choices.rationale: This is the point of the reference. In context, bringing up the fact that we don’t focus on the mirror itself, but rather “into” the mirror, shows that mirrors produce a three-dimensional simulation.

choices.text: illustrate the fact that we typically deal directly with mental constructs rather than with perceptions
choices.rationale: This isn't the purpose of the reference. Again, the point about not focusing on mirrors is a separate topic from the discussion of mental constructs. The mirror point refers specifically to perceptual qualities of mirrors, rather than making a broader point about cognition.

choices.text: emphasize the degree to which the psychological activity of the observer modifies the shape of the object being perceived
choices.rationale: This is not why the reference was made. The point about the mirror does not deal with psychology; rather, it remarks on the illusory nature of our perception of mirrors by making a point about how, because of the mechanics of mirrors, we use them in a way that is very different from other objects.

passages.text:
Charles Darwin objected to all attempts to reduce his theory of evolution to its doctrine of natural selection. "Natural selection has been the main but not the exclusive means of modification," he declared. Nonetheless, a group of self-proclaimed strict constructionist Darwinians has recently risen to prominence by reducing Darwin's theory in just this way. These theorists use the mechanism of natural selection to explain all biological phenomena; they assert that natural selection is responsible for every aspect of every species' form and behavior, and for the success or failure of species in general.

Natural selection is generally held to result in adaptation, the shaping of an organism's form and behavior in response to environmental conditions to achieve enhanced reproductive success. If the strict constructionists are right, the persistence of every attribute and the survival of every species are due to such adaptation. But in fact, nature provides numerous examples of attributes that are not adaptations for reproductive success and of species whose success or failure had little to do with their adaptations.

For example, while it is true that some random mutations of genetic material produce attributes that enhance reproductive success and are thus favored by natural selection, and others produce harmful attributes that are weeded out, we now know from population genetics that most mutations fall into neither category. Research has revealed that neutral, nonadaptive changes account to a large extent for the evolution of DNA. Most substitutions of one unit of DNA for another within a population have no effect on reproductive success. These alterations often change the attributes of species, but their persistence from one generation to the next is not explainable by natural selection.

Additionally, the study of mass extinctions in paleontology has undermined the strict constructionist claim that natural selection can account for every species' success or failure. The extinction of the dinosaurs some 65 million years ago was probably caused by the impact of an extraterrestrial body. Smaller animal species are generally better able to survive the catastrophic changes in climate that we would expect to follow from such an impact, and mammals in the Cretaceous period were quite small because they could not compete on the large scale of the dominant dinosaurs. But while this scenario explains why dinosaurs died off and mammals fared relatively well, it does not conform to the strict constructionist view of the adaptive reasons for the success of species. For that view assumes that adaptations are a response to conditions that are already in place at the time the adaptations occur, and mammals could not have adapted in advance to conditions caused by the impact. In a sense, their success was the result of dumb luck.

From a critical discussion of the work of Victorian photographer Julia Margaret Cameron.

What Cameron called her "fancy-subject" pictures—photographs in which two or more costumed sitters enacted, under Cameron's direction, scenes from the Bible, mythology, Shakespeare, or Tennyson—bear unmistakable traces of the often comical conditions under which they were taken. In many respects they have more connection to the family album pictures of recalcitrant relatives who have been herded together for the obligatory group picture than they do to the masterpieces of Western painting. In Raphael and Giotto there are no infant Christs whose faces are blurred because they moved, or who are looking at the viewer with frank hatred. These traces, of course, are what give the photographs their life and charm. If Cameron had succeeded in her project of making seamless works of illustrative art, her work would be among the curiosities of Victorian photography—like Oscar Gustave Rejlander's extravagantly awful The Two Ways of Life—rather than among its most vital images.

It is precisely the camera's realism—its stubborn obsession with the surface of things—that has given Cameron's theatricality and artificiality its atmosphere of truth. It is the truth of the sitting, rather than the fiction which all the dressing up was in aid of, that wafts out of these wonderful and strange, not-quite-in-focus photographs. They are what they are: pictures of housemaids and nieces and husbands and village children who are dressed up as Mary Madonnas and infant Jesuses and John the Baptists and Lancelots and Guineveres and trying desperately hard to sit still. The way each sitter endures his or her ordeal is the collective action of the photograph, its "plot" so to speak. When we look at a narrative painting we can suspend our disbelief; when we look at a narrative photograph we cannot. We are always aware of the photograph's doubleness—of each figure's imaginary and real personas. Theater can transcend its doubleness, can make us believe (for at least some of the time) that we are seeing only Lear or Medea. Still photographs of theatrical scenes can never escape being pictures of actors.

What gives Cameron's pictures of actors their special quality—their status as treasures of photography of an unfathomably peculiar sort—is their singular combination of amateurism and artistry. In The Passing of Arthur, for example, the mast and oar of the makeshift boat representing a royal barge are obviously broomsticks and the water is white muslin drapery. But these details are insignificant. For once, the homely truth of the sitting gives right of place to the romantic fantasy of its director. The picture, a night scene, is magical and mysterious. While Cameron's fancy-subject pictures have been compared to poor amateur theatricals, The Passing of Arthur puts one in mind of good amateur theatricals one has seen, and recalls with shameless delight.

Some critics of advertising have assumed that the creation of false needs in consumers is the principal mechanism underlying what these critics regard as its manipulative and hegemonic power. Central to this type of critique are the writings of political theorist Herbert Marcuse, who maintained that modern people succumb to oppression by believing themselves satisfied in spite of their living in an objectively unsatisfying world. This process occurs because in mass market culture the powerful psychological techniques of advertising create "needs" that are false and whose satisfaction thus contributes, not to the genuine well-being of consumers, but rather to the profit—and thereby the disproportionate power—of corporations.

Marcuse supposed that we all have certain real needs, both physical and psychological. Advertising appropriates these needs for its own purposes, forging psychological associations between them and consumer items, e.g., between sex and perfume, thereby creating a false "need" for these items. Since the quest for fulfillment is thus displaced from its true objects to consumer items, the implicit promises of advertisements are never really fulfilled and the consumer remains at some level unsatisfied.

Unfortunately, the distinction between real and false needs upon which this critique depends is extremely problematic. If Marcusians are right, we cannot, with any assurance, separate our real needs from the alleged false needs we feel as a result of the manipulation of advertisers. For, in order to do so, it would be necessary to eliminate forces of persuasion that are so prevalent in society that they have come to inform our instinctive judgments about things.

But, in fact, Marcusians make a major mistake in assuming that the majority of consumers who respond to advertising do not do so autonomously. Advertising techniques are unable to induce unwilling behavior in rational, informed adults, and regulations prohibit misinformation in advertising claims. Moreover, evidence suggests that most adults understand and recognize the techniques used and are not merely passive instruments. If there is a real need for emotional fulfillment, and if we can freely and authentically choose our means of obtaining it, then free, informed individuals may choose to obtain it through the purchase of commodities or even through the enjoyment occasionally provided by advertisements themselves. It is no doubt true that in many—perhaps even most—cases the use of an advertised product does not yield the precise sort of emotional dividend that advertisements seem to promise. This does not mean, however, that consumers do not freely and intentionally use the product as a means to another sort of fulfillment, or even that its genuine fulfillment of needs must be less than the advertisement suggests.

Passage A

There are two principles that are fundamental to a theory of justice regarding property. The principle of justice in acquisition specifies the conditions under which someone can legitimately come to own something that was previously not owned by anyone. The principle of justice in transfer specifies the conditions under which the transfer of property from one person to another is justified.

Given such principles, if the world were wholly just, the following definition would exhaustively cover the subject of justice regarding property:

1. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in acquisition is entitled to that property.

2. A person who acquires property in accordance with the principle of justice in transfer, from someone else who is entitled to the property, is entitled to the property.

3. No one is entitled to any property except by (repeated) applications of 1 and 2.

However, not all actual situations are generated in accordance with the principles of justice in acquisition and justice in transfer. Some people steal from others or defraud them, for example. The existence of past injustice raises the issue of the rectification of injustice. If past injustice has shaped present ownership in various ways, what, if anything, ought to be done to rectify that injustice? A principle of rectification would use historical information about previous situations and injustices done in them, and information about the actual course of events that flowed from these injustices, to produce a description of the property ownership that should have resulted. Actual ownership of property must then be brought into conformity with this description.

Passage B

In 1790, the United States Congress passed the Indian Nonintercourse Act, which requires that all transfers of lands from Native Americans to others be approved by the federal government. The law has not been changed in any relevant respect, and it remains in effect today. Its purpose is clear. It was meant to guarantee security to Native Americans against fraudulent acquisition by others of the Native Americans' land holdings. Several suits have been initiated by Native American tribes for recovery of lands held by them when the Nonintercourse Act took effect.

One natural (one might almost say obvious) way of reasoning about Native American claims to land in North America is this: Native Americans were the first human occupants of this land. Before the European invasion of North America, the land belonged to them. In the course of that invasion and its aftermath, the land was illicitly taken from them. The current owners lack a well-founded right to the land, which now lies illicitly in their hands. Ideally, the land should be restored to its rightful owners. This may be impractical; compromises might have to be made. But the original wrong can most easily be righted by returning the land to them—or by returning it wherever that is feasible.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Evidence from two areas of science undermines the strict constructionist claim that natural selection is the only driving force behind evolution.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The main point of this passage is to debunk the strict constructionist understanding (that evolution can be explained entirely by natural selection). The author uses examples from two areas of science (DNA mutation and mass extinction) to prove this point.

choices.text: According to strict constructionist Darwinians, new evidence suggests that natural selection is responsible for the failure of most extinct species.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. Strict constructionists believe that natural selection is responsible for the failure of all extinct species. Also, notice that no specific new evidence is introduced in the passage; the author debunks the strict constructionist view with only vague reference to past research.

choices.text: New evidence demonstrates that natural selection can produce nonadaptive as well as adaptive changes.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The passage uses nonadaptive change as evidence that all evolution isn’t produced by natural selection. Also, notice that no specific new evidence is introduced in the passage; the author debunks the strict constructionist view with only vague reference to past research.

choices.text: Strict constructionist followers of Darwin maintain that natural selection is responsible for all evolutionary change.
choices.rationale: This is too narrow to be the main point of the passage. While this is true, it is stated clearly in the first paragraph. The remainder of the passage works to refute this strict constructionist viewpoint.

choices.text: Evidence from the study of population genetics helps to disprove the claim that natural selection results in the survival of the fittest species.
choices.rationale: This is too narrow to be the main point of the passage. Evidence from the study of population genetics is only one of multiple arguments used to refute the claims of strict constructionists.

questions.stem: According to the author, mammals were able to survive catastrophic environmental changes that occurred roughly 65 million years ago because they

choices.text: had adapted previously to similar changes
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. There is no mention in the passage of similar catastrophic changes. Instead, the passage suggests mammals survived due to their size.

choices.text: were relatively small
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The passage notes that “Smaller animal species are generally better able to survive . . . catastrophic changes in climate”. It was mammals’ size that enabled them to survive.

choices.text: were highly intelligent
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. Intelligence was not mentioned as a factor that might have helped mammals survive catastrophic climate change.

choices.text: lived in a wide range of environments
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. Mammals and dinosaurs were in competition, according to the passage, which suggests that they shared environments. Instead, the passage suggests mammals survived due to their small size.

choices.text: were able to reproduce quickly
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. Reproduction rate is not mentioned as a factor that might have enabled mammals to survive catastrophic climate change.

questions.stem: The author asserts which one of the following regarding mutations of genetic material?

choices.text: The majority of such mutations are not passed on to subsequent generations.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. According to the passage, many nonadaptive changes are passed on from one generation to the next, though “their persistence from one generation to the next is not explainable by natural selection.”

choices.text: The majority of such mutations occur during periods when mass extinctions take place.
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The passage doesn’t specify when mutations might occur and doesn’t relate nonadaptive changes to mass extinctions at all.

choices.text: The majority of such mutations change species' behavior rather than their appearance.
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The passage doesn’t say whether most mutations are behavioral or formal.

choices.text: The majority of such mutations have no effect on reproductive success.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The passage tells us that most genetic changes are neither positive or negative: “most substitutions of one unit of DNA for another within a population have no effect on reproductive success.”

choices.text: The majority of such mutations occur in larger rather than smaller species.
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The author doesn’t make any distinctions about how physical size might affect number of mutations in a species.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: Natural selection is responsible for almost none of the characteristics of existing species.
choices.rationale: This choice goes much further than what the author says in the passage. The passage states that natural selection isn’t responsible for all of species’ traits. We can infer that the author still believes a good deal of characteristics of species are due to natural selection.

choices.text: The fact that a species flourishes in a certain environment is not proof of its adaptation to that environment.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. In the final paragraph, the author writes that “mammals could not have adapted in advance to conditions caused by the impact.” And yet, mammals flourished in the aftermath of the environmental change. From this example, we can infer that the author believes that a species can flourish in an environment that it is not adapted to.

choices.text: Only evolutionary changes that provide some advantage to a species are transmitted to subsequent generations.
choices.rationale: This contradicts the passage. The author asserts that most of the traits transmitted to subsequent generations don’t provide any advantage.

choices.text: Large animal species are generally unable to survive in harsh environmental conditions.
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The passage states that smaller animals are better equipped to handle “catastrophic changes in climate”, but it doesn’t assert that larger animals are unable to survive harsh conditions in general.

choices.text: Natural selection is useful for explaining the form but not the behavior of most species.
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The author describes natural selection as a factor, though not the only factor, in the accumulation of both physical and behavioral traits.

questions.stem: The author's stance toward the arguments of the strict constructionist Darwinians can most accurately be described as one of

choices.text: emphatic disagreement
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The author of the passage strongly disagrees with the strict constructionist Darwinians, and the passage is a refutation of their arguments. The author characterizes the claims of strict constructionists as fundamentally conflicting with the intent of Darwin’s theory.

choices.text: mild disapproval
choices.rationale: This isn’t strong enough to describe the author’s stance. We can tell from the passage that the author emphatically rejects the claims of the strict constructionists. “Mild disapproval” doesn’t capture the extent of author’s disagreement.

choices.text: open-minded neutrality
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. Far from expressing “neutrality”, the author presents strong disapproval of the strict constructionists’ arguments.

choices.text: conditional agreement
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The author doesn’t agree with the strict constructionists, nor do they discuss the possibility of agreement. Instead, they express strong rejection of the claims of the strict constructionists.

choices.text: unreserved endorsement
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. “Unreserved endorsement” means “strong agreement”. The author, on the other hand, expresses strong disagreement with the arguments of the strict constructionists.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately and completely describes the function of the second paragraph of the passage?

choices.text: It outlines the objections to traditional evolutionary theory raised by the strict constructionists mentioned in the first paragraph.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the function of the second paragraph. It doesn’t outline any objection to traditional evolutionary theory. Rather, it prepares readers for the examples that follow, which refute the strict constructionists' arguments.

choices.text: It lists recent evidence suggesting that the strict constructionist claims described in the first paragraph are incorrect.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the function of the second paragraph. It doesn’t list any recent evidence, even though it does introduce why evidence which comes in the following paragraphs will be relevant (it will debunk the strict constructionist viewpoint).

choices.text: It describes the strict constructionists' view of evolutionary theory in order to explain why the evidence described in subsequent paragraphs has recently gotten so much attention.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the function of the second paragraph. The second paragraph never mentions the “attention” received by the evidence presented in the rest of the passage.

choices.text: It enumerates the arguments for the strict constructionist position that are rebutted in the paragraphs that follow.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the function of the second paragraph. Rather than “enumerate the arguments” for the strict constructionist position, it explains the ultimate conclusion resulting from the strict constructionist viewpoint. In fact, the passage doesn’t present any arguments for the strict constructionist position.

choices.text: It explains the ramifications of the strict constructionists' claims and helps clarify the relevance of evidence offered in subsequent paragraphs.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The function of the paragraph is to explain the ultimate conclusion resulting from the strict constructionists’ claims and to preface the relevance of the examples that follow, which refute those claims.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

choices.text: argue in favor of a recently proposed hypothesis
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the passage. The passage doesn’t “argue in favor” of any recently proposed hypothesis. Rather, it “refutes” the hypothesis of the strict constructionists.

choices.text: summarize a contemporary debate
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the passage. Rather than summarize a debate, the passage attempts to convince the reader that one side of a debate is correct and the other side is incorrect.

choices.text: demonstrate that a particular view is incorrect
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The purpose of the passage is to show readers that the view of the strict constructionists is incorrect.

choices.text: criticize the proponents of a traditional theory
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the passage. The passage doesn’t “criticize the proponents” of a theory, but rather it demonstrates that a theory is incorrect. In addition, nothing in the passage suggests that the strict constructionist view is traditional (it has “recently risen to prominence”).

choices.text: explain why a particular theory is gaining popularity
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the passage. The purpose of the passage is to show that a theory is incorrect, not to explain the reasons for its popularity.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: The circumstances under which Cameron's fancy-subject pictures were taken render them unintentionally comical.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the main point of the passage. While there may be a comical element to Cameron’s work, the broader point that the passage makes is that the artistic value of the fancy-subject pictures comes from both the circumstances of their creation as well as the epic scenes that they portray.

choices.text: The peculiar charm of Cameron's fancy-subject pictures derives from the viewer's simultaneous awareness of the fictional scene portrayed and the circumstances of its portrayal.
choices.rationale: This is the main point of the passage. The passage argues that Cameron’s work inspires delight by combining mythical scenes with the mundane idiosyncrasies of photographic flaws: “These traces, of course, are what give the photographs their life and charm.”

choices.text: The implicit claim of Cameron's fancy-subject pictures to comparison with the masterpieces of Western painting is undermined by the obtrusiveness of the sitters.
choices.rationale: This is too narrow to be the main point of the passage. While the passage does suggest Cameron’s theatrical subjects are limited by the intrusion of the sitter’s “real” self, this is only part of the broader identification of the merits of Cameron’s pictures. They may not compare to masterpieces of painting, but they excel as documents of the photography process.

choices.text: The most successful of Cameron's fancy-subject pictures from an aesthetic point of view are those in which the viewer is completely unaware that the sitters are engaged in role playing.
choices.rationale: This contradicts the passage. In fact, the passage argues that, for pictures in which the viewer is aware of the sitters’ role playing, “These traces, of course, are what give the photographs their life and charm.” It is this “doubleness” that is the most successful element of Cameron’s work.

choices.text: The interest of Cameron's fancy-subject pictures consists in what they tell us about the sitters and not in the imaginary scenes they portray.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The passage argues that it is the juxtaposition of the imaginary scenes with the sitters’ that gives the pictures their power.

questions.stem: The author mentions the props employed in The Passing of Arthur as

choices.text: examples of amateurish aspects of the work
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The passage mentions the props in The Passing of Arthur as an example of an element of fancy-subject pictures that is similar to an amateurish theater production.

choices.text: evidence of the transformative power of theater
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the reference. Given the context, the example of the props in The Passing of Arthur illustrates the amateurish qualities of Cameron’s photographs, not the transformative power of theater.

choices.text: testimonies to Cameron's ingenuity
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the reference. The props in The Passing of Arthur are an example of an amateurish aspect of Cameron’s work, not her ingenuity.

choices.text: indications that the work is intended ironically
choices.rationale: This choice is in conflict with the passage. Nothing in the example of the props in The Passing of Arthur (or anything else in the passage) suggests that Cameron’s work was intended ironically.

choices.text: support for a negative appraisal of the work
choices.rationale: This choice contradicts the passage. Far from negatively appraising the work, the author of the passage delights in the amateurish aspect of the props in The Passing of Arthur, likening them to fond memories of amateur theater productions.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to explain the claim about suspension of disbelief (near the middle of the second paragraph)?

choices.text: Sitting for a painting typically takes much longer than sitting for a photograph.
choices.rationale: If true, this statement doesn’t help explain the claim about “suspension of disbelief”. If anything, the long time duration required to sit for a painting should give paintings less of a natural feeling and be less believable.

choices.text: Paintings, unlike photographs, can depict obviously impossible situations.
choices.rationale: If true, this statement doesn’t help explain the claim about “suspension of disbelief”. If anything, the ability of paintings to depict impossible scenarios would make them harder to believe, which conflicts with claim in the passage.

choices.text: All of the sitters for a painting do not have to be present at the same time.
choices.rationale: If true, this statement doesn’t help explain the claim about “suspension of disbelief”. The number of models sitting for a painting doesn’t have anything to do with the eventual believability of the painting.

choices.text: A painter can suppress details about a sitter that are at odds with an imaginary persona.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. If this statement is true, we can imagine that a painter might choose to suppress some details about a sitter to make the painting more believable, perhaps by giving them a more appropriate facial expression. This would make the painting more believable than a photograph in which the sitter looks bored or distracted.

choices.text: Paintings typically bear the stylistic imprint of an artist, school, or period.
choices.rationale: If true, this statement doesn’t help explain the claim about “suspension of disbelief”. If anything, this statement serves to weaken the claim made in the passage—if paintings bear stylistic imprints of the conditions of their creation, then it might be harder to believe the mythical or historical scenes that they portray.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Based on the passage, Cameron is most like which one of the following in relation to her fancy-subject pictures?

choices.text: a playwright who introduces incongruous elements to preserve an aesthetic distance between characters and audience
choices.rationale: This isn’t an analogous relation. Cameron doesn’t preserve a distance between characters and audience. In fact, the ordinariness of the sitters allows viewers to relate to the photographs.

choices.text: a rap artist whose lyrics are designed to subvert the meaning of a song sampled in his recording
choices.rationale: This isn’t an analogous relation. For this relation to be analogous, Cameron’s methods and materials would have to have been designed to undercut the scenes portrayed in her work. Cameron, however, earnestly wished to portray biblical and mythical scenes—we have no reason to believe she sought to subvert them.

choices.text: a sculptor whose works possess a certain grandeur even though they are clearly constructed out of ordinary objects
choices.rationale: This relation is analogous to Cameron’s relation to her work. Her success despite her humble costumes and models is like this sculptor’s success despite the ordinary objects they use in construction.

choices.text: an architect whose buildings are designed to be as functional as possible
choices.rationale: This isn’t an analogous relation. For this relation to be analogous, Cameron’s work would have to be highly functional, whereas the passage portrays it as highly decorative.

choices.text: a film director who employs ordinary people as actors in order to give the appearance of a documentary
choices.rationale: This isn’t an analogous relation. This choice might be tempting, because it involves employing “ordinary people”. But in this statement, the purpose of employing ordinary people is to give the appearance of a documentary, whereas in the case of Cameron, it was not for effect but rather for a lack of alternatives.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, the author would agree with each of the following statements except:

choices.text: A less realistic medium can be more conducive to suspension of disbelief than a more realistic medium.
choices.rationale: The author would agree with this choice. The passage states that painting is less realistic than photography and that painting is more conducive to the suspension of disbelief than photography is. Therefore, we can infer the author believes less realistic media can be more conducive to the suspension of disbelief.

choices.text: Amateurishness is a positive quality in some works of art.
choices.rationale: The author would agree with this choice. The author regards amateurishness as a positive quality both in Cameron’s The Passing of Arthur and in “good amateur theatricals” mentioned in the final paragraph.

choices.text: What might appear to be an incongruity in a narrative photograph can actually enhance its aesthetic value.
choices.rationale: The author would agree with this choice. In fact, this underlies the main point of the passage, which argues that the incongruity in Cameron’s narrative photography actually enhances its aesthetic value.

choices.text: We are sometimes aware of both the real and the imaginary persona of an actor in a drama.
choices.rationale: The author would agree with this choice. The passage says, “We are always aware of the photograph's doubleness—of each figure's imaginary and real personas.” We can infer that the author thinks similarly about actors in a drama and actors in a photograph, in that viewers are aware of both their real and imaginary personas. The passage states that theater only transcends doubleness “some of the time”.

choices.text: A work of art succeeds only to the extent that it realizes the artist's intentions.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice, because we can infer the author would disagree with it. While the intention of Cameron’s fancy-subject pictures might have been a straightforward depiction of mythical scenes, the passage argues that Cameron succeeded in producing an effect far beyond the artist’s intention.

questions.stem: The passage provides the most support for inferring that in Cameron's era

choices.text: there was little interest in photographs documenting contemporary life
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The passage discusses some of the works produced by a single photographer, but doesn’t suggest anything about general trends in photography at the time.

choices.text: photography was practiced mainly by wealthy amateurs
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage, which focuses on a single photographer’s work. The passage doesn’t give any more general information about most photographers at the time.

choices.text: publicity stills of actors were coming into vogue
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The passage makes no mention of publicity stills of actors, and Cameron’s own work, which employed actors, was very different from publicity stills.

choices.text: there were no professional artist's models
choices.rationale: This can’t be inferred from the passage. While Cameron’s work relied on ordinary people instead of professional models, the passage doesn’t suggest that there were no professional models to be found.

choices.text: the time required to take a picture was substantial
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The passage describes the actors in photographs as “trying desperately hard to sit still”, implying that taking a picture was not the quick snap that it is today.

questions.stem: The discussion of suspension of disbelief in the second paragraph serves which one of the following purposes?

choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the passage, for which the discussion of Cameron's fancy-subject pictures serves as a case study.
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported. The point about the suspension of disbelief is not the main conclusion of the passage. The main point of the passage is to critique Cameron’s fancy-subject pictures, and the point about the suspension of disbelief is just one conclusion in that undertaking.

choices.text: It introduces a contrast the author uses in characterizing the peculiar nature of our response to Cameron's fancy-subject pictures.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The discussion of the suspension of disbelief helps us better understand the unusual effect Cameron’s fancy-subject pictures have on the viewer by pointing out a key difference between painting and photography. In photography, the ability to entertain fantasy is limited by the real human beings that appear in the work.

choices.text: It is the key step in an argument supporting the author's negative appraisal of the project of narrative photography.
choices.rationale: This contradicts the passage. Far from giving a negative appraisal of narrative photography, the author of the passage delights in the contrasts that it can produce.

choices.text: It is used to explain a criticism of Cameron's fancy-subject pictures that the author shows to be conceptually confused.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the discussion. The author doesn’t present (or refute) any criticism of Cameron’s work. The discussion of the “suspension of disbelief” is part of the author’s own argument about unique elements of photography that elicit a unique reaction in viewers.

choices.text: It draws a contrast between narrative painting and drama to support the author's conclusion that Cameron's fancy-subject pictures are more like the former.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The purpose of the discussion is to highlight a key difference between narrative painting and narrative photography. Only later in the passage does the author compare Cameron’s work to theatrical works.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: The main purpose of the passage is

choices.text: to chronicle Cameron's artistic development as a photographer, which culminated in her masterpiece The Passing of Arthur
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the passage. The author spends little time discussing Cameron’s development, and The Passing of Arthur is included as an example of one aspect of her work, not as a masterpiece.

choices.text: to argue that the tension between Cameron's aims and the results she achieved in some of her works enhances the works' aesthetic value
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The author argues that there is a discrepancy between Cameron’s aims and the results she achieved. Her aims were to portray mythical scenes; her results were photographs of costumed, human actors. The author argues that the art produced was not a failure, but rather that this discrepancy enhanced the intrigue of Cameron’s works and made them even more enduring.

choices.text: to show that Cameron's essentially theatrical vision accounts for both the strengths and the weaknesses of her photographic oeuvre
choices.rationale: This isn’t the main purpose of the passage. The passage doesn’t regard Cameron’s vision as “essentially theatrical”, but rather compares some aspects of her work to the theater. The passage also identifies the realities of the actors, not Cameron’s theatrical representations, as the strengths of the photos.

choices.text: to explain why Cameron's project of acquiring for photography the prestige accorded to painting was doomed to failure
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the passage. The passage is concerned with arguing for the artistic value of Cameron’s work, not explaining how her choice of medium might affect the prestige she could attain. The prestige of photography and painting isn’t compared in any detail.

choices.text: to defend Cameron's masterpiece The Passing of Arthur against its detractors by showing that it transcends the homely details of its setting
choices.rationale: This isn’t the primary purpose of the passage. The purpose of the passage is to make a broader point about the aesthetic value of Cameron’s collected works, of which The Passing of Arthur is just one example.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Advertising has greater social value than Marcusians have supposed, because it is both an effective means of informing consumers and often an intrinsically entertaining medium of mass communication.
choices.rationale: This is too strong to be the main point of the passage. While the passage doesn’t condemn advertising like the Marcusians do, it certainly doesn’t regard advertising as an “effective means of informing consumers”, and instead notes that rational consumers know to be skeptical of advertisements.

choices.text: Even if, as Marcusians have argued, there is a theoretical difference between real and false needs, that difference is obscured in practice by the relationship of consumers to the forces of persuasion in profit-motivated, consumer-oriented societies.
choices.rationale: This is too narrow to be the main point of the passage. The difference between real and false needs is only one element in a larger discussion about the plausibility of the Marcusian viewpoint.

choices.text: Marcusian arguments regarding advertisers' creation of false needs are mistaken, because individuals are able to make autonomous decisions regarding their needs and are even able to use the elements of mass market culture to achieve genuine fulfillment.
choices.rationale: This is the main point of the passage. The passage argues that Marcuse’s argument is wrong, because individuals can make their own decisions with regard to the pursuit of fulfillment.

choices.text: Critics of advertising typically focus on the development of false needs in the consumer and do not fully consider the ability of people to make independent choices by distinguishing their own real needs from the apparent needs that advertising induces.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the main point of the passage. The main point of the passage is a critique of Marcuse’s argument in particular, not critics of advertising in general.

choices.text: The problematic distinction that Marcusians have drawn between real and false needs provides an inadequate basis for their attacks on advertising, because the distinction overlooks consumers' physical and psychological needs.
choices.rationale: This is too narrow to be the main point of the passage. The difference between real and false needs is only one element in a larger discussion about the plausibility of the Marcusian viewpoint.

questions.stem: The author states that Marcuse believed that advertisers

choices.text: base many of their manipulative strategies on psychological research findings
choices.rationale: This isn’t supported by the passage. The passage makes no mention of psychological research findings.

choices.text: appeal to people's real needs in order to create false needs
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The passage states that Marcuse believed advertisers appealed to real needs to create the false needs. Specifically, the passage noted that advertising forges “psychological associations between [real needs] and consumer items.”

choices.text: are restricted to a degree by regulations prohibiting misinformation
choices.rationale: This is a belief of the author but not of Marcuse. It is the author who brings up the claim that “regulations prohibit misinformation in advertising claims.”

choices.text: exaggerate the consumer's need for independent decision-making
choices.rationale: This mischaracterizes Marcuse’s belief as it is portrayed in the passage. Marcuse believed that advertisers actually obscured consumers’ decision-making by introducing false needs.

choices.text: deny that the needs they create in people are less real than other needs
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. Marcuse wouldn’t deny, but would agree that the needs advertisers create in people (i.e., “fake needs”) are less real than other needs.

questions.stem: The main function of the first paragraph is to

choices.text: summarize the political and economic context from which Marcusian critiques of advertising arise
choices.rationale: This mischaracterizes the purpose of the paragraph. The “political and economic context” of Marcusian critique are not summarized in the first paragraph (or anywhere else in the passage).

choices.text: outline the mechanisms by which false needs originate in mass market culture
choices.rationale: This is too narrow to be the purpose of the first paragraph. The first paragraph doesn’t mention any mechanisms by which false needs originate.

choices.text: evaluate the psychological processes by which the manipulative techniques of mass market advertising influence individuals
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the first paragraph. The first paragraph doesn’t evaluate psychological processes (or anything else), but rather gives a description of Marcusian views.

choices.text: describe the prevailing views among contemporary critics of advertising and categorize Marcuse's theories in relation to those views
choices.rationale: This isn’t the purpose of the first paragraph. The first paragraph doesn’t describe any critical views except Marcuse’s.

choices.text: describe Marcusian views regarding mass market manipulation and indicate their role in certain criticisms of advertising
choices.rationale: This is the purpose of the first paragraph. First, the paragraph contextualizes Marcuse’s views as being “central” to critiques of advertising. Then it provides a description of Marcuse’s views regarding the “oppression” of “modern people” because of the false needs created by advertising (mass market manipulation).

questions.stem: Which one of the following is a claim that the author attributes to Marcuse?

choices.text: In modern society, advertising helps lead people to think that they are satisfied.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. In explaining Marcuse’s critique of advertising, the author attributes this claim to him, saying “modern people succumb to oppression by believing themselves satisfied” due to the fulfillment of the false needs of advertising.

choices.text: Modern societies differ from earlier societies in that they fail to satisfy basic physical needs.
choices.rationale: This isn’t something the author attributes to Marcuse. The author doesn’t provide any information about what Marcuse might have thought about earlier societies, or whether modern societies satisfy basic physical needs.

choices.text: It is impossible to draw any meaningful distinction between real and false psychological needs in modern society.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the ideas that the author attributes to Marcuse. According to the passage, Marcuse does draw a meaningful distinction between real and false needs as the basis for his critique of advertising.

choices.text: Advertising in modern society has sometimes become a tool of oppression working to the benefit of totalitarian political systems.
choices.rationale: This isn’t something the author attributes to Marcuse. Totalitarian political systems aren’t mentioned in the passage.

choices.text: Advertising exploits basic human needs by deriving from them certain secondary needs which, though they become real needs, subtly work to the detriment of consumers.
choices.rationale: This isn’t something the author attributes to Marcuse. The passage doesn’t discuss “secondary needs” but rather false needs, which never “become real needs”. When false needs are satisfied, they still leave consumers unfulfilled, because real needs continue to go unsatisfied.

questions.stem: By the term "forces of persuasion" (last sentence of the third paragraph), the author most probably refers to

choices.text: intentionally dishonest claims that some theorists argue are common in advertising
choices.rationale: This isn’t what “forces of persuasion” means in context. This choice might be tempting, because it refers to external influences (in advertising). But forces of persuasion don’t have to be “intentionally dishonest”. This choice is too strong to be correct.

choices.text: innate, instinctual drives that some theorists say are fundamental to human behavior
choices.rationale: This isn’t what “forces of persuasion” means in context. The theorists described in the passage focus on the external motivations of advertising (which is what “forces of persuasion” refers to), not the internal drives of human nature.

choices.text: emotional pressures that some theorists claim are exerted over individuals by society as a whole
choices.rationale: This isn’t what “forces of persuasion” means in context. “Emotional pressures” aren’t mentioned in the passage, which focused on physical and psychological needs.

choices.text: subtle practices of social indoctrination that some theorists say are sponsored by the state
choices.rationale: This isn’t what “forces of persuasion” means in context. The passage doesn’t discuss ways in which the state could be involved in indoctrination.

choices.text: manipulative influences that some theorists say go unrecognized by those affected by them
choices.rationale: This is a good definition for “forces of persuasion” as it’s used in the passage. In context, “forces of persuasion” are said to “inform our instinctive judgments about things.” So, we can define “forces of persuasion” as hidden, manipulative influences that affect our thinking without us knowing it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following sentences would most logically complete the passage?

choices.text: Therefore, while in principle there might be grounds for holding that advertising is detrimental to society, the Marcusian critique does not provide such grounds.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice to complete the passage. The passage concludes that the Marcusian critique isn’t sufficient for proving that advertising is detrimental to society. The passage doesn’t argue conclusively whether advertising is detrimental to society.

choices.text: Therefore, although Marcusian claims about advertising are rationally justified, the mistake of many recent critics of advertising is in their use of these claims for political gain.
choices.rationale: This statement couldn’t complete the passage. The passage doesn’t view Marcusian claims as “rationally justified”, and it makes no mention of critiques using Marcusian claims for political gain.

choices.text: Therefore, any shift in basic assumptions required to correct the abuses of advertising will require a change in the perception of human nature held by corporate leaders.
choices.rationale: This statement couldn’t complete the passage. The passage doesn’t regard advertising as abusive, and wouldn’t recommend a change “to correct the abuses of advertising”.

choices.text: Therefore, while emphasizing only detrimental social aspects of advertising, Marcusians have failed to consider that such aspects are clearly outweighed by numerous social benefits.
choices.rationale: This statement couldn’t complete the passage. Even though the passage argues against the Marcusians’ claims, it never suggests that the positives of advertising outweigh the negatives.

choices.text: Therefore, the Marcusian critique of advertising is mistaken except in its claim that advertisers exert economic power over those few people who are unable or unwilling to distinguish real from false needs.
choices.rationale: This statement couldn’t complete the passage. The passage doesn’t discuss the set of people who are unable to distinguish real from false needs.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the main purpose for which passage A was written and the main purpose for which passage B was written?

choices.text:
Passage A: to propose a solution to a moral problem

Passage B: to criticize a proposed solution to a moral problem
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the purposes of the passages. Passage A doesn’t propose a solution to a moral problem; it sketches out a theory of justice regarding property. Passage B doesn’t criticize a proposed solution to a moral problem; it analyzes a case of a moral problem.

choices.text:
Passage A: to sketch a general outline of a branch of moral theory

Passage B: to give a particular moral analysis of a real case
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. Passage A sketches an outline of the a branch of moral theory, specifically a theory of justice regarding property. Passage B gives a moral analysis of the case of the theft of Native American lands.

choices.text:
Passage A: to spell out the details of two fundamental principles

Passage B: to examine a case that exemplifies a moral ideal
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the purposes of the passages. Passage B examines a case that conflicts with the moral ideals of property ownership.

choices.text:
Passage A: to argue for a particular moral ideal

Passage B: to question the assumptions of a moral theory
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the purposes of the passages. Passage A doesn’t argue for a moral ideal; it provides a rough outline of a part of a moral theory. Passage B doesn’t question the assumptions of a theory; it analyzes the morality of a particular case.

choices.text:
Passage A: to advocate the use of certain moral principles

Passage B: to provide a counterexample to some widely held moral principles
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the purposes of the passages. Passage A doesn’t advocate for certain moral principles; it provides a rough outline of a part of a moral theory. Passage B isn’t a counterexample to any widely held moral principles; it's a moral analysis of a particular case.

questions.stem: Both passages explicitly mention which one of the following?

choices.text: transfer of property from one owner to another
choices.rationale: Both passages explicitly mention this topic. Passage A mentions it with regard to the “principle of justice in transfer” of property. Passage B mentions it with the example of the transfer of Native American land (its usurpation by invading Europeans) and later with the suggestion that the land be returned to the Native Americans.

choices.text: a legal basis for recovery of property
choices.rationale: This isn’t explicitly mentioned in both passages. Passage A outline a moral basis for recovery of property, not a legal basis. Passage B mentions a legal basis for protection of property (the Indian Nonintercourse Act) and a moral basis for recovery of property (return of Native American lands), but never a legal basis for the recovery of property.

choices.text: entitlement to property in a wholly just world
choices.rationale: This isn’t explicitly mentioned in both passages. Passage A does explicitly mention the entitlement to property in a wholly just world, but passage B doesn’t.

choices.text: practicability of rectification of past injustice
choices.rationale: This isn’t explicitly mentioned in both passages. Passage A mentions the rectification of past injustice, but doesn’t mention its practicability.

choices.text: injustice committed as part of an invasion
choices.rationale: This isn’t explicitly mentioned in both passages. Passage A doesn’t explicitly mention injustice committed as part of an invasion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is true of the relationship between passage A and the second paragraph of passage B?

choices.text: The second paragraph of passage B attempts to develop a broader version of the theory presented in passage A.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the relationship. The second paragraph of passage B is a particular example, not a broader version.

choices.text: The second paragraph of passage B purports to state facts that bolster the argument made in passage A.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the relationship. The example in passage B relies on the argument in passage A; it doesn’t support it.

choices.text: The argument in the second paragraph of passage B is structurally parallel to the argument in passage A, but the subject matter of the two is different.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the relationship. The second paragraph of passage B is an example that relies on the reasoning in passage A, not parallelism with different subject matter. Passage A is general, and applies its theories to no specific subject matter.

choices.text: Passage A presents a theory that tends to support the argument presented in the second paragraph of passage B.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. The second paragraph of passage B is an argument for particular example which is an application of the theory in passage A. More concretely, the second paragraph of passage B argues that land should be returned to the Native Americans, and it uses reasoning about justice regarding property that is supported by the theory introduced in passage A.

choices.text: The second paragraph of passage B attempts to undermine the theory presented in passage A.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe the relationship. Far from attempting to undermine the theory of passage A, the second paragraph of passage B relies on the reasoning in passage A.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Based on what can be inferred from their titles, the relationship between which one of the following pairs of documents is most analogous to the relationship between passage A and passage B?

choices.text:
"Card Counting for Everyone: A Can't-Lose System for Beating the Dealer"

"The Evils of Gambling"
choices.rationale: This isn’t analogous to the relationship between the passages. The first title sounds like a how-to guide on a subject and the second title sounds like a moral condemnation of that subject (which isn’t at all the relationship between the passages).

choices.text:
"Mayor McConnell Is Unfit to Serve"

"Why Mayor McConnell Should be Reelected"
choices.rationale: This isn’t analogous to the relationship between the passages. The first title sounds like an argument against someone and the second title sounds like an argument for someone. But passage A and passage B don’t contradict one another.

choices.text:
"Pruning Fruit Trees: A Guide for the Novice"

"Easy Recipes for Beginning Cooks"
choices.rationale: This isn’t analogous to the relationship between the passages. These titles seem to be introductions to two different topics. Passage A and passage B both discuss the same topic: property rights.

choices.text:
"Notable Failures of the STORM Weather Forecasting Model"

"Meteorologists' Best Tool Yet: The STORM Forecasting Model"
choices.rationale: This isn’t analogous to the relationship between the passages. The first title sounds like a study of the failures of a model, and the second title sounds like a study of the successes of that model.

choices.text:
"Fundamentals of Building Construction and Repair"

"Engineering Report: The Repairs Needed by the Thales Building"
choices.rationale: This is analogous to the relationship between the passages. The first title sounds like an introduction to a subject, and the second title sounds like a case study of that subject. Likewise, passage A is a primer on a theory of justice, and passage B is a case study in how that theory of justice is applied.

questions.stem: The author of passage A would be most likely to characterize the purpose of the Indian Nonintercourse Act as which one of the following?

choices.text: legitimization of actual property holdings during the eighteenth century
choices.rationale: We can’t infer that the author of passage A would agree with this. The Indian Nonintercourse Act protects the land of Native Americans by delegitimizing the property holdings of some Europeans in the eighteenth century, especially in the view of the author of passage A, who believes in “rectification of injustice”.

choices.text: clarification of existing laws regarding transfer of property
choices.rationale: We can’t infer that the author of passage A would agree with this. Passage A doesn’t say whether the author has any knowledge of laws before the Indian Nonintercourse Act.

choices.text: assurance of conformity to the principle of justice in acquisition
choices.rationale: We can infer that the author of passage A would disagree with this idea. The Indian Nonintercourse Act is concerned with the transfer of land from Native Americans to Europeans, so, if anything, it would assure conformity to the principle of justice in transfer.

choices.text: prevention of violations of the principle of justice in transfer
choices.rationale: We can infer that the author of passage A would agree with this idea. The purpose of the Indian Nonintercourse Act, as described in the passage, was to protect Native Americans from the fraudulent seizure of their land. This is a violation of the principle of justice in transfer (as defined by passage A) because it concerns property changing ownership.

choices.text: implementation of a principle of rectification
choices.rationale: We can infer that the author of passage A wouldn’t agree with this. The Indian Nonintercourse Act (rather than attempt to rectify past injustices) seeks to protect Native American lands before they are usurped. Therefore, the author of passage A would describe the Indian Nonintercourse Act as a implementation of the principle of justice in transfer.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the difference in approach taken by passage A as compared to passage B?

choices.text: Passage A espouses a general view without providing details, while passage B sketches an argument that it does not necessarily endorse.
choices.rationale: This is the best choice. Passage A gives us an introduction to a theory of justice regarding property. It doesn’t provide details on the principles it lists. Passage B sketches an argument about why land should be returned to Native Americans. It describes this argument as “natural”, but it never explicitly endorses the position.

choices.text: Passage A argues for the superiority of one view over competing views, while passage B considers only a single view.
choices.rationale: This mischaracterizes the approach of passage A. Only one theory is presented in passage A, but the passage doesn’t argue for the superiority of that theory over competing theories.

choices.text: Passage A invokes commonly held principles to support a policy recommendation, while passage B relies on the views of established authorities to support its claims.
choices.rationale: This mischaracterizes the approaches of the passages. Passage A invokes principles, but it isn’t clear whether those principles are “commonly held”. Passage B doesn’t appeal to the views of any “established authorities”.

choices.text: Passage A briefly states a view and then provides an argument for it, while passage B provides a detailed statement of a view but no argument.
choices.rationale: This mischaracterizes the approaches of the passages. Passage A doesn’t provide an argument for the theory it presents. Passage B does include an argument.

choices.text: Passage A provides an argument in support of a view, while passage B attempts to undermine a view.
choices.rationale: This mischaracterizes the approaches of the passages. Passage A presents a theory but doesn’t provide an argument to support that theory. Passage B doesn’t undermine a view; it simply explains one view.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument in the editorial?

choices.text: Certified technicians receive higher pay than uncertified technicians.
choices.rationale: This comparison isn’t necessary for the editorial to work. The argument never addresses pay, but rather qualifications.

choices.text: There are no contractors with fewer than 40 percent of their technicians certified.
choices.rationale: This isn’t necessary for the editorial to work. The argument is focused on one particular contractor, and what other contractors do isn’t relevant.

choices.text: Technicians who lack certification are not qualified technicians.
choices.rationale: This is an assumption required by the editorial’s argument, which essentially equates not certified with unqualified. To test whether (C) has to be true, suppose that it’s false: what if technicians who lack certification are qualified technicians? In that case, the editorial’s argument would fall apart because it wouldn’t necessarily be true that 60% of the contractor’s technicians are unqualified.

choices.text: Qualified technicians installed the heating systems to be upgraded.
choices.rationale: This isn’t necessary for the editorial to work, because it doesn’t matter who installed the heating systems. The editorial’s author is outraged by the contractor’s seemingly “unqualified” technicians, based on their lack of certification. Whether qualified or unqualified technicians actually installed the heating systems doesn’t affect that connection.

choices.text: The contractor hired by the city has personal ties to city officials.
choices.rationale: This isn’t necessary for the argument to work, because personal ties aren’t relevant. It could help explain why the contractor was hired to begin with, but it doesn’t affect whether the technicians are either qualified or unqualified.

questions.stimulus: Editorial: The city has chosen a contractor to upgrade the heating systems in public buildings. Only 40 percent of the technicians employed by this contractor are certified by the Heating Technicians Association. So the city selected a contractor 60 percent of whose technicians are unqualified, which is an outrage.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the discrepancy that Jeneta observes in people’s responses?

choices.text: Customers regard themselves as doing salespeople a favor by buying from them as opposed to someone else.
choices.rationale: This actually deepens the mystery. It makes the customer/salesperson transaction interaction even more similar to the friend/friend favor interaction, which makes it even more puzzling that the responses to each situation are so different. If (A) is true, then we would expect the customers to respond, “You’re welcome” when the salesperson thanks them—not “Thank you”.

choices.text: Salespeople are often instructed by their employers to thank customers, whereas customers are free to say what they want.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the discrepancy. It helps explain why salespeople say, “Thank you” to begin with, but it doesn’t address the difference between the customer/salesperson transaction interaction and the friend/friend favor interaction.

choices.text: Salespeople do not regard customers who buy from them as doing them a favor.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the discrepancy. The fact that salespeople say “Thank you” suggests that they do regard customers as doing them a favor.

choices.text: The way that people respond to being thanked is generally determined by habit rather than by conscious decision.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the discrepancy. Whether responses are determined by habit or by conscious decision, we still see a significant difference between how a customer responds and how a friend responds. (D) doesn’t explain why that difference exists.

choices.text: In a commercial transaction, as opposed to a favor, the customer feels that the benefits are mutual.
choices.rationale: This helps to explain the discrepancy between a customer’s response and a friend’s response. If (E) is true, then there’s a difference between commercial transactions and favors—and if the customer feels that the benefits are mutual in a commercial transaction, then it would be reasonable for the customer to thank the other party for the benefit received.

questions.stimulus: Jeneta: Increasingly, I’ve noticed that when a salesperson thanks a customer for making a purchase, the customer also says “Thank you” instead of saying “You’re welcome.” I’ve even started doing that myself. But when a friend thanks a friend for a favor, the response is always “You’re welcome.”

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism in that the argument

choices.text: draws a general conclusion on the basis of just one individual case
choices.rationale: This describes a flaw in the argument. The arguer concludes that selling the movie rights for popular games is “rarely good from a business perspective.” That’s a pretty general statement. However, the arguer supports this generalization with only one specific instance—that isn’t enough to demonstrate the conclusion, since we can’t tell if the Nostroma example is representative of other instances.

choices.text: infers that a product will be disliked by the public merely from the claim that the product was disliked by critics
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the argument. The arguer doesn’t infer anything about the public’s dislike, but rather explicitly states that both the public and critics disliked the film adaptation.

choices.text: restates as a conclusion a claim earlier presented as evidence for that conclusion
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the argument, which never restates any of its claims.

choices.text: takes for granted that products with similar content that are in different media will be of roughly equal popularity
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the argument. The arguer concludes that popular games don’t become popular movies, which conflicts with the reasoning of (D).

choices.text: treats a requirement for a product to be popular as something that ensures that a product will be popular
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the argument, which doesn’t say what is required for—or ensures—popularity.

questions.stimulus: Some video game makers have sold the movie rights for popular games. However, this move is rarely good from a business perspective. After all, StarQuanta sold the movie rights to its popular game Nostroma, but the poorly made film adaptation of the game was hated by critics and the public alike. Subsequent versions of the Nostroma video game, although better than the original, sold poorly.

questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments conforms most closely to the principle stated above?

choices.text: The president of the Troskco Corporation is definitely overpaid, since he receives in salary and benefits almost 40 times more than the average employee of Troskco receives.
choices.rationale: The conclusion is that this executive is "definitely" overpaid, which is a stronger conclusion than the principle would allow to be drawn, so this answer is incorrect.

choices.text: The president of the Troskco Corporation is probably overpaid, since his total annual compensation package was determined five years ago, when the company's profits were at an all-time high.
choices.rationale: The premise of this answer has nothing to do with consultants, so it's incorrect.

choices.text: The president of the Troskco Corporation is probably not overpaid, since his total compensation package was determined by the Troskco board of directors without retaining the services of an external compensation consultant.
choices.rationale: The principle in the stimulus allows a conclusion to be drawn that an executive is "likely to be overcompensated," not that they are probably not overpaid, so this answer is incorrect.

choices.text: The president of Troskco Corporation is probably overpaid, since the Troskco board of directors determined his compensation by following the advice of an external consultant who has many other contracts with Troskco.
choices.rationale: This answer concludes that an executive is "probably overpaid" based on the salary being set by a consultant with "many other contracts" with the same company the executive works for—and other contracts certainly count as business interests. This answer aligns with the details of the principle in the stimulus and reaches a conclusion that can be justified by it, so it's the correct answer.

choices.text: The president of Troskco Corporation is definitely not overpaid, since the external consultant the board of directors retained to advise on executive salaries has no other contracts with Troskco.
choices.rationale: This answer's conclusion is that someone is definitely not overpaid—stronger and the opposite of the conclusion that can be drawn based on the principle in the stimulus.

questions.stimulus: Principle: The executive in a given company whose compensation package is determined by advice of an external consultant is likely to be overcompensated if the consultant also has business interests with the company the executive manages.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the science writer's reasoning?

choices.text: The conclusion is derived partly from assertions attributed to a purported expert whose credibility is not established.
choices.rationale: The conclusion is that Lemaitre's theory is inadequate, so it's not appealing to his expertise. And the alternative theory isn't attributed to anyone, so this argument isn't making an inappropriate appeal to an expert.

choices.text: The conclusion is based on a shift in meaning of a key term from one part of the argument to another part.
choices.rationale: The conclusion is about Lemaitre's theory and inadequacy—the theory is still referring to the same theory, and the argument never before discusses inadequacy, so this answer is incorrect.

choices.text: The science writer takes for granted the existence of a causal connection between observed phenomena.
choices.rationale: The argument never assumes causality—it simply raises a prediction that flows from a theory that happens to be true.

choices.text: The science writer fails to see that one theory's correctly predicting observed data cannot itself constitute evidence against an alternative theory that also does this.
choices.rationale: This answer choice highlights that two competing theories making the same prediction don't provide evidence against each other. While two theories making the same prediction means that evidence supporting that prediction can't help determine between the two theories which is correct, it doesn't mean that either theory is inadequate, either.

choices.text: The science writer presumes, without providing justification, that there are only two possible explanations for the phenomena in question.
choices.rationale: The stimulus doesn't get into the explanations (or their number) for the phenomenon in question (the acceleration of the galaxies)—for all we know, the oscillating universe theory could also be based on an explosion that formed the universe. And just because the Writer only raises two theories doesn't mean that there aren't others out there.

questions.stimulus: Science writer: Lemaître argued that the universe began with the explosion of a "primeval atom," a singular point of infinite gravity in space and time. If this is correct, our current observations should reveal galaxies accelerating away from one another. This is precisely what we observe. Yet because there is another theory—the oscillating universe theory—that makes exactly this same prediction, Lemaître's theory must be considered inadequate.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in the critic's argument?

choices.text: Films should be judged on how well they accurately capture the world.
choices.rationale: If this principle were true, then the criticism of Quirks for having unrealistic characters—i.e., not accurately capturing the world—would be valid, not misguided.

choices.text: Films are successful as long as they are popular.
choices.rationale: While the Critic does note that Quirks is popular, she doesn't use that to support the conclusion that criticism of it for not being realistic is misguided. Rather, it's the success at the characters in being funny that justifies the conclusion.

choices.text: Film comedies should find their humor in their stylistic portrayals.
choices.rationale: The argument isn't about where comedies should find their comedy, but rather whether a comedy that has found its comedy succeeds despite being unrealistic.

choices.text: Films are successful if they succeed within their genre.
choices.rationale: The Critic concludes that criticism of Quirks is misguided because the unrealistic characters are funny, which is what's important in a comedy. In other words, Quirks succeeds as a comedy, which, according to this answer, means it succeeds as a film, justifying the conclusion in the stimulus that criticism of it for being unrealistic is misguided. This answer justifies the argument and is thus correct.

choices.text: Films should try to stay entirely within a single genre.
choices.rationale: The argument isn't about what films should do, but rather how to determine if a film is successful in doing whatever it sets out to do—e.g., is a comedy funny?

questions.stimulus: Critic: The criticism of the popular film comedy Quirks for not being realistic is misguided. It is certainly true that the characters are too stylized to be real people. That could be problematic, but in this case the resulting film is funny. And that is the important thing for a comedy.

questions.stem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.text: The plaintiff accuses the defendant of violating campaign laws, but the accusations are ill founded. While the defendant's actions may violate certain laws, they are not immoral, because the laws in question are unjust.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t contain flawed reasoning similar to the passage’s flawed reasoning. The passage dismisses Party Y’s accusations on the basis that Party Y (the accuser) was guilty of the same bad behavior. This choice focuses only on the defendant (the accused), and not the accuser.

choices.text: The plaintiff accuses the defendant of violating campaign laws, but these accusations show the plaintiff to be hypocritical, because the plaintiff has engaged in similar conduct.
