choices.rationale: The passage never states that Dunham discovered that the dance traditions of the Caribbean were derived from earlier African dance traditions. In fact, the first sentence of the third paragraph implies that it was already known that these dance traditions had African origins: “Starting in 1935, Dunham conducted a series of research projects into traditional Caribbean dance forms, with special interest in their origins in African culture.” So this doesn’t reflect any point in the passage, let alone the main point.

choices.text: Katherine Dunham's anthropological and choreographic expertise enabled her to make contributions that altered the landscape of modern dance in North America.
choices.rationale: This accurately sums up the main point of the passage. Overall, the passage argues that the combination of Dunham’s skills as a social researcher and as a dancer/choreographer are what enabled her to make such a big impact on North American modern dance. Each paragraph serves that broader goal: The first paragraph states this thesis; the second explains why other social researchers had ignored dance as an area of study; the third discusses Dunham’s unorthodox method of learning and participating in the dances themselves; and the final paragraph connects her method of immersion with the significant legacy she left by being the first to incorporate African themes into modern dance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Dunham's work in anthropology differed from that of most other anthropologists in the 1930s in that Dunham

choices.text: performed fieldwork for a very extended time period
choices.rationale: The passage never says that Dunham performed fieldwork for a very extended time period, and it also never says that the other anthropologists of the 1930s didn’t do just that. So there’s no support for this in the passage.

choices.text: related the traditions she studied to those of her own culture
choices.rationale: There’s no support for this choice; the passage never says or implies that other anthropologists didn’t related the traditions they studied to those of their own cultures.

choices.text: employed a participative approach in performing research
choices.rationale: The second paragraph describes how Dunham’s anthropological approach “differed radically” from the prevailing methodology in the 1930s in that Dunham did not gather data “from a position of complete detachment,” but rather “eschewed such caution and participated in the dances herself.” In other words, her work in anthropology differed from other anthropologists’ work in that she participated in performing her research.

choices.text: attached a high degree of political significance to her research
choices.rationale: This is out of scope. The passage never says that other anthropologists of the 1930s didn’t attach a high degree of political significance to their research. Also, although the passage might imply that Dunham's work, by correcting the exclusion of African American themes from modern dance, had political (or at least social) consequences, the passage does not state that Dunham herself considered her work highly political.

choices.text: had prior familiarity with the cultural practices of the peoples she set out to study
choices.rationale: This is out of scope. The passage never says that Dunham had prior familiarity with the cultural practices of the peoples she set out to study, or that this is what makes her work distinctive from other anthropologists of the time.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the "peers" mentioned in the second sentence of the second paragraph would have been most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the study of dance?

choices.text: Most social scientists who have attempted to study dance as a cultural phenomenon have misinterpreted it.
choices.rationale: The passage states that “Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry.” We can infer from this that the “peers” would have believed that the study of dance can’t be scientifically rigorous—not that most social scientists have misinterpreted dance. In fact, this excerpt suggests that almost no social scientists even attempted to study dance as a cultural phenomenon before Dunham, let alone attempted and misinterpreted it.

choices.text: Social scientists need not be well versed in dance traditions in order to obtain reliable data about them.
choices.rationale: The passage states that “Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry.” We can infer that the “peers” would have believed that the study of dance can’t be scientifically rigorous.

choices.text: Research into dance as a cultural form cannot be conducted with a high degree of scientific precision.
choices.rationale: The passage states that “Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry.” We can infer that these “peers” would have believed the study of dance does not lend itself to scientifically rigorous inquiry, i.e., studies would be unable to be conducted with a high degree of scientific precision.

choices.text: Most experts in the field of dance are too preoccupied to conduct studies in the field of dance ethnology.
choices.rationale: The passage states that “Previously, dance had been neglected as an area of social research, primarily because most social scientists gravitated toward areas likely to be recognized by their peers as befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry.” We can infer that the “peers” would have believed that the study of dance can’t be scientifically rigorous. The passage does go on to mention experts in the field of dance, but no views about those dance experts are ascribed to social scientists of the 1930s and earlier (the “peers”), and there’s no indication that anybody considered dance experts “preoccupied.”

choices.text: Dance forms are too variable across cultures to permit rigorous means of data collection.
choices.rationale: There’s nothing in the passage to suggest that the “peers” would have believed that dance forms are too variable—the reason why the study of dance was not believed to be “befitting scientifically rigorous, and therefore legitimate, modes of inquiry” is never given.

questions.stem: In the last sentence of the second paragraph, the author mentions "experts in dance" primarily in order to

choices.text: suggest why a group of social scientists did not embrace the study of a particular cultural form
choices.rationale: This paragraph does offer an explanation for why social scientists in general did not embrace the study of dance, but there’s no group of social scientists singled out—it’s implied that most, if not all, social researchers didn’t embrace dance ethnology. So the reason the author brings up “experts in dance” is actually to contribute to their explanation of why dance ethnology had been neglected by social researchers as a whole before Dunham.

choices.text: suggest that a certain group was more qualified to study a particular cultural form than was another group
choices.rationale: Both “groups” brought up here (dance experts and social scientists) are described as being unqualified to study dance ethnology, because each group lacks training in one area or the other. So this can’t be the reason the author mentions "experts in dance."

choices.text: identify an additional factor that motivated a particular social scientist to pursue a specific new line of research
choices.rationale: The “experts in dance” are not brought up as part of explaining Dunham’s motives. In this paragraph, the author first posits that dance had been neglected by social scientists, and then states three points explaining why: that social scientists gravitated toward areas of study that came off as more legitimate; that no other social scientists of the time had the training in dance necessary to evaluate dance techniques; and that (conversely) no “experts in dance” had the anthropological training necessary to engage in that kind of study themselves. Thus, the reason the author brings up “experts in dance” in this context is actually to contribute to their explanation of why dance ethnology had been neglected by social researchers before Dunham.

choices.text: contribute to an explanation of why a particular field of research was not previously pursued
choices.rationale: In this paragraph, the author first posits that, before Dunham, dance ethnology had been neglected as a field of research, and then states three points explaining why: that social scientists gravitated toward areas of study that seemed more legitimate; that no other social scientists of the time had the training in dance necessary to evaluate dance techniques; and that (conversely) no “experts in dance” had the anthropological training necessary to engage in that kind of study themselves. Thus, the reason the author brings up “experts in dance” in this context is to contribute to their explanation of why dance ethnology had been neglected by social researchers before Dunham.

choices.text: indicate an additional possible reason for the tension between the members of two distinct fields of research
choices.rationale: No tension between members of distinct fields of research is brought up—in fact, the “experts in dance” are not identified as members of a field of research at all. In this paragraph, the author first posits that dance had been neglected by social scientists, and then states three points explaining why: that social scientists gravitated toward areas of study that came off as more legitimate; that no other social scientists of the time had the training in dance necessary to evaluate dance techniques; and that (conversely) no “experts in dance” had the anthropological training necessary to engage in that kind of study themselves. Thus, the reason the author brings up “experts in dance” in this context is actually to contribute to their explanation of why dance ethnology had been neglected by social researchers before Dunham.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following was true of the dance forms that Dunham began studying in 1935?

choices.text: They were more similar to dance forms used in Pacific-island cultures than to any other known dance forms.
choices.rationale: There’s nothing in the passage to indicate that this statement is true of the dance forms Dunham began studying in 1935. The first paragraph says that various forms of the dance-isolation technique, which Dunham incorporated into North American dances, “have long been essential to traditional dances of certain African, Caribbean, and Pacific-island cultures.” But the passage never claims that the dance forms Dunham studied were more similar to those in Pacific-island cultures than to those of the other cultures mentioned.

choices.text: They represented the first use of the technique of dance-isolation within a culture outside of Africa.
choices.rationale: There’s nothing in the passage to indicate that this statement is true of the dance forms Dunham began studying in 1935. The first paragraph says that “various forms of the technique [of dance-isolation] have long been essential to traditional dances of certain African, Caribbean, and Pacific-island cultures.” Then, the third paragraph says that Dunham specifically studied Caribbean dance forms that had origins in African culture. But the passage never says that these Caribbean cultures had used dance-isolation before the Pacific-island cultures did, so we can’t say that the dance forms Dunham began studying in 1935 represented the first use of the technique of dance-isolation within a culture outside of Africa.

choices.text: They shared certain rhythmic characteristics with the dance forms employed in North American ballets.
choices.rationale: There’s nothing in the passage that states that the dance forms Dunham began studying in 1935 had anything in common with dance forms employed at the time in North American ballets, let alone that they shared certain rhythmic characteristics.

choices.text: They had already influenced certain popular dances in North America.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage, which implies that Dunham was the first to introduce the Caribbean dance forms she studied into North American dances, meaning they couldn’t have already influenced certain popular dances in North America before she began studying them.

choices.text: They were influenced by the traditions of non-Caribbean cultures.
choices.rationale: The passage discusses the dance forms Dunham began studying in 1935 in the third paragraph. The first sentence reads: “Starting in 1935, Dunham conducted a series of research projects into traditional Caribbean dance forms, with special interest in their origins in African culture.” In other words, these Caribbean dance forms were influenced by African cultural traditions.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to Dunham's work in anthropology and choreography as that work is described in the passage?

choices.text: A French archaeologist with training in musicology researches instruments used in seventeenth century France, and her findings become the basis for a Korean engineer's designs for devices to simulate the sounds those instruments most likely made.
choices.rationale: This is an example of a professional from one field incorporating the results of a professional from another field into their own work. So it’s not quite analogous to Dunham’s work, as described in the passage—Dunham applied her own results from one field to another.

choices.text: An Australian medical researcher with training in botany analyzes the chemical composition of plants that other researchers have collected in the Philippines, and then an Australian pharmaceutical company uses her findings to develop successful new medicines.
choices.rationale: This is an example of a company building upon the results of an individual researcher, all within the same field. So it’s not quite analogous to Dunham’s work, as described in the passage—Dunham applied her own results from one field to another.

choices.text: A Canadian surgeon uses her skill in drawing to collaborate with a Vietnamese surgeon to develop a manual containing detailed illustrations of the proper techniques for certain types of reconstructive surgery performed in both countries.
choices.rationale: This is an example of a two different people from the same field but different countries collaborating. So it’s not quite analogous to Dunham’s work, as described in the passage—Dunham applied her own results from one field to another.

choices.text: A Brazilian teacher with training in social psychology conducts a detailed study of teaching procedures while working with teachers in several Asian countries, then introduces the most effective of those procedures to teachers in his own country.
choices.rationale: This is analogous to Dunham’s work, as described in the passage: a professional with training in two different fields (Dunham, or in this case the Brazilian teacher) goes abroad and leverages their skills in one of the fields to conduct research into the other field, then broadens the latter field at home by incorporating the results of this research.

choices.text: An Italian fashion designer researches the social significance of clothing design in several cultures and then presents his research in a highly acclaimed book directed toward his colleagues in fashion design.
choices.rationale: This is close, but it’s not quite analogous to Dunham’s work, as described in the passage. The key difference between this Italian fashion designer and Dunham is that Dunham actually incorporated the dance forms from the cultures she studied into her own country’s dance forms. So, if the Italian designer had incorporated the different cultures’ fashion designs into Italian fashion, adding to the diversity and multiculturalism of Italian fashion, then this situation would be more analogous.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the colleagues mentioned in the third sentence of the third paragraph?

choices.text: They were partly correct in recommending that Dunham change her methods of data collection, since injury sustained during fieldwork might have compromised her research.
choices.rationale: There’s nothing about injury sustained during fieldwork in the passage, and that’s not the reason Dunham’s “colleagues” advised her to change her methods. Rather, her “colleagues” advised Dunham “not to become too closely involved” in the dances she was studying in order to most effectively gather data—and the author immediately says that this idea is “now fortunately recognized as unrealistic,” so we can infer that the author thinks these colleagues were incorrect.

choices.text: They were partly correct in advising Dunham to exercise initial caution in participating in the Caribbean dances, since her skill in performing them improved with experience.
choices.rationale: There’s nothing about Dunham’s skills improving or not improving at all in the passage. Rather, the “colleagues” advised Dunham “not to become too closely involved” in the dances she was studying in order to most effectively gather data—and the author immediately says that this idea is “now fortunately recognized as unrealistic,” so we can infer that the author thinks these colleagues were incorrect.

choices.text: They were incorrect in advising Dunham to increase the degree of her detachment, since extensive personal investment in fieldwork generally enhances scientific rigor.
choices.rationale: The first part of this is supported: we can infer that the author thinks these colleagues were incorrect. However, the reason why the author believes they were incorrect is not that extensive personal investment in fieldwork generally enhances scientific rigor. Rather, the author believes they were incorrect because complete detachment in data-gathering “is now fortunately recognized as unrealistic.” Besides, according to the passage, Dunham’s personal immersion in the dance forms didn’t necessarily contribute to greater scientific rigor in her studies—rather, her participation in the dance forms led directly to her incorporating these forms into North American dances as a choreographer.

choices.text: They were incorrect in assuming that researchers in the social sciences are able to gather data in an entirely objective manner.
choices.rationale: The “colleagues” advised Dunham “not to become too closely involved” in the dances she was studying in order to most effectively collect data, but the author immediately says that this idea is “now fortunately recognized as unrealistic.” So we can infer that the author believes these colleagues were incorrect in assuming that researchers in the social sciences are even able to gather data in an entirely objective manner.

choices.text: They were incorrect in assuming that dance could be studied with the same degree of scientific rigor possible in other areas of ethnology.
choices.rationale: The first part of this is supported: we can infer that the author thinks these colleagues were incorrect. However, the reason why the author believes they were incorrect is not that dance can’t be studied with the same degree of scientific rigor possible in other areas of ethnology. Rather, the author believes they were incorrect because the idea that complete detachment is even possible for data-gathering in general “is now fortunately recognized as unrealistic.”

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with explaining which one of the following?

choices.text: the human desire to create value
choices.rationale: That the human desire to create value explains the research findings about wealth and happiness is the thesis of passage B, but passage A doesn't touch upon this at all.

choices.text: the relationship between income and happiness
choices.rationale: Though the passages have different theses, both are primarily concerned with explaining the relationship between income and happiness: passage A argues that the phenomena of habituation and rivalry explain this relationship, and passage B argues that the desire to create value is the better explanation.

choices.text: the biological basis of people's attitudes toward wealth
choices.rationale: Passage A doesn’t delve into biological reasoning at all, and passage B only mentions a biological explanation very briefly (which it then dismisses). So neither passage is primarily concerned with the biological basis of people's attitudes toward wealth.

choices.text: the human propensity to become habituated to wealth
choices.rationale: Habituation is a sub-point discussed in passage A, but this is too narrow to be the primary concern of the passage—and passage B doesn't discuss habituation at all.

choices.text: the concept of "required income"
choices.rationale: “Required income” is discussed in passage A, but this is too narrow to be the primary concern of the passage. The concept is somewhat implicitly woven into passage B, but it isn't discussed outright, and is still too narrow to encompass the primary concern.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: The desire to demonstrate that one is wealthier than others is a remnant of human beings' primeval past.
choices.rationale: Author B brings up this theory in the first paragraph, but then rebuts it (writing that “it is not the explanation best supported by the evidence”) in favor of the theory that what human beings really desire is to create value. So we can infer that author B doesn’t agree with this statement.

choices.text: Very few people would be willing to accept a lower standard of living in return for greater relative wealth.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the findings of the Solnick and Hemenway study, which suggest that most people would be willing to accept a lower standard of living in return for greater relative wealth. Author B implicitly accepts these findings: the passage is spent offering an explanation for them, not refuting them. So we can infer that author B doesn’t agree with this statement.

choices.text: Being wealthier than other people would not make one happier if one believed that one's wealth was due merely to luck.
choices.rationale: Author B’s overall argument is that having more wealth than others is not what increases happiness—rather, it is the sense of having created value that leads to happiness, and when we create value, we are often rewarded with relative prosperity (i.e. wealth). In the third paragraph, author B states this directly: “it is the success—not the money per se—that provides the happiness. We use material wealth to show not just that we are prosperous, but that we are prosperous because we create value.” From this, we can infer that the author agrees that if one didn’t create value but is only wealthy by luck, this person would not be happier than others.

choices.text: Gradual increases in employees' wages do not increase their job satisfaction.
choices.rationale: From passage B’s general argument, we can infer that author B believes that increases in wages likely reflect an increase in the value the employee creates, which would lead to greater happiness for the employee. However, happiness is not the same as job satisfaction, which author B never discusses. So we can’t be sure that author B would disagree or agree with this statement—it’s out of scope.

choices.text: The overall level of happiness in a society usually increases as the society becomes wealthier.
choices.rationale: Author B doesn’t discuss the correlation between wealth and the overall happiness level of a society. Rather, author B’s argument focuses on explaining the correlation between relative wealth and happiness—why at any given time, people would prefer to be wealthier than others within that same society. So we can’t infer that the author would agree with this statement—it’s out of scope.

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to regard the conclusion that the Solnick and Hemenway study points to the existence of a "phenomenon of rivalry" (first sentence of the fourth paragraph of passage A) as

choices.text: ungenerous in its view of human nature and mistaken in its interpretation of the evidence
choices.rationale: The Solnick and Hemenway study found that most people would rather have a low absolute income that is higher than everyone else’s than have a high absolute income that is lower than everyone else’s. Author A says that the phenomenon of rivalry explains these findings. But Author B argues that “the data show” something else—that there’s actually a more altruistic motive at work: “what scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society” (last paragraph of passage B). So Author B would likely view Author A’s conclusion of rivalry as both ungenerous (assuming “ignobility” in humans) and an incorrect interpretation of the findings.

choices.text: flattering in its implications about human nature but only weakly supported by the available evidence
choices.rationale: Though the second part of this statement is somewhat supported, author B describes the rivalry explanation as unflattering in the last paragraph: “what scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society.”

choices.text: plausible in its account of human nature but based largely upon ambiguous evidence
choices.rationale: There’s nothing to suggest that author B thinks the rivalry explanation is based on “ambiguous” evidence. Rather, author B thinks the value explanation is better supported by the data (second paragraph). Plus, author B does not think the rivalry explanation is plausible in its account of human nature. Most directly, we can see this in the last paragraph of passage B: “what scholars often portray as an ignoble tendency—wanting to have more than others—is really evidence of a desire to create value. Wanting to create value benefits society.”

choices.text: unflattering in its implications about human nature but more or less valid in the conclusions drawn from the evidence
choices.rationale: Though the first part of this statement is supported, Author B does not think that the rivalry explanation is more or less valid in the conclusions drawn from the evidence—rather, author B thinks that the evidence best supports the value explanation (second paragraph).

choices.text: accurate concerning human nature and strongly supported by the evidence
choices.rationale: Author B doesn’t think the rivalry explanation is accurate concerning human nature. Rather, author B thinks that what scholars often portray as an “ignoble” tendency in humans—the desire to have more wealth than others—is actually the altruistic desire to create value, which benefits society (last paragraph of passage B). And author B does not think that the rivalry explanation is strongly supported by the evidence—rather, author B thinks that the evidence best supports the value explanation (second paragraph).

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs most accurately describes why the authors of passage A and passage B, respectively, mention the study by Solnick and Hemenway?

choices.text:
to present a view that will be argued against

to present a view for which additional evidence will be provided
choices.rationale: Passage A brings up the Solnick and Hemenway study to provide evidence for the rivalry theory, which is one of two explanations given for the phenomenon of the rising income “norm.” Passage A never argues against the rivalry explanation, so the first reason in (A) doesn’t fit.

choices.text:
to present a view that will be argued against

to provide evidence for one explanation of a phenomenon
choices.rationale: Passage A brings up the Solnick and Hemenway study to provide evidence for the rivalry theory, which is one of two explanations for the phenomenon of the rising income “norm.” It never argues against the rivalry explanation, so the first reason in (B) doesn’t fit.

choices.text:
to provide evidence for one explanation of a phenomenon

to present a view for which additional evidence will be provided
choices.rationale: Passage A brings up the Solnick and Hemenway study to provide evidence for the rivalry theory, which is one of two explanations for the phenomenon of the rising income “norm.” So the first part fits.

choices.text:
to provide evidence for one explanation of a phenomenon

to introduce the main topic to be discussed
choices.rationale: Passage A brings up the Solnick and Hemenway study to provide evidence for the rivalry theory, which is one of two explanations for the phenomenon of the rising income “norm.” So the first part fits.

choices.text:
to introduce the main topic to be discussed

to present a view that will be argued against
choices.rationale: The Solnick and Hemenway study comes late in passage A and doesn’t introduce the main topic. Rather, passage A brings up the Solnick and Hemenway study to provide evidence for the rivalry theory, which in turn is only one of two explanations for the phenomenon of the rising income “norm”; the main purpose of passage A is to provide explanations for this phenomenon (and those explanations are brought up well before the study is referenced). So the first part doesn’t fit.

questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs of terms would most likely be used by the authors of passage A and passage B, respectively, to describe a person who wants to make more money than his or her neighbors?

choices.text: insular, cosmopolitan
choices.rationale: This doesn’t match either author’s description of ‘comparers.’

choices.text: altruistic, egocentric
choices.rationale: This doesn’t match either author’s description of ‘comparers.’

choices.text: happy, miserable
choices.rationale: This doesn’t match either author’s description of ‘comparers.’

choices.text: misguided, admirable
choices.rationale: Author A discusses people’s desire to make more money than others in their “reference group” as the phenomenon of rivalry—which explains why happiness levels don’t increase as society grows richer over time. For example, writes author A, in East Germany, “living standards have soared since 1990, but the level of happiness has plummeted because people now compare themselves with West Germans, rather than with people in other Soviet bloc countries” (last sentence). We can infer from the author’s tone and overall argument that such comparers are misguided—that their viewpoint is too narrow and doesn’t take into account how their situation has improved over time.

choices.text: lucky, primitive
choices.rationale: This doesn’t match either author’s description of ‘comparers.’

questions.stem: In arguing for their respective positions, the author of passage A and the author of passage B both do which one of the following?

choices.text: explain a phenomenon by pointing to its biological origins
choices.rationale: Author A doesn’t discuss biological origins at all, let alone within an explanation for a phenomenon. And author B only offers up the biological-origin explanation to then reject it in favor of their own theory, which they believe is better supported by the data.

choices.text: endorse a claim simply because it is widely believed
choices.rationale: Neither author does this. Author A doesn’t discuss whether or not any of their claims are widely believed, and author B directly rejects a widely believed explanation in the second paragraph.

choices.text: accept a claim for the sake of argument
choices.rationale: Neither author does this. Both authors argue for their own position without accepting any claim for the sake of argument.

choices.text: attempt to resolve an apparent paradox
choices.rationale: Author A does this, but author B doesn’t try to resolve any “paradox”—rather, author B focuses on interpreting the findings of the Solnick and Hemenway study, offering a less common but better supported (in their opinion) alternative explanation for the results. In other words, author B doesn’t treat the findings, or the competing theories, as any kind of “paradox.”

choices.text: assert that their positions are supported by data
choices.rationale: Both authors do this. Author A brings up several different pieces of supporting evidence, albeit implicitly—he only names the Solnick and Hemenway study, but presumably the other evidence he cites (including the “required income” discussion and the East Germany discussion) come from studies as well. And author B directly asserts that “the data show that earning more makes people happier because relative prosperity makes them feel that they are successful, that they have created value.”

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: In general, whether people characterize a risk as voluntary or involuntary depends on whether they approve of the purpose for which the risk is taken.
choices.rationale: This is one of the flaws in voluntariness considerations that the author brings up, but it’s too narrow to encompass the main point. Rather, the main point is that the government shouldn’t use considerations of voluntariness to shape policy about protecting people from risks, and should instead shape such policy around saving as many people as possible.

choices.text: Decisions about government intervention to protect people from risks should be based primarily on how many lives can be saved rather than on whether the risks are considered voluntary.
choices.rationale: This sums up the main point. The first paragraph states the thesis, that the government shouldn’t use considerations of voluntariness to shape risk intervention policy. The second and third paragraph further explains the author’s reasoning, and the last paragraph asserts that the government should instead shape policy around saving as many lives as it can.

choices.text: Though laypeople may object, experts should be the ones to determine whether the risk incurred in a particular action is voluntary or involuntary.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The author believes that judgments about voluntariness are flawed, and are thus “of little utility in guiding policy decisions.” Whether or not experts or laypeople are doing the judging is irrelevant—and in fact, the author says that it’s mostly laypeople who care about voluntariness in the first place, while policy experts “tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake” (first paragraph).

choices.text: Public-policy decisions related to the protection of society against risk are difficult to make because of the difficulty of distinguishing risks incurred voluntarily from those incurred involuntarily.
choices.rationale: The author neither states nor implies that public-policy decisions related to the protection of society against risk are difficult to make in general, let alone that distinguishing voluntariness from involuntariness is the reason—rather, the author argues that such decisions should not be based on voluntariness, and should instead be based on saving as many lives as possible. The difficulty of the decision-making is out of the scope of the passage.

choices.text: People who make judgments about the voluntary or involuntary character of a risk are usually unaware of the complicated motivations that lead people to take risks.
choices.rationale: First, this choice is too narrow. Purposes for taking risks are mentioned in paragraph three, but they are related to only one of the author's reasons (for why judgments about voluntariness are often really about something else). So this choice doesn't account for the reason discussed in paragraph two, and, more importantly, it doesn't account for the author's overall argument about what should guide policy decisions.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that which one of the following is usually a significant factor in laypeople's willingness to support public funding for specific risk-reduction measures?

choices.text: an expectation about the ratio of dollars spent to lives saved
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the third paragraph, where the passage says that “it is unlikely that people would want to pour enormous taxpayer resources into lowering the risks associated with skydiving, even if the ratio of dollars spent to lives saved were quite good.” In other words, according to the passage, the ratio of dollars spent to lives saves is not a significant factor in laypeople's willingness to support public funding for specific risk-reduction measures

choices.text: deference to expert judgments concerning whether the government should intervene
choices.rationale: The passage doesn’t state or imply that laypeople ever defer to expert judgments; in fact, by saying that the considerations of the laypeople differ from the considerations of the experts (laypeople weigh voluntariness; experts weigh aggregate lives saved), the passage implies that laypeople don’t usually defer to expert judgments.

choices.text: a belief as to whether the risk is incurred voluntarily or involuntarily
choices.rationale: In the third paragraph, the author states that laypeople would be unwilling to pour enormous taxpayer resources into lowering the risks associated with skydiving, because they would categorize that as a “voluntary” risk (although, the author argues, what’s really going on is that they probably just don’t approve of skydiving as an activity). So we know that judgments about the voluntariness of the risk are usually a significant factor in laypeople's willingness to support public funding for specific risk-reduction measures.

choices.text: a judgment as to whether the risk puts a great number of lives at stake
choices.rationale: This consideration is attributed to the experts, not the laypeople: “Policy experts tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake; laypeople care a great deal whether a risk is undertaken voluntarily” (first paragraph).

choices.text: a consideration of the total resources available for risk reduction
choices.rationale: This isn’t described as a significant factor in laypeople's willingness to support public funding for specific risk-reduction measures. The author argues that the government should primarily factor in the number of lives saved, “subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction.” But this doesn’t imply that a consideration of the resources is key for laypeople to support public funding.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following do laypeople generally consider to involve risk that is not freely assumed?

choices.text: traveling in outer space
choices.rationale: Though it’s not discussed in the passage, given that laypeople think skydiving involves voluntarily risk, they would likely think that traveling in outer space is a voluntary-risk activity as well.

choices.text: participating in skydiving
choices.rationale: Skydiving is considered a voluntary-risk activity by laypeople (third paragraph).

choices.text: serving as a firefighter
choices.rationale: According to the passage, laypeople often characterize risks as "voluntary" when they do not approve of the purpose for which people run the risks. Skydiving is contrasted with firefighting in this regard, as skydiving doesn’t have an approved-of purpose, while firefighting does. However it’s still a personal choice to become a firefighter, and therefore the risk assumed is not totally involuntary (i.e., the risk is freely assumed). So if laypeople say that firefighting involves involuntary risk, what they really mean, according to the author, is that the risk is for an approved-of purpose—to put out fires.

choices.text: traveling in airplanes
choices.rationale: The second paragraph states that “risks incurred by airline passengers are typically thought to be involuntary, since passengers have no control over whether a plane is going to crash.” In other words, laypeople generally consider traveling in airplanes as an activity that involves risks that are not freely assumed.

choices.text: climbing mountains
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. In the first paragraph we’re told that laypeople think the government shouldn’t intervene to protect people from risks associated with mountain climbing. Then we’re told that when laypeople think the government shouldn’t intervene to protect people from risks associated with an activity, it’s because they consider the risks involved in that activity to be voluntarily assumed. So we can infer that laypeople do consider mountain climbing to be an activity that involves freely assumed risk.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: People should generally not be protected against the risks incurred through activities, such as skydiving, that are dangerous and serve no socially useful purpose.
choices.rationale: According to the author, when it comes to risk-protection policy, the government should “attempt to save as many lives as it can,” and that any deviations from this policy shouldn’t be based on voluntariness but rather on more specific considerations (last paragraph). Whether or not an activity is dangerous and doesn’t serve a socially useful purpose is out of scope, so we can’t say that the author would agree with this statement.

choices.text: The fact that plane crash victims chose to fly would usually be deemed by policy experts to be largely irrelevant to decisions about the government's role in regulating air safety.
choices.rationale: According to the author, policy experts “tend to focus on aggregate lives at stake” rather than on the voluntariness of the risk (first paragraph). So the author would likely agree that, in making decisions about the government’s role in regulating air safety, the policy experts would not consider the fact that plane crash victims chose to fly.”

choices.text: Both the probability of occurrence and the probability of resulting death or injury are higher for plane crashes than for any other kind of risk incurred by airline passengers.
choices.rationale: The author doesn’t ever discuss (let alone compare) different types risks incurred by airline passengers. So we can’t say that the author would agree with this statement.

choices.text: For public-policy purposes, a risk should be deemed voluntarily incurred if people are not subject to that risk unless they make a particular choice.
choices.rationale: The author argues that voluntariness should not be factored at all into risk-protection policy, as judgments about voluntariness are flawed. So we can’t say that the author would agree with this statement.

choices.text: The main category of risk that is usually incurred completely involuntarily is the risk of natural disaster.
choices.rationale: The author does imply that natural disasters are one example of a 100% involuntary-risk incurrence (second paragraph, in the discussion of an asteroid collision). But the author doesn’t say or imply that this is the “main” category of involuntary-risk incurrence—there are likely other events that the author would agree fits that bill. So this statement goes too far beyond what we can infer from the passage.

questions.stem: The author's use of the phrase "no special magic" (second to last sentence of the third paragraph) is most likely meant primarily to convey that notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary"

choices.text: do not exhaustively characterize the risks that people commonly face
choices.rationale: The author likely agrees that notions like "voluntary" and "involuntary" don’t exhaustively characterize the risks people commonly face, but that's not the purpose of saying that such notions have “no special magic.” Rather, the author means to convey that we can't rely on judgments about the voluntariness of incurring risk for guidance in shaping policy. Also, in this paragraph, the author isn’t talking about just risks that “people commonly face,” but also risks that are not commonly faced (such as the risks associated with skydiving and firefighting).

choices.text: have been used to intentionally conceal the factors motivating government efforts to protect people from risks
choices.rationale: The author never states or implies that the notions of “voluntary” and “involuntary” have been used to intentionally conceal the factors motivating government efforts to protect people from risk. The author argues that judgments about the voluntariness of taking on risk—a paradigm often favored by laypeople—are flawed, and that they reflect other kinds of judgments (subconsciously) buried within them. But there's never any accusation of intentionally concealing the other factors at play, either on the part of the government, the policy experts, or the laypeople.

choices.text: have no meaning beyond their literal, dictionary definitions
choices.rationale: This is too strong. The author argues that when it comes to incurring risk, notions of “voluntary” and “involuntary” are very flawed—but not that these concepts have no meaning at all beyond their dictionary definitions. Rather, by stating that they have “no special magic” when it comes to policy decisions about risk intervention, the author means to convey that we can't rely on such judgments for guidance.

choices.text: are mistakenly believed to be characteristics that inform people's understanding of the consequences of risk
choices.rationale: The author doesn't use the phrase “no special magic” to say anything about consequences. In fact, the consequences of risk are out of the scope of the passage entirely. Rather, the author means to convey that we can't rely on judgments about the voluntariness of incurring risks to shape policy.

choices.text: provide a flawed mechanism for making public policy decisions relating to risk reduction
choices.rationale: The sentence concludes two paragraphs that each delve into a reason why the voluntariness of incurring risk isn’t a valuable tool for shaping public policy decisions—first, it’s difficult to nail down when a risk is voluntarily incurred in the first place; and second, people often (incorrectly) characterize risks as "voluntary" when they don’t approve of the purpose of taking the risk. Thus, that such judgments are flawed and can’t be used to guide risk-reduction policy is the author’s intention behind saying that these notions have “no special magic.”

questions.stem: The passage most strongly supports the inference that the author believes which one of the following?

choices.text: Whenever an activity involves the risk of loss of human life, the government should intervene to reduce the degree of risk incurred.
choices.rationale: The author argues that risk-reduction policy should be based on saving as many lives as possible, subject to the limited resources devoted to risk reduction (last paragraph). So the author may not believe that an activity that involves the risk of just one or just a few lives merits any government intervention. Hence, we can’t infer that the author would agree with this statement.

choices.text: Some environmental risks are voluntary to a greater degree than others are.
choices.rationale: In the second paragraph, the author argues that “with most environmental, occupational, and other social risks, [voluntariness] is not an all-or-nothing matter, but rather one of degree.” This implies that the author believes there are different degrees of voluntariness involved in environmental risks, with some involving more than others.

choices.text: Policy experts are more likely than laypeople to form an accurate judgment about the voluntariness or involuntariness of an activity.
choices.rationale: The author never implies that policy experts are more accurate in judgments about the voluntariness of risk than laypeople are—in fact, the author states that policy experts tend to “focus on aggregate lives at stake” instead of voluntariness (first paragraph). The author only claims that laypeople care more about voluntariness than experts.

choices.text: The government should increase the quantity of resources devoted to protecting people from risk.
choices.rationale: In the last paragraph, the author writes that “the government should attempt to save as many lives as it can, subject to the limited public and private resources devoted to risk reduction.” The author never argues that these resources aren’t enough and should be increased—just that the government must work within the limits of what resources there are.

choices.text: Government policies intended to reduce risk are not justified unless they comport with most people's beliefs.
choices.rationale: This choice conflicts with the author’s views. The author states that laypeople tend to care deeply about the voluntariness of the risk incurred, but then goes on to argue that such judgments are flawed and shouldn’t be used to guide policy, despite what these laypeople want. So it’s unlikely that the author would agree that policy should comport with most people’s beliefs.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude in the passage?

choices.text: chagrin at the rampant misunderstanding of the relative risks associated with various activities
choices.rationale: Chagrin is too strong of a word to describe the author’s attitude in any part of the passage. The author is certainly doubtful of the utility of voluntariness in guiding risk-management policy, and the author focuses on poking holes in the logic of “voluntary” versus “involuntary” risk to prove that point. But “chagrin” implies distress or embarrassment that isn’t there in the author’s (more scholarly) tone.

choices.text: concern that policy guided mainly by laypeople's emphasis on the voluntariness of risk would lead to excessive government regulation
choices.rationale: This is out of scope. The author never expresses any concern about excessive government regulation. In fact, the author doesn’t bring up “excessive” regulation at all, let alone linking it to laypeople's emphasis on the voluntariness of risk.

choices.text: skepticism about the reliability of laypeople's intuitions as a general guide to deciding government risk-management policy
choices.rationale: The author states that laypeople tend to care deeply about whether or not a risk is incurred voluntarily or involuntarily when considering government risk-management policy (first paragraph). However, throughout most the passage, the author argues that their judgments about voluntariness in risk are highly flawed and therefore not useful in shaping policy. The author ultimately comes down on the side of the policy experts, who tend to focus on aggregate lives saved instead. From this, we can infer that the author is skeptical about the reliability of laypeople's intuitions as a general guide to deciding government risk-management policy.

choices.text: conviction that the sole criterion that can justify government intervention to reduce risk is the saving of human lives
choices.rationale: This is too strong. The author says that government risk-reduction policy should focus on saving as many lives as possible, but that when this principle must be deviated from, we should strive to justify the reasoning with something deeper than voluntariness (last paragraph). So the author anticipates needing to deviate from the “aggregate lives saved” principle at some point. Hence, we can’t say the author believes the sole criterion that can justify government intervention to reduce risk is the saving of human lives.

choices.text: eagerness to persuade the reader that policy experts' analysis of risk is distorted by subtle biases
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the passage. The author ultimately comes down in favor of the policy experts’ focus on aggregate lives at stake instead of the voluntariness of the risk incurred. In fact, we can infer that the author believes the laypeople’s analysis of risk is the one distorted by subtle biases.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the conclusion drawn above?

choices.text: The ten people were randomly assigned to either the group that tasted only coffee or the group that was also given chocolate, although some people had asked to be in the group that received chocolate.
choices.rationale: This could actually strengthen the conclusion in the passage. (A) removes the possibility that the group assignments weren’t random, which would have weakened the experiment. Removing a potential weakener results in a net effect of strengthening a position.

choices.text: Similar results were achieved when the experiment was repeated with a different, larger group of people.
choices.rationale: This could actually strengthen the conclusion in the passage. If the experiment’s results were reproduced with a different, larger group of people, then it’s less likely that the experiment was an anomaly.

choices.text: Chocolate is normally consumed as a solid, whereas coffee is normally consumed as a liquid.
choices.rationale: This comparison doesn’t affect the argument. How chocolate and coffee are normally consumed is irrelevant to whether chocolate interferes with the ability to taste differences in coffee.

choices.text: The five people who were originally given chocolate were asked a week later to taste coffee samples without chocolate, and they still detected no differences between the coffee samples.
choices.rationale: This weakens the conclusion that chocolate interferes with one’s ability to taste coffee. If (D) is true, then the five people (who were originally given chocolate and couldn’t taste the difference among samples of coffee) still couldn’t taste the difference later without chocolate to influence them. That strongly suggests that something else is responsible for their inability to taste the differences—not chocolate.

choices.text: Some subjects who tasted just coffee reported only subtle differences between the coffee samples, while others thought the differences were considerable.
choices.rationale: This comparison doesn’t affect the argument. It remains true that the people in the group that ate chocolate could detect hardly any differences between the coffee samples, so learning about a range of differences among the subjects in the other group is neither helpful nor harmful to the conclusion that chocolate interferes with the ability to taste coffee.

questions.stimulus: In an experiment, ten people were asked to taste samples of coffee and rank them. Five of the people were given chocolate with the coffee, and this group subsequently reported that all the coffee samples tasted pretty much the same as one another. Five others tasted coffee only, and they were able to detect differences. Clearly, then, chocolate interferes with one's ability to taste coffee.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning of the residents opposed to building the house?

choices.text: Every possible effort should be made to preserve historic buildings that are well known and well loved.
choices.rationale: The situation in the stimulus is about preserving landscape, not a building, so this answer is out of scope.

choices.text: Communities that seek to preserve undeveloped areas of landscape or historic neighborhoods should purchase those properties for the public trust.
choices.rationale: The stimulus never discusses purchasing land for the public trust, so this answer is out of scope.

choices.text: Artists who choose to represent actual landscapes in their paintings have the right to demand that the owners of the land represented do not significantly alter the landscape.
choices.rationale: The artist in question isn't the one pushing for the preservation of this land—in fact, that painter recently died.

choices.text: The right to build on one's own property is constrained by the artistic and historical interests of the community at large.
choices.rationale: This answer choice provides justification for using artistic and historical interests to oppose building property on someone else's private land, thus strengthening the position of the residents of this community.

choices.text: In historic communities, the building and zoning regulations should prohibit construction that obstructs access to historic sites.
choices.rationale: First, there's no indication that this community is historic (just that it has a historic heritage). Second, the current zoning laws allow for this development, and the argument isn't about changing those laws. Third, this answer doesn't provide justification for residents to oppose something.

questions.stimulus: Residents of a coastal community are resisting the efforts of one family to build a large house on the family's land. Although the house would not violate any town codes, the land in question is depicted in a painting by a famous and beloved landscape painter who recently died. Residents argue that the house would alter the pristine landscape and hence damage the community's artistic and historic heritage.

questions.stem: The reasoning in Moore's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: takes for granted that there are no other possible health benefits of using sunscreen lotions other than blocking skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t a flaw in Moore’s argument, which focuses on how well sunscreen lotions block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation. Whether sunscreen lotions bring other possible health benefits isn’t relevant to how effectively the lotions prevent skin cancer.

choices.text: fails to distinguish between the relative number of cases of skin cancer and the severity of those cases in measuring effectiveness at skin cancer prevention
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in Moore’s argument, which addresses the rate at which two groups of people develop skin cancer, period. The severity of the cancer isn’t in question here.

choices.text: fails to consider the effectiveness of sunscreen lotions that are not specifically designed to block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t a flaw in Moore’s argument, which focuses on how effective sunscreen lotions are that are designed to block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation. Learning about how effective other sunscreen lotions are wouldn’t resolve any flaws in this argument.

choices.text: relies on evidence regarding the probability of people in different groups developing cancer that, in principle, would be impossible to challenge
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in Moore’s argument, which never addresses the “probability” of people developing cancer—only the rate of people developing cancer. Additionally, it isn’t clear that any of the evidence provided would be “impossible to challenge.”

choices.text: overlooks the possibility that people who consistently use sunscreen lotions spend more time in the sun, on average, than people who do not
choices.rationale: This describes a flaw in Moore’s argument. Moore makes a comparison in the support between people who have consistently used sunscreen lotions and people who have rarely, if ever, used sunscreen lotions. In order for this argument to work, these two groups would need to be sufficiently comparable.

questions.stimulus: Moore: Sunscreen lotions, which are designed to block skin-cancer-causing ultraviolet radiation, do not do so effectively. Many scientific studies have shown that people who have consistently used these lotions develop, on average, as many skin cancers as those who have rarely, if ever, used them.

questions.stem: The reasoning technique employed by the psychologist is that of attempting to undermine an argument by

choices.text: introducing a principle that contradicts the one on which the argument is based
choices.rationale: The opposing point can be said to be based on a principle (difficult/time consuming things are the most effective), but the Psychologist doesn't introduce a competing principle that contradicts that. Rather, she introduces an analogous scenario that calls that principle into question—and an analogous scenario isn't a competing principle.

choices.text: questioning the truth of its premises
choices.rationale: The premises of the opposing argument are that Freudian psychotherapy is difficult and time consuming. The Psychologist doesn't call that into question (and, in fact, relies on it by bringing in an analogous scenario that also involves something that's difficult and time consuming).

choices.text: presenting an analogous argument whose conclusion is thought to be obviously false
choices.rationale: This answer choice highlights that the Psychologist calls the argument's conclusion into question by bringing up an analogous scenario where the same conclusion would "never be accepted." Using an analogy to point out the flaws in an argument is a common method of reasoning (sometimes referred to by the fancy Latin phrase reductio ad absurdum).

choices.text: claiming that the argument is based on a false analogy
choices.rationale: The Psychologist uses an analogy to prove her point, she doesn't claim that the opposing point is using a bad analogy.

choices.text: suggesting that a supposed cause of a phenomenon is actually an effect of that phenomenon
choices.rationale: There's no discussion of cause and effect in the stimulus, so this answer is out of scope.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: Some have argued that Freudian psychotherapy is the most effective kind because it is so difficult and time consuming. But surely this does not follow. Similar reasoning—e.g., concluding that a car-repair chain has the most effective technique for repairing cars because the cars it services receive so much work and spend so much time in the shop—would never be accepted.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the argument?

choices.text: Biodiversity does not require that all existing species continue to exist.
choices.rationale: This statement expresses the argument’s conclusion, which is in the first sentence. The second sentence explains why not all existing species need to continue existing in order to maintain biodiversity: if a given ecological niche could be filled by species A, B, or C, for example, then only one of these three would need to survive. Because (A) is supported by the second sentence, and doesn’t in turn support any other statements, it’s the argument’s conclusion.

choices.text: There are various ecological niches that must be filled if there is to be life on Earth.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion, because it forms part of the support for why biodiversity doesn’t require the survival of every currently existing species.

choices.text: The survival of life on Earth depends upon biodiversity.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion. It’s part of the sentence that contains the conclusion (that biodiversity doesn’t require all existing species to survive), but it’s not what the arguer is trying to prove. Nothing in the passage serves to explain why the survival of life on Earth depends upon biodiversity. This statement is something that the arguer addresses and then moves on from.

choices.text: There are many ecological niches that can be filled by more than one species.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion, because it forms part of the support for why biodiversity doesn’t require the survival of every currently existing species.

choices.text: The species most indispensable for biodiversity fill more than one ecological niche.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the argument’s conclusion, because nothing about the species “most indispensable for biodiversity” was ever stated anywhere in the passage.

questions.stimulus: While biodiversity is indispensable to the survival of life on Earth, biodiversity does not require the survival of every currently existing species. For there to be life on Earth, various ecological niches must be filled; many niches, however, can be filled by more than one species.

questions.stem: Which one of the following would be most useful to know in order to evaluate the clinician's argument?

choices.text: How large is the class of drugs that increase the risk of developing osteoporosis?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. Whether it’s a large class or a small class of drugs that increase the risk of developing osteoporosis, that doesn’t affect whether patients with immune system disorders should take the new drug.

choices.text: Why are immune system disorders treated with drugs that increase the risk of developing osteoporosis?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. We’re told that patients with immune system disorders are currently treated with these drugs, and it’s reasonable to assume that doctors have a good reason for prescribing these drugs, regardless of the side effects. Knowing (or not knowing) the exact reason doesn’t help us determine whether these patients should take the new drug.

choices.text: Is the new drug more expensive than the drug that helps to preserve existing bone?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. The proposal is that the new drug be taken with the old drug, not instead of it. The comparative costs of these drugs aren’t relevant.

choices.text: How long has the drug that helps to preserve existing bone been in use?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question isn’t useful to know. We’d have to make a lot of assumptions—something we should avoid on Test Day—in order to make (D) be relevant. For example, some students are tempted to assume that longevity of use means that a drug is better, but that isn’t demonstrated.

choices.text: To what extent does the new drug retain its efficacy when used in combination with the other drugs?
choices.rationale: The answer to this question is useful to know in order to evaluate the clinician’s argument. If the new drug doesn’t retain its efficacy when used in combination with the other drugs, then we would be less inclined to agree with the clinician. If, on the other hand, the new drug does retain its efficacy when used in combination with the other drugs, we would be more inclined to agree with the clinician. Remember—we’re not trying to prove or disprove an argument with the answer; we’re looking for the question that would be helpful to know the answer to.

questions.stimulus: Clinician: Patients with immune system disorders are usually treated with a class of drugs that, unfortunately, increase the patient's risk of developing osteoporosis, a bone-loss disease. So these patients take another drug that helps to preserve existing bone. Since a drug that enhances the growth of new bone cells has now become available, these patients should take this new drug in addition to the drug that helps to preserve existing bone.

questions.stem: The critic's reasoning most closely conforms to which one of the following principles?

choices.text: A civic building that is located in a downtown area should, if possible, be located on an elevated site.
choices.rationale: This answer doesn't address whether a civic building is successfully serving its purpose, just where it should be built if possible. And since the Critic believes the art museum is successful without mentioning where it's built, she can't believe it's all that relevant. Finally, the image of the "city on the hill" is dismissed as not guaranteeing a truly elevated purpose.

choices.text: A city needs to have civic buildings if it is to have social cohesion.
choices.rationale: This answer sets up civic buildings as a necessary part of creating social cohesion, but it doesn't establish social cohesion as a purpose of civic buildings. This answer is a bit of a reversal of what we're looking for—a principle establishing social cohesion as a necessary element of a successful civic building.

choices.text: A civic building with an elevated purpose should be located on a spectacular site.
choices.rationale: The argument is about whether a civic building serves its purpose, not whether it has an "elevated purpose" and should be on a spectacular site. If anything, in suggesting that the art museum is successful despite being located in the heart of downtown, it's saying that there are factors much more important than the spectacle of the location.

choices.text: The downtown area of a city should be designed in a way that complements the area's civic buildings.
choices.rationale: There's no discussion of how areas of a city should be designed—just what a successful civic building should do, regardless of its location.

choices.text: The purpose of a civic building is to encourage social cohesion and to make a city more alive.
choices.rationale: This answer provides a principle establishing the purpose of civic buildings. The Critic states that the art museum succeeds as a civic building where the concert hall fails because the former encourages social cohesion and makes the city feel alive. If those are the purposes of a civic building, as this answer choice states, then the conclusion holds.

questions.stimulus: Critic: The perennial image of the "city on a hill" associates elevated locations with elevated purposes. The city's concert hall—its newest civic building—is located on a spectacular hilltop site. But because it is far from the center of the city, it cannot fulfill the purpose of a civic building. An example of a successful civic building is the art museum, which is situated in a densely populated downtown area. It encourages social cohesion and makes the city more alive.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can most reasonably be concluded on the basis of the researchers' findings?

choices.text: Fluoride-bearing minerals are not the primary source of fluoride found in groundwater.
choices.rationale: The stimulus establishes that these minerals are how fluoride enters the groundwater, so this answer is contradicted.

choices.text: Rainfall does not affect fluoride concentrations in groundwater.
choices.rationale: Incorrect. The relationship in the stimulus held rainfall constant, thus removing it from the equation. Different levels of rainfall could result in different fluoride levels, but the amount of rain has the same effect on those levels.

choices.text: Sodium-bearing minerals dissolve at a faster rate than fluoride-bearing minerals.
choices.rationale: There's no comparison between fluoride levels and sodium levels, just a note that high levels of each go hand in hand.

choices.text: Sodium in groundwater increases the rate at which fluoride-bearing minerals dissolve.
choices.rationale: This answer connects the high sodium levels where there's high fluoride levels when all else is held constant to the means by which fluoride gets into the groundwater. If the only relevant difference between areas with different fluoride levels is sodium, and the source of fluoride in groundwater is dissolved minerals, then the sodium must act to get that fluoride from the minerals faster.

choices.text: Soil that contains high concentrations of sodium-bearing minerals also contains high concentrations of fluoride-bearing minerals.
choices.rationale: High fluoride is correlated with high sodium levels, not the other way around. This answer reverses the relationship.

questions.stimulus: Fluoride enters a region's groundwater when rain dissolves fluoride-bearing minerals in the soil. In a recent study, researchers found that when rainfall, concentrations of fluoride-bearing minerals, and other relevant variables are held constant, fluoride concentrations in groundwater are significantly higher in areas where the groundwater also contains a high concentration of sodium.

questions.stem: The statement that there is no evidence that Bosch was a member of the Brethren figures in the argument in which one of the following ways?

choices.text: It is a premise that, when combined with the other premises, guarantees the falsity of Fraenger's assertion.
choices.rationale: The argument isn't designed to show the F's hypothesis is wrong but that it is "unlikely to be correct." This answer is too strong.

choices.text: It is used to support the claim that Bosch was a member of a mainstream church.
choices.rationale: While an implication of the argument is that B was a member of a mainstream church, that isn't the main point. Additionally, the statement in question is meant to call into question F's hypothesis that B was in a cult, not that he was in a mainstream church—a subtle difference, but a difference nonetheless.

choices.text: It is used to dispute Fraenger's hypothesis by questioning Fraenger's credibility.
choices.rationale: This answer is describing an ad hominem attack, but there's no questioning of F's credibility. Bringing up reasons to doubt someone's argument isn't questioning their credibility.

choices.text: It is intended to cast doubt on Fraenger's hypothesis by questioning the sufficiency of Fraenger's evidence.
choices.rationale: This answer highlights the role of the statement in question. It's a premise that is used to rebut F's argument by stating that there's no evidence backing it up.

choices.text: It is intended to help show that Bosch's choice of subject matter remains unexplained.
choices.rationale: The author does agree that F's hypothesis explains B's strange subject matter, but she doesn't state that it's the only potential explanation. The argument also isn't designed to establish that the subject matter is, was, or remains unexplained.

questions.stimulus: Fraenger's assertion that the artist Hieronymus Bosch belonged to the Brethren of the Free Spirit, a nonmainstream religious group, is unlikely to be correct. Fraenger's hypothesis explains much of Bosch's unusual subject matter. However, there is evidence that Bosch was a member of a mainstream church, and no evidence that he was a member of the Brethren.

questions.stem: The vacuum cleaner salesperson's argument is most vulnerable to the criticism that it

choices.text: ignores the possibility that dirt remained in the carpet even after the Super XL had been used in the test
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The Super XL could still be the superior vacuum, even if it didn’t clean all the dirt in the carpet.

choices.text: takes for granted that the Super XL will still perform better than the old vacuum cleaner when it is the same age as the old vacuum cleaner
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The salesperson concludes that the Super XL is the better vacuum than the old vacuum now—presumably in order to convince the vacuum owner that they should replace the old vacuum with the Super XL. How they’ll perform when they’re the same age isn’t relevant.

choices.text: takes for granted that because the Super XL outperforms one vacuum cleaner it is the best vacuum cleaner available
choices.rationale: This doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The salesperson never claims that the Super XL is the best vacuum cleaner available, but rather that the Super XL is better than the owner’s current, old vacuum.

choices.text: ignores the possibility that the amount of dirt removed in the test by the old vacuum cleaner is greater than the amount of dirt removed by the Super XL
choices.rationale: This choice tempts some students, but it doesn’t describe a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The old vacuum could very well have picked up more dirt than the Super XL, just by virtue of having gone first—but this tells us nothing about the quality of the two vacuums. The salesperson’s real flaw is in assuming that the Super XL would have picked up all the original dirt and the leftover dirt that the old vacuum left behind.

choices.text: ignores the possibility that if the Super XL had been used first it would have left behind just as much dirt as did the old vacuum cleaner
choices.rationale: This describes a flaw in the salesperson’s argument. The salesperson didn’t run a second test—one in which the Super XL was used first and the old vacuum second. The salesperson is assuming that the Super XL would have picked up the amount of dirt that the old vacuum did, plus the extra dirt that the old vacuum left behind. But this isn’t necessarily so.

questions.stimulus: Vacuum cleaner salesperson: To prove that this Super XL vacuum cleaner is better than your old vacuum cleaner, I ran your old vacuum once over this dirty carpet. Then I ran the Super XL over the same area. All that dirt that the Super XL picked up is dirt your old vacuum left behind, proving the Super XL is the better vacuum.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the manager's argument?

choices.text: Some people argue that the supply-chain problem is so far in the future that there is no need to address it now.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s conclusion. This is an assumption of the manager’s argument. The manager refutes the position of those people who argue that the problem is too far in the future to address.

choices.text: It would be irresponsible to postpone changes to the vendor contracts just because the supply chain will not develop weaknesses for a long time.
choices.rationale: This is the manager’s overall conclusion. Some students identify the passage’s first sentence as the conclusion, but note that the support explains why it’s a bad idea to not act on the basis of an event being far off in the future. The support isn’t backing up the claim of the first sentence: why the supply chain will develop significant weaknesses unless the company makes changes. That is something the manager is taking for granted, and they spend no time trying to prove the validity of that claim.

choices.text: If no changes are made to the vendor contracts, the supply chain will eventually develop significant weaknesses.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s overall conclusion, though it does sound like it could be at first.
