However, the manager’s support explains why it’s a bad idea to not act on the basis of an event being far off in the future. It isn’t explaining why the supply chain will develop significant weaknesses unless the company makes changes. That is something the manager is taking for granted, and spends no time trying to prove the validity of that claim.

choices.text: In planning to meet its future obligations, a company should follow the same practices that are appropriate for an individual who is planning for retirement.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s conclusion, because it’s never stated. Just because the manager uses an analogy to prove a point doesn’t mean that the manager thinks the company should follow the same practices as those in the analogy. The point is that it’s inappropriate for the financial planner to not act, just like it would be inappropriate for the company to not act.

choices.text: Financial planners should advise their clients to save money for retirement only if retirement is many years away.
choices.rationale: This isn’t the manager’s conclusion, because it’s never stated. Furthermore, the conclusion is about the company, not about the financial planning situation—the analogy involving the financial planner forms the support for why it’s a bad idea to put off action just because an event is far in the future.

questions.stimulus: Manager: This company's supply chain will develop significant weaknesses unless we make changes to our vendor contracts now. Some will argue that this problem is so far in the future that there is no need to address it today. But that is an irresponsible approach. Just imagine if a financial planner offered the same counsel to a 30-year-old client: "Don't worry, Jane, retirement is 35 years away; you don't need to save anything now." That planner would be guilty of gross malpractice.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: Last year there were more cookbooks sold that were not intended for beginners than in any previous year.
choices.rationale: Looking at this answer, it seems to be making an inference from statements #2 and 3. We do know that there were more cookbooks sold last year than ever before, and that, for the "first time ever" most of them weren't for beginners. Since previous years had fewer than half of the cookbooks sold targeted not at beginners, and fewer books were sold, last year having more books sold and most of them targeted at not beginners means that there were more of these books sold than any other year. This answer is supported by the information in the stimulus.

choices.text: The best-selling cookbook last year was a cookbook that was intended for beginners.
choices.rationale: There's no indication of what the best-selling book was, so this answer isn't supported.

choices.text: Sales of cookbooks intended for beginners were lower last year than in previous years.
choices.rationale: While sales of books targeted at beginners fell below the 50% mark of cookbooks sold last year for the first time ever, that could have come from a surge in sales of other books, not a decline in sales of beginners books. Selecting this answer would mean that you fell for a percent to amount flaw.

choices.text: Most of the cookbooks purchased last year that were not intended for beginners were purchased by professional cooks.
choices.rationale: While more cookbooks than ever were purchased by professional cooks, the majority of those non-beginner books could have been purchased by home cooks who have some skills. More than ever doesn't mean most.

choices.text: Problem-Free Cooking sold more copies last year than did any cookbook written for professional cooks.
choices.rationale: While PFC was available on every continent, there's no indication in the stimulus of how well it sold compared to other books, so this answer is out of scope.

questions.stimulus: Worldwide, more books were sold last year than in any previous year. In particular, there were more cookbooks sold. For the first time ever, most of the cookbooks sold were not intended for beginners. Indeed, more cookbooks than ever were purchased by professional cooks. However, one of the few books available on every continent is a cookbook written for beginners, entitled Problem-Free Cooking.

questions.stem: The argument relies on the assumption that

choices.text: Mars had no methane in its atmosphere prior to 2003
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. If (A) were true, then it would guarantee the truth of the conclusion (as long as “recently” means since 2003), but we aren’t looking for a sufficient assumption; we’re looking for something that has to be true in order for the argument to work. The year could just as easily be 1999, and the argument would still work, so (A) doesn’t have to be true.

choices.text: all methane in the Martian atmosphere is eventually exposed to sunlight
choices.rationale: This is an assumption that’s necessary in order for the argument to work. To test it, suppose that (B) were false. What if there were some methane in the Martian atmosphere that’s never eventually exposed to sunlight? In that case, the argument would fall apart! It would be possible for there to be methane found in the Martian atmosphere that wasn’t released there relatively recently, since that methane could have just escaped the threat of sunlight for centuries (for example).

choices.text: methane cannot be detected until it has started to fall apart
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. There’s no indication in the passage of any relationship between detection and degradation of methane.

choices.text: the methane that the scientists detected had been exposed to ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. Whether the methane that the scientists detected had or hadn’t been exposed to ultraviolet radiation isn’t relevant to determining how recently the methane had been released.

choices.text: methane in Earth's atmosphere does not fall apart as a result of exposure to ultraviolet radiation
choices.rationale: This isn’t an assumption that’s necessary for the argument to work. What happens in Earth’s atmosphere isn’t necessary (or even relevant) to an argument about what happens in Mars’s atmosphere.

questions.stimulus: In early 2003, scientists detected methane in the atmosphere of Mars. Methane is a fragile compound that falls apart when hit by the ultraviolet radiation in sunlight. So any methane in the Martian atmosphere must have been released into the atmosphere relatively recently.

questions.stem: The environmentalist's statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.text: The cost of pollution from driving should not be reflected in the price of gasoline unless the amount of pollution produced would be reduced as a result.
choices.rationale: The Environmentalist doesn't state that lowering pollution is a necessary condition for having the price of gas reflect its (environmental) costs.

choices.text: Heavier taxes on gasoline would increase consumers' awareness of the kinds of environmental problems to which pollution from driving contributes.
choices.rationale: The Environmentalist does believe that higher taxes would result in less pollution, but that doesn't come from awareness of environmental problems—it comes from people using less gas since it costs more.

choices.text: Consumers would purchase less gasoline, on average, if the cost of the environmental problems to which pollution from driving contributes were fully reflected in the price of gasoline.
choices.rationale: This answer highlights the connection that the Environmentalist draws between higher taxes and less pollution. The cost of gas doesn't reflect environmental costs of pollution, and so it doesn't affect consumer decisions. Higher taxes would "result" in less pollution, thus justifying this answer.

choices.text: The only cost considered by most consumers when they are deciding how much to drive is the cost of gasoline.
choices.rationale: The Environmentalist states that the cost of gasoline is considered by consumers when considering how much to drive, but it's not laid out as the only consideration.

choices.text: Pollution from gasoline burned by cars will be reduced only if consumers give more consideration to the cost of that pollution when deciding how much to drive.
choices.rationale: While the Environmentalist believes that consumers giving more consideration to the cost of pollution will reduce that pollution, she never states that it's the only thing that can reduce pollution.

questions.stimulus: Environmentalist: Pollution from gasoline burned by cars contributes to serious environmental problems. But the cost of these problems is not reflected in gasoline prices, and hence usually does not affect consumers' decisions about how much to drive. Heavier taxes on gasoline, however, would reflect this cost, and as a result consumers would pollute less.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the surprising fact?

choices.text: Red devil crayfish dig chambers that remain filled with water even when the surrounding wetlands dry up.
choices.rationale: This helps explain why dragonfly populations are likelier to remain healthy in areas with the crayfish than without. If (A) is true, it introduces a benefit (water, which dragonfly larvae need to survive) of the presence of red devil crayfish that may well offset the danger that that same presence introduces.

choices.text: Red devil crayfish present no threat to adult Hine's emerald dragonflies.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the situation, which is surprising because dragonfly larvae are in danger from red devil crayfish. If too many larvae were killed, we would expect the dragonfly population to be unhealthy—regardless of whether or not adult dragonflies are threatened.

choices.text: The varied diet of the red devil crayfish does not include any animal species that prey on dragonfly larvae.
choices.rationale: This actually makes the situation even more surprising. If the red devil crayfish did eat other predators of the dragonfly larvae, and those other predators were more dangerous to the larvae, then that could help explain why dragonfly populations are safer in the presence of one predator than without. But since (C) tells us that this isn’t the case, then the situation becomes even more puzzling—why do dragonfly populations do better in the presence of red devil crayfish?

choices.text: Red devil crayfish are found in many more locations than Hine's emerald dragonflies are.
choices.rationale: This comparison doesn’t explain the situation, because it’s not helpful to have information about how many places red devil crayfish are found in versus how many places the dragonflies are found in. The question is why dragonfly populations are healthier when they do overlap with red devil crayfish populations than when they don’t.

choices.text: Populations of red devil crayfish in a wetland do not drop significantly if the local population of Hine's emerald dragonflies dies out.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help explain the situation, which is surprising because dragonfly larvae are in danger from red devil crayfish. What happens to populations of red devil crayfish if the dragonflies disappear doesn’t shed any light on the situation.

questions.stimulus: Hine's emerald dragonflies are an endangered species that live in wetlands. The larvae of these dragonflies can survive only in the water, where they are subject to predation by several species including red devil crayfish. Surprisingly, the dragonfly populations are more likely to remain healthy in areas where red devil crayfish are present than in areas without red devil crayfish.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: For at least some people, having lower blood pressure has at least some tendency to cause their stress levels to be reduced.
choices.rationale: This answer reverses the established causal relationship, so it's incorrect.

choices.text: Most people with high blood pressure can lower their blood pressure by reducing their stress levels.
choices.rationale: This answer reflects the second sentence, which was said to apply to "some people," not most.

choices.text: Most people who do not exercise regularly have higher stress levels as a result.
choices.rationale: While exercise is noted as being one way to calm one's mind and thus lower stress levels, it doesn't establish it as the primary, only, or best way to do so, so people who don't exercise might still have low stress levels because they, say, meditate.

choices.text: Engaging in exercise can directly lower one's blood pressure.
choices.rationale: The stimulus establishes that exercise can help calm one's mind, and calming one's mind can lower stress, which can lower blood pressure. That's an indirect relationship, not a direct one.

choices.text: For at least some people, engaging in exercise can cause their stress levels to be reduced.
choices.rationale: While this answer doesn't use all the premises, it does reflect the causal chain that we developed. Exercise can calm the mind, which is stated as lowering stress, supporting this answer.

questions.stimulus: Stress is a common cause of high blood pressure. By calming their minds and thereby reducing stress, some people can lower their blood pressure. And most people can calm their minds, in turn, by engaging in exercise.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: In cities where there are high concentrations of many air pollutants but little if any soot in the air, the frequency of the ailment is just as high, on average, as it is in cities where there are large amounts of soot in the air.
choices.rationale: This actually strengthens the argument, which concludes that soot by itself doesn’t cause the ailment. (A) provides information that suggests that the other air pollutants that often accompany soot actually cause the ailment also, and in the absence of soot. So, if (A) is true, it actually suggests that the air pollutants cause the ailment—that helps the passage’s argument that it’s not soot itself that causes the ailment.

choices.text: If the ailment rarely occurs except in cities in which there are large amounts of soot in the air, then the soot is probably the cause of the ailment.
choices.rationale: This condition doesn’t weaken the argument. It doesn’t actually add anything to the argument, since it doesn’t address the presence (or absence) of the other air pollutants in question. Additionally, the rarity of the ailment isn’t necessarily a factor in this argument, so (B)’s condition might never be triggered.

choices.text: In each of the cities where there are large amounts of soot in the air but little other air pollution, the frequency of the ailment is at least as high as it is anywhere else.
choices.rationale: This weakens the argument, which concludes that soot by itself doesn’t cause the ailment in question, because high amounts of soot are often accompanied by high amounts of other pollutants. If (C) is true, it provides information about places where soot is found without those other air pollutants, and the frequency of the ailment is essentially unaffected by that absence. That makes it more likely that soot alone can cause the ailment, which makes the passage’s conclusion less likely to follow from its support.

choices.text: If high concentrations of many different pollutants in a city's air are correlated with a high frequency of the ailment among that city's population, then it is possible that two or more of those pollutants each causally contributes to the ailment.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t weaken the argument. Like (B), this choice provides a condition that isn’t necessarily relevant to this argument—it might never be triggered, which would leave the argument unaffected.

choices.text: In cities in which there are high concentrations of many air pollutants, there are generally also high concentrations of other forms of pollution that are very likely to contribute causally to the ailment.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t weaken the argument. (E) states a correlation between air pollutants and other forms of pollution that cause the ailment, but that doesn’t shed any light on whether soot by itself can cause the ailment.

questions.stimulus: A positive correlation has been found between the amount of soot in the atmosphere of cities and the frequency of a certain ailment among those cities' populations. However, the soot itself probably does not cause this ailment, since in cities where there are large amounts of soot in the air, there are usually also high concentrations of many other air pollutants.

questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following arguments?

choices.text: Aisha has finished proofreading all but the last two pages of an issue of the journal Periodos and has encountered no errors. However, there are sometimes a few errors in an issue of the journal Periodos. So there may be errors in the pages that Aisha has not yet checked.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. In fact, (A)’s argument is reasonable: it concludes that there may be errors based on the fact that there are sometimes a few errors. That doesn’t match the passage, which erroneously concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

choices.text: There are generally few errors in an issue of the journal Periodos. Aisha has finished proofreading all but the last two pages of an issue of this journal but has encountered no errors. Hence, there are probably no errors in the pages that Aisha has not yet checked in this issue of the journal.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. A problem with (B)’s argument is that it concludes that there are probably no errors in the remaining pages, due to the fact that there are generally few (not many) errors. [Note that “few” isn’t the same as “a few.”] That doesn’t match the passage, which concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

choices.text: On average, there are a few errors in an issue of the journal Periodos. Aisha has finished proofreading all but the last two pages of an issue of this journal but has encountered no errors. So there are probably errors in the pages she has not yet checked in this issue of the journal.
choices.rationale: This argument has a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. The passage erroneously concludes that something will probably happen just because it usually happens. (C) commits a similar flaw: it concludes that there are probably errors in the remaining pages just because there are on average (or, usually) a few errors in the journal as a whole.

choices.text: Aisha has proofread several issues of the journal Periodos and has encountered no errors. But there are seldom any errors in an issue of this journal. So there will probably be no errors in the next issue of the journal Periodos that she proofreads.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. (D) concludes that there will probably be no errors based on the fact that there are seldom any errors. That doesn’t match the passage, which erroneously concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

choices.text: There usually are errors in each issue of the journal Periodos. Since Aisha has finished proofreading the latest issue of this journal and has detected no errors, Aisha has probably made a mistake in her proofreading.
choices.rationale: This argument doesn’t have a flaw that matches the passage’s flaw. (E) concludes that Aisha has probably made a mistake because she hasn’t detected any errors. That doesn’t match the passage, which concludes that something will probably happen because it usually happens (and hasn’t happened yet).

questions.stimulus: So far this summer there has been no rain in the valley. But usually a few inches of rain fall there each summer. Since only one week of summer is left, it will probably rain in the valley within the next week.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.text: Motivating people to work to solve humanity's problems will enable them to believe that the future can be better and will cause them to be less pessimistic.
choices.rationale: This answer choice reverses the connection needed for the stimulus to work. The stimulus requires enabling people to view a better future as driving them to have motivation to change, not creating the motive in order to make people more optimistic.

choices.text: Enabling people to believe that better futures are possible will help prevent the loss of motivation that results from pessimistic beliefs about the future.
choices.rationale: This answer choice connects the proposed solution to the problem—making people more optimistic prevents a loss of motivation to make the world a better place. If enabling people to view a better future doesn't prevent that loss of motivation, then the proposed solution from the stimulus won't work to solve the problem.

choices.text: Optimism about the future is better than pessimism, even if that optimism is based on an illusory vision of what is likely to occur.
choices.rationale: The argument doesn't require one view to be "better" than another—just to lead to a certain outcome (motivation to make the world a better place).

choices.text: If future generations believe that the future can be better, then pollution, poverty, and war will be eliminated.
choices.rationale: The argument is about motivation and viewpoint, not actually solving these problems, so this answer is out of scope. Even when discussing these specific problems, it's framed as what young people "believe"—not whether they're actually solvable.

choices.text: The current prevalence of such problems as pollution and poverty stems from previous generations' inability to believe that futures can be better.
choices.rationale: The cause of the problems that young people view as unsolvable are out of scope of an argument about motivation to solve those problems.

questions.stimulus: Young people believe efforts to reduce pollution, poverty, and war are doomed to failure. This pessimism is probably harmful to humanity's future, because people lose motivation to work for goals they think are unrealizable. We must do what we can to prevent this loss of motivation and therefore must enable our children to believe that better futures are possible.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: Any neurotransmitter that leaks from a damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cell will damage surrounding nerve cells.
choices.rationale: This actually weakens the argument. If any neurotransmitter that leaks from a damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cell will damage the nerve cells, then it might not be glutamate that’s causing the brain damage—and it could just be a coincidence that glutamate is present in the blood.

choices.text: Stroke patients exhibit a wide variety of abnormal chemical levels in their blood.
choices.rationale: This could actually weaken the argument. If (B) is true, then other chemical abnormalities—not glutamate—might actually be the cause of the brain damage.

choices.text: Glutamate is the only neurotransmitter that leaks from oxygen-starved or physically damaged nerve cells.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t strengthen the argument, though it’s sometimes tempting to students. Even if (C) is true, there could still be other proteins that cause the brain damage—proteins that come from somewhere other than oxygen-starved or physically damaged nerve cells. In other words, glutamate’s presence could still be completely coincidental to the brain damage.

choices.text: Leakage from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is the only possible source of glutamate in the blood.
choices.rationale: This strengthens the argument, which concludes causation from a correlation. If (D) is true, and leakage from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is the only way that glutamate could be found in the blood, then other potential reasons for glutamate’s presence are eliminated. That makes it more likely that glutamate is the cause of the brain damage. It doesn’t prove the argument’s truth, but it doesn’t have to—we’re asked to strengthen the argument, not prove it.

choices.text: Nerve cells can suffer enough damage to leak glutamate without being destroyed themselves.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t affect the argument, because the process of nerve cell damage isn’t relevant to whether the glutamate leaked from nerve cells is damaging to brain cells.

questions.stimulus: In a recent study of stroke patients, those who exhibited continuing deterioration of the nerve cells in the brain after the stroke also exhibited the highest levels of the protein glutamate in their blood. Glutamate, which functions within nerve cells as a neurotransmitter, can kill surrounding nerve cells if it leaks from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells. Thus glutamate leaking from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is a cause of long-term brain damage resulting from strokes.

questions.stem: The reasoning in which one of the following arguments is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.text: The only pets the Gupta family has ever owned are fish and parrots. Most parrots are very noisy. So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is a parrot, it will probably be very noisy.
choices.rationale: This argument isn’t similar to the passage’s argument. In order for (A) to be a match, it would have to conclude: “So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is not a fish, it will probably be very noisy.” But (A) doesn’t eliminate one option the way the passage does (“if the next song...is not a blues song”).

choices.text: Most parrots are very noisy. The Gupta family has never owned any pets other than fish and parrots. So if the Gupta family has ever owned a noisy pet, it was probably a parrot.
choices.rationale: This argument isn’t similar to the passage’s argument. In order for (B) to match the passage, it would need to conclude: “So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is not a fish, it will probably be very noisy.” But (B)’s conclusion is about past pets (“has ever owned”).

choices.text: All the pets the Gupta family has ever owned have been fish and parrots. Most parrots are very noisy. So any pet the Gupta family ever owns that is not a fish will probably be very noisy.
choices.rationale: This argument isn’t similar to the passage’s argument. In order for (C) to match the passage, it would need to conclude: “So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is not a fish, it will probably be very noisy.” That’s subtly different than a conclusion about any pet the Gupta family ever owns.

choices.text: Every pet the Gupta family has ever owned has been a fish or a parrot. Most parrots are very noisy. So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is not a parrot, it will probably not be very noisy.
choices.rationale: This argument isn’t similar to the passage’s argument. In order for (D) to match the passage, it would need to conclude: “So if the next pet the Gupta family owns is not a fish, it will probably be very noisy.” We don’t know that most fish are not very noisy, so (D)’s conclusion doesn’t follow from its support.ere, the argument is that:

choices.text: The Gupta family has never owned any pets other than fish and parrots. Most parrots are very noisy. So the next pet the Gupta family owns will probably be very noisy if it is not a fish.
choices.rationale: This reasoning matches the passage’s reasoning. Remember that two arguments do not have to have similar topics in order to have similar reasoning.

questions.stimulus: The only songs Amanda has ever written are blues songs and punk rock songs. Most punk rock songs involve no more than three chords. So if the next song Amanda writes is not a blues song, it probably will not involve more than three chords.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

choices.text: There has recently been increased demand at LargeCo stores for the chain's own brand of yogurt as well as for other brands of yogurt.
choices.rationale: This actually makes the discrepancy worse. If (A) is true, we would expect yogurt sales to have increased more than milk sales, and by a larger margin than what we would have expected from the passage’s information. Yogurt sales should be helped by the advertisement and the recent increased demand—instead, milk sales increased more than yogurt sales did.

choices.text: The typical shopper going to LargeCo for the purpose of buying milk does not go with the intention of also buying yogurt.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help resolve the discrepancy. The habits of the typical shopper don’t tell us why store-brand milk sales recently increased more than store-brand yogurt sales.

choices.text: Shoppers at LargeCo tend to purchase the chain's own brand of dairy products more frequently than other brands of dairy products.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help resolve the discrepancy. (C) only compares LargeCo’s dairy products in general to other brands of dairy products, so there’s no distinction between yogurt and milk that can help us shed light on the situation described in the passage.

choices.text: Supermarkets throughout the entire nation have experienced a sharp decrease in sales of yogurt recently.
choices.rationale: This helps resolve the discrepancy. If (D) is true, then yogurt sales are facing a significant challenge. Therefore, it could be true that the LargeCo advertising did affect the yogurt sales more than it did the milk sales, and that the yogurt sales might not have even increased at all without the help of the advertising.

choices.text: Consumers tend to purchase store brands of yogurt, but purchase whichever brand of milk is least expensive.
choices.rationale: This doesn’t help resolve the discrepancy. We don’t have information in the passage about the relative costs of milk brands. We can’t assume that the store-brand milk is the least expensive, the most expensive, or anything in between. And even if it were the least expensive, that would put it exactly on par with the store brands of yogurt—people would buy store-brand yogurt, and they would buy store-brand milk. It still wouldn’t explain why sales of its store-brand milk increased more than sales of its store-brand yogurt.

questions.stimulus: Advertising tends to have a greater influence on consumer preferences regarding brands of yogurt than it does on consumer preferences regarding brands of milk. Yet, since the LargeCo supermarket chain began advertising its store-brand products, sales of its store-brand milk increased more than sales of its store-brand yogurt.

questions.stem: The principle, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning in which one of the following arguments concerning the problem?

choices.text: If Shayna congratulates Daniel, she will avoid hurting his feelings, so she should congratulate him.
choices.rationale: The principle isn't about whether or not someone's feelings would be hurt, so this answer is out of scope.

choices.text: Daniel might prefer for Shayna to congratulate him—even if insincerely—rather than for her to express her true feelings, and so Shayna would be doing nothing wrong in insincerely congratulating Daniel.
choices.rationale: The principle is about what Shayna "believes" Daniel would prefer, so this answer about his actual preference is out of scope.

choices.text: Shayna believes that kindness should be preferred to dishonesty when speaking to others, so she should not tell Daniel her true feelings.
choices.rationale: The principle is about a speaker's belief about what the person being spoken to would prefer, so Shayna's preferences on kindness vs. honesty are out of scope.

choices.text: Daniel's feelings would be hurt if he knew that congratulations from Shayna were insincere, so Shayna should not congratulate him.
choices.rationale: First, this answer is about feelings being hurt, not preferences, so it's out of scope. Additionally, it doesn't establish what Shayne does or doesn't believe about Daniel's preferences, so it's out of scope again!

choices.text: Shayna has no opinion about whether Daniel would prefer kindness to honesty, so she should not congratulate him.
choices.rationale: However, the sufficient condition of the principle is that a speaker doesn't believe the listener would prefer kindness to honesty—that's subtly different from believing the listener wouldn't prefer kindness to honesty. Since this answer states that Shayna has no opinion on Daniel's preferences, she doesn't think that he'd prefer kindness to honesty, and so the principle applies—establishing that Shayna should be sincere. According to the problem, that means she shouldn't congratulate him.

questions.stimulus:
Problem: If Shayna congratulates Daniel on his award, she will misrepresent her true feelings. However, if Shayna does not congratulate Daniel, she will hurt his feelings.

Principle: One should never be insincere about one's feelings, except possibly where one believes that the person with whom one is speaking would prefer kindness to honesty.

questions.stem: The argument's conclusion is properly inferred if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.text: All societies that have effective news media are thriving democracies.
choices.rationale: The premises already connect to establishing something about a thriving democracy, so this answer choice doesn't fill in the missing gap. This answer is a reversal of the conclusion.

choices.text: If an electorate has access to unbiased information about the government, then that electorate will be knowledgeable about important political issues.
choices.rationale: This answer is a reversal of one of the conditional premises.

choices.text: A democracy will thrive if its electorate is knowledgeable about important political issues.
choices.rationale: This answer is a reversal of the first part of the second sentence.

choices.text: A democracy cannot thrive if the electorate is exposed to biased information about the government.
choices.rationale: The stimulus never mentions exposure to biased information—just access to unbiased information. The negation of that also doesn't guarantee exposure to biased information—not having access to unbiased information could follow from having no information about the government! Since this answer raises a concept that isn't mentioned in the stimulus, it's out of scope.

choices.text: Without effective news media, an electorate will not have access to unbiased information about the government.
choices.rationale: This answer connects the necessary elements to allow the conclusion to follow from the premises. The conclusion featured a new term—Effective news media—that was a shift from the related term in the premises—Access to unbiased information. In bridging this gap, the answer justifies the conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Clearly, a democracy cannot thrive without effective news media. After all, a democracy cannot thrive without an electorate that is knowledgeable about important political issues, and an electorate can be knowledgeable in this way only if it has access to unbiased information about the government.

questions.stem: The reasoning above is flawed in that it

choices.text: infers from a correlation between tiredness and yawning that tiredness causes yawning
choices.rationale: While the argument does mention yawning, it ends up being a throwaway since Roberta losing her keys is sufficient to establish that she's tired.

choices.text: assumes the conclusion that it sets out to prove
choices.rationale: The argument uses Roberta losing her keys to reach its conclusion, not a premise about her being irritable to reach the same conclusion. This answer is the circular reasoning answer, which isn't present here.

choices.text: generalizes on the basis of a single instance
choices.rationale: The conclusion is about whether Roberta is currently irritable, which isn't a generalization. (The premises, however, are generalizations, as almost all conditionals are.)

choices.text: takes a necessary condition for Roberta's losing things to be a sufficient condition
choices.rationale: So close! However, the argument doesn't reverse the logic of the second conditional. The argument uses that conditional properly, basing a premise about Roberta losing things to lead to an inference that she's tired. The issue is when it applies the first conditional to that inference.

choices.text: takes a necessary condition for Roberta's being irritable to be a sufficient condition
choices.rationale: This answer highlights the flaw in the argument. Roberta being tired is necessary for her being irritable. However, the argument establishes that Roberta is tired and from that concludes that she's irritable. That's treating being tired as a sufficient condition for irritability.

questions.stimulus: Roberta is irritable only when she is tired, and loses things only when she is tired. Since she has been yawning all day, and has just lost her keys, she is almost certainly irritable.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption the farmer's argument requires?

choices.text: Use of the crops that have been genetically engineered to resist insect pests in place of crops that have been sprayed with insecticides will cause less harm to wildlife populations.
choices.rationale: This answer compares the harm to wildlife by GMO crops to that of insecticides, stating that they do less harm—a necessary assumption for the argument to work. If the GMO crops do as much or more damage as insecticides, then switching to them won't help wildlife populations to recover and the argument falls apart.

choices.text: Wildlife populations that have been harmed by the excessive spraying of insecticides on croplands are likely to recover if the amount of insecticides sprayed on those croplands is reduced even slightly.
choices.rationale: The conclusion is about using GMO crops, not avoiding using pesticides. While the two go together, it's also possible to use less insecticide without switching to GMO crops, so this answer isn't necessary for the argument to work.

choices.text: Crops that have been genetically engineered to resist insect pests are never sprayed with insecticides that harm wildlife populations.
choices.rationale: This answer is too extreme in stating that GMO crops are "never" sprayed with insecticides. While the argument relies on some GMO crops not being sprayed by insecticides, if they are sometimes sprayed, the argument could still work.

choices.text: Use of crops that have been genetically engineered to resist insect pests is no more costly to farmers than the use of insecticides on crops that are not genetically engineered.
choices.rationale: The argument is about whether this shift would work if it happens, not if it's feasible to make happen. As such, the economics of it are out of scope.

choices.text: If a wider use of certain crops that have been genetically engineered to resist insect pests is likely to help at least some wildlife populations to recover, it is likely to have that effect only because its use will prevent excessive and ineffective spraying of insecticides on croplands.
choices.rationale: First, this answer reverses the logic in the argument by starting with the use of GMO crops helping wildlife to recover. Second, it's too extreme in stating that the "only" reason GMO crops would help wildlife recover is because of the decreased use of insecticides—if there are other benefits, as well, the argument still holds.

questions.stimulus: Farmer: Crops genetically engineered to produce toxins that enable them to resist insect pests do not need to be sprayed with insecticides. Since excessive spraying of insecticides has harmed wildlife populations near croplands, using such genetically engineered crops more widely is likely to help wildlife populations to recover.

passages.text:
The late 1950s and early 1960s were a time of profound growth for the civil rights movement in the United States. Although racial segregation in the public schools had been outlawed in 1954, the ruling applied only to this one category of discriminatory practice in U.S. society. But it furthered within the African-American community the anticipation of broader changes. It was in this climate that the student sit-in demonstrations of the early 1960s were born. The technique of the sit-in was simple—African Americans occupying "whites only" seats in racially segregated establishments—but this new type of student activism galvanized established civil rights organizations, brought about the creation of new ones, and generated support for the civil rights movement among many new segments of the populace.

Initiated by four students of the North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College, the first sit-in occurred at a lunch counter in February 1960. Sit-ins then spread rapidly through the southern U.S., involving over 70,000 participants by August 1961. The sit-ins provided an important model for nonviolent protest and showed students that they could affect the political process. The influence of these demonstrations on the determination of the student activists was particularly visible in two events: the formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and the birth of a second form of sit-ins called Freedom Rides.

The formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee followed the first sit-in by just a few months and not only solidified student involvement in the civil rights movement but also placed students in leadership roles for the first time. It operated independently of other civil rights organizations and relied on strong local leadership, helping to transform student involvement from participation in small-scale protests into a sustained effort to challenge discrimination throughout the U.S. But the development that marked the clearest turning point for the civil rights movement was the Freedom Rides. The goal of the rides, which were organized in 1961 by the already well-established Congress of Racial Equality, was to challenge segregation through the occupation of "whites only" seats on interstate buses and in facilities at the various terminals at which the buses stopped. Because the rides inspired violent reprisals in some regions, the U.S. government began using force to protect the safety of the Freedom Riders; this was the first government action taken explicitly in support of the cause of desegregation outside the public schools. The Freedom Rides thus helped take the civil rights movement to a new level by underscoring to the U.S. government, and to U.S. society generally, the harsh realities of the segregation system, and by providing, for students and their elders alike, examples of the methods they might use to achieve a more equal society.

Grammarians of the prescriptive school take it as part of their task to distinguish correct from incorrect usage in language and thereby to encourage the former. They believe that in so doing they play an essential role in preventing a constantly changing language from falling into disarray. In contrast, descriptive grammarians are so called because they are content to describe the way language is actually used by members of a community. In their eyes, those who seek to preserve some forms of usage while preventing others from gaining a foothold are being unscientific and are, moreover, doomed to almost certain failure. Descriptivists point to numerous examples of usage that were once judged by prescriptivists to be incorrect but that over time and through continual use have come to be almost universally accepted. One example is the use of "data" as a singular noun in English: prescriptivists have typically regarded the phrase "the data is incomplete" as ungrammatical, on the grounds that "data" is the plural of the Latin noun "datum" and should continue to be treated as a plural in English out of respect for the word's origins. Descriptivists argue that "data," in addition to its use as a plural, has acquired a widespread use as a singular mass term, like "water." It would be pointless, they say, to try to reverse this trend.

This example illustrates the two main objections of descriptivists to prescriptivism. The first is the scientific objection: the transformation of language is governed by laws not unlike the laws of nature, and those trying to hold back linguistic change might as well attempt to defy the law of gravity. The second is the egalitarian objection: the prescriptivists are simply trying to impose their own linguistic practices, which are usually those of an educated and affluent elite, upon other members of society. The suggestion is that the attempted imposition is somehow immoral.

With regard to the scientific objection, it should be noted that while many attempts to regulate language have failed, some have succeeded. Descriptivists may respond that in the latter cases the usages favored by prescriptivists were in accordance with the laws governing linguistic change and would have prevailed without their assistance. But this is in large measure an article of faith. In the end it must be acknowledged that the laws governing the transformation of language are not like the laws of physics. Language usage depends on choices made by individuals, who are subject to persuasion. In response to the egalitarian objection, prescriptivists point to the importance of standard language usage for the free exchange of ideas. Those to whom preservation of the standard is entrusted inevitably possess some of the attributes of an elite, but their aim is one of inclusion rather than exclusion.

Passage A is from a newspaper article. Passage B is from UNESCO's 1999 Draft Convention on the Protection of Underwater Cultural Heritage.

Passage A

A North American company that found what is believed to be the HMS Sussex during expeditions in the Mediterranean from 1998 to 2001 has signed an agreement with the British government, which owns the Sussex, to raise what may be history's richest sunken treasure and to split the proceeds. The agreement is a legal breakthrough that could allow the recovery of perhaps US$4 billion in gold coins lost with the Sussex in a storm in 1694.

As robots, sonar, and other technologically advanced gear have opened the deepest oceans to exploration and recovery, governments have begun asserting ownership over their sunken vessels. But governments often lack the money and skills to retrieve cultural riches and, until now, there had been no legal precedent for a private company to join with a government to salvage the government's treasure. This agreement could end the days of freelance treasure hunting and allow nations to oversee the recovery of their lost fleets.

The company, which is funding the venture, agrees with British historians that the ship carried coins, most likely gold, worth £1 million in 1694. The US$4 billion figure is the coins' theoretical value if sold to collectors. The agreement calls for archaeological integrity—a difficult technical feat at such depths and a goal that critics of for-profit archaeology are likely to doubt. Many archaeologists abhor the sale of recovered artifacts, arguing that this inhibits scholarly analysis and public display. The agreement, however, draws a distinction between different classes of artifacts, recognizing that cultural items have greater archaeological value than coins, which it allows to be sold to help pay for the project.

Passage B

"Underwater cultural heritage" (UCH) means all traces of human existence that have been partially, totally, or periodically situated underwater for at least 100 years.

1. The protection of UCH is best achieved through in situ (original site)preservation, which should be considered as the first option. Accordingly, activities directed at UCH shall be authorized by the competent authority of the concerned State only when they make a significant contribution to knowledge, protection, and/or enhancement of UCH.

2. The commercial exploitation of UCH for trade, sale, barter, or speculation...is fundamentally incompatible with the protection and proper management of the UCH.

3. Activities directed at UCH shall not adversely impact UCH more than is necessary for the objectives of the project;

4. must use nondestructive techniques and prospection and limited sampling in preference to recovery of objects. If excavation is necessary for the purpose of scientific studies, the methods and techniques used must be as nondestructive as possible and contribute to the preservation of the remains;

5. shall avoid the unnecessary disturbance of human remains or venerated sites;

6. shall be strictly regulated to ensure proper recording of historical, cultural, and archaeological information.

7. Public access to conduct activities relating to UCH that are nonintrusive (such as photography) should, where practicable, be encouraged.

Some environmentalists claim that the higher the international debt a nation carries, the more likely it is that the quality of life in that nation will suffer. These environmentalists argue that in a variety of ways the effort a nation must expend to pay its debt hastens the depletion of its natural resources, increases pollution, or hampers domestic spending. The most common reason given by the environmentalists is known as the exports promotion hypothesis. According to this hypothesis, in order to increase foreign trade in a way that better allows it to repay international debt, a nation must divert resources away from sectors generating domestic goods and toward the production of export goods. Partly because of the greater volume involved, this causes more environmental damage than does production of goods for domestic consumption. One possible scenario frequently cited by environmentalists is that a nation might raze its forests for timber or to open up land on which to plant cash crops. Another reason the environmentalists give for their claims is that domestic spending can fall when a nation shifts money toward repayment of its debt. A nation may take funds away from health care, education, or improvements in such public services as water quality or sanitation. It can also adjust its economy in other potentially harmful ways in order to cut costs—for example, through the elimination of government subsidies for practices that reduce pollution or conserve natural resources.

But the evidence for the environmentalists' claims is weak. With respect to the exports promotion hypothesis, one recent study does suggest a positive correlation between international debt and deforestation, but also indicates that other factors besides debt may play a stronger role. Another study found only a slight positive correlation between debt and deforestation; in fact, in one nation the correlation was negative, contrary to the environmentalists' expectations. The impact of debt on environmental indicators such as pollution or depletion of other resources has not yet been studied. Similarly, with respect to the domestic spending argument, while debt-saddled nations might shift money away from programs designed to enhance quality of life, it is just as likely that they would shift the money from plans that, if implemented, would have a negative impact on the environment. For example, they might abandon plans to build new dams or roads, or eliminate subsidies that promote fertilizer or pesticide use. The extent, then, to which a nation's quality of life is connected to the size of its international debt must be considered unknown. Indeed, a case could be made that at least some of the fiscal discipline or economic restructuring imposed by debt may rein in potentially harmful spending.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to

choices.text: describe how the successful use in the early 1960s of a new tactic to combat discriminatory social practices led to the transformation of the U.S. civil rights movement
choices.rationale: This matches our anticipated primary purpose: “show why a movement of civil rights protests and organizations that started with sit-ins was historically significant.” We anticipated that this movement “started with sit-ins,” so it's accurate to say a “new tactic” eventually “led to the transformation of the U.S. civil rights movement.” This answer choice also correctly identifies that sit-in demonstrations and ensuing movements were intended to “combat discriminatory social practices.” The only part of this answer choice we may need to check is its claim that sit-ins were successfully used in the early 1960s, but the first paragraph corroborates that claim (P1, S4-S5). Once we verify this matter, we can select (A) and advance directly to the next question.

choices.text: chronicle the activities of the U.S. civil rights movement during the late 1950s and early 1960s that led to the first use by student activists of sit-in demonstrations
choices.rationale: This doesn't match our anticipated primary purpose: “show why a movement of civil rights protests and organizations that started with sit-ins was historically significant.” While our anticipated main point discusses the movements that “started with sit-ins,” this answer choice focuses on the civil rights movement before sit-in demonstrations. The passage only discusses the climate before set-in demonstrations in the first three sentences. The rest of the passage discusses the sit-ins and their aftermath.

choices.text: contrast various techniques and tactics used by U.S. civil rights organizations in the early 1960s to expose the injustice of racial segregation and achieve a more equal society
choices.rationale: This doesn't quite match our anticipated primary purpose: “show why a movement of civil rights protests and organizations that started with sit-ins was historically significant.” The author isn't concerned with “contrast[ing]” various civil rights tactics. The author discusses tactics that were inspired by the sit-in demonstration, but the author doesn't point out these tactics' differences.

choices.text: argue that confrontational sit-in tactics were necessary in order for the U.S. civil rights movement to make inroads against racial discrimination in the late 1950s and early 1960s
choices.rationale: This doesn't quite match our anticipated primary purpose: “show why a movement of civil rights protests and organizations that started with sit-ins was historically significant.” The author, whose tone toward sit-in demonstrations is entirely approving, would probably not use a loaded term like “confrontational” to describe sit-ins. Moreover, the author never argues that sit-ins were “necessary” for the civil-rights movement. The author argues that sit-ins inspired other civil rights protests and organizations, but the author doesn't claim that these protests and organizations could not have grown without sit-ins.

choices.text: provide information on the extent to which the activities of the U.S. civil rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s were rooted in the earlier successes of the movement
choices.rationale: So close! However, this answer choice messes up the dates. The passage discusses how the sit-in demonstrations of the early 1960s inspired new tactics and protests like the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and Freedom Rides. So, it's probably fair to say that the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and Freedom Rides were “rooted in the earlier successes of the movement,” but it would be ahistorical to say they were from the 1950s. Moreover, this answer choice goes a little too far when it says the passage's “primary purpose” is to show “the extent to which” activities like the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and Freedom Rides were rooted in earlier civil rights successes. The author really just asserts that both were influenced by sit-in demonstrations and doesn't elaborate (P3, S4).

questions.stem: According to the passage, the outlawing of segregation in the U.S. public schools in 1954 had which one of the following consequences?

choices.text: It led directly to the formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee.
choices.rationale: Does this refer to one of three consequences we found in the first paragraph (not making segregation illegal elsewhere, leading the African-American community to anticipate broader changes, inspiring sit-in demonstrations)? Nope. For this reason, we can cross off (A). In fact, the passage makes it seem like the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee was directly inspired by the sit-in demonstrations (P2, S4; P3, S1), not the outlawing of segregation in public schools.

choices.text: It served to encourage African Americans to expect similar changes in other parts of society.
choices.rationale: Does this refer to one of three consequences we found in the first paragraph (not making segregation illegal elsewhere, leading the African-American community to anticipate broader changes, inspiring sit-in demonstrations)? Yes! This refers to the second consequence we identified. The passage claims that the outlawing of segregation also led the African-American community to anticipate “broader changes” (P1, S3). “Broader changes” in that context means changes beyond just making segregation illegal in public schools. So, it's accurate to say that the outlawing of segregation in schools encouraged “African Americans to expect similar changes in other parts of society.” Because this answer choice conforms to our anticipation, we can select it.

choices.text: It provided a useful example of a method students might use to achieve a more equal society.
choices.rationale: Does this refer to one of three consequences we found in the first paragraph (not making segregation illegal elsewhere, leading the African-American community to anticipate broader changes, inspiring sit-in demonstrations)? Not quite. While this decision eventually inspired sit-in demonstrations, it would be a stretch to say that the decision “provided a useful example of a method students” could use to fight discrimination. The case didn't directly provide an example—it's not as if Chief Justice Warren and Thurgood Marshall showed students how to occupy segregated areas in Brown v. Board of Education. It's more accurate to say that the outlawing of segregated schools inspired African Americans to expect more changes and fight for those changes with techniques like the sit-in. So, we can eliminate this answer choice. If we check the passage, we'll see that the author says that the Freedom Rides, not the outlawing of segregated schools, provided a useful example of a method students might use “to achieve a more equal society.”

choices.text: It dramatically concluded a period of profound growth in the U.S. civil rights movement.
choices.rationale: Does this refer to one of three consequences we found in the first paragraph (not making segregation illegal elsewhere, leading the African-American community to anticipate broader changes, inspiring sit-in demonstrations)? Not at all. This passage's main point says that outlawing segregation in public schools led to sit-ins, which inspired a new movement of civil rights activism through the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and Freedom Rides. It didn't conclude the “period of profound growth” at all!

choices.text: It galvanized established U.S. civil rights organizations and led immediately to the creation of new ones.
choices.rationale: Does this refer to one of three consequences we found in the first paragraph (not making segregation illegal elsewhere, leading the African-American community to anticipate broader changes, inspiring sit-in demonstrations)? Not quite. The author implies that outlawing segregation in public schools eventually, indirectly led to sit-in demonstrations. It would be a stretch to say that outlawing segregation in public schools immediately “galvanized established U.S. civil rights organizations” or led to “the creation of new ones.” So, we can eliminate this answer choice. If we checked the passage, we'd see that the author says that the sit-ins, not the outlawing of segregated schools, “galvanized established civil rights organizations” and “brought about the creation of new ones” (P1, S5).

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which one of the following can be most reasonably inferred about the Freedom Rides?

choices.text: They were primarily a spontaneous phenomenon.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with the facts we reviewed in our note on the Freedom Rides or in the third paragraph? Nope. This isn't reflected in our notes on the Freedom Rides, so we can justifiably eliminate—or at least table—(A) and move on to the next answer choice. Besides, if we reviewed the third paragraph, we'd already know that these were not “spontaneous” affairs. They were “organized in 1961 by the already well-established Congress of Racial Equality” with deliberate objectives (P3, S4). So, (A) is a false statement.

choices.text: They were directed against the U.S. government.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with the facts we reviewed in our note on the Freedom Rides or in the third paragraph? No. This isn't reflected in our notes on the Freedom Rides, so we can justifiably eliminate—or at least table—(B) and move on to the next answer choice. Besides, if we reviewed the third paragraph, we'd already know that the Freedom Rides were not necessarily directed against the U.S. government. Ostensibly, they were directed at “interstate buses” and the “facilities at the various terminals” (P3, S4). We don't know if the U.S. government operated these in the early 1960s. Moreover, the author only mentions the U.S. government in the third paragraph to say that the U.S. government began using force to protect the safety of the Freedom Riders and later became more aware of the harsh realities of segregation (P3, S5-S6). So, while the Freedom Rides may have changed the U.S. government, they weren't necessarily directed against the government.

choices.text: They were less important to the U.S. civil rights movement than were the original sit-in demonstrations.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with the facts we reviewed in our note on the Freedom Rides or in the third paragraph? Negative. This isn't reflected in our notes on the Freedom Rides, so we can justifiably eliminate—or at least table—(C) and move on to the next answer choice. Besides, if we reviewed the third paragraph, we'd already know that the author calls the Freedom Rides “the clearest turning point for the civil rights movement” (P3, S3). The author thinks the Freedom Rides were very important, perhaps even more important than the original sit-in demonstrations.

choices.text: They were based on a different philosophy than the original sit-in demonstrations.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with the facts we reviewed in our note on the Freedom Rides or in the third paragraph? Again, no. This isn't reflected in our notes on the Freedom Rides. Moreover, our anticipated main point suggests that the sit-in demonstrations inspired the Freedom Rides. So, we can justifiably eliminate (D) and move on to the next answer choice. Besides, if we reviewed the third paragraph, we'd already know that the Freedom Rides seem very similar to the original sit-in demonstrations. After all, like the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides involved occupying “'whites only' seats” in segregated spaces to protest this discrimination (P3, S4). The similarity of these two approaches further suggests that (D) is false.

choices.text: They were modeled on the original sit-in demonstrations.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with the facts we reviewed in our note on the Freedom Rides or in the third paragraph? Yep. While this isn't reflected in our notes on the Freedom Rides, our anticipated main point suggests that the sit-in demonstrations inspired the Freedom Rides. This strongly suggests that the Freedom Rides were modeled on the original sit-in demonstrations. Moreover, if we reviewed the third paragraph, we'd already know that the Freedom Rides seem very similar to the original sit-in demonstrations. Like the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides involved occupying “'whites only' seats” in segregated spaces to protest this discrimination (P3, S4). Since these two tactics are so similar, we can combine that with the main point to validly infer that the Freedom Rides were modeled on the original sit-in demonstrations. Additionally, the second paragraph refers to the Freedom Rides as a “second form of sit-ins” (P2, S4). All of these facts suggest that (E) is supported.

questions.stem: The discussion of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee in the third paragraph is intended primarily to

choices.text: argue for the preeminence of a particular U.S. civil rights organization
choices.rationale: Does this say the author discusses the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show a civil rights movement that was inspired by the sit-in demonstrations? Nope. We can quickly cross off (A). Besides, the author doesn't argue that any particular type of civil rights organization is “preeminent” or superior to others.

choices.text: serve as a contrast to discussion of the efforts of student sit-in demonstrators
choices.rationale: Does this say the author discusses the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show a civil rights movement that was inspired by the sit-in demonstrations? No. The author doesn't think the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and the sit-in demonstrations are contrasting efforts. The author argues that the sit-in demonstrations inspired the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee by showing students that they can affect change in the civil rights movement.

choices.text: summarize the historical background against which the Freedom Rides flourished
choices.rationale: Does this say the author discusses the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show a civil rights movement that was inspired by the sit-in demonstrations? Negative. For that reason, we can immediately eliminate (C). Besides, the author doesn't introduce the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee as a background detail in the story of the Freedom Rides. The author says that the sit-in demonstrations influenced two important events: the formation of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee and the Freedom Rides. The author brings up the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show how it and the Freedom Rides were inspired by the sit-ins. The author doesn't mention the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show how it inspired the Freedom Rides.

choices.text: describe an important outgrowth of the student sit-in demonstrations
choices.rationale: Does this say the author discusses the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show a civil rights movement that was inspired by the sit-in demonstrations? Yes, it does! Based on our review of our notes and the third paragraph, we can validly conclude that the author brings up the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show an “important outgrowth” of the sit-in demonstrations. We can select (D) and advance straight to the next question.

choices.text: explain why local sit-in demonstrations require nationally coordinated efforts
choices.rationale: Does this say the author discusses the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee to show a civil rights movement that was inspired by the sit-in demonstrations? No. So we can cross off (E). Besides, the author never claims that sit-in demonstrations require nationally coordinated efforts.

questions.stem: Which one of the following statements most accurately expresses the author's view in the passage regarding the Freedom Rides?

choices.text: By exposing the harsh realities of the segregation system, the Freedom Rides induced the U.S. government to address segregation.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with our note for the third paragraph or what we can recall from the third question in this set? Yes! Our note for the third paragraph says that the Freedom Rides “led to government protection” and “showed segregation's harsh realities.” This answer choice says exactly that! Therefore, we can review the third paragraph to confirm that the author would agree with this. Upon reviewing the third paragraph, we'll see that the author says, “Because the rides inspired violent reprisals in some regions, the U.S. government began using force to protect the safety of the Freedom Riders; this was the first government action taken explicitly in support of the cause of desegregation outside the public schools” (P3, S5). The author also claims that the “Freedom Rides thus helped take the civil rights movement to a new level by underscoring to the U.S. government, and to U.S. society generally, the harsh realities of the segregation system” (P3, S6). So, these details confirm that the Freedom Rides exposed the harsh realities of the segregation system and induced the U.S. government to address segregation. We can select (A) and wrap up this passage.

choices.text: The Freedom Rides were the final contribution of student activists in their effort to defeat the segregation system.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with our note for the third paragraph or what we can recall from the third question in this set? Nope. Our note doesn't suggest that the Freedom Rides were the last contribution from students. Moreover, the phrase “the final” is a strong, hard-to-support phrase that we don't like to see in Author Agree answer choices. Therefore, we can cross this off without checking the passage. Besides, if we had to check the passage, we'd see that the author claims that the “Freedom Rides thus helped take the civil rights movement to a new level” and provided, “for students and their elders alike, examples of the methods they might use to achieve a more equal society” (P3, S6). So, far from being the end of student involvement with civil rights, the Freedom Rides marked the beginning of a new era of student involvement.

choices.text: The Freedom Rides introduced an entirely new technique into the U.S. civil rights movement that served as a model for later protest.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with our note for the third paragraph or what we can recall from the third question in this set? Nope. Our note doesn't suggest that the Freedom Rides were an “entirely new technique.” Moreover, the word “entirely” is a strong, hard-to-support word that we don't like to see in an Author's Agree answer choice. So, we can cross off (C) without reviewing the passage. Besides, if we had to check the passage, we'd see that the Freedom Rides were very similar to the original sit-in demonstrations. After all, like the sit-ins, the Freedom Rides involved occupying “'whites only'” seats in segregated spaces to protest this discrimination (P3, S4). The similarity of these two approaches further suggests that the author would disagree with (C). In fact, the author claims in the second paragraph that the freedom rides were “a second form of sit-ins” (P2, S4).

choices.text: Because the Freedom Rides provoked violent reprisals against demonstrators, they reversed earlier progress in the cause of desegregation.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with our note for the third paragraph or what we can recall from the third question in this set? No. Our note for the third paragraph says the Freedom Rides led to violent reactions, but that the violence “led to government protection” of the demonstrators. So, far from “revers[ing] earlier progress,” the Freedom Rides led to greater protection against discrimination. We can cross off (D) without reviewing the passage. Indeed, if we checked the passage, we'd also see that the author says that “Freedom Rides thus helped take the civil rights movement to a new level” (P3, S6), which shows that the author disagrees with (D).

choices.text: The Freedom Rides transformed a series of uncoordinated local student protests into a movement with national scope.
choices.rationale: Is this consistent with our note for the third paragraph or what we can recall from the third question in this set? Negative. Our note doesn't suggest that the Freedom Rides started out as uncoordinated. Therefore, we can eliminate—or at least table—(E) without checking the passage. Besides, if we had to check the passage, we wouldn't find any evidence that the Freedom Rides started off as a series of uncoordinated student protests. On the contrary, the author says the Freedom Rides were “organized in 1961 by the already well-established Congress of Racial Equality” and had deliberate objectives (P3, S4). This suggests that the author would disagree with (E).

questions.stem: The passage says that the aim of descriptivist grammarians is to

choices.text: criticize the habits of language users
choices.rationale: Does this match our anticipation that the aim of the descriptivists is to “describe language as it's used”? Nope. This sounds more like those fuddy-duddy prescriptivists, although “criticize” might be too harsh of a word for them. Regardless, we can cross off (A).

choices.text: observe how language is actually used
choices.rationale: Does this match our anticipation that the aim of the descriptivists is to “describe language as it's used”? This is pretty close! We don't love the word “observe”—the word “describe,” which is used in the passage and our notes, suggests the descriptivists take a more active role in their approach. Still, this is otherwise such a close match to our anticipation that we can mark it as a strong contender and quickly evaluate the remaining choices. If all the remaining choices are further from our anticipation, we'll select (B) confidently.

choices.text: facilitate communication among language users
choices.rationale: Does this match our anticipation that the aim of the descriptivists is to “describe language as it's used”? No. Neither the notes nor the part of the passage we reviewed suggests that the descriptivists want to help people communicate with each other. That's enough reason to eliminate (C). Besides, if you have a good memory of the last paragraph, you may recall that the author says one of the prescriptivists' aims is to promote “the free exchange of ideas” (P3, S6). So, like (A), this answer choice describes the prescriptivists.

choices.text: slow the pace of linguistic change
choices.rationale: Does this match our anticipation that the aim of the descriptivists is to “describe language as it's used”? Nope. Like (A) and (C), this describes the prescriptivists. They want to slow linguistic change before language falls into disrepair (P1, S2). We can eliminate (D).

choices.text: influence laws that govern language usage
choices.rationale: Does this match our anticipation that the aim of the descriptivists is to “describe language as it's used”? Not quite. Once again, this answer choice describes the prescriptivists. They're the ones who want to influence whatever laws govern language by imposing their standards (P1, S2). We can eliminate (E).

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: The author's defense of the prescriptivist approach in the fourth and fifth sentences of the final paragraph would be most strengthened if which one of the following were true?

choices.text: A study showed that communities left to formulate their own rules of grammar typically develop rules very similar to those of other communities.
choices.rationale: Does this strengthen the argument that language change does not follow certain observable, unchangeable laws because people are persuadable? No. In fact, this makes language seem more law-like. If two separate communities—presumably with people who are persuadable in all sorts of different ways—end up developing very similar grammar rules, it seems like language resembles a scientific law. If people were so unique and persuadable, as this author contends, we'd expect the grammatical rules created by different people to vary. Instead, these languages are all subject to the same rules, much like the groups would be subject to the same scientific laws. Therefore, (A) weakens the author's argument.

choices.text: A study found a strong correlation between emphasis on grammar instruction in primary schools and lifelong adherence to the rules of usage taught there.
choices.rationale: Does this strengthen the argument that language change does not follow certain observable, unchangeable laws because people are persuadable? Yes! This answer choice shows that people can be persuaded enough to overcome any observable, immutable laws. If people adhere to the grammar rules taught in their early schooling, that shows that people are highly influenceable. If there were strong laws that governed linguistic change, we'd expect these people's linguistic behavior to change according to those rules at some point. However, since these people's linguistic behavior doesn't change much after early grade school, it supports the author's argument that language is not very law-like. While most test-takers wouldn't feel comfortable selecting the first answer choice that appears to strengthen the argument, we can at least mark (B) as a strong contender and take a quick look at the remaining choices. After eliminating (C) through (E), we can select (B) with confidence.

choices.text: A cross-cultural study found that nations with extensive formal education systems and those with minimal education systems demonstrate a similar range of variation in language use.
choices.rationale: Does this strengthen the argument that language change does not follow certain observable, unchangeable laws because people are persuadable? Nope. Like (A), this makes language seem more law-like. If two nations with different education systems produce “a similar range of variation in language use,” that doesn't make it seem like education systems are very good at changing the way people speak. If even an “extensive formal education system” can't influence people to speak more “correctly,” that might suggest that language use is governed by something akin to scientific laws. (We're hedging with “might” because we don't know the extent to which these education systems address grammar or usage.) At the very least, we can confidently say that this doesn't strengthen the author's contention that language change doesn't follow law-like rules.

choices.text: A study showed that groups of students left to formulate their own rules of grammar usage were more likely to reach agreement if they had little prior instruction in correct usage.
