(Compare this to a different version of (B), which says, “It takes for granted that the only reason mammals need to move their forelimbs quickly is to attack prey.” While the author doesn't necessarily believe this, this would at least strengthen the argument if true.)

choices.text: It overlooks the possibility that Megatherium could have been a successful predator even if it did not have a short olecranon process.
choices.rationale: When we see “overlooks the possibility” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the author's argument if true?” This definitely wouldn't weaken the author's argument. Even if the Megatherium was a successful predator without a short olecranon process, it would still be a predator. That would support the author's conclusion that the Megatherium was probably a predator

choices.text: It takes for granted that, on average, the olecranon processes of extinct mammals were no shorter than those of living mammals are.
choices.rationale: When we see “takes for granted” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, it's easy to assume that the author believes that the olecron processes were not generally shorter for extinct mammals. After all, the author bases the conclusion on the fact that the Megatherium had a “short olecranon process.” If extinct mammals generally had shorter olecranon processes, the Megatherium could have had an average olecranon process for its era. However, the author doesn't make any statements about “extinct mammals” generally. So, it's a stretch to say the author definitely believes that the olecranon processes of extinct mammals were no shorter than living mammals'. Moreover, (D) wouldn't weaken the author's argument if true. Even if extinct mammals generally had shorter olecranon processes, it would still be true that “the shorter the olecranon process, the faster the forelimbs can typically be moved.” So, extinct mammals would generally be able to move their forelimbs very fast. This would help a mammal like the Megatherium attack prey, which would still support the conclusion that the Megatherium was probably a predator.

choices.text: It fails to address the possibility that a longer olecranon process may confer some other advantage, such as greater strength.
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to address” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the author's argument if true?” This definitely wouldn't weaken the author's argument. A longer olecranon process could provide some advantages, but those advantages would not necessarily outweigh the advantages of a shorter olecranon process for a predatory mammal. Therefore, the Megatherium's short olecranon process could still provide evidence that the Megatherium was probably a predator.

questions.stimulus: The olecranon process is a bony part of the mammalian elbow. The shorter the olecranon process, the faster the forelimbs can typically be moved. Predatory mammals must move their forelimbs very quickly when attacking prey, and thus generally have short olecranon processes. It has recently been found that the extinct mammal Megatherium had a short olecranon process. Hence, in all probability, Megatherium was a predator.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the essayist's reasoning?

choices.text: Any commitment that is morally neutral either has outlasted its original justification or deserves no praise, or both.
choices.rationale: The “if” part of this principle says a commitment is morally neutral. That part should go in the “then” part of the principle because that's the conclusion the essayist reaches. Moreover, the “has outlasted its original justification or deserves no praise” part should go on the “if” side since those are premises the essayist uses. For this reason, (A) is incorrect.

choices.text: Commitment to a relationship or career is virtuous when, but only when, the relationship or career is good.
choices.rationale: This principle won't justify the essayist's conclusion that all commitments are morally neutral. It would establish that the commitments made to bad careers and relationships are not morally virtuous. That doesn't imply that these commitments are morally neutral, however. They could be morally bad! Moreover, this principle would establish that commitments made to good careers and relationships are morally virtuous, not neutral.

choices.text: If a commitment deserves no praise, then that commitment is morally neutral.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is tempting, but it won't help justify that all commitments are morally neutral. The essayist states that some commitments deserve no praise. According to this principle, those commitments would be morally neutral. But what about the commitments that deserve praise? Are those morally neutral, too? This principle doesn't tell us that, so it doesn't strengthen the essayist's reasoning.

choices.text: If a commitment has outlasted its original justification, then it cannot be virtuous.
choices.rationale: The essayist establishes that some commitments outlast their original justification. According to this principle, that would mean that those commitments are not morally virtuous. But that doesn't mean that they're morally neutral. They could be morally bad. Moreover, this principle doesn't tell us whether other commitments are morally neutral. Therefore, it doesn't establish that all commitments are morally neutral.

choices.text: All commitments are morally neutral if there are any commitments that are undeserving of praise.
choices.rationale: This connects one of the essayist's premises to their conclusion.” Translated to a more straightforward “if-then” statement, this says, “If any commitments are undeserving of praise, then all commitments are morally neutral.” This connects the essayist's premise that “commitment to a relationship that benefits none of the people involved deserves no praise” to the conclusion that “all commitments should be seen as morally neutral.” The essayist identifies one commitment undeserving of praise, so this principle would establish that all commitments must be morally neutral. Therefore, this principle bridges the gap between the essayist's premise and conclusion. We can confidently select (E).

questions.stimulus: Essayist: Commitment to relationships or careers is commonly held to be virtuous. But all commitments should be seen as morally neutral. After all, what one is committed to might be either good or bad; for example, commitment to a relationship that benefits none of the people involved deserves no praise. Often, commitment is nothing more than involvement that has outlasted its original justification.

questions.stem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.text: No children who spend their free time reading stories fail to develop a lifelong interest in literature.
choices.rationale: To translate this, we'll need to use the “No,” a “then-denying” keyword. That would give us this “if-then” statement and flipside: if Read stories, then NOT fail to develop a lifelong interest in literature (if Fail to develop a lifelong interest in literature, then NOT read stories). If we use a “positive mindset” on the “NOT fail” double negative, we can translate that to simply “develop a lifelong interest in literature”: if Read stories, then Develop a lifelong interest in literature (if NOT Develop a lifelong interest in literature, then NOT read stories). Rather than connect the premise to the new idea in the conclusion, it says that if we don't have the premise, then we won't have the new idea in the conclusion. For this reason, (A) is incorrect.

choices.text: Only those people who currently spend their free time reading stories will develop a lifelong interest in literature.
choices.rationale: We'll need to notice that the “only” is a “then” keyword. That will give us this “if-then” statement and flipside: if Develop a lifelong interest in literature, then Read stories (if NOT read stories, then NOT develop a lifelong interest in literature). The flipside matches our anticipation, so we can confidently select (B). After all, if we add this premise to the argument, it becomes valid. Suppose that (B) is true—suppose that we know that if you don't spend your free time reading, then you won't develop a lifelong interest in literature. In that case, most children who spend their time watching TV rather than reading will not develop a lifelong interest in literature. So, this answer choice makes the argument valid. We can select it.

choices.text: No children who grow up in a household that lacks a television fail to spend their free time reading stories.
choices.rationale: We can eliminate this answer choice immediately because it lacks the new term in the conclusion. It doesn't discuss whether any kids “develop a lifelong interest in literature.” Therefore, this can't make the conclusion valid. You can't have a valid conclusion with a term that doesn't appear in any of the premises, so adding this premise won't make the conclusion follow logically.

choices.text: Few people who watch a great deal of television develop a lifelong interest in literature.
choices.rationale: This doesn't connect the author's premise to their conclusion. Instead, it just establishes that people who watch a “great deal of television” will usually not develop a lifelong interest in literature. However, the author's premises don't say that most children watch a great deal of television. The premises just say that televisions are common and that few children “spend their free time reading stories.” These children may spend their free time watching television instead of stories, but that doesn't mean they're necessarily watching “a great deal of television.” In other words, since the author doesn't include a premise that establishes that most children watch a great deal of television, this answer choice does not connect the author's premise to their conclusion.

choices.text: Few children who spend their free time reading stories watch television.
choices.rationale: Like (C), we can immediately cross this answer choice off once we see that it lacks the new term in the conclusion. It doesn't discuss whether kids “develop a lifelong interest in literature.” Therefore, this can't make the conclusion valid. A conclusion that features an idea that isn't discussed in any of the premises will never be valid, so adding this premise won't make the conclusion follow logically.

questions.stimulus: Because of the ubiquity of television in modern households, few children today spend their free time reading stories, which lack the visual appeal of flashy television programs. Thus, few children today will develop a lifelong interest in literature.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the filmmaker's argument?

choices.text: A documentary with no purpose other than authentically depicting the behavior of its human subjects can be legitimate.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't discuss whether documentaries where the subjects are unaware of the camera's location and act naturally are “more worthwhile” than other documentaries. It just says these documentaries “can be legitimate.” Sure, they're legitimate, but are they worthwhile? This answer choice doesn't say. For these reasons, we can cross off (A).

choices.text: A documentary can be authentic only if it does not include any subjects speaking directly to a camera.
choices.rationale: This principle takes the form “if Documentary authentic, then Subjects do NOT speak directly to the camera.” (The “only” is a “then” keyword, so we have to put that part on the “then” side.) The flipside of this — “if Subjects speak directly to the camera, then Documentary NOT authentic” — would prove that the kinds of documentaries this filmmaker criticizes are “not authentic.” But it doesn't show that these documentaries are not worthwhile. In other words, we can cross this answer choice off because it focuses on documentaries' authenticity rather than their worth.

choices.text: Makers of documentaries do not have a moral obligation to reveal to their subjects the location of the cameras filming them.
choices.rationale: This answer choice only establishes that this filmmaker did not violate a moral obligation. It doesn't discuss whether the filmmaker's documentaries are more worthwhile than any other documentary. Just because something passed a (fairly low) moral bar doesn't mean it's “worthwhile.”

choices.text: The more authentically a documentary depicts its subjects, the more worthwhile it is.
choices.rationale: This principle gets pretty close to our anticipation of “If the subjects of a documentary act more naturally, then the documentary is more worthwhile than documentaries where subjects are aware of the camera's location and that they're being filmed.” It's not a perfect match. The answer choice uses the term “authenticity” rather than “act naturally.” And it's a proportional claim rather than a conditional one. But—crucially—it's the only answer choice so far that brings up how “worthwhile” the filmmaker's documentaries are. So, this answer choice merits a closer examination. Upon review, we can see how this would strengthen the filmmaker's argument. If the filmmaker's subjects don't know where the cameras are and therefore act naturally, we can reasonably argue that these subjects are depicted fairly authentically. These subjects are definitely depicted more authentically than those subjects who speak directly to a camera. This principle would, therefore, establish that the filmmaker's documentaries—which depict their subjects more authentically—would be more worthwhile than other documentaries. Since this isn't a perfect match for our anticipation, we should probably review the remaining answer choice to confirm that it's wrong. But once we confirm that it's wrong (for instance, if we see that it doesn't describe whether the filmmaker's documentaries are worthwhile), we can select (D) confidently.

choices.text: Subjects of documentaries should not try to discover the locations of the cameras filming them.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't discuss whether documentaries where the subjects are unaware of the camera's location and act naturally are “more worthwhile” than other documentaries. It just says these subjects shouldn't look for the cameras. Fine, but are the resulting documentaries “worthwhile”? This answer choice doesn't say, so it's wrong.

questions.stimulus: Filmmaker: I use hidden cameras when filming documentaries, because people behave differently when they are aware of being filmed. Although my subjects have been told that a camera is present, they remain unaware of its location and act naturally. Hence, my documentaries are more worthwhile than documentaries in which, for example, people speak directly to the camera.

questions.stem: The argument requires the assumption that

choices.text: only a few corporations give their employees bonuses that provide strong enough incentives for the employees to keep working hard even when they are not being monitored
choices.rationale: This strengthens the argument, but it isn't necessary. This answer choice strengthens the argument because it establishes that expensive bonuses can incentivize employees to work hard even though they're not being monitored. However, this isn't necessary to the argument because we don't need to know that some corporations already give out these bonuses as an incentive to work hard. Even if no corporations give out these bonuses, these bonuses could still incentivize employees to work hard and thus save highly profitable corporations money. Finally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “Managers' time is more valuable in highly profitable corporations. So, monitoring employees is very costly for highly profitable corporations. Reducing monitoring can save highly profitable corporations money. But, employees need incentives to work hard. But, it's not true that only a few corporations give their employees bonuses that provide strong enough incentives for the employees to keep working hard even when they are not being monitored. So, giving employees expensive bonuses won't save highly profitable corporations money.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. Why would knowing that no corporations give out big bonuses prove that giving out bonuses won't save the corporations money? This argument doesn't provide any evidence that expensive bonuses won't incentivize employees to work hard. So, this answer choice doesn't pass the backup test. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (A).

choices.text: if a highly profitable corporation could save money by giving its employees expensive bonuses, it is because giving such bonuses would reduce the amount of time its managers must spend monitoring those employees
choices.rationale: This answer choice doesn't strengthen the argument. It puts the conclusion in the “if” part of an “if-then” statement. The correct answer to a Strengthen with a Necessary Premise question can't do that. Such statements presuppose that the conclusion is true. However, such a presupposition won't help the argument since we don't know whether the conclusion is true! Alternatively, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “Managers' time is more valuable in highly profitable corporations. So, monitoring employees is very costly for highly profitable corporations. Reducing monitoring can save highly profitable corporations money. But, employees need incentives to work hard. But, it's not true that if a highly profitable corporation could save money by giving its employees expensive bonuses, it is because giving such bonuses would reduce the amount of time its managers must spend monitoring those employees. So, giving employees expensive bonuses won't save highly profitable corporations money.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. The “But, it's not true that part” establishes that a highly profitable corporation can save money through expensive bonuses for reasons other than reducing its need to monitor employees. Even if that's true, the corporation is still saving money through the bonuses. So, giving employees expensive bonuses would save highly profitable corporations money! So, this answer choice doesn't pass the backup test. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (B).

choices.text: the more valuable the managers' time is at a corporation, the less likely it is that the corporation will actually have those managers spend time monitoring employees
choices.rationale: This answer choice doesn't strengthen the argument. In fact, it weakens it! If managers at highly profitable corporations aren't monitoring their employees, then these corporations wouldn't save money through expensive bonuses. These bonuses only save the company money, according to this argument, because they replace the need for managers to use their valuable time monitoring their employees. But if these bonuses aren't replacing that monitoring, they'll only cost the corporation money. Alternatively, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “Managers' time is more valuable in highly profitable corporations. So, monitoring employees is very costly for highly profitable corporations. Reducing monitoring can save highly profitable corporations money. But, employees need incentives to work hard. But, it's not true that the more valuable the managers' time is at a corporation, the less likely it is that the corporation will actually have those managers spend time monitoring employees. So, giving employees expensive bonuses won't save highly profitable corporations money.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. The “But, it's not true that part” establishes that managers of highly profitable corporations monitor their employees' activity. The premises establish that this is very costly. So, it's unclear why replacing this monitoring with bonuses wouldn't save the corporations money, as this conclusion asserts. Giving employees expensive bonuses instead of wasting the manager's valuable time could save highly profitable corporations money! So, this answer choice doesn't pass the backup test. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (C).

choices.text: for people who are employees of highly profitable corporations where monitoring is reduced, expensive bonuses constitute strong incentives to keep working hard
choices.rationale: This answer choice strengthens the argument by establishing that expensive bonuses is a strong incentive for employees of highly profitable corporations to work hard. If employees of highly profitable corporations are given bonuses instead of being monitored, and these bonuses incentivize the employees to work hard, then it makes sense that these bonuses can save the corporation money. After all, these bonuses would replace managers' need to waste their valuable time by monitoring their employees while ensuring the employees continue to work hard. We also need to know this to draw the conclusion. If these bonuses didn't incentivize employees to work hard, then the bonuses might not save the company money. Managers would need to monitor the employees again (wasting their valuable time and costing the corporation money), or the corporation would not function properly (potentially losing money in the process). Since this answer choice strengthens and is needed to draw the conclusion, it is the correct answer. Alternatively, we can also evaluate this answer choice using the backup plan. Here's the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the answer choice to make this easier to read): “Managers' time is more valuable in highly profitable corporations. So, monitoring employees is very costly for highly profitable corporations. Reducing monitoring can save highly profitable corporations money. But, employees need incentives to work hard. But, it's not true that expensive bonuses constitute strong incentives for employees of highly profitable corporations to keep working hard. So, giving employees expensive bonuses won't save highly profitable corporations money.” This makes sense. If expensive bonuses don't ensure that employees work hard, these bonuses won't necessarily save the company money. The bonuses will be costly. And, because employees may not work as hard, the managers might need to monitor the employees again (which would waste their valuable time and cost the corporation money), or the corporation would not function properly (which could be very costly). Since this argument makes sense, (D) also passes the backup test. Therefore, no matter which approach we used, we can be confident that (D) is the correct answer.

choices.text: a highly profitable corporation can save money by reducing its managers' monitoring of employees only if its employees are given expensive bonuses
choices.rationale: If we translate it into a simple “if-then” statement, we'll see that it asserts that if corporations save money by reducing their managers' monitoring, they have to give their employees expensive bonuses. In its translated form, we can see that this answer choice strengthens the argument but isn't necessary. This answer choice strengthens the argument by establishing that expensive bonuses can incentivize employees to work hard even though they're not being monitored. However, this isn't necessary to the argument because we don't need to know that expensive bonuses are the only way to incentivize employees to work hard or for a corporation to save money. The argument only asserts that such bonuses can help a corporation save money. It doesn't assert that there are no other ways to save money or keep employees working hard. For this reason, (D) is not a necessary premise for this argument. Alternatively, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “Managers' time is more valuable in highly profitable corporations. So, monitoring employees is very costly for highly profitable corporations. Reducing monitoring can save highly profitable corporations money. But, employees need incentives to work hard. But, it's not true that a highly profitable corporation can save money by reducing its managers' monitoring of employees only if its employees are given expensive bonuses. So, giving employees expensive bonuses won't save highly profitable corporations money.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. Even if there are other ways to save money, couldn't expensive bonuses still save corporations money? Moreover, this argument doesn't provide any evidence that expensive bonuses won't incentivize employees to work hard. So, this answer choice doesn't pass the backup test. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (E).

questions.stimulus: The more profitable a corporation is, the more valuable its managers' time is. As a result, it is especially costly for highly profitable corporations to have their managers spend time monitoring employees. Such corporations can save money by reducing this monitoring, as long as the employees are given strong incentives to keep working hard. So highly profitable corporations can save money by giving their employees expensive bonuses.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: infers that two phenomena are associated merely from the claim that there are many instances in which both phenomena are present
choices.rationale: The columnist's argument doesn't infer that two phenomena are associated. The columnist's conclusion discusses two phenomena—subjects resenting being given placebos and resenting being given ineffective medicine. But the author doesn't say they're associated—just that the consent forms cast doubt on whether either phenomenon occurs.

choices.text: uses as evidence the opinions of people who are unlikely to be qualified to make informed judgments about the scientific value of placebos
choices.rationale: It's not a flaw that the columnist uses the opinions of unqualified people to make this conclusion. In fact, the columnist's conclusion asserts that test subjects do not actually resent being given placebos or ineffective treatments. To draw that conclusion, the columnist must rely on the test subject's opinions!

choices.text: uses evidence drawn from a sample that is likely to be unrepresentative
choices.rationale: The columnist doesn't even use a sample to draw this conclusion. As far as we can tell, the columnist uses the consent forms of all subjects who sign up for tests of experimental medicines. If we knew that, for instance, the columnist only looked at subjects who were paid to sign up for these tests, this would be an appealing answer choice. But the argument doesn't give us any reason to think the consent forms the columnist cites are unrepresentative of the test subject's general feelings.

choices.text: takes for granted that most test subjects do not change their attitudes toward the chance of taking ineffective substances once the substances they take turn out to be ineffective
choices.rationale: When we see “takes for granted” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, the columnist definitely believes that “most test subjects do not change their attitudes” toward the risk of taking ineffective substances after they take ineffective substances. After all, the columnist uses evidence about what the subjects agree to before the study to conclude how they feel after they take the study. (Notice the shift in verb tense between the premise and conclusion. The premises say the subjects “filled out” the consent forms “prior to their participation in tests.” The conclusion says the test subjects may not “resent” being given placebos or ineffective medicines.) So, the columnist must believe that the subjects' attitudes do not change between filling out the forms and being given ineffective treatments. This assumption isn't necessarily warranted. People change their minds all the time. It would be very understandable and not at all surprising if a test subject given an ineffective treatment for a disease they're suffering from would change their mind and resent the treatment. Additionally, this unwarranted assumption strengthens the columnist's argument. If test subjects do not change their mind after filling out the consent form, they will continue to accept the risk of taking ineffective treatment even after being given an ineffective treatment. Therefore, those forms would cast doubt on the medical ethicists' claims that subjects resent being given ineffective medicine in these studies. Since the columnist relies on this unwarranted assumption to make their conclusion, this is a flaw in their argument. We can select (D) confidently.

choices.text: draws a conclusion that is essentially about a moral issue by appealing to evidence that is purely factual
choices.rationale: The columnist doesn't draw a conclusion about a moral issue. In fact, the columnist's conclusion isn't evaluative or normative; the columnist doesn't argue that subjects should not be or have no right to be resentful. The columnist's conclusion is a factual one—the consent forms undermine the medical ethicists' argument that subjects actually resent being given placebos.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Consent forms filled out by subjects prior to their participation in tests of experimental medicines designed to treat the diseases from which they are suffering show that almost all subjects accept the risk of receiving ineffective substances. This casts doubt on the claim made by some medical ethicists that many test subjects resent being given placebos (as happens to roughly half of all test subjects) or resent being given medicines that turn out to be ineffective (as also often occurs).

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: The use of organic farming methods has recently increased in the commercial apple farming industry.
choices.rationale: This might weaken the argument. If there are more organic apple orchards, the supply of organic apples is up. With more organic apples to sell, this might lower the price organic apples can fetch. This could reduce organic apple orchard's profitability.

choices.text: The apple orchards that tend to be most profitable in the long run tend to be those that are most profitable in the short run.
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument because we have no idea if organic orchards tend to be more profitable in the short run. In fact, we don't know anything about either kind of orchard in “the short run.”

choices.text: Demand for a given kind of apple is based primarily on flavor.
choices.rationale: Here we go! As expected, this answer choice ties organic apples' superior taste to their profitability. If demand for apples is based primarily on flavor, then we can expect more people to want organic apples. If more people want organic apples, organic orchards can sell more organic apples, charge a higher price, or both. If organic orchards can do that, then they'll be more profitable in the long run, especially if they don't cost more to run than conventional orchards. Because (C) strengthens the argument, we can select it.

choices.text: Most people prefer to buy apples that have the lowest price.
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument because we have no idea if organic apples cost less than conventionally grown apples.

choices.text: Many consumers prefer the appearance of apples grown using conventional methods to that of apples grown organically.
choices.rationale: This weakens the argument. If people prefer the appearance of conventionally grown apples, more people may buy them (especially if they can't sample both apples and compare their tastes before purchasing). If more people eschew organic apples to buy conventionally grown apples instead, the organic orchards will probably be less profitable over time.

questions.stimulus: Over the long run, apple orchards that use organic farming methods cost no more to run than, and are just as productive as, apple orchards using conventional methods. However, organically grown apples tend to be better tasting, and thus, organic orchards are likely to be more profitable than conventional orchards in the long run.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion of the argument?

choices.text: In the near future, bank customers will be able to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from their own homes.
choices.rationale: This doesn't match our identified conclusion, so it's a quick cross-off. Besides, this is a misstatement of the first sentence. Bank visionaries “foresee” (predict) this type of banking, but that doesn't mean these banks will soon exist or will ever come to fruition. This argument is about a hypothetical form of banking, not a near-future one.

choices.text: Enabling bank customers to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from their own homes may be more beneficial to banks than to their customers.
choices.rationale: This expresses the same idea as the main conclusion we identified, so we can select it and advance to the following question.

choices.text: As banks eliminate branch offices and customer-service employees, bank customers will have to serve as their own tellers and pay more fees.
choices.rationale: This restates the last sentence in the passage. That sentence is a premise to the argument's main conclusion. According to the argument, the fact that customers will have to serve as their own tellers and pay more fees is why online and telephonic banking “may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers.” In other words, this sentence makes the argument's prediction that online and telephonic will be better for banks than customers more convincing.

choices.text: Eliminating branch offices and customer-service employees would benefit the banking industry.
choices.rationale: This is an assumption the author makes. The author asserts that eliminating branch offices and customer-service employees is why online and telephonic banking “may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers.” In order for that premise and conclusion to have a logical relationship, the author must believe that eliminating these branches and employees is good for the banking industry. In other words, this answer choice reflects an unstated belief the author has when making this argument. This unstated belief cannot be the argument's conclusion. The conclusion must be stated in the argument. And, the conclusion takes the premise and assumption for granted to assert that online and telephonic will be better for banks than customers.

choices.text: Enabling customers to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from their own homes would allow banks to eliminate branch offices and customer-service employees.
choices.rationale: Like (D), this is an assumption the author makes. The author discussses the possible switch to online and telephonic banking in the first sentence. In the last sentence, the author says that this new type of banking will result in banks eliminating branch offices and customer-service employees. In order to get from the first sentence to the third, the author must believe that online and telephonic banking will allow the banks to cut offices and employees. The author doesn't say this out loud, but it's implied by the author's jump from the first to the third sentence. In other words, this answer choice reflects an unstated belief the author has when making this argument. This unstated belief cannot be the argument's conclusion. The conclusion must be stated in the argument. And, the conclusion takes the premises and this assumption for granted to assert that online and telephonic will be better for banks than customers.

questions.stimulus: Banking industry visionaries foresee a bright day in the near future when customers will be able to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from the comfort of their own homes. But that may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers. As banks eliminate their branch offices and customer-service employees, customers will have to serve as their own tellers—and pay more transaction fees for their efforts.

questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that Bernard and Ayla disagree about whether

choices.text: one should always avoid legitimizing a view whose adoption one wishes not to support
choices.rationale: It seems like Bernard and Ayla are in agreement on this issue. Neither wants to legitimize Carl's false views. Bernard just thinks that inviting Carl to speak will legitimize his views, while Ayla thinks that challenging Carl's views will de-legitimize them.

choices.text: people will see the falsity of every dangerous idea for which they are furnished with forceful counterarguments
choices.rationale: While we can infer that Bernard would agree with this answer choice, it is so boldly worded that we don't know whether Ayla agrees with it. Ayla thinks counterarguments are “the best way” to challenge dangerous ideas. But that doesn't imply that Ayla thinks that counterarguments will falsify “every dangerous idea” the public faces. Even Ayla may acknowledge that some dangerous ideas will survive counterarguments.

choices.text: the best way to fight erroneous ideas involves allowing the public expression of these ideas
choices.rationale: Ayla would quite obviously agree with this statement, given that she expresses it in the first sentence. We also have good reason to believe that Bernard would disagree with this statement. He says that allowing one to speak publicly “encourages” the consideration of their false views, thereby legitimizing those views and helping to “support their adoption.” So, Bernard thinks that public expression of erroneous ideas encourages the adoption of those views. So, he would almost certainly disagree with the idea that the best way to fight erroneous ideas involves allowing the public expression of these ideas. Since Ayla would agree with (C) and Bernard would disagree with it, we can select (C) and advance to the following question.

choices.text: people who hold false views tend to pose a danger to society
choices.rationale: This answer choice is so boldly worded that we can't tell whether either Bernard or Ayla would agree with it. Bernard says that Carl's ideas are both false and dangerous, but that doesn't mean Bernard thinks that everyone who holds false views poses a danger to society. Perhaps he would acknowledge that some people possess harmless false ideas. Plus, Ayala doesn't even state or imply that Carl's ideas are dangerous, so we don't know what she thinks about the relationship between false and dangerous ideas.

choices.text: one should not encourage the adoption of dangerous views
choices.rationale: It seems like Bernard and Ayla agree on this issue. Bernard doesn't want to legitimize what he calls Carl's false and dangerous views. Although Ayla doesn't say that Carl's views are dangerous, she calls his views false and wants to refute them publicly. If she thinks it's important to combat false views, it would stand to reason that she would want to refute dangerous views as well.

questions.stimulus:
Bernard: We should not invite Carl to speak at the forum. Carl's views are clearly false, and worse, dangerous. To encourage their consideration will not only legitimize them but also help to promulgate them, both of which we should avoid, since we wish not to support their adoption.

Ayla: The best way to combat false views is to challenge them in public. Once Carl's views are subjected to the kind of public scrutiny the forum provides, people will see them for what they are because the forum will provide convincing arguments against them.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most justifies the above application of the principle?

choices.text: Before returning the camera, James used it extensively to record members of his family engaged in funny activities.
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says that James got all the use out of the camera that he intended, and this answer choice doesn't quite say that. James may have used the camera to record his family acting funny, but that doesn't mean that this was his sole intention or that he was done filming his family. If James intended to film more family antics, he could have returned the camera before he got all the use from it that he intended.

choices.text: James bought the camera to avoid having to hire a professional videographer for his sister's graduation party, and he returned the camera immediately after the party.
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says that James got all the use out of the camera that he intended, and this answer choice says just that! If James bought the camera to avoid hiring a professional videographer for his sister's party and returned it immediately after the party, it certainly seems like recording the party was the only reason he wanted to use the camera. That would mean James would have bought the camera, got all the use out of it he intended, and then returned the camera. According to the principle, James's return would be unethical. Therefore, we can select this answer choice and give the remaining a quick once-over.

choices.text: James used the camera several times but returned it after he had dropped it and then discovered that some of the features did not work.
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says that James got all the use out of the camera that he intended, and this answer choice doesn't say that. In fact, it sounds like James is trying to return the camera because he broke it. The principle doesn't consider whether it's unethical to return a product you break, so this doesn't strengthen the application of the principle.

choices.text: James returned the camera after he discovered that the same model was on sale at another store at a considerably lower price.
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says that James got all the use out of the camera that he intended, and this answer choice doesn't say that. Instead, James is returning the camera because he found a better deal. This answer choice doesn't say whether he's used the camera at all. The principle doesn't consider whether it's unethical to return a product to save some money, so this doesn't strengthen the application of the principle.

choices.text: James used the camera in the manner for which he bought it, and, though he generally enjoyed it, he thought a different one might work better with his new computer.
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says that James got all the use out of the camera that he intended, and this answer choice doesn't quite say that. James may have used the camera “in the manner for which he bought it,” but that doesn't mean that he got all the use out of it that he intended. In fact, it sounds like James wants to use a camera more since he wants a different one that “might work better with his new computer.”

questions.stimulus:
Principle: It is unethical for someone who has bought an item to return it to the store after getting all the use from it that he or she ever intended to get.

Application: James purchased a video camera and returned it to the store two weeks later. This return was unethical.

questions.stem: The situation described above most closely conforms to which one of the following generalizations?

choices.text: Sometimes measures that appear to promote efficiency are actually deleterious to it.
choices.rationale: The passage doesn't say that Taylorism made workers in any way less productive. So, we don't have any evidence that measures that appear to promote efficiency are actually “deleterious” (harmful) to efficiency.

choices.text: Some developments in industry can benefit workers financially while making their work less rewarding in other respects.
choices.rationale: We should anticipate that the correct answer would say something like, “A movement can benefit people in one way and harm them in other ways.” This answer choice is a touch more specific than that anticipation, but it gets across the same basic idea. Moreover, it accurately describes what happened to workers following Taylorism. It benefited these workers financially (as they could enjoy a higher standard of living) while making their jobs less rewarding in other ways (since Taylorism made this work boring and robbed it of some of its intrinsic worth). Moreover, this answer choice uses the weak and wiggly language (“some,” “can”) we need for this question. Therefore, we can select (B) and give the remaining choices an at-most cursory review.

choices.text: Increased efficiency in industrial settings is sometimes accompanied by decreases in the amount of effort workers devote to their jobs.
choices.rationale: The passage doesn't say that Taylorism led workers to decrease the effort they devoted to their jobs. The passage only says that their work became routine and repetitive. But a routine and repetitive task can still take a lot of time and effort to complete!

choices.text: An increase in workers' standards of living will likely involve an accompanying decrease in how much they value their jobs overall.
choices.rationale: We can't validly conclude that increased living standards “will likely” decrease how much workers value their jobs. We know this happened in the early 1900s, but we don't know if this usually happens. For this reason, we can cross off (D).

choices.text: Workers who have greater than average creativity and talent are sometimes less efficient than workers who have average creativity and talent.
choices.rationale: The passage doesn't tell us anything about workers with “greater than average” or “average creativity and talent.” The passage only says that Taylorism made jobs emphasize creativity and talent less. The passage doesn't tell us anything about the creativity and talent the workers possessed.

questions.stimulus: Taylorism, the early-twentieth-century industrial efficiency movement pioneered by Frederick Taylor, has had a profound effect on industrialized societies. Increased productivity resulting from greater efficiency has led to increases in most workers' standards of living. At the same time, Taylor's methods have tended to make these workers' jobs routine and repetitive, thereby robbing their work of some of the intrinsic worth it possessed when it emphasized creativity and talent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument above?

choices.text: Many Winchester residents never use the branch libraries because of the irregular hours each branch keeps.
choices.rationale: This answer choice could either strengthen or weaken the author’s argument. This answer choice shows that the residents can't take advantage of the smaller branch libraries' current hours. If the centralized library fixes this issue and expands the hours, the new library could better meet residents' needs. More people would be able to visit the library and conduct their library-related business. On the other hand, if the centralized library keeps the same hours as the branch libraries, this answer choice would weaken the argument. This would be one reason the new library doesn't do a better job meeting Winchester residents' needs. If an answer choice has an ambiguous effect on the argument—if it could strengthen or weaken the argument based on additional information—it can't be said to truly weaken the argument.

choices.text: Most Winchester residents have complained about the selection of books at the branch libraries.
choices.rationale: This strengthens the argument by showing that residents at least care about the selection of books at the branch libraries. This gives us reason to believe that a centralized library with a broader selection of books would satisfy Winchester residents' bibliographic needs.

choices.text: The only possible site for a new library is not readily accessible to most Winchester residents.
choices.rationale: This definitely weakens the argument. It brings up another factor germane to Winchester residents' needs: convenience and accessibility. If the centralized library can only be built in an inaccessible location, then the library's vast and up-to-date collection won't matter to most Winchester residents. These residents won't be able to access that collection. This makes the argument's conclusion much less convincing, making (C) the correct answer. We can select it and give the remaining choices an, at most, cursory read.

choices.text: It would cost Winchester a significant amount of money to build a larger library.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant to the argument. The argument's conclusion didn't assert that the new library was the right policy choice for the Winchester government. The argument's conclusion only predicted that a new library would better meet residents' needs. So, the argument isn't concerned with the cost the library poses—it's only concerned with whether an improved selection would meet residents' needs. And even if the library would cost a lot of money to construct, that doesn't necessarily mean that the library wouldn't be able to afford to carry a broader and more current collection of books. After all, the centralized library eliminates the need to buy multiple books for the various branch libraries.

choices.text: Each of Winchester's branch libraries attempts to cater to the tastes of the residents of the entire township.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant to the argument. Even if the smaller branch libraries try to cater to the entire township's tastes, that doesn't mean that the libraries succeed in doing so. Winchester residents might still desire a broader and more up-to-date selection of books. Moreover, regardless of what the smaller branch libraries try to stock, it would still be easier for a single, centralized library to cater to the entire town's tastes. After all, the centralized library eliminates the need to buy multiple books for the various branch libraries. So, the centralized library could stock a much broader variety of titles, ensuring that it satisfies the tastes of any Winchester resident.

questions.stimulus: Winchester Township cannot afford to keep its several small branch libraries supplied with a wide selection of current books. However, if the branch libraries were closed, then Winchester could afford to open one large library, which could carry broader and more current selections. Thus, Winchester would better meet its residents' needs by closing its small branch libraries and opening one larger, well-supplied library.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the information in the news report?

choices.text: The technology used to make compound television screens is not appropriate for television sets with relatively small screens.
choices.rationale: Why wouldn't this technology be appropriate for small-screen television? True, one of the main advantages of the new screen is that they can be very large and maintain their brightness. But these new screens could still have advantages over older screens that are apparent even in small-screen televisions. After all, we know that the new screens are only a few inches thick, which could make the small-screen televisions very light and portable.

choices.text: There is a great consumer demand for television sets that are just a few inches thick and that have very large screens.
choices.rationale: Well, these new television screens sound pretty sick, but the passage doesn't tell us whether people actually want to buy them yet. Remember, when we're connecting facts, we need to stick to the facts. We don't know if there's actually “a great consumer demand” for these new screens. Maybe they're too expensive right now, or maybe people don't want them for some other reason.

choices.text: In a television set with a noncompound screen, the thicker the television set, the brighter the screen.
choices.rationale: This misstates a claim from the passage. The passage says, “For a noncompound screen [a few inches thick], the larger the screen is, the dimmer it is.” The last sentence implies that a larger compound screen might also need to be thicker to maintain its brightness. However, this doesn't imply the proportional relationship (C) asserts. There may be limits to how much brighter we can make a screen. After a certain depth, the screen may not get any brighter.

choices.text: Television sets that are just a few inches thick can now be made with screens that are both bright and very large.
choices.rationale: Here it is. The passage implies that we can now make a television screen that's very large, very bright, and not very thick. We can make these sorts of televisions by connecting these small, bright tiles. And we can make this inference by connecting the facts about these small, bright tiles. Let's select (D) and give the last answer choice an, at most, quick glance.

choices.text: Television sets with compound screens do not have any disadvantages relative to sets with noncompound screens.
choices.rationale: This is far too bold. These new television screens sound cool, but they might have many disadvantages. They could be more expensive than older screens. They may project blurrier images than older screens. They may cause more retina damage than older screens. We really only know that the new screens can be bigger, brighter, and less thick than older screens. That doesn't imply that the new screens are better in every way.

questions.stimulus: News report: Some recently invented television screens are built out of small tiles seamlessly joined together, each tile a separate miniature screen. Television sets with these compound screens are just a few inches thick. For a noncompound screen in a set of this thickness, the larger the screen is, the dimmer it is. However, each tile in a compound screen is small enough to be quite bright. Moreover, an unlimited number of the tiles can be joined together, without making the resulting screen any less bright or the set any thicker.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the anthropologist's overall argument by the statement that for early humans who moved from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture, the transition must have been traumatic?

choices.text: It is a premise for which another premise is offered as support.
choices.rationale: Bingo. We're looking for an answer choice that says the phrase is a premise/conclusion. This answer choice doesn't word it that way, but it gets close enough. It describes the first sentence as a “premise,” which is accurate. The first sentence supports the last. This answer choice also says that “another premise is offered as support” for the first sentence, which is also accurate. The second sentence supports the first sentence, as the second sentence explains why the transition to agriculture would be traumatic. Since we have a precise anticipation for this question and (A) matches that anticipation, we can confidently select (A) and advance to the following question.

choices.text: It is background information that plays no logical role in the argument.
choices.rationale: Nope. The first sentence definitely plays a “logical role” in the argument. It supports the main conclusion by describing a major downside of the transition to agriculture, which makes it more likely that the transition to agriculture was due to ulterior motives, like the opportunity to amass wealth. The first sentence is also supported by the second sentence, as the second sentence explains why the transition to agriculture would be traumatic. Since the first sentence is supported by and used to support other claims, it has a logical role in this argument.

choices.text: It is a premise for which no support is offered.
choices.rationale: Nope. The first sentence is supported by the second sentence, as the second sentence explains why the transition to agriculture would be traumatic.

choices.text: It is the conclusion of the argument as a whole.
choices.rationale: Nope. The first sentence supports the third conclusion by describing a major downside of the transition to agriculture, which makes it more likely that the transition to agriculture was due to ulterior motives, like the opportunity to amass wealth. Since the first sentence supports another claim, it is not the argument's main conclusion.

choices.text: It is a claim that the rest of the argument seeks to rebut.
choices.rationale: Nope. The argument doesn't try to rebut or disprove the first sentence. In fact, the first sentence supports the main point by describing a major downside of the transition to agriculture, which makes it more likely that the transition to agriculture was due to by ulterior motives, like the opportunity to amass wealth. Rather than try to rebut the first sentence, the argument relies on the first sentence.

questions.stimulus: Anthropologist: For early humans who moved from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture, the transition must have been traumatic. There would have been increased incidence of disease and injury and a more homogeneous diet lacking vital nutrients more easily obtainable from the richly varied diet of hunter-gatherers. Thus, groups that made the transition were likely motivated by certain benefits that accompany the settled life of the agriculturist, such as opportunities for the accumulation of wealth by those with specialized social roles.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: fails to provide adequate evidence that property in cyberspace is widely considered to be real estate
choices.rationale: This answer choice is pretty tempting, but it misdescribes the author's analogy. The author doesn't argue that because real estate and websites share a few terms, websites should be considered real estate. The author argues that real estate and websites will continue to exist as separate entities, but real estate laws can be extended “to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.” Moreover, the author wouldn't need to provide evidence that “cyberspace is widely considered to be real estate” to argue that real estate laws can be applied to websites. The author would just have to convincingly argue that real estate and websites are similar enough—regardless of what people think about them—that the same laws can work for both areas.

choices.text: has a premise that presupposes what the argument attempts to show in the conclusion
choices.rationale: This doesn't match our anticipation that the correct answer will refer to the relevant differences between real estate and websites. So, we can cross it off without thinking about it too deeply. Besides, this answer choice refers to “circular reasoning.” Circular reasoning occurs when the conclusion merely restates a premise. Arguments that rely on circular reasoning typically have this pattern on the LSAT: “X is true. We know this because, even when X doesn't appear to be true, X still must be true because X is always true.” This argument doesn't rely on circular reasoning. The author never establishes the claim that “it is reasonable to extend that law to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace” as a premise.

choices.text: itself provides significant evidence against the conclusion that it draws
choices.rationale: This doesn't match our anticipation that the correct answer will refer to the relevant differences between real estate and websites. So, we can eliminate this without a second thought. Besides, it's not a flaw to provide “significant evidence against” your conclusion. The author cites that most lawyers think copyright law should protect websites. That's pretty good evidence against the author's conclusion, but that's OK. If the author provided even better evidence that most lawyers are wrong, the author's conclusion could still be persuasive. The author's issue is that they didn't provide adequate evidence to prove their conclusion.

choices.text: fails to provide evidence that the similarities that constitute the analogy are anything but merely verbal
choices.rationale: Here we go! The correct answer should highlight the relevant differences between real estate and websites. If “the similarities that constitute the analogy are anything but merely verbal,” then real estate and websites don't really have much in common. If those two areas don't have much in common, it's not reasonable to extend real estate laws to websites. So, it is definitely a flaw that the author didn't provide evidence that their analogy was based on anything other than verbal similarities. We can justifiably select (D) and advance to the following question.

choices.text: defends a view solely on the grounds that the view is held by many experts
choices.rationale: This doesn't match our anticipation that the correct answer will refer to the relevant differences between real estate and websites. So, we can toss this away without spending much time mulling it over. Besides, the author doesn't rely on experts to make this conclusion. In fact, if it's fair to call most lawyers “experts,” the author argues against the expert view!

questions.stimulus: Most lawyers hold that violations of the rights of those who possess sites on the web are best prevented using copyright law. Yet many of the words used to describe such sites evoke ideas that are usually associated with real estate: for example, the word "site" itself and the term "visiting" as applied to sites. The common law of trespass usually applies to cases of encroachment on real estate. Thus, it is reasonable to extend that law to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.

questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, helps to strengthen the argument except:

choices.text: Only during the day are there more unsafe than safe vehicles on the road.
choices.rationale: This one strengthens the argument by providing more stats that suggest the daytime is more dangerous. If most cars driving during the day are unsafe, then we'd expect the daytime to be the more dangerous time to drive.

choices.text: There is decreased law enforcement presence during the day.
choices.rationale: This one strengthens the argument by providing more stats that suggest the daytime is more dangerous. If there is less law enforcement during the day, there are fewer people to stop dangerous drivers and unsafe vehicles before they harm someone else. That makes it more reasonable to conclude that the daytime is the more dangerous time to drive.

choices.text: Persons drive more cautiously during the night than during the day.
choices.rationale: This one strengthens the argument by providing more stats that suggest the daytime is more dangerous. If people drive more recklessly during the day, then there should be a higher percentage of accidents during the day. This supports the journalist's argument that the daytime is the more dangerous time to drive.

choices.text: The number of travelers per vehicle has increased over the past ten years.
choices.rationale: This doesn't affect the journalist's argument, so it's the correct answer to this Bizarro Strengthen question. The number of people in each car may have increased over the last ten years, but that doesn't suggest that it's more dangerous to drive during the day. Maybe if a higher percentage of cars had more people during the day, then we could expect drivers to be more distracted during the day and thus more likely to get into accidents. But, this answer choice doesn't fill in those details. In fact, it doesn't tell us anything about daytime versus nighttime. Without differentiating those times, this can't meaningfully strengthen this argument.

choices.text: Persons drive faster during the day than during the night.
choices.rationale: This one strengthens the argument by providing more stats that suggest the daytime is more dangerous. If people drive faster during the day, then there should be a higher percentage of accidents at that time. This supports the journalist's argument that driving during the daytime is more dangerous.

questions.stimulus: Journalist: Contrary to popular opinion, it is more dangerous for an individual to drive during the day than during the night. A recent study found that in each of the last ten years, the number of traffic accidents that resulted in death was greater during the day than during the night.

questions.stem: The claim that an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species plays which one of the following roles in the biologist's argument?

choices.text: It is a claim offered in support of the argument's conclusion.
choices.rationale: There it is. We're looking for an answer choice that says the second sentence is a premise that supports the main conclusion. This answer choice says just that. Since we have a precise anticipation for this question and (A) matches that anticipation, we can confidently select (A) and advance to the following question.

choices.text: It is presented to raise a question that sheds doubt on the argument's conclusion.
choices.rationale: Nope. The second sentence supports the argument's conclusion (by ruling out another way that sexual reproduction could have become the norm among species). So, the second sentence doesn't “ shed doubt”  (cast doubt) on the conclusion. It makes the conclusion more likely to be true!

choices.text: It is a claim that the argument is designed to call into question.
choices.rationale: Nope. The second sentence supports the argument's conclusion (by ruling out another way that sexual reproduction could have become the norm among species). So, the argument doesn't call the second sentence into question! The second sentence makes the argument more convincing!

choices.text: It describes an observed phenomenon for which the argument seeks an explanation.
choices.rationale: Nope. The second sentence isn't an observed phenomenon. We can't walk out into nature and see that an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species. And even if the second sentence was a phenomenon, the conclusion doesn't explain that phenomenon. Instead, the conclusion uses that supposed “phenomenon” to rule out an alternative way that sexual reproduction could have become the norm among species.

choices.text: It is presented as the main explanation of the origin of an observed phenomenon.
choices.rationale: Nope. The second sentence isn't an explanation for any other supposed “phenomenon” in this argument. Besides, when an argument has a Phenomenon/Explanation structure, the explanation is always the conclusion. The second sentence is a premise, which shows that it can't be a conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Biologist: The evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction is that it increases the range of genetic variation in a species, which is an advantage for the species as a whole. However, an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species. It follows that the sole reason that sexual reproduction has become the rule among both animals and plants is that natural selection has favored some entire species over others.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: presumes, without providing any justification, that most innocuous everyday occurrences are harmful to society
choices.rationale: When we see “presumes, without providing justification” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, the columnist doesn't believe that innocuous everyday occurrences are harmful to society. In fact, the whole notion of “innocuous everyday occurrences being harmful to society” is oxymoronic. “Innocuous” literally means “harmless.” Besides, the author never claims or implies that anything related to vagrancy is harmful to society. This is enough reason to eliminate (A). If you were relying on the backup plan for this question, we can make this answer choice easier to read by replacing “presumes, without providing justification” with “assumes.” Here's the paragraph we'd read to test this answer choice: “Some people argue that vagrancy laws do not decrease criminal activity because vagrancy laws transform many harmless behaviors into crimes, therefore increasing crime. But, that argument assumes that that most innocuous everyday occurrences are harmful to society. So, vagrancy laws might reduce criminal activity.” That paragraph doesn't make any sense. The argument doesn't appear to assume that most innocuous everyday occurrences are harmful to society. In fact, it appears to assume the opposite—that vagrancy laws take harmless behaviors and make them crimes. Secondly, even if the argument assumed that those innocuous everyday occurrences were harmful to society, that would undermine the notion that vagrancy might reduce criminal activity! Before vagrancy laws, everyday activity was harmful and legal. After vagrancy laws, everyday activity became harmful and illegal. That sounds like vagrancy laws increased crime to us! Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (A).

choices.text: mistakenly infers, from the claim that vagrancy laws are associated with an increase in many innocuous everyday occurrences, that vagrancy laws cause that increase
choices.rationale: This misdescribes the columnist's argument. The columnist never establishes that vagrancy laws are associated with an increase in many innocuous everyday occurrences. In fact, the columnist never says that there is an increase of many innocuous everyday occurrences. The columnist instead says that vagrancy laws take the innocuous everyday occurrences that were already happening and transform them into crimes. For this reason, we can cross off (B). If you were relying on the backup plan for this question, here's the paragraph we'd read to test this answer choice (note that we re-arranged the answer choice a bit to make it easier to read): “Some people argue that vagrancy laws do not decrease criminal activity because vagrancy laws transform many harmless behaviors into crimes, therefore increasing crime. But, that argument mistakenly concludes that vagrancy laws cause an increase in many innocuous everyday occurrences, from the claim that vagrancy laws are associated with that increase. So, vagrancy laws might reduce criminal activity.” That paragraph doesn't make any sense. First, the argument never says that there is an “increase in many innocuous everyday occurrences” associated with vagrancy laws. So, the part that follows “But” seems inaccurate. Moreover, the “But” part acknowledges that there is an increase in innocuous everyday occurrences. If those occurrences are now classified as crimes under vagrancy laws, then it sounds like vagrancy laws increase crime. That makes the “So” part sound false. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (B).

choices.text: fails to specify what is meant by "innocuous everyday occurrences"
choices.rationale: This isn't a flaw. The columnist doesn't have to define “innocuous everyday occurrences” to convincingly reach this conclusion. As long as the columnist establishes that vagrancy laws don't reduce any criminal activity and only reclassify non-criminal, innocuous everyday occurrences as crimes, the columnist can reach this conclusion without defining what they mean by “innocuous everyday occurrences.” For this reason, we can cross off (C). If you were relying on the backup plan for this question, here's the paragraph we'd read to test this answer choice: “Some people argue that vagrancy laws do not decrease criminal activity because vagrancy laws transform many harmless behaviors into crimes, therefore increasing crime. But, that argument fails to specify what is meant by 'innocuous everyday occurrences.' So, vagrancy laws might reduce criminal activity.” That paragraph doesn't make any sense. The fact that the argument doesn't specify what “innocuous everyday occurrences” means doesn't prove that vagrancy laws might reduce criminal activity. The “But” and the “So” sentences sound unrelated and disconnected, which is a strong signal that this answer choice does not point out a flaw in the argument's reasoning.

choices.text: fails to consider the possibility that crime will increase even in the absence of vagrancy laws
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to consider” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the argument if it were true?” In this case, crime increasing in the absence of vagrancy laws would not weaken the conclusion that vagrancy laws do not reduce criminal activity. “Crime” is a broad enough term that there could be multiple, unconnected increases. For instance, vagrancy laws could increase criminal activity by, as this columnist says, reclassifying everyday occurrences into crimes. Separate and apart from this phenomenon, there could be a nationwide increase in shoplifting. Even without the vagrancy laws, there would still be this nationwide increase in shoplifting. Still, we could say that the vagrancy laws increase criminal activity, as they're adding to the number of crimes on top of the nationwide increase in shoplifting. So, the fact that some crimes could increase without vagrancy laws doesn't undermine the notion that vagrancy laws increase criminal activity. This is enough reason to eliminate (C). If you were relying on the backup plan for this question, here's the paragraph we'd read to test this answer choice: “Some people argue that vagrancy laws do not decrease criminal activity because vagrancy laws transform many harmless behaviors into crimes, therefore increasing crime. But, that argument fails to consider the possibility that crime will increase even in the absence of vagrancy laws. So, vagrancy laws might reduce criminal activity.” That paragraph doesn't make much sense. Even if crime would increase without vagrancy laws, vagrancy laws could still add to the total number of crimes. So, the “But” part doesn't provide strong evidence supporting the “So” part. This is a strong signal that this answer choice does not point out a flaw in the argument's reasoning.

choices.text: does not adequately distinguish between an increase in criminal activity and the reclassification of certain occurrences as crimes
choices.rationale: This one points out the flaw that eagle-eyed test-takers may have noticed. There's a big difference between the conclusion and the premise and premise/conclusion: the former discusses “criminal activity,” while the latter discusses “crime.” Those aren't necessarily the same thing. Increased criminal activity sounds like more people are out there committing crimes. There's more theft, vandalism, assaults, etc. But an increase in “crime” based on the reclassification of formerly legal, harmless activity? That doesn't sound like it's the same thing as an increase in “criminal activity.” If we reclassify harmless behavior as “crimes,” we won't necessarily see a spike in theft, vandalism, assault, etc. So, it's a problem that the author doesn't “adequately distinguish” these two things. The argument would be much more persuasive if it said, “The amount of criminal activity may stay the same under vagrancy laws, but vagrancy laws will increase the number of crimes committed.” Moreover, even if vagrancy laws increase the amount of crimes committed, it could still decrease the amount of criminal activity. Perhaps knowing they can get cited for violating vagrancy laws will compel “vagrants” from doing other crimes. If loitering is now illegal under vagrancy laws, perhaps people won't loiter or commit the other crimes they typically commit while loitering. That would reduce the amount of criminal activity, even if it increases the number of crimes. If you were relying on the backup plan for this question, here's the paragraph we'd read to test this answer choice: “Some people argue that vagrancy laws do not decrease criminal activity because vagrancy laws transform many harmless behaviors into crimes, therefore increasing crime. But, that argument does not adequately distinguish between an increase in criminal activity and the reclassification of certain occurrences as crimes. So, vagrancy laws might reduce criminal activity.” That paragraph makes sense. Yes, the number of crimes might increase once vagrancy laws reclassify previously legal behaviors as crimes. But that doesn't necessarily mean the amount of criminal activity will go up. Vagrancy laws might compel “vagrants” to engage in less criminal activity (like theft, vandalism, and assault), even if it adds to the number of crimes by reclassifying previously legal behavior as crimes. Whichever method we use, we can select (E) with confidence.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Vagrancy laws are supposed to reduce criminal activity, but they don't. Making vagrancy illegal means transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes. Thus, vagrancy laws increase crime while purporting to reduce it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the political theorist's argument?

choices.text: Governments alone are not able to convince individuals to take a reasoned approach to getting what they want.
choices.rationale: This doesn't even strengthen the argument, so it can't be necessary to the argument either. The conclusion is an “if-then” statement that puts the “people take a reasoned approach to getting what they want” in the “if” part of the premise. When strengthening an argument, we don't have to worry about making the “if” part come true. The conclusion is already assuming that the “if” part is true. In fact, we can treat the “if” part as a premise if that makes more sense to us. Rather than worrying about making the “if” part come true, we should focus on strengthening the “then” part. In this argument, that would involve showing that a reasoned approach to getting what you want involves not injuring other people. So, this answer choice, which only addresses whether governments can make the “if” part happen, does not strengthen the argument. (And, for what it's worth, this answer choice only makes the “if” part less likely to be true.) For that reason, we can cross (A) off.
