Splitters, on the other hand, tend to use the increasingly popular phylogenetic species concept, which defines a species as a "diagnosable" population, among which there is a pattern of ancestry and descent. A phylogenetic species is a population in which members share a distinctive, genetically traceable feature that distinguishes it from other populations.

The late Charles G. Sibley, a prominent ornithologist and one of the fomenters of a controversial revolution in avian taxonomy, could be called a splitter. He used a process known as DNA-DNA hybridization—which compares DNA from different species—to determine the relationships of the various families of birds. From his studies he concluded that many earlier classifications of the relationships of bird families were wrong. For instance, he said that vultures found in North and South America were more closely related to storks than to European vultures, and that loons and grebes, which many taxonomists had argued were closely related, were not.

Sibley's work has not been widely accepted. "What the DNA data can give you is an approximation of how different the genes of two isolated populations are," one critic has written, "but how you interpret those differences is basically arbitrary, as arbitrary as any decision made in any species concept." Sibley might not have disagreed, at least not entirely. In 1996 he wrote that "Evolution produces all degrees of genetic differences between populations of organisms, but, for practical reasons, we must limit the number of degrees we choose to 'recognize' by names. We assign names of populations and proposed definitions of taxonomic categories based on various criteria, but the 'species concept' is slippery because there are so many examples in nature of populations that refuse to fit our limited set of definitions and names."

Whatever the merits of each position, the species question undoubtedly has political and economic stakes. For example, increasing the number of species would probably increase the number needing protection as well.

This passage was adapted from an article published in 1991.

Because it is relatively easy and inexpensive to produce copycat computer programs, most people believe that some form of legal protection should be extended to creators of computer software. Without a legal deterrent to copycat programming, the resources expended by an individual or a company to develop an innovative software program could be unfairly exploited by rivals who develop a similar product and rush it to market at a lower price. The occurrence of such exploitation would leave software developers with little financial incentive to develop innovative products. While most legal commentators agree that copyright has generally proven to be an effective means of preventing this exploitation, some contend that patent protection is also needed to combat copycatting.

In essence, every piece of software is an encoding of one or more algorithms. An algorithm is simply defined as a series of steps to be followed in carrying out a task; to be usable in computer applications, an algorithm must be expressed in terms that can be processed by a computer. Proponents of software patents assert that in providing a specific way of achieving a desired result, the encoding of algorithms is analogous to the design of a process. Process designs (for example, an innovative way of inducing a series of chemical reactions) do, in fact, fall under the scope of patent protection. However, in order for any design to be patentable, it must be genuinely a product of invention (rather than, say, a law of nature or a logical axiom). For example, while a particular innovative windmill design might be patentable, the principle that wind can be harnessed to produce energy would clearly not be. On similar grounds, software algorithms, because they represent generic principles underlying the specific processes by which tasks are to be carried out by computers, should not be considered patentable.

Issuing patents for computer programs would extend protection to software developers beyond that afforded by copyright when there is really no compelling justification for doing so. Insofar as software programs constitute the expression of ideas in the form of specific texts (i.e., sequences of computer code), they fall more appropriately within the established domain of copyright law. Whereas patents protect the underlying design of an invention, even if it is never actually executed, copyright protects only the particular way in which the underlying ideas are expressed. Because the value of software lies in its form of expression, protection should be given only for particular applications—expressions of algorithms in an encoded form. Such protection could be more effectively afforded with only slight modification to existing copyright laws, and the financial incentive to develop innovative software could thereby be preserved.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Newly established independent record companies must find innovative approaches in order to compete effectively with established major companies.
choices.rationale: This author only described the conditions that favored Motown's success. The author never said that other independent record companies should emulate Motown's approach. Moreover, the idea of competing with “established major companies” is perhaps alluded to in the second paragraph, but it's certainly not part of the explanation that defines the passage's main point.

choices.text: The high quality of Motown recordings was made possible by African American musicians trained in the music-education program of Detroit's public schools.
choices.rationale: Many test-takers may conclude that there's nothing “wrong” with this answer choice — meaning it doesn't misdescribe the passage or change the scope of the discussion — and select it. This passage does, however, completely remove the discussion of Berry Gordy, Jr. and electric instruments from the author's explanation. Because it doesn't fully capture the author's explanation of Motown's success, this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: Berry Gordy, Jr.'s faith in local talent and local financing was vindicated by the success of Motown Records.
choices.rationale: Like (B), this answer choice is too narrowly focused on Berry Gordy, Jr. to fully capture the author's explanation. This answer choice almost makes it seem like Gordy's faith in local talent and financing was the phenomenon described in this passage. But, Motown's success is the phenomenon described in this passage. Besides, “local financing” wasn't discussed in this passage at all.

choices.text: Berry Gordy, Jr. deserves credit that is long overdue for having brought about a revolution in the culture of popular music in the United States in the 1960s.
choices.rationale: Like (C), this answer choice makes it seem like Berry Gordy, Jr. is the topic of this passage. However, Motown's success is the phenomenon, and the author only identifies Gordy as one factor that contributed to Motown's success. That one problem is serious — and would probably lead to quick elimination from an experienced test-taker — but there are other issues as well. There's nothing in this passage to suggest that Gordy's credit is “long overdue,” and the revolution discussed in the final paragraph was caused by musicians' embrace of electric instruments, not Gordy.

choices.text: Motown Records became a highly successful and culturally influential company through the efforts of an entrepreneurial individual in a favorable artistic environment.
choices.rationale: Some test-takers may find issue with the general phrasing here. Rather than elaborate on all three parts of the explanation, this answer choice compresses them to “the efforts of an entrepreneurial individual in a favorable artistic environment.” As long as this compression is accurate and doesn't omit anything substantial, however, it's fine. And “the efforts of an entrepreneurial individual” clearly refers to Berry Gordy, Jr., while the “favorable artistic environment” could refer both to the public music-education programs in Detroit and the electric revolution in pop music. So, this answer choice best describes the author’s explanation and is correct.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes Gordy's attitude concerning the potential for Motown's recordings to have widespread appeal?

choices.text: uncertainty in light of past trends in the music industry
choices.rationale: An experienced LSATer wouldn't need to read past “uncertainty.” Remember, Gordy “insisted” that Motown's records could appeal to all, so “uncertainty” is the exact opposite of what we're looking for. Moreover, Gordy thought Motown could defy “past trends”; he certainly wouldn’t let past trends deter him, then.

choices.text: willingness to accept anticipated popular indifference
choices.rationale: Does a person who “insisted” that his small record label could make massive, universal hits sound this reserved to you? The author never says that Gordy would be willing to accept that audiences would be indifferent to Motown's music. The author never even claimed that anyone anticipated that audiences would be indifferent to Motown's music.

choices.text: courage in the face of unpromising statistics
choices.rationale: “Courage” would be a slightly strange, but not entirely inaccurate, way to describe Gordy's confidence. Do you recall reading anything about “unpromising statistics,” though? An experienced test-taker would recognize that they don't recall any references to “unpromising statistics” and defer to see if a more familiar description of Gordy's attitude appears in another answer choice. Better yet, such a test-taker would take their lack of familiarity as a sign that “statistics” was not discussed in this passage and eliminate this outright.

choices.text: confidence rooted in firm personal conviction
choices.rationale: “Confidence” is a promising start. This answer choice says this confidence is “rooted in firm personal conviction,” which the passage never explicitly claims. However, note the verbs used to describe Gordy throughout the second paragraph: he “rejected” common practices (P2, S2), and he “insisted” that his music would appeal to the masses (P2, S3). Both of these words are strong action verbs. They are used to show that someone is acting boldly and without reservation. And in the first paragraph, the author claims he had a “belief” in his economic independence (P1, S3). All of these suggest that Gordy had “strong personal conviction” — a steadfast belief in and commitment to his vision. For these reasons, (D) is supported by the passage and is correct.

choices.text: optimism based on changing economic conditions
choices.rationale: “Optimism” is a great start and arguably a more apt description of Gordy than “confidence” in (D). But this answer choice suffers from a similar problem as (C). Do you recall reading anything about “changing economic conditions”? An experienced test-taker would recognize that they don't remember any references to “economic conditions” and check the passage to see if any references were made to economic conditions. Better yet, such a test-taker would take their lack of familiarity as a sign that “economic conditions” was not discussed in this passage and eliminate this outright.

questions.stem: The passage provides information sufficient to answer which one of the following questions?

choices.text: What musical innovation by African American musicians influenced other musicians?
choices.rationale: This answer choice discusses a musical innovation by African American artists. This could reflect the Motown musicians who embraced electric instruments. If necessary, we can check the final paragraph to see if their use of electric instruments was (1) characterized as an innovation and (2) something that influenced other musicians. The supporting information for (A) shouldn't be difficult to find if you highlighted the electric bass example. During that discussion, the author claims that "African American musicians were among the first to use the electric bass," confirming that this was an innovation by African American musicians. The author then claims this "distinctive sound" would inspire "other musicians to experiment with this new musical technology" (P4, S2). So the passage definitely provides an answer to (A). What musical innovation by African American musicians influenced other musicians? The use of the electric bass.

choices.text: What musical styles were favored by African American recording companies established before Motown Records?
choices.rationale: You could eliminate (B) after reading “before Motown records.” We hear very little about what happened at African American recording companies before Motown. We hear very little about music in general before Motown, other than a few contrasts drawn between Gordy and the major record companies at the time. Since the passage never answers this question, it is incorrect.

choices.text: How long after Hitsville, USA was founded did it come to be known as Motown Records?
choices.rationale: You could eliminate this answer choice for asking a very specific question about “Hitsville, USA.” A search could confirm that this passage mentions “Hitsville, USA” at the very beginning and nowhere else. In this brief reference, the author never discusses when or how “Hitsville, USA” became known as “Motown.” So, the passage does not provide an answer to this question.

choices.text: Why did Berry Gordy, Jr. insist on following certain standard practices of recording companies in the 1960s?
choices.rationale: You could eliminate this one for conflicting with the passage's main point. Berry Gordy, Jr. didn't follow other recording companies' standard practices. One part of the passage's main point was that Gordy's business skills and independence allowed him to defy standard record company practices. The passage never claims that Gordy adopted any standard operations, so this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: Why did E. Azalia Hackley dedicate herself to the musical education of African American youth?
choices.rationale: You could refer back to the third paragraph to look for an answer to this question. In the second sentence of that paragraph, the author says, “E. Azalia Hackley adopted the musical education of African American youth as her personal mission.” But the author never elaborates on why she made this her mission, so we don't have an answer to this question.

questions.stem: Based on information in the passage, it can be inferred that the author most likely believes which one of the following?

choices.text: Gordy's own expertise in the technical aspects of record production ensured that Motown's recordings would be of the highest possible quality.
choices.rationale: The main point we anticipated for this passage had little to do with Berry Gordy, Jr.'s technical expertise. Additionally, the claim that Gordy's expertise “ensured that Motown's recordings would be of the highest possible quality” is extremely strong and difficult to support. A time-conscious test-taker would likely defer on this answer choice or eliminate it outright. Indeed, this topic is only brought up at the end of the second paragraph. In that brief discussion, the passage never claims that Gordy personally possessed the technical expertise — only that “he devoted the necessary resources to this endeavor.”

choices.text: The great popularity of Motown recordings in the 1960s was largely due to the dearth of innovative popular music being produced by other record companies at that time.
choices.rationale: The main point we anticipated did not include a lack of competition as a cause of Motown's success. Additionally, the claim that Motown's success was “largely” due to a lack of other innovative music is strong and difficult to support, especially in a passage that lists out several contributing factors. A time-conscious test-taker would likely defer on this answer choice or eliminate it outright. That would be a wise decision, as this passage did not explicitly discuss what was being produced by other record companies. The only discussion of that sort is in the last paragraph. There, the author claims that there was a “revolution in popular music” during Motown's heyday, suggesting that there was plenty of innovative popular music being produced elsewhere.

choices.text: The revolution in popular music brought about by the use of electric instruments would not have occurred if Motown musicians had never used the electric bass.
choices.rationale: We don't have to look too closely before realizing that this describes a hypothetical situation — it discusses what would have happened in some theoretical world in which Motown's musicians didn't use the electric bass. It's nearly impossible to provide the requisite evidence to support a hypothetical like this. The author would have needed to claim that Motown's electric bass-playing musicians were the only possible people who could have initiated the electric instrument revolution. Of course, the author never makes any preposterous claims of that sort, so this answer choice is wrong.

choices.text: Gordy's unconventional ideas would have been harder for him to implement if his company had been a subsidiary of a major recording company.
choices.rationale: Although it presents a hypothetical, the prediction is much weaker than the one in (C). So, is there reason to believe that the author thinks it would have been harder for Gordy to implement his unconventional ideas if Motown was owned by a big record company? In the second paragraph, the author writes, “Motown's status as an independent company allowed Gordy considerable freedom to oppose recording industry convention” (P2, S1). So, the author thinks Motown's independence led to Gordy's freedom to defy convention. It stands to reason that if Motown lacked that freedom, it would have been harder for Gordy to deviate from standard practices in the record industry. Notably, this answer choice never claimed it would have been impossible for Gordy to do so. That claim would be difficult to support. But this weaker claim is well supported by the second paragraph, and this answer is correct.

choices.text: Motown songs would have been equally popular if they had been performed instead by established artists from other record companies.
choices.rationale: Our anticipated main point did not include some hypothetical reality in which “established artists” recorded Motown songs. In fact, the main point was that Gordy's unconventional approach — such as not letting established artists cover Motown songs (P2, S3) — helped contribute to Motown's success. So this answer choice is one the author probably would disagree with.

questions.stem: The author states which one of the following about Berry Gordy, Jr.?

choices.text: He relied on Detroit's public school music teachers to help him recruit talented performers.
choices.rationale: This answer choice inserts one part of the passage into another. We know that the second paragraph discusses Berry Gordy, Jr. at length. The third paragraph discusses the talented performers in Detroit at length. Gordy never came up in the third paragraph. And just because public school music teachers were fostering the local talent doesn't mean that Gordy was reaching out to those music teachers.

choices.text: He had worked in the music industry prior to founding Motown Records.
choices.rationale: We really don't get much about Berry Gordy, Jr.'s biography. A time-conscious test-taker would acknowledge that fact and quickly eliminate this answer choice. It's possible that Gordy worked at another record label before founding Motown, but it's never discussed in this passage.

choices.text: He devoted resources to ensuring high-quality recordings at Motown Records.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is explicitly supported by the passage. At the end of the second paragraph, the author claims that Berry Gordy, Jr. aimed to produce the “highest possible technical quality in Motown's recordings” and “devoted the necessary resources to this endeavor” (P2, S4). So this answer choice is correct.

choices.text: He was educated in the Detroit public school system.
choices.rationale: As was the case for (B), a quick-moving test-taker would recognize that we got very little biographical information about Berry Gordy, Jr. and eliminate this answer choice. The passage never confirms that Gordy also went to the Detroit public schools that produced Motown's seminal artists — we never even learned whether Gordy was from Detroit.

choices.text: He founded Motown Records largely to promote the extensive use of electric instruments.
choices.rationale: Like (A), this attempts to connect two distinct parts of the passage. The first paragraph tells us Berry Gordy, Jr. founded Motown and the final paragraph tells us Motown musicians were among the first to use electric instruments. But at no point does the passage state or imply that Gordy founded Motown with the goal of promoting the use of electric instruments.

questions.stem: The author most clearly intends to include which one of the following within the scope of the phrase "the artistic situation" (third sentence of the first paragraph)?

choices.text: the willingness of Detroit financiers to take risks on artistic ventures
choices.rationale: This question is eminently anticipatable — we know we're looking for an answer that refers to Detroit's public music education programs or the artists and technicians who came from those programs. This answer choice brings up “financiers” and can be eliminated without much consideration. A review of the passage would reveal that financiers are not a topic of this passage.

choices.text: Detroit residents' ready access to musical training in public schools
choices.rationale: This answer choice is precisely what we're looking for: access to Detroit's well-developed, public music education program. This access to music education is the “artistic situation” that is first referenced in the first paragraph and then described in detail in the third paragraph.

choices.text: a Detroit instrument manufacturer's production of electric instruments
choices.rationale: This question allows us to be very precise in our anticipation. We are looking for an answer that refers to Detroit's public music education programs or the artists and technicians who came from those programs. This answer choice brings up electric instruments, which is enough to eliminate it. A review of that passage would reveal that this passage never stated that electric instruments were manufactured in Detroit.

choices.text: Detroit residents' disenchantment with prevailing trends in popular music
choices.rationale: We know what we're looking for on this question. Any answer choice that doesn't bring up Detroit's public music education programs or the artists and technicians who came from those programs should be eliminated straight away. This answer choice discusses Detroit r

choices.text: Detroit's well-established tradition of supporting independent recording businesses
choices.rationale: Yet again, an answer choice that doesn't mention Detroit's public music education programs or the artists and technicians who came from those programs. We can eliminate it without reviewing the passage, but if we did review the passage we'd find that Detroit's history of supporting independent record companies was never discussed.

questions.stem: The author's discussion of E. Azalia Hackley serves primarily to illustrate

choices.text: the existence of a long-standing tradition of musical education for African American young people in Detroit
choices.rationale: This hits the right note. The purpose of the third paragraph as a whole, and the reference to E. Azalia Hackley in particular, was to show that there were public music education programs in Detroit, which provided Motown with talented African American musicians and technicians.

choices.text: the specific type of musical education that was provided in Detroit's public schools
choices.rationale: We never learn what “specific type” of musical education E. Azalia Hackley established in Detroit. So this answer choice is a bit too specific to accurately convey the purpose of including the reference to E. Azalia Hackley.

choices.text: the extent to which many Motown performers had been directly influenced by Hackley
choices.rationale: Like (B), this is a bit too specific to describe the author's purpose in including the reference to E. Azalia Hackley. We learn from the third paragraph that Hackley mentored “locally renowned public school music teachers,” who created the “vibrant musical atmosphere” in Detroit's public music education programs. But we don't know that Hackley directly influenced Motown's musicians and technicians. Perhaps those music teachers developed their own styles and approaches that conflicted somewhat with Hackley's, and those new styles and techniques directly influenced Motown's artists.

choices.text: the way in which music instruction in Detroit's public schools had changed over the years
choices.rationale: Did Detroit's public music education change over the years? Perhaps, but we never get any explicit confirmation of that in the passage. We don't even know whether this is true, so it can't be the purpose behind the reference to E. Azalia Hackley.

choices.text: the author's belief that music instruction in Detroit would have languished without such ardent supporters
choices.rationale: Does the author believe that Detroit's music education would have suffered without people like E. Azalia Hackley? Perhaps, but the author never makes this claim in the passage. We don't even know whether this is true, so it can't be the reason the author included the reference to E. Azalia Hackley.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?

choices.text: Is collective wisdom more reliable than individual judgment?
choices.rationale: Both passages discuss the “collective wisdom” of markets, but neither compares that collective wisdom to “individual judgment.” The latter topic is not mentioned in either passage, so this answer choice can be swiftly eliminated.

choices.text: What can be learned from studying the movement of stock markets?
choices.rationale: A test-taker who anticipated what the correct answer should say — and relied on this anticipation when appraising the answer choices — would likely note that this didn't mention anything about the “reliability” of markets and would move on to the next option without much thought. To less-prepared test-takers, however, this answer choice may be tempting. But beyond lacking “reliability,” there are a few issues here. One, “stock markets” were merely an example of a market in passage A (PA, P1, S1) but were never explicitly mentioned in passage B. In fact, both passages focus on prediction/forecast markets far more than stock markets. Second, we can infer what the authors think we can learn from price movement on stock markets. The author in passage A might say this is evidence that people realize the company's value is changing. In contrast, the author of passage B would probably say the only thing changing is the majority's opinion of the value. But neither passage explicitly addresses this issue, so this can't be the correct answer to a Main Point question.

choices.text: Can markets be used to elicit reliable information?
choices.rationale: One way to check whether an answer is correct on this type of question is to see if the authors' main points provide an answer. Both main points answer this question. Passage A concludes that markets are reliable reflections of the collective knowledge of many investors with remarkable efficiency. So passage A would answer this question with a resounding “Yes.” In contrast, passage B concludes that markets are not inherently reliable. So, passage B would answer this question with a defiant “No.”

choices.text: Are opinions more likely to be true when people will stake money on them?
choices.rationale: A test-taker relying on their anticipation would likely note that this answer choice didn't mention anything about the “reliability” of markets and would eliminate this option without much thought. To other test-takers, however, this answer choice may be tempting because it describes a topic both passages address. However, both passages bring up this topic to support the main points; this topic is not the main point.

choices.text: Are markets that are engineered to predict election results as efficient as actual stock markets?
choices.rationale: “Stock markets” were merely an example of a market in passage A, but stock markets were never explicitly mentioned in passage B. Moreover, neither passage compares the efficiency of stock markets to that of prediction markets. Passage B doesn't even bring up the topic of efficiency at all.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: The purpose of passage A and the purpose of passage B, respectively, are to

choices.text: persuade and inform
choices.rationale: “Persuade” and “inform” are not contrasting descriptions we'd expect from a passage with an Opposing Viewpoints Meta-Structure. Moreover, “inform” as a purpose suggests the author is taking a passive role in the passage — that the author just wants to convey facts, not opinions. That's a poor description of passage B, which definitely wants to convince us that markets aren't as reliable or predictive as many believe.

choices.text: challenge and defend
choices.rationale: “Challenge” and “defend” are antonymic, at least. However, the author of passage A isn't challenging the use of markets in any way. According to passage B's characterization (PB, P1, S2), passage A asserts the conventional view on markets. And passage B's author is definitely not attempting to “defend” markets. So while these two words do reflect the opposing viewpoints, it gets the words backward. Remember, we were looking for an answer choice in which the first word connotes a positive view and the second word connotes a skeptical one.

choices.text: present and interpret
choices.rationale: “Present” and “interpret” are not contrasting descriptions we'd expect from a passage with an Opposing Viewpoints Meta-Structure. Moreover, “present” as a purpose suggests the author is taking a passive role — that the author just wants to convey facts, not opinions. That's a poor description of passage A's author, who definitely wants to convince us that markets are very reliable and efficient.

choices.text: entertain and educate
choices.rationale: “Entertain” and “educate” are not exactly the contrasting descriptions we'd expect from a passage with an Opposing Viewpoints Meta-Structure. Moreover, “entertain” as a purpose is a poor description of passage A. There's very little use of humor, analogy, or anecdote that might get used in a passage that wants to entertain. (“Entertain” might be a more apt description of passage B, which uses several offbeat comparisons and word choices — like “get over it,” “nag,” and “random spoofing.” Still, the primary purpose is to convey doubt about the reliability of markets, not to entertain the reader.)

choices.text: advocate and deflate
choices.rationale: “Advocate” and “deflate” are the contrasting descriptions we'd expect from a passage with an Opposing Viewpoints Meta-Structure. Plus, “advocate” connotes a positive view about markets — passage A's author definitely wants to advocate for the reliability and efficiency of markets — and “deflate” connotes a skeptical view — passage B's author intends to deflate economists' beliefs about the reliability of markets. This matches our prediction, and it is correct.

questions.stem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to agree on which one of the following statements about markets?

choices.text: They are a much better predictor of future events than any expert.
choices.rationale: The author of passage A probably agrees with this statement. We can infer that view when that author notes that markets don't benefit the opinions of anyone with “the most degrees after their name” (PA, P1, S3). However, the author of passage B has no express opinion on this issue. The issue of expertise is never brought up or alluded to in that passage. And based on the author of passage B's general view on the reliability of markets, they'd be far more likely to disagree with this statement than to agree with it. Because the latter author has no opinion on this answer choice, it is incorrect.

choices.text: They move in completely random and unpredictable ways.
choices.rationale: Both authors probably disagree with this sentiment. The author of passage A claims that markets are very efficient — they quickly and accurately reflect what informed people know (PA, P3, S1). So markets are not erratic; instead, markets move toward the truth that only “insiders” know about. And the author of passage B claims, in the analogy to racetracks, that markets move predictably. As the author implies in that analogy, the markets reflect the general opinion about an asset's “health” or value (PB, P3). When the asset begins to look more valuable, the market will reflect that. Since both authors would disagree with this statement, this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: They are easily manipulated for long periods by people with inside knowledge.
choices.rationale: Although the author of passage A discusses the effect people with “inside knowledge” can have on markets, that author never claims that such people can “easily manipulate” markets “for long periods.” In fact, that author likely believes the opposite; in the third paragraph, they discuss the efficiency with which inside information becomes reflected in market prices. And passage B's author never brings up “inside knowledge.” Either of these issues would be enough to eliminate this answer choice.

choices.text: They are affected by new information as it becomes publicly available.
choices.rationale: We can infer that both authors think markets are affected by new information becoming public. In the study cited in the third paragraph, passage A's author suggests that when certain “insiders” begin trading with new information, that information affects how others buy and sell on markets. As that author puts it, “within seconds, everyone was acting as if they were insiders” (PA, P3, S5). And the author of passage B claims, in the analogy to racetracks, that markets respond to new information. As the author implies in that analogy, the markets change based on the general opinion about an asset's “health” or value (PB, P3). When the asset starts to look more valuable, the market will reflect that. Since both authors agree with this statement, this answer choice is correct.

choices.text: They are no better at predicting elections than most polls are.
choices.rationale: Both authors would disagree with this statement, making this answer choice incorrect. Both claim that markets are at least somewhat more reliable than polls, as markets require people to back up their opinions with money (PA, P1, S2; PB, P4, S4). So neither author would claim that markets are “no better” at predicting elections than polls.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: The relationship between which one of the following pairs of essays, based on what can be inferred from their titles, is most analogous to the relationship between passage A and passage B, respectively?

choices.text: "The Future of Computing" and "Futurists' Sorry Track Record"
choices.rationale: A time-saving test-taker would likely eliminate this one solely on the first title. Passage A's main point isn't analogous to “The Future of Computing.” Passage A is all about the present reliability of the markets — it's not about what the markets might look like in the future. So while “Futurists' Sorry Track Record” may match the skepticism in passage B, we can eliminate this answer choice based on the first title alone.

choices.text: "Computer Models for Predicting Elections" and "Margins of Error in Prediction of Electoral Results"
choices.rationale: “Computer Models for Predicting Elections” matches the second paragraph of passage A — arguably, it's too close a match since analogous titles rarely match the subject matter this closely. However, this doesn't quite reflect passage A's main point, which was all about the author's trust in the reliability of markets. Nothing in this title suggests the author trusts computer models to predict elections. Moreover, “Margins of Errors in Prediction of Election Results” doesn't match passage B's distrust of or skepticism toward markets. In other words, this doesn't reflect the oppositional relationship of the two passages, and it is incorrect.

choices.text: "The Pace of Computer Innovation" and "Will Computing Hit a Speed Bump?"
choices.rationale: This is another answer choice that doesn't quite match the oppositional relationship of passages A and B. “The Pace of Computer Innovation” doesn't exhibit passage A's advocacy for markets' reliability, while “Will Computing Hit a Speed Bump?” doesn't quite evince passage B's skepticism toward markets. With a slight tweak we could make this more analogous to the passages (“The Remarkable Pace of Computer Innovation” and “The Lack of Innovation in Computing”), but it is incorrect as written.

choices.text: "Computer Simulations of Stock Prices" and "Program Outperforms Fund Managers"
choices.rationale: A time-conscious test-taker might quickly eliminate this for at least one of two reasons. First, its subject matter — stock markets — is far too close to the passages'. Analogous titles rarely match the subject matter this closely. Second, and more importantly, “Computer Simulations of Stock Prices” and “Program Outperforms Fund Managers” do not embody the oppositional relationship of the two passages. “Computer Simulations of Stock Prices” suggests a far more descriptive (and less opinionated) passage than the author of passage A wrote. And “Program Outperforms Fund Managers” takes a far more positive stance towards its subject than the author of passage B.

choices.text: "Computers as Thinking Machines" and "Computers Don't Think: They Execute Programs"
choices.rationale: This is the only answer choice in which the titles mirror the oppositional relationship of the two passages. “Computers As Thinking Machines” describes a belief in the reliability of its subject matter, while “Computers Don't Think: They Execute Programs” expresses skepticism toward that same topic. This is what we were looking for and is correct.

questions.stem: Passage B, but not passage A, advances its argument in part by referring to which one of the following?

choices.text: market crashes
choices.rationale: Do you remember reading anything about “market crashes” in either passage? Probably not. A time-conscious test-taker might take that lack of memory as a tell-tale sign that “market crashes” were not mentioned in either passage. If you really wanted to check, reviewing the passage would reveal that the topic of “crashes” was not mentioned at all.

choices.text: racetracks
choices.rationale: The third paragraph of passage B compares markets to racetracks. This analogy shows how passage B's author thinks markets just reflect the general opinion about an asset's “health” or value (PB, P3). The author of passage A thinks markets are far more predictive than this, so it's unsurprising that passage A never mentions racetracks when making its argument. So, this answer choice presents a detail included in passage B but not A, and it is correct.

choices.text: insiders
choices.rationale: “Insiders” is a concept described in passage A (PA, P3) but not in B. This makes (C) incorrect.

choices.text: polls
choices.rationale: We noted that the authors agree on markets' superiority to polls (PA, P1, S2; PB, P4, S4), so we can quickly eliminate this answer choice.

choices.text: contracts
choices.rationale: Do you remember reading anything about “contracts” in passage B? Probably not. A time-conscious test-taker might take that lack of memory as a tell-tale sign that “contracts” were not mentioned in passage B. In fact, the topic of “contracts” was only mentioned in passage A, in its description of the Iowa Electronic Markets.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Suppose that, in an attempt to manipulate the Iowa Electronic Markets, several people invest large sums in contracts for long-shot candidate X. The price of contracts for X briefly spikes, but well-informed traders promptly sell their contracts for X at a profit, and the effect of the investments quickly vanishes. This outcome would tend to support

choices.text: passage A, since it shows that contracts for an initially unpopular candidate cannot have a sustained increase in value
choices.rationale: Passage A never claims that initially unpopular candidates cannot have a sustained increase in value. According to passage A, if the initially unpopular candidate has an increasingly high chance of winning an election, their value should increase in a prediction market. Since this is not a claim passage A asserts, this cannot be the correct answer.

choices.text: passage A, since it provides evidence that accurate information is quickly and accurately disseminated throughout the market
choices.rationale: This is just what we predicted, and it is correct. This hypothetical supports passage A because it shows that markets are efficient, meaning they disperse accurate information quickly throughout the market.

choices.text: neither passage, since the attempt at manipulation was so unsuccessful and short-lived that it proves nothing
choices.rationale: This hypothetical supports passage A. An expert test-taker likely wouldn't read past “neither passage.” Moreover, the fact that manipulation was “unsuccessful and short-lived” could support either passage. If the manipulation was short-lived because accurate information was disseminated quickly throughout the market, it would support passage A. If the manipulation was short-lived because people remained convinced that the long-shot candidate couldn't win and acted accordingly, it would support passage B.

choices.text: passage B, because it shows that a losing candidate can be temporarily ahead of the winning candidate
choices.rationale: This hypothetical supports passage A. An expert test-taker likely wouldn't read past “passage B.” Moreover, this answer choice seems to suggest that the point of passage B was that prediction markets are inherently inaccurate; however, passage B never made such a claim. Passage B instead claimed that such markets are unreliable because they merely reflect the general opinion (which is sometimes accurate and sometimes inaccurate). And, to point out one final issue with this answer choice, this question stem never said the “long-shot” candidate was the “losing” candidate.

choices.text: passage B, because it shows that the market simply reflects majority opinion in the population as a whole
choices.rationale: This hypothetical supports passage A. An expert test-taker likely wouldn't read past “passage B.” Plus, this hypothetical doesn't suggest that the market merely reflects the majority opinion of the population. The price for the long-shot candidate didn't rise because more people suddenly thought the candidate would win — it was just through market “manipulation.”

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: The relation between the conception in passage A and the conception in passage B, respectively, of how markets handle the knowledge of their participants, is most analogous to the relation between

choices.text: a typewriter and a word processor
choices.rationale: What are the differences between a typewriter and a word processor? A typewriter is slower, older, and produces more permanent outcomes than a word processor. This doesn't reflect the contrast in how knowledge is described in the two passages, so this is incorrect.

choices.text: a thermostat and a thermometer
choices.rationale: What's the difference between a thermostat and a thermometer? A thermostat produces changes in the temperature, while a thermometer merely records the current temperature. This is very similar to how each passage characterizes knowledge. Passage A argues that knowledge can change the market, while passage B thinks markets are a mere measurement of knowledge. This is the correct answer.

choices.text: a bicycle and a motorcycle
choices.rationale: What's the difference between a bicycle and a motorcycle? Bicycles are older, slower, safer, and powered by the user rather than by gasoline or electricity. This doesn't reflect the contrast in how knowledge is described in the two passages, so this is incorrect.

choices.text: a news broadcast and a magazine
choices.rationale: What's the difference between a news broadcast and a magazine? News broadcasts, unlike magazines, are a more recent medium, include an audio and televisual component, and are more responsive. This doesn't reflect the contrast in how knowledge is described in the two passages, so this is incorrect.

choices.text: a digital camera and a camera that uses film
choices.rationale: What's the difference between a digital camera and film camera? Digital cameras are newer, feature more storage, and provide more immediate and malleable results. This doesn't reflect the contrast in how knowledge is described in the two passages, so this is incorrect.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Classifying biological populations into different species has long posed problems for proponents of biodiversity, but many of these problems are closer to resolution thanks to the work of Charles G. Sibley and others.
choices.rationale: This answer choice attempts to assert the primacy of Charles G. Sibley. Sibley wasn't the most important subject in this passage — the debate itself was — nor did Sibley help resolve this debate. (Arguably, Sibley's controversy has only made the debate harder to reconcile.) So this answer choice completely mischaracterizes the subject of the passage and Sibley's role therein, so it is wrong.

choices.text: Although scientists often disagree on the classification of biological populations into species, most agree that all such classification systems contain arbitrary elements.
choices.rationale: There are two scientists who note that classification systems are arbitrary, both mentioned in the third paragraph. There's the scientist who criticized Charles G. Sibley, and there's Sibley. Unless this passage was written in some alternative universe in which there are only three scientists, that's not enough scientists to account for “most” scientists. This answer choice also over-emphasizes the discussion of classification systems' arbitrary nature, which was confined to just the third paragraph.

choices.text: How biological populations are classified into species is a controversial scientific issue with practical implications in current debates over the preservation of biodiversity.
choices.rationale: This answer choice asserts that there is a debate (or, in this answer choice's terms, a “controversial scientific issue”), as is often the case when the passage utilizes a Describe a Debate Meta-Structure. It also includes the author's conclusion from the final paragraph: that resolving this debate has “practical implications.” Some test-takers might take issue with the reference to “the preservation of biodiversity,” but this topic was raised by the author in the first sentence. Because this answer choice includes both the debate and the author's view, it best captures the main point.

choices.text: Traditional methods of classifying biological populations into species continue to have their supporters, but these methods have been called into question by the work of Charles G. Sibley.
choices.rationale: Another answer choice that over-emphasizes the role of Charles G. Sibley in this passage. The main focus of this passage was not Sibley's work or his revisions to classification systems. Instead, the focus was the debate. Sibley was merely an example of someone on one side of the debate.

choices.text: Charles G. Sibley developed revolutionary methods of classifying biological populations into species, but these methods have not been widely accepted.
choices.rationale: Yet again, this answer choice places too much weight on the role of one Charles G. Sibley. The discussion of Charles G. Sibley was confined to the second and third paragraphs. This answer choice is missing the larger debate described in the first paragraph and the author's views conveyed by the last paragraph.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which one of the following is true of the phylogenetic species concept?

choices.text: It has effectively discredited other methods of species classification.
choices.rationale: If the splitters effectively “discredited” other methods of species classification, that would mean the debate was effectively resolved. We know the debate is still ongoing, so we can eliminate this without reviewing the passage.

choices.text: Its popularity has declined since the death of Charles G. Sibley.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading anything about Charles G. Sibley's death or a decline in splitters' popularity? Probably not. (If anything, test-takers will recall that the splitters' approach is becoming increasingly popular.) If you don't remember reading about a detail, simply defer and move on to the next answer choice. If you did review the passage, you'd see that their approach is described as “increasingly popular” (P1, S6).

choices.text: It is more useful in ornithology than in most other biological sciences.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading anything about biological sciences other than ornithology? Probably not. If you don't remember reading about a detail, simply defer and move on to the next answer choice. If you did review the passage, you wouldn't find any references to other biological sciences.

choices.text: It has more proponents now than it had in the past.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading anything about the number of “splitter” proponents? Perhaps not, but at least two references might allow you to remember this fact. First, when describing the “lumpers,” the author notes that that was the “dominant approach” until recently (P1, S4). That suggests the alternative approach, the splitters', is getting more popular and thus has more proponents. Second, the author notes that the splitters' approach is getting “increasingly popular” (P1, S6). This confirms that the splitters approach now has more proponents. So whether you recalled that this answer choice was supported, or you found that confirmation after deferring on or eliminating the rest of the answer choices, this is the answer choice that must be true based on the passage.

choices.text: It was pioneered by Charles G. Sibley.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading that Charles G. Sibley pioneered the splitters' approach? Probably not. If you don't remember reading about a detail, simply defer and move on to the next answer choice. If you did review the passage, you would only see that author says Charles G. Sibley “could” be called a splitter, which would suggest that he has a tangential relationship with that group and that he didn't pioneer it.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that Charles G. Sibley would have been most likely to agree with which one of the following views?

choices.text: Splitters are somewhat more likely than lumpers to be motivated by political and economic, rather than purely scientific, concerns.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading that Charles G. Sibley's views on “lumpers,” or of political or economic motivations at all? Probably not. If you don't remember reading about a detail, simply defer and move on to the next answer choice. If you did review the passage, you wouldn't find any commentary on lumpers' motives from Sibley.

choices.text: The total number of animal species in the world today is probably accurately estimated.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading that Charles G. Sibley claimed that the total number of species in the world today is “accurately estimated”? Probably not. In fact, you may believe the opposite is true. If Sibley is making controversial and major revisions to the previously dominant “lumpers” theory, it's unlikely that he thinks the consensus view of species classification is accurate. That's enough to eliminate, rather than defer on, this answer choice.

choices.text: A proper goal for ornithologists engaged in taxonomic research is to simplify the classification system so as to reduce the total number of species.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading that Charles G. Sibley wanted to simplify the classification system or reduce the total number of species? Probably not. In fact, you may recall that the author says that Sibley belongs to the “splitters,” who are increasing, not reducing, the total number of species (P2, S1). That's enough to eliminate, rather than defer on, this answer choice.

choices.text: The degree of genetic difference that two populations display with respect to each other should have little bearing on the decision about whether to classify them as belonging to the same species.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading that Charles G. Sibley didn't think genetic similarities between populations should affect how we classify species? Probably not. In fact, you may remember that the author notes that Sibley is a “splitter,” and they are all about using genetic similarities to classify species (P1, S7). And you may also remember that Sibley uses DNA in his classification system (P2, S2), which certainly involves species’ genes. That's enough to eliminate, rather than defer on, this answer choice.

choices.text: Disagreements about species classification are likely to persist even if techniques like DNA-DNA hybridization are further refined.
choices.rationale: We've seen four unpromising answer choices, so hopefully this one looks good. So do we recall reading anything about Charles G. Sibley's views on disagreements about species classification? Perhaps. In his defense of his DNA-DNA hybridization approach, he notes that “the 'species concept' is slippery because there are so many examples in nature of populations that refuse to fit our limited set of definitions and names” (P3, S5). So he believes that classifying species is “slippery,” and that nature always is more complicated than “our limited set of definitions and names.” So even if his DNA-DNA hybridization approach improved, it would still rely on limited definitions and names, so disagreements could still persist. This answer choice has textual support, and unlike (B) through (D), it doesn't explicitly contradict Sibley's views. Therefore, this answer choice is correct.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately illustrates the biological species concept, as described in the passage?

choices.text: There is strong evidence that bird populations X and Y share a common ancestor. Therefore, they should be classified as belonging to the same species, even though they do not resemble each other in certain respects.
choices.rationale: We are looking for a situation involving interbreeding bird populations. This doesn't discuss interbreeding at all. A time-savvy test-taker would eliminate this without reservation, especially if they remembered that this illustrates the phylogenetic approach taken by the “splitters,” not the biological species concept used by the “lumpers.”

choices.text: Bird populations X and Y interbreed in the wild, but they have never been known to do so in captivity. Therefore, they should be classified as belonging to different species.
choices.rationale: This answer choice at least mentions interbreeding, so it warrants a closer inspection. However, it says that the populations interbreed in the wild. Based on the biological approach, these populations should be classified as the same species, irrespective of how they interbreed in captivity. For this reason, this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: Bird populations X and Y are visually indistinguishable from each other and live in similar, though mutually isolated, habitats. Therefore, they should be classified as belonging to the same species.
choices.rationale: We are looking for a situation involving interbreeding bird populations. This doesn't discuss interbreeding at all. A time-conscious test-taker would eliminate this without a second thought. Some test-takers who made a less precise anticipation may overthink the answer choice’s reference to being “isolated.” However, the passage referred to isolation as “reproductive isolation,” which was defined as two non-interbreeding species (P1, S5).

choices.text: Although bird populations X and Y have differently shaped beaks and head feathers, they nevertheless interbreed. Therefore, they should be classified as belonging to the same species.
choices.rationale: We were looking for a situation in which two bird populations interbreed and are classified as the same species, and this answer choice states exactly that. Don't overthink the morphological dissimilarities — we only need to focus on the interbreeding part.

choices.text: Although bird populations X and Y have never been known to interbreed, they resemble each other in appearance, and examination of their DNA indicates a common ancestor. Therefore, they should be classified as belonging to the same species.
choices.rationale: This answer choice at least mentions interbreeding, so it warrants a closer inspection. However, it says that the populations don't interbreed in the wild. Based on the biological approach, these populations should be classified as different species, irrespective of their morphological or genetic similarities. For this reason, this answer choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: If valid, Charles G. Sibley's findings, as described in the last two sentences of the second paragraph, most seriously challenge which one of the following assertions?

choices.text: A stork population from Europe is likely to be of the same species as one from North America.
choices.rationale: The correct answer will either say a North or South American vulture is related to a European vulture or that loons and grebes are related. This is all about the relationship between European and North American storks. A time-conscious test-taker would quickly jettison this choice and move on.

choices.text: A stork population from South America is likely to be of a different species than one from Europe.
choices.rationale: The correct answer will either say a North or South American vulture is related to a European vulture or that loons and grebes are related. This is all about the relationship between European and South American storks. An expedient test-taker would quickly eliminate this choice and move on to the next one.

choices.text: A vulture population from North America is likely to be of the same species as one from Europe.
choices.rationale: Just as we predicted: an answer choice that says a North American vulture is related to a European vulture. There is no need to second-guess or double-check — select this and move on.

choices.text: A vulture population from South America is likely to be of a different species than one from Europe.
choices.rationale: Assuming they didn't select (C) and move on, an efficient test-taker would quickly note that this is consistent with the first example of Charles G. Sibley's findings, and move on.

choices.text: A vulture population from North America is likely to be of the same species as one from South America.
choices.rationale: Assuming they didn't select (C) and move on, an efficient test-taker would quickly note that Charles G. Sibley's findings aren't inconsistent with this assertion. Sibley didn't note whether North and South American vultures were the same species, only that each was more closely related to storks than to European vultures.

questions.stem: The passage provides information sufficient to answer which one of the following questions?

choices.text: When did Charles G. Sibley begin using DNA-DNA hybridization in species classification?
choices.rationale: Dates tend to stick out in passages. A quick glance at the second paragraph would confirm no dates mentioned were there. So the passage does not provide the information needed to answer this question. We can eliminate this.

choices.text: What are two continents on which storks are found?
choices.rationale: We just answered Question 19, which required us to review the reference to storks in the second paragraph. Although we learned that vultures are found in the Americas and Europe, we never were told which continents storks can be found. So the passage does not provide the information needed to answer this question. We can eliminate this.

choices.text: What common traits led taxonomists to classify loons and grebes as related species?
choices.rationale: We just answered Question 19, which required us to review the reference to the commonly held belief that loons and grebes are related. But in our review, we never learned why loons and grebes are thought to be related. So the passage does not provide the information needed to answer this question. We can eliminate this.

choices.text: What is one objection to applying Sibley's work to species classification questions?
choices.rationale: The existence of at least “one objection” to Sibley's work is certainly consistent with the main point of this passage. If there's a debate between “lumpers” and “splitters” like Sibley, then there will be a few objections among the parties. Reviewing our notes, if necessary, we can see the beginning of the third paragraph describes one objection to Sibley's approach — that it's “arbitrary” (P3, S2). So the passage provides enough information to answer this question, making this the correct answer.

choices.text: What is one non-avian animal population on whose classification lumpers and splitters have disagreed?
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading anything about non-avian (non-bird) species? Probably not. Assuming they hadn't already selected (D) and moved on, an expedient test-taker would defer on this choice and look for support for (D) (which is consistent with the main point) in the passage. And any search for references to non-avain species would be in vain, as no such references were made in this passage.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a proponent of the biological species concept would be most likely to disagree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: There are considerably more bird species in the world today than are currently recognized.
choices.rationale: We know that lumpers want to “lump,” or group, similar bird populations together. So, lumpers almost certainly do not think there are “considerably more bird species” than we currently recognize. They either think that there should be fewer bird species than we currently recognize or (since their view is dominant) the right number of bird species. Therefore, this assertion is something the lumpers would disagree with, making this the correct answer.

choices.text: Members of two bird populations that differ from each other in certain physical characteristics might nevertheless belong to the same species.
choices.rationale: Assuming they didn't select (A) and simply move on to the last question, a time-savvy test-taker would quickly eliminate this. The lumpers think that bird populations are the same species if they interbreed. They do not base their decisions solely on the birds' physical attributes. So, physically dissimilar bird populations could be part of the same species — as long as those birds interbreed.

choices.text: Some animal species that are considered extinct in fact have surviving members.
choices.rationale: Assuming they didn't select (A) and simply move on to the last question, an efficient test-taker would eliminate this without much consideration. “Extinction” was not a topic most would remember reading about; an efficient test-taker would take that as a sign that “extinction” was not in the passage and that this claim was not something we know the lumpers would disagree with.

choices.text: There is less biodiversity in the world today than there was 50 years ago.
choices.rationale: Assuming they didn't select (A) and simply move on to the last question, a fast-moving test-taker would eliminate this without thinking twice. Such a test-taker would note that “biodiversity” was a topic only the author broached in this passage. For that reason, we can't say that the lumpers would disagree with this claim.

choices.text: Current debates over what constitutes a species are sometimes motivated by political rather than by scientific concerns.
choices.rationale: Assuming they didn't select (A) and simply move on to the last question, a speedy test-taker would quickly eliminate this. Such a test-taker would probably not remember reading about “political” motivations and would take that as a sign that this topic was not in the passage at all. So, they'd (correctly) conclude we cannot say whether the lumpers would disagree with this answer choice's claim.

questions.subtype: Applying the Argument to New Contexts
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would provide the strongest support for the author's assertion in the final sentence of the passage about the effects of increasing the number of recognized species?

choices.text: It is becoming increasingly difficult to enact international agreements to protect endangered species.
choices.rationale: The author didn't make any claims about actually protecting endangered species, so this is irrelevant to the author's assertion.

choices.text: Increasing the number of species through reclassification is more likely to result in new avian species than in new mammalian species.
choices.rationale: Even if it's true that reclassifying species will create more bird populations than mammal populations, it doesn't necessarily follow that more species will need protection following reclassification. And that's because this doesn't address the part vs. whole issue. If the lumper-defined species considered endangered each have only one population regarded as endangered, it wouldn't matter how many new species we made after reclassification. Even if we split the species up as finely as possible, to the point that each population is now considered a new species, we still wouldn't increase the number of endangered species.

choices.text: In disputes over protection of endangered species, economic considerations often outweigh scientific ones.
choices.rationale: This is wrong for the same reason as (A). The author didn't make a claim about how easy it will be to actually protect the species. The author only asserted that the number of species that need protection will increase. So, this answer choice is irrelevant to the author's assertion at the end of the passage.

choices.text: Advances in scientific techniques like DNA-DNA hybridization will probably favor the efforts of proponents of the phylogenetic species concept.
choices.rationale: So what? The author never claimed that the most likely result of species reclassification is more species. The author just said that if there are more species, there will probably need to be more species needing protection. Another irrelevant answer choice.

choices.text: Proponents of the phylogenetic species concept are less likely to contest an established species classification if none of the biological populations involved is endangered.
choices.rationale: This answer choice fixes one of the problems we identified. We identified one situation in which increasing the number of species might not result in more species needing protection. As described in the final paragraph of that section, let's assume the lumpers grouped the populations A, B, and C into one species, but none of populations A, B, or C were regarded as endangered. In that case, the lumpers wouldn't think the species as a whole needed protection. Even if the splitters came along and divided that species into three new species, none of the new species would need protection either. This answer choice fixes this issue by saying that the splitters wouldn't both reclassify the lumpers' A/B/C species. So the only times the splitters would reclassify species is when the species has one or more endangered populations. This would make it more likely that increasing the number of species through “splitting” would result in more species needing protection. Therefore, this strengthens the argument, and it is the correct answer.

questions.subtype: Identifying Main Points and Primary Purposes
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.text: Although patent protection is needed for a software program's underlying algorithms, existing copyright laws adequately protect the expression of those algorithms.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker wouldn't need to read past “patent protection is needed.” That's the exact opposite sentiment the author expresses in this passage, so this can be eliminated without further reading. If you did, you would also note it claims “existing copyright laws adequately protect” software programs' algorithms, which conflicts with the author's assertion that algorithms don’t need protection and the claim at the end of the passage that protection of software requires a “slight modification to existing laws.”

choices.text: Legal protection for software programs beyond that which could be provided through the modification of existing copyright laws is unwarranted.
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes the authors' resolution of the debate accurately — that we only need to modify existing copyright law to protect software programs. Some test takers may take issue with this choice because it doesn't explicitly mention patent law. But that is not an issue here, since the reference to legal protection “beyond that which could be provided through ... copyright laws” would naturally include patent law. So patent law is acknowledged by this answer choice tacitly.

choices.text: Without the legal protection afforded by patents, software developers will have little financial incentive to innovate.
choices.rationale: The author argues the opposite of this — that patent law is not needed to protect software developers' financial incentive to develop innovative software.

choices.text: Issuing patents for software programs would give software developers more protection against copycat programming than granting copyright does.
choices.rationale: This is the third answer choice to suggest that the author prefers or sees merit in using patent law to protect software. The author claimed that there's “no compelling justification” for such protection (P3, S1), so we can cast off this choice.

choices.text: Copyright protects only the unique manner in which a software program's underlying algorithms are expressed.
choices.rationale: This is true, but it's not the author's main point. The author's main point was that this copyright protection is the only legal protection needed to maintain the financial incentive to create innovative software.

questions.stem: On the basis of the passage, which one of the following is most likely to be a view held by the author?

choices.text: An algorithm is analogous to a law of nature or a logical axiom.
choices.rationale: This doesn't conflict with the author's main point. Remember, the author thinks that patent protection should not cover computers' software or constituent algorithms. And, whether we can recall the following fact on our own or need to consult our notes or the passage, we can recall that patents do not protect laws of nature or logical axioms (P2, S5). So, there's reason to believe that the author thinks that algorithms are similar to laws of nature and logical axioms. An efficient test-taker may note that this answer choice was consistent with the author's main point and is probably correct. Then, they'd look to see if they could eliminate the remaining answer choices without reviewing the passage before returning and selecting this answer choice. If they weren't able to eliminate the remaining choices, they could return to the passage and find the reference to laws of nature and logical axioms in the third paragraph. They'd see that the text supports the inference that the author believes algorithms are similar to laws of nature and logical axioms. They'd notice how the author says, after claiming that patents do not protect laws of nature and logical axioms, that patents shouldn't protect algorithms “[o]n similar grounds” (P2, S7). There, the author draws a line connecting algorithms to laws of nature and logical axioms, making this the correct answer.

choices.text: The discovery of an algorithm that can be used in a software program usually requires genuine inventive effort.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the author's main point. Remember, the author does not think that patent protection should cover computers' software or constituent algorithms. We should also recall that patents cover “genuine inventive efforts.” So the author almost certainly disagrees with this sentiment, and it should be eliminated without consulting the passage.

choices.text: Sequences of computer code should not be copyrightable unless they encode a previously unused algorithm.
choices.rationale: Do you remember reading anything about copyright requiring algorithms to be “previously unused”? Probably not. A risk-averse test-taker might defer on this answer choice. On the other hand, a more risk-accepting test-taker would take that as a sign that this topic was not discussed in the passage, so we cannot say whether the author agrees with it. And if you did eventually review the passage, you wouldn't find any references to “previously unused algorithms.”

choices.text: Proponents of software patents underestimate the severity of the problem of copycat programming.
choices.rationale: This conflicts with the main point. The author didn't think patent proponents underestimated the risk of copycat programming or that patent protection was inadequate to deter copycat programming. The author acknowledges that patent and copyright proponents seek to protect software innovators from copycat programmers (P1, S4). The author's main point was that patent protection is unnecessary to accomplish this goal. So the author almost certainly disagrees with this sentiment, and it should be eliminated without consulting the passage.

choices.text: The encoding of algorithms is not analogous to the composition of a literary work.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading about “literary works”? Probably not. If you don't remember reading about a detail, simply defer and move on to the next answer choice. A risk-averse test-taker might defer on this answer choice. On the other hand, a more risk-accepting test-taker would take that as a sign that this topic was not discussed in the passage, so we cannot say whether the author agrees with it. And if you did eventually review the passage, you wouldn't find any comparisons to literary works.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the assertion that software programs constitute the expression of ideas in the form of specific texts functions primarily as

choices.text: an example of a counterintuitive claim
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says the claim from the question stem is there to advance the author's conclusion. This answer choice does not say that, so it should be quickly crossed off. If you wanted another reason to eliminate this choice, a “counterintuitive claim” means the claim is inconsistent with commonly held beliefs or common-sense expectations. The author did not discuss any such claims in the third paragraph.

choices.text: a rationale for the author's position
choices.rationale: “Rationale” just means “reason” in this context. The author included the claim from the question stem to provide a reason for their position. This is correct.

choices.text: a causal explanation for a particular phenomenon
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says the claim from the question stem is there to advance the author's conclusion. This answer choice does not say that, so we should eliminate it without reservation. If you wanted another reason to get rid of this choice, there are no causal claims or phenomena described in this paragraph.

choices.text: a layperson's definition of a technical legal term
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says the claim from the question stem is there to advance the author's conclusion. This answer choice does not say that, so we should cross it off without giving it a second thought. But if you wanted another reason to eliminate this answer choice, a "layperson's definition" simply refers to a definition that could be understood by a non-expert. Such definitions generally use simplified language or analogies to commonly understood concepts. The statement from the question stem uses neither, so we have no reason to believe that this was intended to be a "layperson's definition."

choices.text: a point of consensus between opposing viewpoints
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that says the claim from the question stem is there to advance the author's conclusion. This answer choice does not say that, so we should rule it out. And, of course, the author does the exact opposite of finding a point of consensus between opposing viewpoints in the third paragraph. The author uses the third paragraph to conclude that one side is wrong and the other is right.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, it can be inferred that proponents of software patents are most likely to hold which one of the following views?

choices.text: The sequences of computer code through which a computer programmer expresses algorithms are more genuinely a product of the programmer's inventiveness than the underlying algorithms are.
choices.rationale: Do you recall reading that the patent proponents thought that coding was more inventive than creating the algorithms? Probably not. If you don't remember reading about a detail, simply defer and move on to the next answer choice. If you did review the passage, you wouldn't find any support for this claim. The pro-patent folks claimed that encoding algorithms was “analogous to the design of a process” and thus fell under patent law, which covers processes that are the products of invention (P2, S3-S5).
