Many test-takers will anticipate the correct answer to say, “Some types of honey that are unusually high in antioxidants are made from sage nectar.” But it is equally valid to say, “Some types of honey that are made from sage nectar are unusually high in antioxidants.” And that is because “some” statements are reversible. Claiming that some types of honey that are unusually high in antioxidants are made from sage nectar is equivalent to saying there's at least one type of honey that is both high in antioxidants are made from sage nectar. If that's true, then it must also be true that there's at least one type of honey that is both made from sage nectar and high in antioxidants.

choices.text: Most plants produce nectar that, when harvested by bees, results in light-colored honey.
choices.rationale: Is there anything in the passage that discusses the nectar produced from “most plants”? No. We don't know that most plants produce nectar, and we certainly don't know what colored honey the nectar from these plants would produce. We only know some plants that produce sage nectar, which results in light-colored honey when harvested. Therefore, we don't have any support to draw this conclusion, and this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: Light-colored honey tends to be more healthful than dark honey.
choices.rationale: We know that at least one type of light-colored honey is very healthful. But we can't use that single example to conclude that light-colored honey tends to be more healthful than dark-colored honey. That would be an unsupported generalization. (Experienced test-takers will recognize this as a sampling flaw.) In fact, we know that dark-colored honey tends to have more antioxidants than light-colored honey, which suggests (although not definitively) that the dark-colored varieties are generally more healthful than their light-colored counterparts.

choices.text: Certain strains of honey produced by bees harvesting primarily sage nectar are unusually low in antioxidants.
choices.rationale: We can validly conclude that some types of honey harvested from sage nectar are unusually high in antioxidants. But there are a few reasons why that does not imply that some of these types are unusually low in antioxidants. First, “some” statements do not exclude the possibility of “all.” Even though the passage just said “certain” strains of honey from sage nectar are healthful, and thus high in antioxidants, it could be the case that “all” strains of honey from sage nectar are healthful and thus high in antioxidants. Second, even if some strains of honey from sage nectar weren't high in antioxidants, that doesn't necessarily mean they must be unusually low in antioxidants. They could simply have an average or slightly below-average amount of antioxidants. (Experienced test-takers will recognize this as an exclusivity flaw.)

choices.text: The strain of honey that has the highest antioxidant content is a light-colored honey.
choices.rationale: We can validly conclude that some light-colored types of honey are unusually high in antioxidants. But that doesn't imply that the type of honey with the most antioxidants is light-colored. The superlative language used by this answer choice is extremely difficult to support and, unsurprisingly, the passage doesn't provide the evidence to validly infer this claim.

questions.stimulus: Dark honey tends to have a higher antioxidant content than light-colored honey, and the most healthful strains of honey are all unusually high in antioxidants. However, certain strains of honey produced by bees harvesting primarily sage nectar are among the most healthful strains of honey, even though they are also among the lightest-colored strains of honey.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the researcher's argument?

choices.text: The recommended height for computers is different for children than for adults.
choices.rationale: Even if this is true, we still don't know that elementary school children are less likely to be injured by the computers' positioning. This answer choice could weaken the researcher's argument if said office workers' computers are positioned more out of line from their recommended height. But, as written, the answer choice provides no information about how office workers' computers are positioned relative to the recommendations.

choices.text: Children spend more time working with computers at home than at school.
choices.rationale: This answer choice may tempt some test-takers, who assume that the computers schoolchildren use at home are not positioned awkwardly. However, that assumption is unfounded. It's possible that the home computers are also positioned much higher than the recommendations and that children maintain unhealthy postures on these computers too. Moreover, the conclusion is only about the school computers' effect on children. Any effect home computers have is irrelevant.

choices.text: The greater suppleness of children's bodies makes them less susceptible than adults to repetitive stress injuries.
choices.rationale: If we can get past the inherent ickiness of the phrase “suppleness,” we can see that this answer choice weakens the argument. It points out a relevant dissimilarity between schoolchildren and office workers that suggests schoolchildren are less likely to be injured by the computers. If schoolchildren are less susceptible to repetitive stress injury than adults, then the claim that children and adults are at the “same risk” of those injuries is questionable.

choices.text: Office workers' keyboards and monitors are usually not at the recommended heights for healthy postures for adults.
choices.rationale: This strengthens the argument by presenting a similarity between the computers used by schoolchildren and office workers. If office workers' computers are also not set the recommended height, they may also adopt similarly harmful postures. This could make their risk of repetitive stress injuries comparable to the school children.

choices.text: Office workers are more likely to report injuries than children are.
choices.rationale: This conclusion is about whether schoolchildren are at the same risk of injury as adults. The likelihood that schoolchildren or adults report these injuries has no bearing on whether either will actually be injured. So this answer choice has no effect on the argument.

questions.stimulus: Researcher: In a recent study of elementary school computers, we found that all keyboards and most monitors were positioned higher than recommended for children. Consequently, children were seated in ways that encouraged craned necks, awkwardly placed wrists, and other unhealthy postures. Evidently, most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on posture, and thus put children at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the sociologist's argument?

choices.text: can save those cultures capable of reflecting on their customs and envisioning alternatives
choices.rationale: This sociologist does not think the anthropologists' strategy can “save” cultures. The sociologist claims that each culture's tradition is “essential” to the culture's identity. So even if the cultures can envision and implement alternative customs, the culture would still be chipping away at its identity by eliminating customs.

choices.text: will ensure the elimination of a culture rather than prevent its decay
choices.rationale: This might read as slightly over-the-top (even histrionic) to some, but it completes the sociologists' argument with a valid conclusion. After all, the sociologist claims that each culture's tradition is “essential” to the culture's identity. That means the sociologist thinks each tradition is necessary to maintain a culture's identity. In other words, the sociologist thinks a culture's identity will vanish after removing one of its traditions. So the sociologist must believe that the anthropologists' strategy of abandoning or replacing traditions will eliminate a culture rather than preserving it. Therefore, this is the correct answer.

choices.text: can be implemented by all and only those cultures studied by anthropologists
choices.rationale: The sociologist does not think the anthropologists' strategy should be adopted by any culture. Certainly, the sociologist wouldn't conclude that every culture studied by the anthropologists should adopt this strategy.

choices.text: constitutes the most effective response to the threat of cultural decay
choices.rationale: The sociologist disagrees with the anthropologists and does not believe their strategy is a viable solution to the threat of cultural decay. So, the sociologist definitely doesn't think that their strategy is the “most effective” solution.

choices.text: can succeed if adopted by cultures whose traditions have been adopted only recently
choices.rationale: The sociologist doesn't make any distinction between recent and long-standing traditions, so we have no reason to believe that sociologist thinks that the anthropologists' strategy could work for cultures with recently adopted traditions. Perhaps if the sociologist claimed that “each of its long-standing traditions is essential to a culture's identity,” this answer choice would be an apt conclusion. Instead, the sociologist said that each tradition—irrespective of its history—is essential to a culture's identity. Therefore, we must eliminate this answer choice.

questions.stimulus: Sociologist: Some anthropologists claim that cultures can most effectively respond to the threat of cultural decay by replacing or abandoning many of their traditions so that other traditions may endure. But since each of its traditions is essential to a culture's identity, this strategy _______.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the scholar's argument by the statement that the purpose of a law is to deter certain actions by threatening to punish those performing the actions?

choices.text: It is offered in support of the implicit conclusion that a legal system needs a significant number of police officers.
choices.rationale: There is no “implicit conclusion” that a legal system needs a significant number of police officers. Although the scholar notes that people will be deterred from committing crimes only if they think they'll be caught, the scholar's solution is not to increase the number of police. It's instead to limit the number of prohibited acts.

choices.text: It is the conclusion of the argument.
choices.rationale: The last sentence is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.text: It is a premise of the argument.
choices.rationale: This is correct! The first sentence is a premise that supports the last sentence of this argument.

choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion.
choices.rationale: An intermediate (AKA subsidiary conclusion) is a statement that is supported by a premise, which in turn supports another conclusion. There is no intermediate (AKA subsidiary) conclusion in this argument. None of the premises in the first three sentences support one another. For instance, we don't need to know that threat of punishment is effective only if people think they'll be punished, or that people don't think they'll be punished when laws ban a ton of behaviors, to establish that the purpose of laws is to deter bad acts. So, each premise is an independent fact that directly supports the main conclusion.

choices.text: It is the view that the argument as a whole is designed to discredit.
choices.rationale: The scholar is not trying to argue against the claim that the purpose of laws is to deter bad acts through the threat of punishment. In fact, the author needs to establish this to draw a conclusion about a “successful legal system.”

questions.stimulus: Scholar: The purpose of a law is to deter certain actions by threatening to punish those performing the actions. This threat works only if potential violators believe that they are likely to be punished. But the likelihood that someone will be apprehended and punished for committing a prohibited act decreases as the number of types of prohibited actions increases. Therefore, a successful legal system prohibits only those few behaviors that citizens find absolutely intolerable.

questions.stem: The historian's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: fails to address adequately the possibility that the Oromo people did not use the structures as tombs
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to address” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the conclusion if true?” This answer choice wouldn't weaken the conclusion. Even if the Omoro people did not use the large-pillared and paneled-facade structures as tombs, the style of these structures could have still influenced the Swahili culture. The historian's argument wasn't about the use of the structures influencing the Swahili culture; instead, it was about the style influencing the Swahili culture.

choices.text: concludes, simply because one event occurred earlier than another event, that the first event caused the second event
choices.rationale: This answer choice gestures toward the temporal flaw, but it misdescribes how the argument is made. If an answer choice says a variation of, “Concludes, simply because ...” we need to make sure the claim that follows the “because” was a premise in the argument. But the premises never establish that “one event occurred earlier than another event in this argument.” In fact, the problem with this argument is that the historian never claimed that the Omoro people began constructing these tombs before the Swahili people. So, this answer choice misdescribes what the premises assert in this argument, making this answer choice incorrect.

choices.text: draws a restricted conclusion from premises that provide strong support for a much broader conclusion
choices.rationale: It's not a flaw to “draw a restricted conclusion” even if your premises support “a much broader conclusion.” If the premises suggested that every African civilization in the fourteenth and fifteenth century built tombs with large pillars and paneled facades, we could certainly conclude the Swahili civilization built such tombs, even though the premises would support a more expansive conclusion.

choices.text: takes for granted that there was no third civilization responsible for creating the first tombs of the kind found in both the Oromo and Swahili cultures
choices.rationale: When we see “takes for granted” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the questions we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” We don't have any evidence that the historian believes there wasn't a third civilization that first created the tombs found in the Oromo and Swahili cultures. The historian thinks that the Oromo people built these tombs first and influenced the Swahili tombs. But the historian may think another civilization constructed these tombs before the Oromo people and influenced the Oromo tombs. Remember, the historian just concludes that Oromo people influenced Swahili culture. The historian didn't conclude that the Oromo people originated this style. For this reason, this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: takes for granted that the Oromo people began constructing tombs with large pillars and paneled facades earlier than the Swahili civilization did
choices.rationale: This answer choice perfectly describes the historian's assumption. If you didn't anticipate this, and needed to assess this answer choice, you could simply ask yourself, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” The historian definitely believes the Oromo people began constructing this style of tomb first. Otherwise, the historian's conclusion that the Oromo culture influenced the Swahili culture wouldn't make any sense. And the Oromo people producing this style of tomb first would strengthen the argument, by eliminating the alternative explanation that the Swahili culture influenced the Oromo culture. Therefore, this answer choice is correct.

questions.stimulus: Historian: In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, the Swahili civilization of East Africa built tombs with large pillars and paneled facades. Such structures are widespread among the Oromo people of Somalia and Kenya, but are unknown among any other people with whom the Swahili civilization had contact. This indicates that Swahili culture was, to some extent, influenced by Oromo culture.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?

choices.text: The narrator in a novel is never deceptive.
choices.rationale: This is a tempting answer choice. It would be correct if a narrator avoiding deception implied that the narrator never introduced information that conflicts with the rest of the novel. Is that true? Not quite. A narrator can always be straightforward and still introduce information that conflicts with the rest of the novel. Perhaps the author wants to convey that the narrator is unreliable, so the author has the narrator introduce a bunch of information that conflicts with the novel's plot, setting, or characters. For this reason, this answer choice does not strengthen the argument. Moreover, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is not necessary to the argument. Suppose it was the case that the narrator is sometimes deceptive. Would this weaken the argument? Would this show that the narrator acts like a chorus, and introduces information that conflicts with the novel? Not necessarily. A narrator could be deceptive without introducing information that conflicts with the novel. The narrator could deceive the reader by, for instance, withholding information about the novel's plot, setting, or characters. Therefore, this answer choice is not necessary to the argument and is incorrect.

choices.text: The voice of a narrator is sometimes necessary in plays that employ a chorus.
choices.rationale: This answer choice may entice some, as it uses the weak, wiggly language (“sometimes”) that is often found in correct answers to Strengthen with Necessary Premise questions. However, it doesn't strengthen the argument, and it isn't necessary to the argument. We don't need to know that narrators are sometimes necessary in plays to establish that narrators and choruses are not the same. The argument consistently specifies that narrators are used in novels and choruses are used in plays, so there is no use in asserting that narrators are necessary for plays.

choices.text: Information necessary for the audience to understand events in a play is sometimes introduced by the chorus.
choices.rationale: This answer choice may appeal to some, as it uses the weak, wiggly language (“sometimes”) that is often found in correct answers to Strengthen with Necessary Premise questions. Even so, it doesn't strengthen the argument, and it isn't necessary to the argument. We know that both narrators and choruses introduce information about the context in which characters' actions take place. This is a trait narrators and choruses share. This answer choice just presents a stronger version of that trait—that sometimes this information is “necessary” to understand a play. But this conclusion wants to establish that choruses and narrators are different. Rather than focus on a difference between narrators and choruses, this just gives more information about a trait narrators and choruses share.

choices.text: Information introduced by a narrator in a novel can never be inconsistent with the rest of the information in the novel.
choices.rationale: This answer strengthens the argument by providing a difference between narrators in a novel and choruses in a play. We know choruses sometimes introduce information inconsistent with the play. This answer choice shows that narrators never do that in a novel. Moreover, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is necessary to the argument. Suppose that narrators sometimes introduced information that was inconsistent with the rest of the novel. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Yep. We would have no reason to believe that narrators and choruses were different, as the argument would have listed out a bunch of similarities between the two. Therefore, this answer choice is necessary to the argument and is correct.

choices.text: Authors sometimes use choruses in plays to mislead audiences about events in the plays.
choices.rationale: Like (B) and (C), this answer choice may allure some test-takers, since it uses the weak language (“sometimes”) often found in correct answers on Strengthen with Necessary Premise questions. However, this doesn't strengthen the argument. Perhaps it would if we knew that authors never used narrators to mislead audiences about the events of a novel. But we do not know that, so this doesn't not present a difference between choruses and narrators.

questions.stimulus: The chorus in a play, like a narrator in a novel, introduces a point of view not tied to any of the characters, and both chorus and narrator allow the author to comment on the characters' actions and to introduce information about the context in which these actions take place. However, since the information introduced by the chorus in a play is sometimes not consistent with the rest of the information in the play, the chorus in a play is not equivalent to the narrator in a novel.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?

choices.text: Some species are more deserving of protection than are other species.
choices.rationale: This principle would not help justify this argument's conclusion because the argument did not conclude that the pygmy bears were more deserving of being protected than any other species. Instead, the conclusion asserted that the bears definitely should be saved. Just because an animal is more deserving of protection doesn't mean the animal should be protected. Moreover, this answer choice doesn't refer to any of the premises offered in the argument. Any one of these issues would be enough to eliminate (A).

choices.text: Rare animals should not be moved from one habitat to another unless these habitats are similar to one another.
choices.rationale: If Rare Animals Should Be Moved, then Similar Habitats. This is the reversal of what we're looking for. “if Similar Habitats, then Rare Animals Should Be Moved” would justify the reasoning in this argument, as a premise asserts that the neighboring island is the only place with a similar habitat to the bears' native island. But as written, (B) can't justify this argument's conclusion—it could only justify concluding that the habitats are similar or that rare animals shouldn't be moved.

choices.text: If a species is in danger of extinction, whatever is most likely to prevent the extinction should be undertaken.
choices.rationale: If Species in Danger of Extinction, then Should Do Whatever Is Most Likely to Prevent Extinction. This is not exactly what we predicted, but it's close enough. We know the pygmy bears are facing extinction, so this principle applies to the argument's premises. We also know that moving the bears to the nearby island is the “only viable chance” of saving the bears. If moving the bears is the only viable way to prevent the bears' extinction, it is definitely the measure most likely to prevent their extinction. So, this applies to the argument's conclusion as well. This principle would therefore strengthen the reasoning in the argument, and (C) is the correct answer.

choices.text: The rarer a species of plant or animal is, the more that should be done to protect that species.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would quickly eliminate this answer choice once they noticed it didn't mention whether one “should” move an endangered species. Upon closer inspection, this principle wouldn't strengthen the reasoning in this argument because we don't know how rare these pygmy bears are. Are they only somewhat rare? If so, this may not support the idea that we should move the bears to a new island.

choices.text: If an animal's original habitat is in danger of being lost, it is permissible to try to find a new habitat for the animal.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would quickly eliminate this answer choice once they noticed the weak language used in this answer choice. We need a principle with the strength to support the claim that we should move the bears to a new island. Saying it's “permissible” to try to find a new habitat would only support a conclusion that “we can start looking for a new habitat for the pygmy bears.”

questions.stimulus: Some of the rare pygmy bears should be moved from their native island to the neighboring island. The bears risk extinction from the loss of habitat on their native island, and since the neighboring island is the only place that has a similar habitat, this move represents the only viable chance of saving these valuable animals.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the argument?

choices.text: In the future, most private correspondence and diaries of public figures will be stored as encrypted text.
choices.rationale: This claim is a premise. It supports the subsidiary conclusion (the most interesting, revealing material won't be available to historians without a password), which, in turn, supports the main conclusion.

choices.text: The widespread use of encryption software will cause the writing of biographical history to decline significantly or cease.
choices.rationale: This accurately conveys the same idea as the argument's main conclusion, so this is the correct answer. The claims that encryption software will “bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end” and that the software “will cause the writing of biographical history to decline significantly or cease” are identical. On a very predictable question like this, a time-conscious test-taker would be justified in selecting this and moving on to the next question, or giving the remaining answer choices just a cursory glance.

choices.text: Historians will probably not have access to much of the private correspondence and diaries of public figures in the future.
choices.rationale: This expresses a similar idea to the argument's subsidiary conclusion. The subsidiary conclusion states that the most interesting, revealing material won't be available to historians unless the historian has a password. That implies that historians will not have as much access to material from public figures in the future. However, this idea supports the main conclusion that encryption software will bring an end to biographical writing.

choices.text: In the future, biographers' access to the most interesting, revealing material will be determined by their knowledge of the necessary passwords.
choices.rationale: This is similar to the argument's subsidiary conclusion. That subsidiary conclusion supports the main conclusion that encryption software will bring an end to biographical writing.

choices.text: Public figures' private correspondence and diaries are the most interesting and revealing sources for the writing of biographical history.
choices.rationale: This is implied by the argument's premise and subsidiary conclusion. The premise tells us that public figures' private correspondence and diaries will be stored as encrypted text. The subsidiary conclusion tells us that means the most interesting, revealing material won't be available to biographers. So, these ideas, taken together, imply this answer choice. But this is used to support the argument's main conclusion that encryption software will bring an end to biographical writing.

questions.stimulus: The widespread use of encryption software, which makes electronic documents accessible by password only, will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end. Public figures' private correspondence and diaries are intended to be confidential when written, but they later become biographers' principal sources. In the future, most such documents are likely to be stored as encrypted text, so the most interesting, revealing material will be unavailable to historians unless they have the necessary passwords.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument fails to consider the possibility that

choices.text: this galaxy contains no celestial objects that reflect light other than planets
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that will weaken the argument's conclusion. So, does this weaken the conclusion? Nope. If planets are the only celestial objects that reflect light, that strongly supports the claim that some non-star objects in this galaxy generate light. This strengthens rather than weakens the conclusion, so it is incorrect. (Note: if the question stem asked us to identify what the author “takes for granted” or “presumes without justification,” this would be the correct answer. This answer choice expresses an unstated, unsubstantiated belief the author has—not something the author “fails to consider.” Let this serve as a reminder that reading the question stem carefully, and using the question stem to figure out what you're looking for in the answer choices, is a crucial part of answering questions!)

choices.text: celestial objects in this galaxy comprise only a minute percentage of all the celestial objects in the universe
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that will weaken the argument's conclusion. So, does this weaken the conclusion? Not at all. This information is entirely irrelevant to the conclusion. The conclusion is only about the celestial objects in this galaxy, so whether there are a lot of celestial objects outside of this galaxy is immaterial.

choices.text: celestial objects in this galaxy are not the only celestial objects that generate light
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that will weaken the argument's conclusion. So, does this weaken the conclusion? Again, no. This answer choice asserts that celestial objects outside this galaxy generate light. But, as discussed in (B), the argument's conclusion only applies to celestial objects in this galaxy. Facts about celestial objects outside this galaxy won't tell us anything about the objects inside this galaxy, so this information is irrelevant.

choices.text: there are numerous features that distinguish stars from planets besides the ability to generate light
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that will weaken the argument's conclusion. So, does this weaken the conclusion? Once again, no. The conclusion discussed whether celestial objects in this galaxy generate or merely reflect light. Whether there are other features to distinguish planets and stars is irrelevant. Those features cannot tell us whether non-star objects in this galaxy generate light.

choices.text: planets are not the only celestial objects that do not generate light
choices.rationale: We're looking for an answer choice that will weaken the argument's conclusion. So, does this weaken the conclusion? Finally, yes. If planets are not the only celestial objects that do not generate light, maybe every non-star object in this galaxy doesn't generate light. This substantially weakens the conclusion that non-star objects in this galaxy generate light, and it does so by pointing out the exclusivity flaw the author commits.

questions.stimulus: Unlike stars, planets do not generate light, but only reflect it. Besides stars, there are many other celestial objects in this galaxy that are not planets. Hence, there are celestial objects in this galaxy that generate light but are not stars.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the psychologist's argument?

choices.text: Some of the great creative geniuses in history were first-born children.
choices.rationale: This conclusion asserts that first-born children will be less adventurous than their younger siblings. The argument doesn't assert that first-born children will be more creative than their siblings (and we have no reason to believe that being creative is associated with being unadventurous). Plus, this answer choice is very weak (“some”) and unlikely to strengthen a general conclusion like this one.

choices.text: In most cases, the more younger siblings one has, the greater one's cognitive plasticity.
choices.rationale: First-born children, by definition, have the most younger siblings in their family. If those first-born children also have more cognitive plasticity than their siblings, that directly contradicts the findings in this psychologist's study. Rather than strengthen the argument, this weakens it by casting doubt on the psychologist's study.

choices.text: Other studies have shown a correlation between cognitive plasticity and the willingness to take risks.
choices.rationale: This answer choice fixes the problem: the jump from low cognitive plasticity to a lack of adventurousness. This answer choice shows that cognitive plasticity is associated with a willingness to take risks. So, if you have low cognitive plasticity, you'll be less likely to take risks. Being adventurous certainly involves taking risks. So, if you have low cognitive plasticity, you probably won't be very adventurous. This strengthens the psychologist's conclusion and is thus the correct answer.

choices.text: A study of business executives shows that several industry leaders have older siblings.
choices.rationale: This conclusion asserts that first-born children will be less adventurous than their younger siblings. It doesn't argue that first-born children will be less successful or less likely to lead industries than their siblings (and we have no reason to believe that being successful is associated with being adventurous). Plus, this answer choice is very weak (“several”) and unlikely to strengthen a general conclusion like this one.

choices.text: Most of the participants in the study had characterized themselves as more adaptable than other people.
choices.rationale: This answer choice raises the possibility that the study did not measure a representative sample of the population. If the people in the study all thought they were more adaptable, there's a chance the study did not include participants with the lowest cognitive plasticity. Without including those participants, it's difficult to draw any conclusions about people with less cognitive plasticity. So, this answer choice weakens the argument by suggesting that the study is flawed. (Now, just because the participants said they were more adaptable doesn't mean they are more adaptable. Still, the possibility that this study's sample was unrepresentative is enough to weaken, at least slightly, this argument. At any rate, raising a potential problem with a premise will certainly not strengthen an argument.)

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: We measured the “cognitive plasticity,” or the willingness to accept new ideas, of a group of people of both genders and of all ages. The first-born children in the study consistently exhibited less cognitive plasticity than did their siblings. It is reasonable to think that those who are open to new ideas will be adventurous in other ways. Hence, our study suggests that siblings of first-born children will tend to be more adventurous than will the first-borns.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to reconcile the historians' apparent counterexample with their general rule?

choices.text: The political systems that have emerged since the time of Plato and Aristotle have in various ways been different from the political system in ancient Athens.
choices.rationale: This describes a difference between ancient Athens and other political systems in which intellectual advancements occurred. However, it doesn't describe a difference that would explain why Plato and Aristotle could make intellectual achievements despite the political unrest. Just stating that the systems are different isn't enough to resolve this paradox.

choices.text: The citizens of ancient Athens generally held in high esteem people who were accomplished intellectually.
choices.rationale: This is tempting, but there are a few unacceptable issues. First, we don't know that Plato and Aristotle were “accomplished intellectually” in ancient Athens. Yes, historians acknowledge that Plato and Aristotle made significant intellectual accomplishments, but we have no idea if the ancient Athenian citizens also recognized those accomplishments. And, even if the citizens did recognize Plato and Aristotle's accomplishments, that doesn't explain how they were able to make those accomplishments during a time of political unrest in the first place.

choices.text: Financial support for intellectual endeavors is typically unavailable in unstable political environments, but in ancient Athens such support was provided by wealthy citizens.
choices.rationale: As expected, this presents a difference between most politically unstable systems and ancient Athens. In most unstable political systems, intellectuals can't find funding. However, wealthy citizens funded Aristotle and Plato in ancient Athens. So Aristotle and Plato didn't rely on certain governments or regimes for their funding—their funding came from wealthy citizens, regardless of the political or social unrest. This resolves the paradox by affirming the general rule that significant intellectual advances occur in politically stable systems while explaining how Plato and Aristotle made intellectual advancements in the politically unstable ancient Athens.

choices.text: Significant intellectual advances sometimes, though not always, lead to stable political environments.
choices.rationale: A time-conscious test-taker would likely table or eliminate this answer choice based on its weak language. “[S]ometimes, though not always” is a very wishy-washy claim. We typically need stronger, more informative assertions to resolve a paradox. Moreover, this answer choice just says that some intellectual advancements occur in cities or countries that initially lacked a stable political system. That doesn't explain why Plato and Aristotle made such advancements during great political unrest or why political stability is generally favorable for intellectual advances.

choices.text: Many thinkers besides Plato and Aristotle contributed to the intellectual achievements of ancient Athens.
choices.rationale: This misses the mark entirely. We need to explain why Plato and Aristotle made intellectual advances in ancient Athens, despite it's instability. Asserting that other thinkers were able to make advancements as well offers little insight into how Plato and Aristotle were able to do so.

questions.stimulus: Historians have found that significant intellectual advances generally occur in cities or countries that have a stable political system. But these same historians acknowledge that in ancient Athens, Plato and Aristotle made unparalleled intellectual progress during a period of great political and social unrest.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?

choices.text: Only if the cost of transporting materials from Earth to Mars decreases will human habitation be established on Mars.
choices.rationale: This answer choice reads: “if Human Habitation on Mars, then Cost of Transporting Materials Decreases.” After taking the contrapositive, it would read: “if Cost of Transporting Materials DOESN'T Decrease, then No Human Habitation on Mars.” This conclusion asserts that it's not economically feasible to colonize Mars, so the necessary condition that there will be no human habitation on Mars applies to this conclusion. Therefore, this would strengthen the argument if a premise asserted that the cost of transporting materials from Earth to Mars won't decrease. But no premises says that. The premise only asserts that the cost of transporting materials is “so high”—not that it won't decrease. Because this answer choice doesn't apply to any of the premises in this argument, it doesn't strengthen it.

choices.text: The cost of transporting basic materials through space is not expected to decrease in the near future.
choices.rationale: When assessing answer choices on a Strengthen with Necessary Premise question, some test-takers find it helpful to ask, “Do we need to know this?” So, do we need to know that the cost of transporting materials through space won't decrease? Not necessarily. Even if the costs of transporting materials through space decreased significantly, it could still be too high to make colonizing Mars economically feasible. (For instance, the transportation cost could drop from $100 billion per pound of material to $50 billion per pound of material, and it would still likely be cost-prohibitive.) So while this may strengthen the argument, it doesn't need to be true to draw the conclusion.

choices.text: Earth is the only source of the basic materials that would be needed to establish human habitation on Mars.
choices.rationale: Do we need to know that Earth is the only source of the materials required to colonize Mars? Not necessarily. Even if other planets or moons could provide the materials, it might still be too costly to transport them through space. We could maybe travel from Earth to our moon or to Saturn to get the materials. But doing so would still require transporting the materials through space, which could still make it economically unfeasible to transport these materials to Mars. So while this answer choice strengthens the argument, it doesn't need to be true to draw the conclusion.

choices.text: No significant benefit would result from establishing human habitation on Mars.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the conclusion. The conclusion didn't claim that it's pointless or not worthwhile to colonize Mars. It only argues that it won't be economically feasible to do so. Therefore, asserting that there's no benefit to colonizing Mars does little strengthen the claim that it's not economically viable to do so.

choices.text: Mars is not a practical source of the basic materials required for establishing human habitation there.
choices.rationale: This certainly strengthens this argument, as it shows that assembling the requisite materials on Mars will require transporting the materials through space. Moreover, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is necessary to the argument. Suppose Mars is a practical source of the basic materials required for establishing human habitations there. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Yep. If we can get the materials from Mars, we won't have to transport them there, and it may not be cost-prohibitive to establish colonies there. Therefore, this answer choice is necessary to the argument and is correct.

questions.stimulus: To establish a human colony on Mars would involve assembling tremendous quantities of basic materials at the site of the colony. But because the costs of transporting such materials through space would be so high, it will not be economically feasible to colonize Mars.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that effectiveness of different practitioners in bringing about major improvement cannot differ at all if their effectiveness in bringing about any improvement does not differ
choices.rationale: When we see “presumes, without providing justification” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” This author only discusses patients making “major improvements.” The author never discusses the percentage of patients who experience “any improvement.” So, we have no reason to think the author agrees with this statement, and we can eliminate it.

choices.text: provides no information about the kinds of injuries that require short-term as opposed to long-term treatment
choices.rationale: This is true, but the author doesn't need to distinguish the types of injuries that require short-term versus long-term physical therapy. Although the premises discuss these time frames (assuming less than six weeks is “short-term” and more than three weeks is “long-term”), the conclusion is about any patient who requires physical therapy. So there may be some injuries that require long-term therapy, and some that require only short-term therapy. The author's point is whatever therapy you need, your chances of making major improvements does not depend on whether you see a general practitioner or a specialist. (Put another way, this answer choice brings up a difference between the types of therapy you may require when we should look for a difference between the types of patients the two practitioners treat.)

choices.text: overlooks the possibility that patients are more strongly biased to report favorably on one of the two types of medical professionals than on the other
choices.rationale: When we see “overlooks the possibility” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the conclusion if true?” So, would the possibility that patients may be biased to report favorably on one of the physical therapists weaken this conclusion? Not at all. The premises were not based on the patients' subjective assessments of the practitioner. The premises were based on whether the patients “showed major improvement.” That's an objective fact, which can be corroborated through medical records. This could weaken the argument if the premise and conclusion were about whether the patients liked or had favorable experiences with their physical therapist. However, this argument was about whether the patients actually healed. So this answer choice would not weaken the argument's conclusion, and it is incorrect.

choices.text: fails to indicate whether the number of patients surveyed who saw a general practitioner was equal to the number who saw a specialist
choices.rationale: The author doesn't need to establish that the number of patients who saw a general practitioner equaled the number of patients who saw a specialist. The premises were based on the percentage of patients who saw improvements, and the conclusion was about the likelihood that one would improve through physical therapy. Neither requires the group sizes to be exactly the same. Perhaps there would be a small-sample issue if the records were only based on a few patients who saw a general practitioner. But as long as both group sizes were large, studies based on unequal group sizes would be acceptable in this argument.

choices.text: overlooks the possibility that specialists and general practitioners each tend to excel at treating a different type of injury
choices.rationale: When we see “overlooks the possibility” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the conclusion if true?” So, would the possibility that specialists and general practitioners excel at treating different injuries weaken this conclusion? Yes, absolutely. In that case, one's chances of improving through physical therapy would depend on whether they saw the practitioner who excelled at treating their type of injury. Whether you were able to anticipate this as a potential difference between the two physical therapists, or you knew you needed to look for some relevant difference between them, we can conclude that this is an error in the argument's reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Records reveal that of physical therapy patients who received less than six weeks of treatment, about 31 percent showed major improvement, regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist. Of patients who received physical therapy for a longer time, again regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist, about 50 percent showed major improvement. Therefore, the choice between seeing a specialist or a general practitioner for necessary physical therapy will not affect one's chances of major improvement.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption the argument requires?

choices.text: If two stars are in two different galaxies, it is not possible to determine whether or not they are approximately the same distance from Earth.
choices.rationale: This argument is about two stars in the same distant galaxy. We don't need to know anything about two stars in two different distant galaxies to draw this argument's conclusion.

choices.text: If any two stars are in the same distant galaxy, differences in the elements each is burning will be detectable from Earth.
choices.rationale: This answer choice says that we can observe differences in at least one characteristic—the elements the star is burning—in “any two stars” in the same distant galaxy. This claim strengthens the argument's conclusion by showing that we can observe at least one characteristic other than brightness in two distant stars. If this answer choice were true, we'd at least be able to figure out how brightness correlates with which element the star is burning. But does this answer choice need to be true to draw the argument's conclusion? Let's turn to the negation test to check. Suppose it wasn't true that differences in the elements burning in any two stars in the same distant galaxy were detectable from Earth. Or, put another way, suppose that there were some stars in the same distant galaxy in which we couldn't detect differences in the elements burning. Would that weaken this conclusion? Not necessarily. This conclusion didn't assert we'd be able to determine how brightness correlates to every trait in every star in distant galaxies. Even if we couldn't observe differences in the elements burning in some stars, we may be able to observe this difference in most stars. And those observations would allow us to develop a general impression of how brightness correlates to elements burning. Moreover, even if we couldn't observe differences in the elements burning in some stars, we still may be able to detect other differences in these stars, and figure out how those differences correlate to brightness. Since negating this answer choice doesn't weaken this conclusion, this answer choice is not necessary and incorrect.

choices.text: The stars in our own galaxy are not all approximately the same distance from Earth.
choices.rationale: This argument is about two stars in the same distant galaxy. We don't need to know anything about two stars in our galaxy to draw this argument's conclusion.

choices.text: There are stars in distant galaxies that have characteristics, other than brightness, discernible from Earth.
choices.rationale: This answer choice strengthens this argument. If stars in distant galaxies have detectable characteristics, other than brightness, we can be much more confident that we can determine how brightness correlates to other characteristics. Additionally, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is necessary to the argument. Suppose there weren't stars in distant galaxies that had characteristics, other than brightness, discernable from Earth. Or, put another way, suppose that brightness was the only trait we could observe in distant stars. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Yep. If we couldn't detect any trait other than a star's brightness from Earth, we couldn't determine how the star's brightness correlates with different traits. Therefore, this answer choice is necessary to the argument and is correct.

choices.text: If there are significant differences in how far away two stars are from Earth, then those stars will differ significantly in apparent brightness.
choices.rationale: This argument is about stars in the same distant galaxy. The first premise establishes that these stars will be approximately the same distance from Earth. Therefore, we don't need to know anything about two stars that have a significantly different distances from Earth.

questions.stimulus: The differences in distance from Earth between the stars in any one distant galaxy are negligible compared to the vast distance to the galaxy itself. Thus, if two stars are in the same distant galaxy, any significant difference in the apparent brightness of those stars results from differences in how brightly each is actually burning. Therefore, we should be able to determine how a star's relative actual brightness correlates with other characteristics by studying stars in the same distant galaxy.

questions.stem: Each of the following, if true, contributes to an explanation of the repressors' characteristics mentioned above except:

choices.text: Repressors are better able than sensitizers to focus on their work and to avoid distractions.
choices.rationale: Repressors' ability to focus on work and avoid distractions—perhaps because they're not constantly, histrionically overreacting to every negative thought—would help explain how they got better grades. This explains the surprising findings, so we should eliminate it.

choices.text: Repressors are less apt than sensitizers to alienate people by expressing their emotions.
choices.rationale: If repressors don't alienate people by expressing their emotions, this would explain how they had “superior social skills.” So, even if this answer choice doesn't provide the most flattering portrait of people's ability to empathize with others' emotions, it does explain the surprising finding. We'll need to eliminate it.

choices.text: Parents and other caregivers tend to reward repressors more than they reward sensitizers for academic performance and social behavior deemed desirable.
choices.rationale: Getting rewarded more for academic success and desirable social behavior would help explain why repressors have greater self-esteem (they feel good when they get lavishly rewarded), and why they get better grades and social skills (they have more incentive than the sensitizers). This helps explain the surprising finding, so we should eliminate it.

choices.text: Some psychologists have hypothesized that the desire to maintain social and academic success and self-esteem strengthens repressors' tendency to repress upsetting thoughts and feelings.
choices.rationale: Just because psychologists have hypothesized that the desire to maintain social and academic success is correlated to the repressors' tendency to repress upsetting thoughts and feelings doesn't mean those psychologists are correct. There may be no evidence that corroborates this hypothesis. Further, this answer choice gets the cause and effect backwards. We're looking for reasons why repressors' tendency to repress causes their better social skills and grades. This answer choice describes a possible reason why repressors' desire for better social skills and grades causes their tendency to repress. Therefore, this answer choice does not contribute to an explanation of the surprising findings, and it is correct.

choices.text: Sensitizers tend to focus more than repressors do on the difficulties of succeeding in their projects rather than on factors that are likely to contribute to success.
choices.rationale: If we know that sensitizers focus more on the negative and consequently can't focus on ways to succeed, we can better understand why sensitizers have worse grades than repressors, have a harder time tolerating frustration, and are more anxious. This contributes to an explanation of the surprising findings, so it is incorrect.

questions.stimulus: A research psychologist used a personality test to classify high school students as "repressors"—people who repress upsetting thoughts and feelings from conscious awareness—or as "sensitizers"—those especially attuned to internal states who freely express distress. The researcher found that, compared to sensitizers, the repressors were less shy and anxious, could better tolerate frustration, and had superior social skills, higher grades, and a greater sense of self-esteem.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?

choices.text: No known form of bacteria is complicated enough in structure to engage in a sexual type of reproduction.
choices.rationale: This has no effect on the argument. We know that nanobes are significantly smaller than bacteria, which means nanobes don't have a reproductive mechanism. This answer choice perhaps suggests that nanobes can't engage in sexual reproduction, but that doesn't give us any more information than what we already had.

choices.text: Single-celled creatures can combine to form a multicelled structure and then reproduce before they disband into separate single cells again.
choices.rationale: If you noticed the equivocation between life and lifeform, this should be a very appealing answer choice. This suggests how members of a species can reproduce without each member possessing a reproductive mechanism. If single-celled creatures can combine, Voltron-style, into a multicelled creature, reproduce, and divide back again, perhaps nanobes also can do this. In that case, nanobes could be a lifeform, even if each member is too small to have a reproductive mechanism. Some test-takers may bristle at certain elements of this answer choice. They may point out that we don't know that nanobes are single-celled creatures or that a combination of nanobes would be complicated enough to reproduce. They may also point out that we don't even know that these single-celled creatures lack a reproductive mechanism. All of these objections are valid. But it's worth reviewing our goal on a Weaken question: to make the conclusion less convincing, even if that effect is slight. We don't need to prove that the conclusion is false. So (B) doesn't prove that this conclusion is false. However, it shows that very simple organisms can reproduce, which suggests that maybe the tiny, simplistic nanobes can as well. Therefore, this answer choice weakens the conclusion, and it is correct.

choices.text: The material phenomena that some scientists claim are the fossilized remains of bacteria in meteorites from Mars are approximately the same size as nanobes.
choices.rationale: This answer choice states that some scientists claim they found the fossilized remains of bacteria on Martian meteorites, and these remains are approximately the same size as nanobes. It's easy to see the appeal in this answer choice. If bacteria are lifeforms, finding evidence of bacteria that are the same size as nanobes would suggest that nanobes might also be lifeforms. However, that's not quite what this answer choice says. First, this answer choice only says scientists “claim” they found the remains of bacteria. Just because they said it's bacteria doesn't necessarily mean it is bacteria. Second, the answer choice says the remains are the same size as nanobes. But the remains might refer to the remnants of part of a bacterium. Maybe the entire bacterium wasn't fossilized and its size is much larger than a nanobe. So, this answer choice doesn't provide enough information to weaken the argument.

choices.text: Previous definitions of life were based on research done with inferior microscopes no longer in use.
choices.rationale: “Previous definitions of life” have no bearing on this argument. Nothing in this argument suggests that only “previous definitions of life” hold that life requires reproductive mechanisms or that nanobes are too small to possess such mechanisms.

choices.text: Animals such as cold-blooded lizards can be physiologically simpler, though still larger, than other animals.
choices.rationale: This answer choice suggests that an animal's simplicity doesn't necessarily correlate with its size. But, even if that's true, it doesn't necessarily weaken this argument. First, we don't think nanobes are animals, so it's unclear if this even applies to nanobes. Even if we ignore that issue, this answer choice doesn't address the fact that nanobes aren't large enough to have reproductive mechanisms, and that lifeforms require reproduction. So this answer choice may only suggests that nanobes might not be simplest entities, but it doesn't imply that they can reproduce.

questions.stimulus: A geologist recently claimed to have discovered in clay a previously unknown form of life: "nanobes," one-tenth the size of the smallest known bacteria. However, it is unlikely that nanobes truly are living things. They are probably inanimate artifacts of the clay's microscopic structure, because a nanobe is too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, a prerequisite for life.

questions.stem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to the flawed reasoning exhibited in the argument above?

choices.text: Each officer of this club must be a member of two years standing, or be a committee member, or have special qualifications. Evelyn cannot be an officer, for she has only been a member for one year and is not a committee member.
choices.rationale: This is an invalid argument, but not because it ignores a middle ground between two extremes. The premise asserts that officers must have “two years standing” or be a “committee member” or have “special qualifications.” We know Evelyn lacks two years of standing and isn't a committee member, but she could still be an officer if she has special qualifications.

choices.text: In order to thrive, this plant needs to be located in a sunny spot and to be watered regularly. So, since this spot is not sunny, and since I did not water this plant regularly, that explains why this plant is not as healthy as it should be.
choices.rationale: This argument takes the contrapositive of a conditional statement, so it's valid. If plants need sun and water to thrive, and this plant received neither sun nor water, we have a good explanation for why it hasn't thrived.

choices.text: This book has been widely reviewed and hasn't received even one hostile review. Hence we can conclude that, so far, all the critics have loved this book.
choices.rationale: Like the passage, this answer choice jumps from one extreme to the other. The critics didn't give this book any “hostile” reviews. But that doesn't mean they “loved” the book. They could think the book is pretty good, just OK, or slightly below-average. In other words, this argument ignores the middle ground between “hate” and “love,” just like the passage ignored the middle ground between “friend” and “enemy.” It is the correct answer.

choices.text: A decision in favor of developing the northern border of the town logically implies that it would be equally acceptable to develop the southern, eastern, or western borders. So, it is possible that at least one of these other borders will also be developed.
choices.rationale: This argument is flawed, but not because it ignores a middle ground between two extremes. Even if it's “acceptable” to develop the southern, eastern, or western borders doesn't mean that it's “possible” that at least one will be developed. This is an equivocation between two related but distinct concepts.

choices.text: If everyone were an author, poet, or academic, then society would come crashing to a halt. But most people are not poets or authors. Nor are there many academics in our society. Therefore, our society will not come crashing to a halt.
choices.rationale: This argument is flawed, but not because it ignores a middle ground between two extremes. This commits a negates-but-doesn't-reverse flaw. We know that society would crash if everyone were an author, poet, or academic. But not everyone is an author, poet, or academic. But that doesn't mean society won't crash. Perhaps society will crash for some other reason. In other words, this argument tries to draw a conclusion by negating a sufficient condition. This is flawed, but not for the same reason as the passage.

questions.stimulus: Devan has never bothered to be kind to me. Nor has he offered help or companionship. So, since he does not meet any of these basic criteria for friendship, he is my enemy.

questions.stem: The journalist's reasoning most closely conforms to which one of the following principles?

choices.text: When people believe that there are several measures they could take to reduce the risk associated with a certain activity, generally they will take only the measure that they believe will most reduce that risk.
choices.rationale: The conclusion of this argument is about people engaging in risky behaviors (like smoking), not taking measures that reduce risk. So this principle would not strengthen the reasoning in this argument.

choices.text: The development of ways to protect people from the consequences of behaviors that would normally harm them often makes people less careful to avoid such behaviors.
choices.rationale: If developing ways to protect people from harmful behavior (like cancer cures) often leads people to be “less careful to avoid such behavior,” we can expect people to be less careful to avoid carcinogens. This strengthens the argument's reasoning by showing that the premise about SUV drivers can apply to other contexts.

choices.text: People generally take special care to avoid behaviors that they believe would likely lead to serious injury to them and generally do not take special care to avoid behaviors that they believe will not harm them at all.
choices.rationale: This argument's conclusion asserts that people will engage in behaviors they know will harm them (like smoking and overexposure to the sun). This principle asserts that people will avoid such behaviors. So this principle weakens the argument's reasoning. (Some test-takers may argue that this principle might strengthen the conclusion, because it shows that people will engage in behaviors known to increase the risk of cancer because they think the cure will prevent cancer from harming them. However, even if the cure eventually protects these people from cancer, they still would be harmed by getting the cancer in the first place.)

choices.text: People generally exercise more care when performing activities they know to have risky consequences than when performing activities of unknown risk.
choices.rationale: This argument's conclusion asserts that people will exercise less care when engaging in activities they know to be risky. This principle suggests that people will be careful when engaging in those activities. Therefore, this principle weakens the argument, and this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: Avoiding serious harm to themselves is given a high priority by people in their behavior, but avoiding lesser harms is frequently outweighed by various desires.
choices.rationale: This argument's conclusion asserts that people will engage in behaviors they know can lead to the serious harm of cancer. This principle asserts that people will make it a priority to avoid that harm. Once again, this principle weakens the argument, making this answer choice incorrect.

questions.stimulus: Journalist: Drivers of sport utility vehicles correctly tend to believe that occupants of such vehicles carry lower risk of serious injury as a result of accidents, and such drivers therefore tend to drive less carefully than they would in more traditional vehicles. Thus, the discovery of powerful cures for certain high-incidence forms of cancer would probably trigger an increase in behaviors such as smoking and overexposure to sun that are known to increase the risks of such cancers.

questions.stem: The filmmaker's conclusion is properly drawn if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.text: A creation has absolute integrity as a work of art if the artistic decisions made in creating it were unaffected by the need to make profits.
choices.rationale: This could validate a conclusion that claimed that a work of art had absolute integrity. But it cannot validate a conclusion that a work of art lacks absolute integrity. Therefore, this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: If any of the artistic decisions made in creating something were affected by the need to make profits, then that creation does not have absolute integrity as a work of art.
choices.rationale: The filmmaker's conclusion would be valid if we added this to the argument. The filmmaker established that the artistic decisions made by independent filmmakers are affected by profits. Therefore, if this answer choice is true, we must conclude that films made by independent filmmakers do not have absolute integrity as works of art.

choices.text: The creations of individuals have more integrity as works of art, on average, than those of groups.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this as soon as they saw it lacked the conclusion's new idea: that independent films “do not have absolute integrity as works of art.” We need to prove that independent films do not have absolute integrity. An answer choice that claims that creations of individuals tend to have more integrity than creations of groups cannot do that. For one, it's not clear whether independent films are the creations of individuals or groups. Second, a relative claim (“more integrity”) cannot prove an non-relative claim (“do not have integrity”).

choices.text: The unconventionality of a creation has no bearing on its integrity as a work of art.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this as soon as they saw it lacked the conclusion's new idea: that independent films “do not have absolute integrity as works of art.” While this may strengthen the argument (it shows that the unconventionality of independent films won't affect their integrity), it doesn't prove that independent films completely lack integrity. Perhaps independent films possess some quality other than unconventionality that give them absolute integrity.

choices.text: A creation has no integrity as a work of art unless the artistic decisions made in creating it were unaffected by views about what is conventional.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this as soon as they saw it added an idea that the argument did not discuss: that decisions were not “unaffected by views about what is conventional.” Correct answers cannot add new ideas on Strengthen with Sufficient Premise questions. Although the argument asserts that independent films are unconventional, we have no idea if the artistic decisions are affected by what is conventional. Are the filmmakers deliberately trying to make their films unconventional? Unclear. So this cannot validate the conclusion because this does not connect to the argument's premise.

questions.stimulus: Filmmaker: Many people feel that independent films have more integrity as works of art than films produced by major studios, since independent films are typically less conventional than major studio films. However, like major studios, all independent filmmakers need to make profits on their films, and this affects the artistic decisions made in creating most independent films. Thus, most independent films do not have absolute integrity as works of art.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.text: If the mayor and the city council had approved the proposed budget, the botanical gardens would be able to open this week. The botanical gardens cannot open this week even though the city council approved the proposed budget. Thus, the mayor must not have approved the proposed budget.
choices.rationale: This has all the key characteristics we're looking for: if Mayor Approve and Council Approve, then Botanical Gardens. NO Botanical Gardens and Council Approve. Conclusion: NO Mayor Approve. This has the same structure as the passage. Like that argument, we satisfy one sufficient condition, but the necessary condition is not satisfied. In both cases, the conclusion asserts that the other sufficient condition must not be satisfied. This is the correct answer.

choices.text: If I see a science fiction movie, I either love it or hate it. I do not hate the movie I am watching now. Therefore, I will probably end up loving the movie, since it is a science fiction movie.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this one as soon as they saw it lacked an “and” in the sufficient condition of a premise. Rather, this has an “or” in a necessary condition. An argument cannot have the same structure if it misplaces an important element like that. Its conclusion also features a different strength of language (“probably”) than the passage's conclusion. In addition to having a different structure than the passage, this is also an invalid argument. This author predicts that they probably will love the movie, because they don't currently hate it. However, even if this author only loves or hates these movies, their opinion may change before the movie is over.

choices.text: If the government or some other party had bought the processing plant, the local economy would have improved. But the local economy did not improve. Therefore, neither the government nor any other party bought the processing plant.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this one as soon as they saw it lacked an “and” in the sufficient condition of a premise. Rather, this has an “or” in the sufficient condition. Moreover, the absolute premise lacks an “and” and the conclusion has an “and.” An argument cannot have the same structure if it misplaces crucial elements like these. While this is a valid argument, its structure is not the same as the argument in the passage.

choices.text: Books at Falling Embers Bookshop are on sale only if they are either used books or paperbacks. The book I am looking for at Falling Embers is on sale. Therefore, if the book I am looking for is not a paperback, it is a used book.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this one as soon as they saw it lacked an “and” in the sufficient condition of a premise. Like (B), this has an “or” in a necessary condition. Additionally, the conclusion is a conditional, rather than an absolute, statement. An argument cannot have the same structure if it misplaces important elements like these. While this is a valid argument, its structure is not the same as the argument in the passage.

choices.text: If Doria owes more money than she can pay back, then she must either get a higher paying job or declare bankruptcy. Doria does in fact owe more than she can pay back, yet she does not want to declare bankruptcy. So, Doria must get a higher paying job.
choices.rationale: An efficient test-taker would eliminate this one as soon as they saw it lacked an “and” in the sufficient condition of a premise. Like (B) and (D) before it, this has an “or” in a necessary condition. An argument cannot have the same structure if it misplaces important elements like this. While this is a valid argument, its structure is not the same as the argument in the passage.

questions.stimulus: If you complete 24 graduate credits and a thesis in our department, you are eligible to receive a master's degree. Roger has completed 24 graduate credits in our department, yet he is not eligible to receive a master's degree. So he must not have finished his thesis yet.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: contains a premise that presupposes the truth of the conclusion
choices.rationale: “Presuppos[ing] the truth” of a conclusion refers to circular reasoning, a flaw in which the conclusion merely restates a premise. That is not the case here, as the premise is about the last two years, and the conclusion is about this year.

choices.text: draws an inference about a future event on the basis of a very limited number of instances of related past events
choices.rationale: This describes the flaw perfectly. The author is drawing an inference about a future event (the amount of rainfall over Browning this year) from premises about a “very limited number of instances of related past events” (two past events: the amount of rainfall over Browning in the last two years). This answer choice accurately describes the temporal flaw discussed above by describing the shift from one time period to another. And, if you thought of this as a sampling flaw, the characterization of the premises as “very limited” also references that.

choices.text: overemphasizes the possibility that average rainfall statistics could be skewed by large rainfall in one year
choices.rationale: Like many incorrect answer choices to Errors in Reasoning questions, this answer choice misconstrues the conclusion drawn in this argument. The author's conclusion was not about “average rainfall statistics” in Browning or anywhere else. That was not a point the author was trying to make, so there’s no way the author could have “overemphasize[d]” how much abnormal rainfall could skew the average.

choices.text: concludes that two phenomena are associated merely from the claim that there are many instances in which both phenomena are present
choices.rationale: When an answer choice uses abstract, nonspecific language like this, try to fill in the vague terms with concrete details from the passage. If you’re unable, or find yourself straining, to find something from the passage that aligns with a vague term, then there’s a good chance that the answer choice misdescribes the argument and is wrong. In this case, what are the “two phenomena” that conclusion claims are “associated”? The conclusion arguably describes Browning rainfall in June and Browning rainfall in September. Still, the author doesn’t claim these phenomena are “associated” — just that there's probably going to be more rainfall in June than September. Moreover, the premises never assert that there are many instances when both these phenomena are present (we’d probably have to bend the space-time continuum to get rain in June and September at the same time). Since we can’t fill in the vague terms from this answer choice with concrete details from the passage, this answer choice misdescribes the argument.

choices.text: uses evidence drawn from a source whose reliability cannot readily be verified
choices.rationale: There’s no reason to believe that we can’t verify the evidence used in this argument. As long as someone or something is keeping track of the rainfall in Browning, we can double-check these figures.

questions.stimulus: In the previous two years, significantly more rain has fallen in Browning in September than in July. Therefore, this year in Browning more rain will probably fall in September than in July.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the educator's argument?

choices.text: Problems faced in daily life usually can be solved effectively using only common sense.
choices.rationale: It's unclear whether interdisciplinary or single-subject courses would be better at helping students acquire the common sense to solve problems. Perhaps neither would.
