This answer choice doesn't address the educator's central comparison between interdisciplinary and single-subject courses, and therefore doesn't strengthen the argument.

choices.text: Most teachers are able to teach courses in a single academic discipline more effectively than they can teach interdisciplinary courses.
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes a downside to interdisciplinary courses that this author overlooks: they're more challenging to teach than single-subject courses. We're looking for an answer choice that strengthens the argument by fixing a problem; this answer choice weakens the argument by stating a problem.

choices.text: Students who take only courses in individual academic disciplines are rarely able to combine knowledge from those disciplines.
choices.rationale: This answer choice eliminates a potential benefit of single-subject courses: that students could be better at learning to solve problems by combining knowledge from several single-subject courses. This answer choice shows this is not the case — students usually cannot combine knowledge from several single-subject courses. In that case, interdisciplinary courses are probably a better way to provide students with the knowledge required to solve life's problems. In other words, this answer choice strengthens the argument by patching up a potential weakness in the educator's reasoning.

choices.text: Most students who are required to take courses that cover only single disciplines can effectively solve many problems faced in daily life.
choices.rationale: So students who are required to take single-subject courses usually get good at solving life's problems anyway? That weakens the argument by showing that the educator's prescribed ban on single-subject course requirements isn't necessary to help students solve life's problems.

choices.text: Most interdisciplinary courses are not designed specifically to teach students how to solve problems faced in daily life.
choices.rationale: This presents an arguable drawback of interdisciplinary courses (arguable because a class that's not designed to teach students how to solve life's problems could still equip students with the knowledge required to solve those problems). So, if this answer choice has any effect on the educator's argument at all, it only weakens it.

questions.stimulus: Educator: Few problems faced in daily life can be solved most effectively, if at all, by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation. Thus, schools should not require students to take courses in individual academic disciplines but should instead require them to take interdisciplinary courses.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the newspaper columnist's argument?

choices.text: Solving a problem never requires finding the root cause of the problem.
choices.rationale: This is a much broader statement than the second sentence of this argument. The columnist believes there are at least two specific situations in which solving a problem doesn't require finding the root cause, but that doesn't mean that the columnist believes solving a problem never requires finding the root cause. The columnist does not necessarily think this statement is true, so it cannot be the columnist's main point.

choices.text: Knowing the cause of the current recession would not necessarily enable people to find a solution to it.
choices.rationale: This misconstrues the columnist's main point ever so slightly. The columnist states that we don't need to know the cause of the recession to solve it. That doesn't mean that the columnist thinks knowing the cause of the recession wouldn't allow us to solve it.To use a favorite device of this columnist and argue by analogy: if you feel sick, you don't need to know what caused your illness to feel better. Usually, rest and fluids will help you out. But knowing what caused your illness could still help you feel better more quickly — you could take certain medications that could expedite the healing process. Perhaps the same is true of the recession.The columnist concludes we don't need to know the cause, not that it wouldn't help. So, the columnist does not necessarily believe that this answer choice is true, and it cannot be the columnist's main point.

choices.text: The question of what caused the current recession is subject to considerable debate.
choices.rationale: Unlike (A) and (B), the columnist believes this statement is true. But it is not the columnist's main point. The tone doesn't suggest that this sentence is the takeaway point the columnist wants to leave us with. Additionally, none of the columnist's statements help explain why or how there's a hot debate over what caused the recession. Because no premises support this assertion, it is not the columnist's main point.

choices.text: One need not ascertain the cause of the current recession in order to improve the economy.
choices.rationale: This is it. This answer choice expresses the same idea as the second sentence, which we've identified as the columnist's main point. It's the takeaway point the columnist wants to leave us with, and it's supported by the central premise in this argument (the analogy to corrective lenses).

choices.text: Long before the cause of myopia was known to be genetic, corrective lenses were being used as an effective treatment for the disease.
choices.rationale: This refers to the columnist's only premise in this argument. We can surmise that this is a premise both from the phrase “after all” (a standard premise indicator) and the fact that it supports why the columnist thinks we don't have to figure out what caused the recession before attempting to fix the recession. Because this answer choice refers to a premise and not the main conclusion, it is incorrect.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper columnist: What caused the current recession is a hotly debated question. It is a mistake, however, to assume that answering this question is essential to improving the economy. Corrective lenses, after all, were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

questions.stem: A questionable aspect of the reasoning above is that it fails to take into account that

choices.text: logicians' being illogical in their discussions of logic constitutes incompetence, whereas physicians' having an unhealthy lifestyle does not
choices.rationale: This answer choice points out a relevant difference between logicians and physicians. A physician having an unhealthy lifestyle wouldn't affect that physician's competency to treat patients. But a logician failing to be logical would make that logician incompetent to discuss logic. That would mean that the logician, unlike the physician, is an example of a person who does need to practice what they preach. The author fails to consider that important difference between physicians and logicians, which makes the author's reasoning very questionable.

choices.text: if a physician's health deteriorates badly, the physician may not be able to treat patients effectively
choices.rationale: This answer choice doesn't really show why a physician might not need to maintain a healthy lifestyle. Maintaining a healthy lifestyle and staying in good health aren't quite the same thing. A physician failing to maintain a healthy lifestyle does not necessarily mean that the physician's health will “deteriorate badly.” (Likewise, physicians’ health can deteriorate even if they maintain healthy lifestyles.) Because this author is discussing physicians maintaining “healthy lifestyles” and not physicians “being healthy,” this answer choice doesn't quite point out why physicians might need to practice what they preach.

choices.text: physicians who are incompetent to practice medicine can cause more harm than can logicians who discuss logic illogically
choices.rationale: This answer choice wants us to believe that this is a relevant difference between physicians and logicians. But, by discussing a physician's incompetence, the answer choice brings up an issue that's irrelevant to the reasoning. This author's point wasn't about physicians being incompetent to practice medicine. It was about physicians who do not maintain a healthy lifestyle. Those are entirely different concepts, so this answer choice does not point out a difference between physicians and logicians that's germane to the reasoning.

choices.text: it is more difficult to become logical in one's discussions of logic than it is to modify an unhealthy lifestyle
choices.rationale: The author's point was that logicians don't need to be logical to do their job. Since the author doesn't think that trait is necessary, the author isn't concerned with how easy it is to acquire that trait. To identify a flaw in this reasoning, we should look for an answer choice that shows why logicians need to be logical, not an answer choice that discusses how difficult it may be to become logical.

choices.text: although it is not necessary for logicians to be logical in order to be competent to discuss logic, it is highly desirable
choices.rationale: To identify a flaw in this reasoning, we can look for an answer choice that shows why logicians need to be logical. The problem with this answer choice is that it concedes that the author's whole point is valid. It says that logicians don't have to be logical to do their job.

questions.stimulus: Generally, it is important that people practice what they preach, yet there are exceptions. For instance, it is no more necessary for logicians to be logical in their discussions of logic than it is for physicians to have healthy lifestyles in order to treat people.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: Domesticated animals cannot be turned into wild species by breeding only those animals that display some wild characteristics.
choices.rationale: As fascinating as it is to contemplate reverse-engineering a wolf by breeding dogs, this argument was not about turning domesticated animals back into wild animals. We're looking for a reason why we can't make every wild species into a domesticated one, not why we can't make every domesticated species into a wild one.

choices.text: In some animal species, wild members mate more frequently than tame members.
choices.rationale: Note the conclusion's scope: any animal could, “in principle,” be domesticated. By qualifying the conclusion with the “in principle,” the author only claims that it's theoretically possible to domesticate any wild animal. This answer choice points to reasons why domesticating some species would be difficult or time-consuming — the tame members we have to use are more reluctant to mate. However, even if it would take a long time and involve a great deal of cajoling, we could still theoretically breed these species. So this answer choice doesn't undermine the claim that it's theoretically possible to domesticate any species.

choices.text: In some animal species, no members ever display tameness.
choices.rationale: This answer choice points out why we wouldn't be as successful domesticating non-lupine species: unlike wolves, some species don't have tame members. As this author's reasoning went, by focusing on just the tame wolves, we created dogs. The author then concludes that by using only the tame members, we could domesticate any wild species. This answer choice points out that some species don't have tame members. Without the ability to select the animals that display tameness, we couldn't necessarily domesticate those species. Therefore, this weakens the author's reasoning and is correct.

choices.text: In some animal species, tame members are less fertile than wild members.
choices.rationale: Note the conclusion's scope: any animal could, “in principle,” be domesticated. By qualifying the conclusion with the “in principle,” the author only claims that it's theoretically possible to domesticate any wild animal. Like (B), this answer choice shows why domesticating some species could be difficult or time-consuming — the tame members are less fertile. However, even if it would take a long time and a great many attempts, we could still theoretically breed these species. So this answer choice doesn't undermine the claim that it's theoretically possible to domesticate any species.

choices.text: In some domesticated animal species, some members are much more tame than other members.
choices.rationale: This answer choice gives us a fact about the tameness of domesticated species. However, this author concluded we could domesticate any species by using only the tame members of that wild species. The tameness of domesticated animals doesn't matter to the author's argument, so this answer choice doesn't weaken the argument.

questions.stimulus: Domesticated animals, such as dogs, have come into existence by the breeding of only the individuals of a wild species that are sufficiently tame. For example, if when breeding wolves one breeds only those that display tameness when young, then after a number of generations the offspring will be a species of dog. Therefore, all animals can, in principle, be bred for domesticity.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why pollution levels in Crystal Bay increase after a heavy rainfall?

choices.text: Compared to the total amount of polluted seawater, the amount of rainwater that falls into Crystal Bay is negligible.
choices.rationale: Even if rainwater accounts for only a tiny percentage of the total water in Crystal Bay, we'd still expect Crystal Bay's pollution levels to go down when the pure rainwater fell directly to the bay. This answer could explain why Crystal Bay's pollution levels don't fall much after rain, but it doesn't explain why the pollution levels increase.

choices.text: Most of the rainwater that eventually reaches Crystal Bay falls on pesticide-treated fields before being carried into the bay.
choices.rationale: As predicted, this answer choice shows that rainwater can reach Crystal Bay through means other than direct rainfall. If most rainwater that winds up in Crystal Bay takes a circuitous path through pesticide-treated fields, that would explain why the pollution levels tend to go up following rain. Rather than falling into Crystal Bay as this passage discussed, the rainwater can become less pure and increase Crystal Bay's pollution levels if it instead picks up some pesticides from fields that carry it to the bay.

choices.text: Most rainwater carried by clouds consists of water that has evaporated from oceans around the world.
choices.rationale: Even if rainwater is mostly evaporated ocean water, the passage tells us the rainwater is pure. So, if the rainwater falls directly into Crystal Bay, we'd still expect the rain to dilute Crystal Bay and reduce its pollution levels. Therefore, this answer does not explain why Crystal Bay's pollution levels are higher following rainfall.

choices.text: The single leading cause of pollution in Crystal Bay is beachgoers' leaving behind their trash and debris, which then blows into the bay.
choices.rationale: Even if the primary source of Crystal Bay's pollution is beachgoers' behavior, we'd still expect Crystal Bay's pollution levels to go down if rain fell directly into the bay and diluted the extant pollution. In fact, since beachgoers typically do not go to the beach on rainy days, this answer choice makes Crystal Bay's high post-rain pollution levels all the more inexplicable.

choices.text: Other nearby ocean areas experience a pattern of pollutant increase and decrease that is extremely similar to that of Crystal Bay.
choices.rationale: This answer choice shows that there's a similar pattern of high post-rain pollution in other oceans. But identifying a pattern is not the same thing as explaining the causes of that pattern. So, this answer choice doesn't address the fundamental mystery the passage presents: why wouldn't the rainfall dilute and reduce the pollution levels in Crystal Bay?

questions.stimulus: Surprisingly, a new study has revealed that shortly after a heavy rainfall, pollution levels in Crystal Bay reach their highest levels. This occurs despite the fact that rainwater is almost totally pure and one would therefore expect that it would dilute the polluted seawater.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the ethicist's argument?

choices.text: Dr. Faris was aware that medication A had no known sleep-inducing properties.
choices.rationale: This would strengthen the case against Dr. Faris. In both legal and everyday usage, deception requires the deceiving party to knowingly misrepresent that truth. This answer choice shows that Dr. Faris was fully aware that Medication A isn't known to help patients sleep, which would strengthen the case against Dr. Faris.

choices.text: A committee at the hospital is currently considering revisions to the hospital's ethics code.
choices.rationale: The committee changing the hospital's ethics code is immaterial to this argument. This ethicist argues that Dr. Faris violated the current code, as presently constructed. Even if the revisions are made, and even if those revisions change the policy against deception — neither of which is inevitable — that wouldn't make Dr. Faris any less guilty of violating the current code.

choices.text: Medication A is a pain reliever that can indirectly lead to sleep due to a reduction in the patient's discomfort.
choices.rationale: This answer choice weakens the case against Dr. Faris by showing that the doctor may have reasonably expected Medication A to help the patient sleep. This argument features an equivocation between the premises and the conclusion. As described by the premises, Dr. Faris's actions might constitute deception, especially if the premises don't explicitly define what would constitute deception. Perhaps to deceive a patient, Dr. Faris would need to knowingly misrepresent the truth. If Dr. Faris had a reasonable expectation that Medication A could indirectly lead to sleep, perhaps Dr. Faris didn't deliberately lie to a patient, which would weaken the case against the doctor.

choices.text: Several other members of the hospital staff prescribed medication A to patients who had trouble sleeping.
choices.rationale: Sure, and these doctors may also be guilty of violating the hospital's code against lying to patients. A practice being widespread doesn't necessarily exculpate people who engage in the practice.

choices.text: Dr. Faris knew that the patient was not taking any other medications that have sleep-inducing properties.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant to the ethicist's argument. The issue is whether Dr. Faris's claim that Medication A would help a patient sleep constitutes deceiving a patient. The other medications the patient may have been taking at the time and whether Dr. Faris knew about those medications have no bearing on whether Dr. Faris's claims about Medication A were deceptive.

questions.stimulus: Ethicist: This hospital's ethics code states that hospital staff must not deceive patients about their medical treatment. But we know that Dr. Faris administered medication A to a patient and informed him that it would help him sleep. Medication A has no known sleep-inducing properties. So, Dr. Faris is clearly in violation of the ethics code, despite the fact that the patient's sleep did improve after taking medication A.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the student's argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.text: discusses the professor's stated criteria in order to draw attention away from the shortcomings of the student's paper
choices.rationale: This student draws a conclusion about the professor's stated criteria, so any discussion of those criteria is appropriate. Further, the student never claims the paper lacks shortcomings, so the argument is not an attempt to deflect from the paper's flaws.

choices.text: attempts to draw an evaluative conclusion solely on the basis of factual claims
choices.rationale: This answer choice mischaracterize's the argument's conclusion. The argument's conclusion is factual, not evaluative. Evaluative conclusions are about an entity's worth, value, merit, etc. Whether the professor correctly applied her guidelines can be established without making an “evaluation” about the professor or the guidelines.

choices.text: takes a condition that is among the requirements for a particular grade to be a condition that is enough to guarantee that grade
choices.rationale: This answer choice accurately describes the Sufficient/Necessary flaw in the student's argument. The “condition” that's a “requirement” for an A is the presence of reliable stats in the paper. The student implies the paper unfairly received a B despite featuring reliable stats, which means the student mistakenly believes that the reliable stats are enough to guarantee the A.

choices.text: is based on the report of a biased participant in the controversy
choices.rationale: The student may be a biased participant in this so-called controversy, but that doesn't render the premises or conclusion inherently flawed. Especially when the central premise — the paper's use of reliable stats — is verified by the teacher. In fact, it would actually be a flaw to assume that because the student has a vested interest, the argument is without merit.

choices.text: fails to make a necessary distinction between the professor's grading criteria and the objective criteria of a paper's quality
choices.rationale: This answer choice, like (A), misconstrues the student's conclusion. The student's argument is about the professor's criteria. It's not about the objective quality of the paper. Because the argument is focused only on the professor's criteria, there's no need to distinguish it from “objective criteria of a paper's quality.”

questions.stimulus: Student: My paper was not graded in accordance with the professor's stated criteria. The professor said that she would give A's only to papers whose conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence. The professor acknowledges that my conclusions were supported by reliable statistical evidence, but she gave my paper a B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the consumer advocate's argument?

choices.text: Providing information on minor drug-related interactions would detract from a patient's attention to serious interactions.
choices.rationale: This answer choice points to a significant downside of requiring drug companies to list “all known drug-related interactions.” If every prescription comes with a tome of potential, minor interactions, then consumers may disregard all the warnings, and not pay attention to or heed warnings about potentially catastrophic interactions. So this answer choice weakens the argument by providing a reason why companies shouldn't notify consumers of all known interactions.

choices.text: Many drugs have fewer documented drug-related interactions than does aspirin.
choices.rationale: This doesn't provide a reason why companies shouldn't notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions. If many drugs have fewer known interactions, then that's no problem. Companies will just have to provide a shorter list of interactions to the consumer. If anything, this may add a reason why companies should notify consumers of all known interactions — a shorter list would probably be cheaper to produce for the company and less overwhelming for the consumer. At any rate, this answer choice does not present a downside to the consumer advocate's recommendation, so it is incorrect.

choices.text: Providing information about all drug-related interactions would result in only negligible price increases for consumers.
choices.rationale: This strengthens the argument by eliminating a potential drawback of the consumer advocate's mandate. This requirement may make drugs even more expensive, maybe even inaccessible to those who need the drugs. But if the mandate leads to just a negligible cost increase, as this answer choice states, then the consumer advocate's conclusion is more persuasive.

choices.text: Current research is such that many drug-related interactions have not yet been identified.
choices.rationale: Like (B), this answer just shows that, for many drugs, the list of known interactions isn't extensive. But that's OK. That doesn't provide a reason why drug companies shouldn't notify consumers of all the interactions they know about. If anything, this may explain why companies should inform consumers of all known interactions — a shorter list would likely be less costly for the company and easier to read and follow for the consumer.

choices.text: Pharmacists usually draw patients' attention to printed warnings that are provided with drugs.
choices.rationale: This answer choice provides a reason why drug companies should notify consumers of all known interactions: pharmacists can point consumers to — and perhaps better understand — the warnings. This may strengthen the argument by eliminating a drawback of the consumer advocate's position, so this answer choice should be eliminated.

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Even relatively minor drug-related interactions can still be harmful to patients. For example, aspirin taken with fruit juice is ineffective. People unaware of this suffer unnecessary discomfort or take more aspirin than necessary. The government should, therefore, require drug companies to notify consumers of all known drug-related interactions.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.text: Any radioactive elements created when the universe began have probably decayed into other, nonradioactive elements.
choices.rationale: Perhaps this could be inferred from the argument, but this claim is never explicitly made in the passage. The author never definitively claims that radioactive elements were created when the universe began, so the author does not make a definitive statement about what happened to those elements.

choices.text: Radioactive elements are being created in the universe today.
choices.rationale: This answer choice refers to the argument's main conclusion. It is supported by every other claim in the argument, and it does not support anything else. Moreover, this answer choice does not distort or misrepresent the idea expressed in the argument's main conclusion. So this is the correct answer.

choices.text: If no new radioactive elements had been created after the universe began, almost no radioactive elements would be left in the universe today.
choices.rationale: This answer choice refers to the argument's second subsidiary conclusion. It is supported by the first subsidiary conclusion (the second part of the third sentence), but it supports the argument's main conclusion.

choices.text: It is possible that radioactive elements were created when the universe began.
choices.rationale: This refers to a concession the author makes at the beginning of the argument. The argument does not try to prove anything about the creation of radioactive elements during the universe's formation, so this answer choice has no role in the argument.

choices.text: Due to their instability, most of the universe's radioactive elements decay within at most a few million years into other, nonradioactive elements.
choices.rationale: This answer choice refers to the first subsidiary conclusion. This claim supports the second subsidiary conclusion (the first part of the last sentence), which in turn is used to support the argument's main conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Radioactive elements may have been created when the universe began. However, even if this occurred, these elements are clearly still being created in the universe today. Radioactive elements are unstable, so most of them decay within at most a few million years into other, nonradioactive elements. So, if no new radioactive elements had been created after the universe began, almost no radioactive elements would be left in the universe today, but there is an abundance of such elements.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?

choices.text: Many ancient cultures had agriculture before they began using fire to clear large tracts of land.
choices.rationale: This answer choice has no effect on this argument. Even if some ancient cultures engaged in agriculture before burning wide swaths of land, that isn't necessarily the “large-scale agriculture” this argument discusses. Moreover, even if this were true, it wouldn't show that this ancient society in question was still a hunter-gatherer society.

choices.text: Hunter-gatherer societies used fire for cooking and for heat during cold weather.
choices.rationale: Sure, hunter-gatherers may need fire for these reasons, but why would they need to burn “large areas of land” to cook or warm themselves? It seems much more practical to use small fires for both of these purposes. In brief, this answer choice may show why this society needed fire, but not the large-scale fires required to burn large tracts of land.

choices.text: Many plants and trees have inedible seeds that are contained in hard shells and are released only when subjected to the heat of a great fire.
choices.rationale: First, we don't know that the areas burned contained these plants with inedible seeds.Second, even if the ancient society burned these plants and trees, this still wouldn't explain why the ancient society had to burn the land to free the edible seeds. Why not just burn the shells? Wouldn't it make more sense to keep the seed-bearing plants and trees intact? Like (B), this answer choice may show why this society needed fire, but not the large-scale fires required to burn large tracts of land.

choices.text: Hunter-gatherer societies are known to have used fire to move animal populations from one area to another.
choices.rationale: This answer choice strengthens the argument by showing why hunter-gatherers would need to clear land with fire: to move herds of animals and (presumably) make it easier to hunt them. Unlike (B) or (C), this answer choice points to a purpose a hunter-gatherer society would have not just for fires but for large-scale, land-clearing fires. If we added this back to the argument, the author's conclusion would seem more convincing, and it is the correct answer.

choices.text: Few early societies were aware that burning organic material can help create nutrients for soil.
choices.rationale: Although this suggests the ancient society was probably not aware of the nutrient-enriching benefit of burning land, it doesn't necessarily undermine the claim that they were burning land for agriculture. A society can do something even it is unaware of all the benefits of doing that thing. This answer choice doesn't explain why a hunter-gatherer society would burn a tract of land. Consequently, it doesn't strengthen the author's conclusion.

questions.stimulus: There is evidence that a certain ancient society burned large areas of land. Some suggest that this indicates the beginning of large-scale agriculture in that society—that the land was burned to clear ground for planting. But there is little evidence of cultivation after the fires. Therefore, it is likely that this society was still a hunter-gatherer society.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in Professor Shanaz's argument by the claim that people generally notice and are concerned about only the most obvious public health problems?

choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the claim that contaminated water currently presents a much more widespread threat to the community than does ozone.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is a premise. However, the statement-in-question supports the conclusion that there probably will not be widespread efforts to tighten air pollution regulations. The claim that contaminated water presents a threat is another premise, not supported by anything in this argument.

choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the claim that there is unlikely to be a widespread, grassroots effort for new, more restrictive air pollution controls at this time.
choices.rationale: This is it. The statement-in-question is a premise. And it supports, as this answer choice states, the conclusion that there probably will not be widespread efforts to tighten air pollution regulations. This answer choice correctly identifies the role of the statement-in-question and accurately describes the conclusion of the argument, so it is the correct answer.

choices.text: It is used to explain the current public awareness of the severity of the problem of contaminated water.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is a principle about public health issues in general. It doesn't offer any specific insight into the contaminated water problem. Rather, the statement is used as a premise to support the conclusion that there probably will not be widespread efforts to tighten air pollution regulations. This answer choice neglects to mention that function, so it is incorrect.

choices.text: It is presented as indisputable evidence that ozone can be dangerous for severe asthmatics even if found in levels much lower than maximum levels permitted by law.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is used as evidence. However, the statement-in-question supports the conclusion that there probably will not be widespread efforts to tighten air pollution regulations. The claim that ozone can be dangerous for asthmatic people is another premise, not supported by anything in this argument.

choices.text: It is the main conclusion drawn in the argument.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is a premise. The argument's main conclusion is that there probably will not be widespread efforts to tighten air pollution regulations.

questions.stimulus: Professor Shanaz: People generally notice and are concerned about only the most obvious public health problems. Although there is indisputable evidence that ozone, an air pollutant, can be dangerous for severe asthmatics even if found in levels much lower than maximum levels permitted by law, most people are currently well aware that contaminated water presents a much more widespread threat to our community. Hence, there is unlikely to be a widespread, grassroots effort for new, more restrictive air pollution controls at this time.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption the psychotherapist's argument requires?

choices.text: Psychotherapists cannot help change their patients' relationships unless those patients focus on other people's troubles.
choices.rationale: This answer choice brings up a new idea: a patient focusing on “other people's troubles.” But the gap in this argument was only about therapists helping their patients and the causes of a patient's troubles. To address that gap, we don't need to establish anything about a patient focusing on “other people's troubles.” Rather than addressing the gap in the argument, this answer choice creates a new gap by introducing a new idea.

choices.text: At least some psychotherapy patients cannot be healed if a psychotherapist helps them change their relationships with other people.
choices.rationale: This answer choice has the type of weak language (“at least some”) we often see in correct answer choices to this type of question. However, it is not necessary to draw the conclusion.Remember, this argument concludes that therapists need to focus on a patient's relationships to help the patient heal. To reach that conclusion, do we need to know that some patients won't be healed even if the therapist focuses on a patient's relationships? Of course not. In fact, the negation test will confirm that answer choice is not necessary. Suppose it wasn't true that some patients won't be healed even if the therapist focuses on a patient's relationships. Or, better put, suppose all patients were healed when the therapist focuses on a patient's relationships. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Definitely not. We'd only strengthen the conclusion if we establish a consistent correlation between healing and focusing on relationships. Therefore, this answer choice is not necessary to the argument and should be eliminated.

choices.text: Those psychotherapy patients who change their relationships with other people will thereby find relief from at least some of their troubles.
choices.rationale: This answer choice has the type of weak language (“at least some”) we often see in correct answer choices to this type of question. Plus, this answer choice gets very close to addressing the gap in the argument. But this answer choice leaves out the therapist's role. Remember, this conclusion argues that the therapist will help the patient heal if the therapist focuses on the patient making positive changes in relationships. This answer choice doesn't address how a therapist can help a patient find relief from troubles, so it doesn't strengthen the argument.

choices.text: No psychotherapist can help a patient heal solely by addressing the internal causes of the patient's troubles.
choices.rationale: This answer choice establishes a link between the conclusion's new idea (a therapist helping a patient heal) and one of the premises (that patient's troubles do not have solely internal causes). By bridging the gap between the two discrete terms, this answer choice strengthens the argument. If a therapist can't help a patient by focusing on the internal causes of their troubles, the therapist will instead need to help patients change their relationships. Moreover, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is necessary to the argument. Suppose it wasn't true that therapists can't help their patients simply by focusing on the internal causes of the patients' troubles. Or, stated another way, suppose therapists could help patients by addressing the internal causes of the patients' troubles. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Yes. A therapist wouldn't have to focus on changing the patient's relationships in that case. Therefore, this answer choice is necessary to the argument and is correct.

choices.text: If a psychotherapist helps patients focus on troubles that are purely internal, then that psychotherapist thereby provides them the relief they seek.
choices.rationale: This weakens the conclusion and is incorrect. Therapists helping patients heal by focusing on the purely internal troubles would show that therapists don't need to focus on helping their patients make positive relationship changes.

questions.stimulus: Psychotherapist: The troubles from which a patient seeks relief through psychotherapy do not have purely internal causes; rather, those troubles result in part from the patient's relationships with other people. Hence, to help the patient heal, the psychotherapist must focus on the need for positive change in those relationships.

questions.stem: Which one of the following displays a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to the one in the argument above?

choices.text: Some high school teachers teach biology. No kindergarten teachers teach biology. Therefore, biology is not taught by all teachers.
choices.rationale: This answer choice features a “some” premise, a conditional premise, and a “some” conclusion (“not ... all” can be translated to “some do not”). However, the non-negated term in the conclusion (“biology”) is not the sufficient condition of the conditional premise (“kindergarten teacher”). This makes this argument structurally dissimilar to the passage, which means it does not commit the same flaw. In fact, this argument is valid. If kindergarten teachers do not teach biology, it must be true that some teachers do not teach biology. Since this argument is not even flawed, it is incorrect.

choices.text: Most school board members were once teachers. No one who was once a teacher prefers administrative work to teaching. Hence, few school board members prefer administrative work to teaching.
choices.rationale: This answer choice features a “most” premise. The argument in the passage did not feature a “most” statement at all, so this answer choice should be eliminated. Obviously, this answer choice cannot make an invalid combination of a “some” premise and a conditional premise if the answer choice does not feature a “some” premise. Moreover, this argument is valid. To validly combine a “most” and a conditional statement, the term shared by both must be the sufficient condition of the conditional statement. When the term shared by both is the “necessary” condition of the “most” statement, we can draw a “most” conclusion with the non-shared terms. Since both criteria are satisfied in the above case, we can validly draw the conclusion that most school board members do not prefer administrative work to teaching. Since this argument is not even flawed, it is incorrect.

choices.text: Some students prefer history to mathematics. No member of the Calculus Club prefers history to mathematics. Thus, some members of the Calculus Club are not students.
choices.rationale: This answer choice features a “some” premise, a conditional premise, and a “some” conclusion (“not ... all” can be translated to “some do not”). Moreover, the non-negated term in the conclusion (“members of the Calculus Club”) is the sufficient condition of the conditional premise. This makes this argument structurally similar to the passage. And, it's invalid for the same reason as the argument in the passage. If we take the contrapositive of the second statement (if Prefer History, then NOT Calculus Club), we can more easily see what a valid combination would look like. Remember the rule of combining a “some” statement and a conditional statement: the term shared by the two statements must be the sufficient condition in the conditional statement; (2) the conclusion must be a “some” statement containing the two non-shared terms. Because the first rule is satisfied, we validly could conclude: Students -some- NOT Calculus Club. However, the stated conclusion (Calculus Club -some- NOT Students) reverses and negates both conditions. Although “some” statements are reversible, we cannot validly negate both conditions — in other words, we cannot validly take the “contrapositive” of a “some” statement. The flawed conclusion in the passage also appeared to be the “contrapositive” of a properly drawn conclusion. So this answer choice is flawed for the same reason as the argument in the passage.

choices.text: Some principals are harsh disciplinarians. No adviser to a debate team is a harsh disciplinarian. Hence, some principals are not advisers to a debate team.
choices.rationale: This answer choice features a “some” premise, a conditional premise, and a “some” conclusion. However, the non-negated term in the conclusion (“principles”) is not the sufficient condition of the conditional premise (“adviser to the debate team”). This makes this argument structurally dissimilar to the passage, which means it does not commit the same flaw. In fact, this argument is valid. Since this argument is not even flawed, it is incorrect.

choices.text: Some teachers who let their students leave early are popular. No coaches allow their students to leave before three o'clock. Therefore, some popular teachers are not coaches.
choices.rationale: This answer choice features a “some” premise, a conditional premise, and a “some” conclusion. However, the non-negated term in the conclusion (“popular teachers”) is not the sufficient condition of the conditional premise (“coach”). This argument is invalid, as it equivocates between “leaving early” and “leaving before three o'clock”. Otherwise, however, it's a valid combination of a “some” statement and a conditional statement. Ignoring that equivocation, if we take the contrapositive of the second premise (“Let Students Leave → NOT Coach”), we can more easily see what a valid combination would look like. Remember the rule of combining a “some” statement and a conditional statement: the term shared by the two statements must be the sufficient condition in the conditional statement; (2) the conclusion must be a “some” statement containing the two non-shared terms. Because the first rule is satisfied, we validly could conclude:Popular -some- NOT Coach. Since this argument is not even flawed, it is incorrect.

questions.stimulus: Some freelance journalists sell their work to magazines that have lax editorial standards. No self-respecting writer sells his or her work to magazines that have lax editorial standards. Therefore, some self-respecting writers are not freelance journalists.

questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.text: Programs that are sold into syndication early tend to be long-running hits that are likely to decline soon.
choices.rationale: This answer choice explains the results of the study. It shows why running new and old episodes of the same show may shed viewers — the shows have been on the air forever and are bound to decline in ratings soon. However, this answer choice doesn't strengthen the argument because it doesn't show that a decline in ratings would affect a network's revenues. In other words, this answer choice fails to address the gap between the two discrete concepts in the argument's premise and conclusion. Therefore, this answer choice does not strengthen this argument, much less with a necessary premise.

choices.text: A drop in ratings has a negative effect on the network's revenues.
choices.rationale: This answer choice establishes a link between the premises (the study showing a drop in ratings for shows that run new and old episodes simultaneously) and the conclusion's new idea (a network losing revenue). By bridging the gap between the two discrete ideas, this answer choice strengthens the argument. Moreover, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is necessary to the argument. Suppose it wasn't true that a drop in ratings “had a negative effect on the network's revenues.” Or, stated another way, suppose a drop in ratings didn't negatively impact a network's revenue. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Yes. We couldn't conclude that selling syndicated rights and simultaneously airing new and old episodes can decrease the network's revenue. Therefore, this answer choice is also necessary to the argument.

choices.text: The price of syndication rights includes some compensation for the network's probable losses.
choices.rationale: This answer choice has the sort of weak language (“includes”) we often see in correct answers on this type of question. Further, it strengthens the argument by asserting that the network has “probable losses” when it sells syndicated reruns of a show. However, it is not necessary to draw the conclusion.In fact, the negation test will confirm that answer choice is not necessary. Suppose the network did not receive compensation for the probable losses when it sold syndication rights. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Is it the case that the network's revenues will not decrease as a result of the sale? Not necessarily. Even if the network received compensation to help offset the losses, it could still lose money following the sale. Since we can draw the argument's conclusion even if we assume this answer choice isn't true, this answer choice is unnecessary and should be eliminated.

choices.text: The audience of a popular program will usually prefer first-run episodes to reruns.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the argument. The audience's preference has no bearing on whether networks experience a revenue decrease when they run new and old episodes of a TV show at the same time.

choices.text: Most programs are never sold into syndication.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the argument. This argument is about what happens when a network sells the syndication rights to a show. This answer choice just states networks won't sell the most shows' syndication rights. That doesn't tell us anything about the shows whose syndication rights are sold.

questions.stimulus: Selling syndicated reruns of a popular network television program while the program is still running on the network can lead to decreased revenues for that network. The show's producers do earn a great deal of money from the sale of the syndication rights because the stations rerunning the program are assured of a successful show. However, a recent study shows that over 80 percent of the programs that are made available as reruns and as first-run episodes during the same season suffer an immediate ratings drop for their first-run episodes.

questions.stem: If all the statements above are true, which one of the following statements must be true?

choices.text: Beliefs for which a person does not have observable evidence are unreasonable.
choices.rationale: This answer choice brings up beliefs that are not grounded on observable evidence. To support this answer choice, we would need to use the second sentence from the passage. That sentence is a “some” statement, but this answer choice discusses all beliefs not grounded on observable evidence. That means the conclusion drawn by this answer choice is logically stronger than its support. Therefore, it is incorrect.

choices.text: Beliefs based on information from a reliable source are self-evident.
choices.rationale: The second premise establishes that some beliefs based on reliable sources are not self-evident. Therefore, this answer choice must be false. How could all beliefs based on reliable sources be self-evident if some of those beliefs are not self-evident?

choices.text: All reasonable beliefs for which a person has no observable evidence are based on information from a reliable source.
choices.rationale: An experienced and decisive test-taker might read three words of this answer choice before eliminating it. The first premise in the passage establishes “reasonable beliefs” as a necessary condition. That is the only mention of reasonable beliefs in this passage. This answer choice attempts to put “reasonable beliefs” as a sufficient condition, which means this answer choice is committing the reverses-without-negating flaw. We cannot conclude anything about “all reasonable beliefs.” We can only make a conclusion about “some” reasonable beliefs.

choices.text: If a belief is not grounded in observable evidence, then it is not self-evident either.
choices.rationale: This answer choice asserts a conditional relationship between a self-evident belief and a belief grounded on observable evidence. From the passage, we can only conclude that some beliefs based on a reliable source and some reasonable beliefs lack both conditions. That doesn't mean that there's a conditional relationship between the two — there could be many self-evident beliefs that are not based on observable evidence.

choices.text: Among reasonable beliefs that are not self-evident, there are some beliefs that are not grounded in observable evidence.
choices.rationale: In its incredibly wordy, difficult-to-parse way, this answer choice expresses the deduction we drew. Let's break it down, piece by piece. This answer choice refers to “reasonable beliefs,” which is synonymous with “beliefs that are reasonable to maintain.” The first part of this answer choice says, “Among reasonable beliefs that are not self-evident.” This tells us these beliefs have two conditions: they're reasonable and NOT self-evident. If we were abbreviating this statement, we could write: Reasonable Beliefs & NOT Self-Evident. Next, the answer choice tells us that some of these beliefs “are not grounded in observable evidence.” If we were to add this to the above, we would get: Reasonable Beliefs & NOT Self-Evident -some- NO Observable Evidence. From the passage, we can validly conclude that there's at least one belief that is (1) reasonable, and (2) not self-evident, and (3) not grounded on observable evidence. Both our initial deduction and this answer choice express that idea. (It would be equally valid to say, “Among beliefs that are not self-evident, there are some that are reasonable and not grounded in observable evidence.”) So this answer choice must be true and is correct.

questions.stimulus: If a belief is based on information from a reliable source, then it is reasonable to maintain that belief. Furthermore, some beliefs are based on information from a reliable source and yet are neither self-evident nor grounded in observable evidence.

questions.stem: The analysis provided for the situation above could be appropriate for each of the following situations except:

choices.text: A math teacher wants her students to understand the mathematical principles taught in her course and wants them to apply these principles routinely in everyday life.
choices.rationale: It's reasonable enough to conclude that a math teacher helping her students understand mathematical principles (her first objective) will help her students apply these principles to everyday life (her second objective). Understanding the principles could make it easier for students to apply the principles. Therefore, applying the analysis “success in the first objective success will bring about success in the second objective” to this situation seems logical. It's close enough, at least, to meet the low bar of “could be appropriate” set by the question stem.

choices.text: A software manufacturer wants its customers to be more satisfied with its product, and it wants them to place fewer calls to the service representative about how to use the product.
choices.rationale: It makes some intuitive sense to conclude that a software manufacturer making its customers more satisfied with its products (its first objective) would result in fewer calls to the customer service representatives (its second objective). After all, if the customers are satisfied with the product, they probably know how to use it, and they will probably not need to place as many calls to customer service. Therefore, applying the analysis “success in the first objective success will bring about success in the second objective” to this situation makes sense. It's close enough, at least, to meet the low bar of “could be appropriate” set by the question stem.

choices.text: A librarian wants fewer of the books borrowed from the library to be lost or stolen, and he wants more of the library's books to be returned on time.
choices.rationale: It makes some sense to conclude that having fewer books lost or stolen from a library (the librarian's first objective) would result in more books being returned on time (the librarian's second objective). After all, if fewer books are lost or stolen, it's probably the case that they're being returned on time, which would result in a higher percentage of the books being returned. Therefore, it's reasonable enough to apply the analysis “success in the first objective success will bring about success in the second objective” to this situation. It's close enough, at least, to meet the low bar of “could be appropriate” set by the question stem.

choices.text: A hardware retail company wants to construct a new, larger warehouse and wants its employees to help plan how the old warehouse will be expanded to meet any need for more space.
choices.rationale: Unlike the other answer choices, this one presents two objectives that appear to be, if not mutually exclusive, at least in direct competition. Constructing a new, expansive warehouse would certainly not help “bring about success” in getting employees to plan how to expand the old warehouse. Making the new, large warehouse would obviate the need to expand the old warehouse. Therefore, we cannot apply the “success in the first objective success will bring about success in the second objective” to this situation.

choices.text: A concert series director wants to present a more varied repertoire and wants to attract new patrons.
choices.rationale: It wouldn't be unfounded to conclude that a concert director introducing a more varied repertoire to the concerns (the first objective) would result in new patrons attending the concerts (the second objective). After all, more variety to the music presented could attract previously uninterested people to attend the concert series. So it's plausible enough to apply the analysis “success in the first objective success will bring about success in the second objective” to this situation. It's close enough, at least, to meet the low bar of “could be appropriate” set by the question stem.

questions.stimulus:
Situation: A physical therapist wants her patients to derive more enjoyment from the challenge of developing physical skills. She also wants them to spend more time practicing those skills.

Analysis: Success in meeting the first objective will bring about success in meeting the second.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the classicist's argument by the claim that you cannot travel back in time to spend a year abroad at Plato's Academy?

choices.text: It is the main conclusion drawn in the argument.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is a premise. The first sentence is the main conclusion of this argument

choices.text: It points up by example a contrast from which the conclusion is drawn.
choices.rationale: As far as we can tell, “point up” is a Britishism meaning “emphasize.” So this answer choice can be roughly translated to, “It is an example intended to emphasize a contrast that supports the conclusion.” However, an adaptable test-taker could get to this answer choice without knowing this definition of “point up.” We know the statement-in-question draws a contrast with how we master modern language. This contrast is used to support the conclusion. So the phrase “a contrast from which the conclusion is drawn” is an apt description of the statement-in-question. Further, an adaptable test-taker could see how the reference to “Plato's Academy” could accurately be called an “example.” To illustrate the same point, the author could have used several other places where Latin or Ancient Greek was spoken — the Roman Colosseum, Virgil's study, Mycenae. The author just chose Plato's Academy as one example. So, even with the strange phrasing, it's possible to determine that this accurately expresses the role played by the statement-in-question.

choices.text: It is a mere rhetorical flourish having no logical relation to the argument's conclusion.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is a premise. The contrast it draws with how we master contemporary languages helps support the main conclusion. So it is inaccurate to say that the statement-in-question has “no logical relation to the argument's conclusion.”

choices.text: It is a premise that guarantees the truth of the argument's conclusion.
choices.rationale: The statement-in-question is a premise. However, this premise does not “guarantee[] the truth of the argument's conclusion.” This argument is flawed, so the conclusion is far from guaranteed. The statement-in-question shows why we can't master ancient languages in the same way we master modern language. But this doesn't guarantee the conclusion's assertion that our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is imperfect, as there could be other ways to gain mastery over those ancient languages.

choices.text: It is an ancillary conclusion drawn in the argument.
choices.rationale: This is a rare appearance of the term “ancillary conclusion” on the LSAT. In the context of law or business, the word ancillary means subordinate, supplemental, or subsidiary. So an “ancillary conclusion” is synonymous with “subsidiary conclusion” or “intermediate conclusion.” You wouldn't need to know that to eliminate this answer choice, however. The statement-in-question is not supported by anything — there's no study cited to disprove the existence of time machines or anything like that — so it cannot be a conclusion at all.

questions.stimulus: Classicist: Our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is at best imperfect. The best students of a modern language may so immerse themselves in a country where it is spoken as to attain nearly perfect knowledge; but you cannot travel back in time to spend a year abroad at Plato's Academy.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the argument's conclusion to be properly drawn?

choices.text: If the water in a pond is not acidic, the conditions at that pond are beneficial to turtles.
choices.rationale: Establishing that acidic ponds are not beneficial for turtles would justify this conclusion, as Wallakim is an acidic pond. But establishing that non-acidic ponds are beneficial does not tell us anything about Wallakim, and therefore does not support this conclusion.

choices.text: The most important factor that determines whether a pond will have a thriving turtle population is the acidity of the water.
choices.rationale: This answer choice establishes a link between a pond's acidity and its turtle population, so it at least addresses the gap in the argument. However, it doesn't establish that acidity is bad or negatively impacts the turtle population. Even if (B) is true, it could be the case that an acidic pond is actually beneficial to turtle populations. So (B) doesn't ensure the validity of this argument's conclusion.

choices.text: The water conditions at Sosachi Pond are more beneficial to turtles than are the water conditions at Wallakim Pond.
choices.rationale: Even if the waters at Sosachi a more beneficial than the waters at Wallakim, that doesn't establish that the waters at Wallakim are not beneficial to turtles. Both Sosachi and Wallakim could have beneficial conditions for turtles, with Sosachi featuring slightly better conditions.

choices.text: Wallakim Pond would have a thriving population of turtles if it were not acidic.
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes a hypothetical about Wallakim Pond — if it was not acidic, it would be beneficial to turtles. One implication of this answer choice is that it's beneficial to turtles if a pond isn't acidic. That's the same conditional relationship that answer choice (A) brings up, so this answer choice is wrong for the same reasons as (A). We know Wallakim is acidic, and establishing that non-acidic ponds are beneficial doesn't tell us anything about Wallakim.

choices.text: The conditions at a pond are beneficial to turtles only if the water in the pond is not acidic.
choices.rationale: This will ensure the conclusion's validity. We can specify this as: if Beneficial Conditions, then NOT Acidic. If we take its contrapositive and add it to our argument, we can see that we have drawn a valid conclusion: (E) Contrapositive: if Acidic, then NOT Beneficial Conditions. Contrapositive: if NOT Beneficial Conditions, then NOT Thriving Turtle Pop. Wallakim: Acidic. Conclusion: Wallakim: NOT Thriving Turtle Pop.

questions.stimulus: For there to be a thriving population of turtles in a pond, conditions at that pond must be beneficial to turtles. The water in Wallakim Pond, unlike that in Sosachi Pond, is acidic. Thus, there must not be a thriving population of turtles at Wallakim Pond.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the information above?

choices.text: The chimpanzee, a higher primate, evolved from the lemur.
choices.rationale: We cannot conclude that any higher primates evolved from the lemur. So we cannot conclude that the chimpanzee, or any other higher primate, evolved from the lemur.

choices.text: No primates indigenous to Madagascar are diurnal higher primates.
choices.rationale: This answer choice must be true. The only primate indigenous to Madagascar is the lemur, and we know lemurs are lower primates. Therefore, if a primate is indigenous to Madagascar, it is a lower primate. So it is true that “No primates indigenous to Madagascar are ... higher primates.” They're all lower primates. This answer choice also mentions that these primates indigenous to Madagascar are not diurnal higher primates. That's also true. We know all primates indigenous to Madagascar are lower primates, which means they're not any kind of higher primates, no matter the sleep pattern.

choices.text: No higher primate is nocturnal.
choices.rationale: This is not supported. Higher primates may have evolved from a diurnal lower primate (or so we think), but that doesn't mean that they're all diurnal as well. Beyond that, the passage doesn't provide any information about the sleep patterns of higher primates.

choices.text: There are some lemurs without opposable thumbs.
choices.rationale: We have no idea if some lemurs lack opposable thumbs. The passage states that if a species has an opposable thumb, it must be a primate. That could imply that all primates have opposable thumbs or that some primates lack opposable thumbs. We can't say for sure. And even if we knew that some primates lacked opposable thumbs, we can't conclude that lemurs are among the species that lack opposable thumbs.

choices.text: There are no nocturnal lemurs.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is too strong. The passage tells us that “some” species of lemur are diurnal. But that doesn't imply that all species of lemur are diurnal. Some, or even most, lemurs could be nocturnal.

questions.stimulus: The study of primates is interesting for many reasons, including the fact that only primates have opposable thumbs. The lemurs are lower primates and the only primates indigenous to Madagascar, a large island off the coast of southeastern Africa. Some species of lemurs are the only living lower primates that are diurnal—that is, active primarily during the day. All higher primates are thought to have evolved from a single diurnal species of lower primates.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the professor's argument?

choices.text: The low visibility of other star systems from Earth would not be adequately explained by the existence of an invisible light-absorbing medium in outer space, even if there were such a medium.
choices.rationale: This answer choice might strengthen the argument if true — it refutes the premise supporting the light-absorbing explanation-favoring scientists' hypothesis — but it isn't a necessary assumption. To draw the conclusion that we have no reason to believe in the light-absorbing explanation, we don't need to establish that the light-absorbing explanation can't even explain star dimness. We just need to show that the alternative explanation is enough, by itself, to explain star dimness.

choices.text: The hypothesis of an invisible light-absorbing medium in outer space is correct only if it adequately explains the low visibility of other star systems from Earth.
choices.rationale: The contrapositive of this answer choice would read, “If the hypothesis of an invisible light-absorbing medium in outer space does not adequately explain the low visibility of other star systems from Earth, then it is not correct.” That answer choice would strengthen this professor's conclusion if the professor established that the light-absorbing explanation didn't explain star dimness. However, the professor never said that. The professor just claimed that there's already the theory-of-relativity explanation that can explain star dimness. As on (A), we don't need to establish that the light-absorbing explanation can't explain star dimness. We just need to show that the theory-of-relativity explanation is enough, by itself, to explain star dimness.

choices.text: A hypothesis is likely to be correct if there is some phenomenon that it adequately accounts for and that is not adequately accounted for by an existing theory.
choices.rationale: We're looking for assumptions that would help support the conclusion that there's no evidence for the light-absorbing explanation. So we need rules for what makes a hypothesis incorrect, not correct.

choices.text: Most scientists who posit the invisible light-absorbing medium accept the general theory of relativity.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant. Correctness does not depend upon public or even scientific acceptance. The Earth revolved around the sun long before most scientists accepted that theory. So whether or not scientists accept the theory of relativity does not affect whether the theory of relativity fully explains star dimness.

choices.text: The general theory of relativity does not depend upon the hypothesis that there exists an invisible light-absorbing medium in outer space.
choices.rationale: This precisely matches our anticipation that the correct answer would show that the theory-of-relativity explanation and the light-absorbing-medium explanation are mutually exclusive. This answer choice states that the theory-of-relativity explanation doesn't rely on the light-absorbing-medium explanation. This strengthens the argument, as it shows that the theory-of-relativity explanation can stand on its own — it doesn't need a light-absorbing medium to explain star dimness. Moreover, the negation test will confirm that this answer choice is necessary to the argument. Suppose that the general theory of relativity depended on the existence of an invisible light-absorbing medium in outer space. In that case, is the conclusion now untrue? Yep. The professor's belief in the theory of relativity's ability to explain star dimness would be evidence in favor of the existence of a light-absorbing medium, not evidence against its existence. Therefore, this answer choice is necessary to the argument and is correct.

questions.stimulus: Professor: Many scientists hypothesize that there is an invisible "light-absorbing medium" in outer space. In support, they argue that the medium's existence would explain the low visibility of other star systems from Earth. But there is actually no reason to believe that the hypothesis is correct, since the low visibility in question is already completely explained by the general theory of relativity.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the method of reasoning used in the argument?

choices.text: appealing to the ambiguity of a word in an attempt to show that a correlation is universal
choices.rationale: This misdescribes the argument. The author didn't claim the correlation (between gesturing and concrete words) is universal. In fact, the conclusion is about how the correlation is not universal.

choices.text: appealing to a universal psychological generalization in an attempt to support a claim about the use of gestures
choices.rationale: Like (A), this misdescribes the argument. The author never claimed the generalization (that we gesture more when saying concrete words) is universal. In fact, the conclusion is about how the correlation is not universal.

choices.text: citing a psychological fact to try to reconcile a generalization with apparently disconfirming evidence
choices.rationale: This answer choice is very close to our anticipation (“attempting to explain why potentially inconsistent evidence is not a reason to reject a generalization”) and is worthy of a closer inspection. Some test-takers may take issue with the abstract phrasing here — especially that which doesn't conform to our anticipation, such as the words “psychological fact” and “reconcile.” However, if we can find an analog in the passage that matches these words, we can be confident that this answer choice accurately describes the technique of reasoning in the passage. So, what could be the “psychological fact” this answer choice references? According to this answer choice, the fact will help reconcile a “generalization” and “disconfirming evidence.” We've already identified the generalization as the belief that people gesture more when describing concrete stuff. And the disconfirming evidence would appear to be that this “correlation is far from universal” — not everyone gestures more when describing concrete stuff. What could this psychological fact be then? The last premise describes how some people “perceive” (a psychological phenomenon) words differently. In other words, the psychological fact is that the perception of particular concepts as concrete or abstract is not the same for everyone. So we can find an analog in the passage for “psychological fact,” which means we shouldn't reject (C) for using this term. For many test-takers, “reconcile” is another keyword that may jump out in this answer choice. Whenever the idea of “reconciling” comes up in Logical Reasoning, it usually means using evidence to show how apparently contradictory facts can both be true. That's what happened here. Yes, it seems contradictory to say that the generalization is (1) not universal and (2) real. But the “psychological fact” can show why both sides are true — we all gesture more on concrete stuff, we just disagree on what is concrete. So no matter how we slice it, (C) correctly describes the argumentative technique in this passage, and it is correct.

choices.text: advocating an explanation for a phenomenon by attempting to demonstrate that other possible explanations are implausible
choices.rationale: Another answer choice that misdescribes the argument. The author never discussed “other possible explanations” for a phenomenon. In fact, the argument didn't even explain why we gesture more when describing concrete stuff. Rather, the issue was whether or not the phenomenon is even valid!

choices.text: offering a reason for believing that a widely accepted generalization requires still more supporting evidence
choices.rationale: This incorrectly characterizes the conclusion of the argument. Our author does not call for additional evidence in their conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Some researchers claim that people tend to gesture less when they articulate what would typically be regarded as abstract rather than physical concepts. To point out that such a correlation is far from universal is insufficient reason to reject the researchers' claim, because some people perceive words like "comprehension" as expressing a physical action, like grasping something, rather than a state of understanding, which is abstract.

questions.stem: It can be properly inferred from the statements above that many sociologists believe that

choices.text: economically motivated decisions by voters need not constitute a complex phenomenon
choices.rationale: Right away, we get our anticipation. If voting based on personal economic interest was a complex phenomenon, the sociologists couldn't use their principle to undermine rational-choice theory. Because they believe the principle undermines rational-choice theory, the sociologists must believe voting based on rational economic interest is not a complex phenomenon. This is correct.

choices.text: a complex phenomenon generally will have many complex causes
choices.rationale: The sociologists seem to believe complex phenomena have complex causes, but nothing here says they believe each phenomenon has more than one cause. They may believe some phenomena have one complex cause.

choices.text: political phenomena often have religious and cultural causes as well as economic ones
choices.rationale: Religion and culture were not mentioned in this passage at all! So this answer choice is simply not supported by the passage.

choices.text: popular support for political parties is never a complex phenomenon
choices.rationale: This contradicts the sociologists' premise. The sociologists use the popular support of a political organization support as an example of a complex phenomenon.

choices.text: the decisions of individual voters are not usually influenced by their beliefs about which policies will yield them the greatest economic advantage
choices.rationale: Since we know the sociologists oppose rational-choice theory. However, this answer choice subtly but significantly misdescribes what rational-choice theory is. Rational-choice theory holds that popular support for a political party is entirely (“sufficiently”) explained by voters making decisions based on their economic self-interest. The sociologists certainly have issues with that. But even though they don't think popular support for a political party isn't entirely explained by that, they could still think that economic self-interest influences voters' decisions. The sociologists think that considerations of economic self-interest don't entirely cause the rise of political parties, not that those considerations never enter into the equation at all.

questions.stimulus: According to rational-choice theory, popular support for various political parties can be explained sufficiently in terms of deliberate decisions by individual voters to support the party whose policies they believe will yield them the greatest economic advantage. This theory is opposed by many sociologists on the grounds that a complex phenomenon such as the rise of a political organization cannot be caused by a simple phenomenon.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the scientist's argument?

choices.text: The genetically engineered plants that have been developed so far have few advantages over plants that are not genetically engineered.
choices.rationale: This is unrelated to the question of GMOs' capacity to cause harm. If they have few advantages but do not cause harm, the scientist's argument is not any weaker.

choices.text: Whatever health risks there are in food from genetically altered plants may be somewhat reduced by other factors such as enrichment of the plants' vitamin and mineral content.
choices.rationale: This answer choice says that even if GMOs were harmful, those harms are mitigated by other factors. Mitigating factors would only strengthen the scientist's claims GMOs' risk is minimal, so this is incorrect.

choices.text: Scientists have yet to determine, for each characteristic of some plants and animals used for food, the precise location of the genes that determine that characteristic.
choices.rationale: This answer choice may be tempting, since it makes it seem like scientists don't really understand the food they're genetically engineering. But really, it is so weak that it doesn't have an effect on the argument. Scientists don't know what all 750,000 genes do in just some plants and animals? Even if that were true, they could still only alter the genes they understand, and the risks of altering those genes could be minimal.

choices.text: There are plants that are known to be toxic to some animals and whose toxicity is known to be affected by the alteration of a single gene.
choices.rationale: Yes! This answer choice presents the same cause (alteration of a single gene) and the same effect (changing the toxicity of the plant). So this answer choice strengthens the claim that altering a single gene might cause harm, which weakens the scientist's claim that changing a single gene is too insignificant to increase the risk of harm. There are a few things that might give us pause about this answer choice. First, it's about plants we know to be toxic, while the passage focused on “foodstuffs,” which are generally not toxic.
