Second, it discusses the toxicity to animals, not necessarily humans. Finally, it just says that the “toxicity is known to be affected” — it doesn't say that the toxicity is increased. However, these doubts should be erased when we remember how strong the scientists' assertion was. The scientist depends entirely on the claim that changing a single gene is just too minor a change to affect a plant's capacity to cause harm when eaten. This answer choice shows an instance when changing a single gene can affect a plant's ability to cause harm. Even if those plants are not ones we eat or genetically modify, even if the change would only affect nonhuman animals, and even if the change actually makes the plan less toxic, the answer choice still weakens the scientist's argument. It undercuts the scientist's claim that altering a single gene “cannot have effects significant enough” to increase the risk of harm. This answer choice shows it's possible alter a single gene and produce significant effects, so it is correct.

choices.text: Research has shown that those consumers who are most strongly opposed to genetically altered foods tend to be ill-informed on the issue.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant. People can be ill-informed about a topic generally but correct about one specific fact (or even about the topic in general). Pointing out that someone is ill-informed may make one's argument less convincing, but it doesn't make their beliefs necessarily false. Even if did, this would only strengthen the scientists' argument.

questions.stimulus: Scientist: Some consumer groups claim that the economic benefits of genetically engineered foodstuffs may be offset by hidden health risks to humans. However, the risk is minimal. In most cases of deliberate alteration of a plant's genetic structure only a single gene in about 750,000 has been changed. Since the change in the organism's genetic structure is so slight, it cannot have effects significant enough to be worrisome.

questions.stem: Of the following judgments, which one most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.text: Jerry's hobby, making home movies, does not harm anyone, nor does it increase the likelihood of harm to anyone. He does it because he thinks that it will benefit his children by preserving a record of their childhoods. So the government is unjustified in interfering with Jerry's moviemaking.
choices.rationale: We don't have any principle that leads to the conclusion “Government NOT justified in interfering,” so we cannot choose an answer that draws this conclusion. We only have NOT justified as a sufficient condition, not as a necessary one.

choices.text: It is well known that a property is aesthetically less pleasing when neighboring properties have unkempt lawns. My neighbor often forgets to mow his lawn for several weeks. The city council, therefore, is justified in fining my neighbor for not mowing his lawn more frequently.
choices.rationale: This argument at least leads to a conclusion our principle could justify — the government justified in interfering — but both halves of the sufficient condition are missing. The lawn isn't causing physical harm, and we don't know if the neighbor overgrows his lawn to help others, so this one is incorrect.

choices.text: Because a motorcyclist who is not wearing a helmet is much more likely to suffer a serious head injury in the event of an accident, the government is justified in requiring motorcyclists to wear helmets.
choices.rationale: Not wearing a helmet is “increasing the likelihood of physical harm,” but not “to others,” so it doesn't meet the first half of our sufficient condition. And the other half is absent as well. We don't know if motorcyclists decline helmets to help others (or — unless they really want to help trauma surgeons practice their craft — how this could feasibly help others).

choices.text: Because Zabziew Pharmaceutical Corporation's research is motivated by the desire to make profits and not by the desire to benefit customers, it has been of little help to people suffering from serious illness. So the government is justified in suspending Zabziew's license to test new drugs.
choices.rationale: Here we have a situation in which it's true that the corporation was “not motivated by the intent to help others,” but it's missing the condition “increases the chance of physical harm to others.” The company may be making ineffective drugs, but that doesn't automatically mean they're harmful.

choices.text: To further her own political ambitions, Jill wanted to give a speech advocating the use of violence to achieve political ends. But her speech would most likely have caused a riot and people would have gotten hurt. Hence, the government was justified in preventing her from giving her speech.
choices.rationale: Finally! A situation in which there is an increased chance of physical harm to others (people getting hurt in a riot) and not a desire to help others (making the speech to further her own political ambitions). Both halves of the sufficient condition are present; therefore the conclusion that interference is permissible is fully justified, and (E) is correct.

questions.stimulus: A government is justified in interfering with a person's action if the action would increase the likelihood of physical harm to others and the action is not motivated by a desire to help others.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.text: The plan to crack down on violations of corporate income tax law is part of a broad campaign against corporate misconduct.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the author’s argument. It doesn’t show that the government is trying to crack down on corporate income tax violations, even if it hasn’t completed any audits this year. This answer choice just provides context to the government’s promise to crack down on corporate income tax violations. If the argument concluded that the government is not trying to reduce “corporate misconduct” because it hasn’t completed any audits, this answer choice would weaken the argument. But the argument concludes that the government isn’t trying to cut down corporate income tax violations, making this answer choice irrelevant.

choices.text: The number of personal income tax returns audited over the past year is greater than in previous years.
choices.rationale: Like (A), this answer choice doesn’t show that the government is trying to crack down on corporate income tax violations, even if it hasn’t completed any audits this year. Instead, this answer choice tells us about “personal income tax” — not “corporate income tax.” The former addresses whether individuals accurately report the incomes they receive; the latter addresses whether corporations accurately report the incomes they pay their employees. If the argument concluded that the government is not trying to reduce “income tax violations” because it hasn’t completed any audits of corporations, this answer choice would weaken the argument. But the argument concludes that the government isn’t trying to cut down corporate income tax violations, making this answer choice irrelevant.

choices.text: Most audits of corporate income tax returns do not reveal any significant violations.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the author’s argument. It doesn’t show that the government is trying to crack down on corporate income tax violations, even if it hasn’t completed any audits this year. This answer choice tells us about the success rate of audits on corporate income tax returns. But that’s irrelevant to the argument’s conclusion, which addresses whether the government is attempting to crack down on violations of corporate income tax law. Whether these audits would reveal fraud is immaterial to whether these attempts are being made.

choices.text: It generally takes longer than one year to complete an audit of a corporate income tax return.
choices.rationale: This definitely weakens the author’s argument. It shows that the government’s audits on corporate income tax returns take longer than a year. So, even if no audits have been completed this year, the government could still be pursuing these audits and thus attempting to uncover corporate income tax law violations. In other words, (D) shows that the government is trying to crack down on corporate income tax violations, even if it hasn’t completed any audits this year.

choices.text: Over the last five years, fewer audits of corporate income tax returns have been completed than in the preceding five years.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the author’s argument, which focuses only on the “past year.” The number of audits over the last “five years” doesn’t tell us anything about the number of audits this past year. Besides, the argument already told us that no audits on corporate income tax returns have been completed this year. Even if this answer choice did tell us about the number of audits completed over the last year, it wouldn’t add any information that could meaningfully affect the author’s argument.

questions.stimulus: The government's tax collection agency has not followed through on its plan, announced a year ago, to crack down on violations of corporate income tax law. Audits are the primary tool for detecting such violations, and over the past year, not a single audit of corporate income tax returns has been completed.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.text: uses the word "environment" in one sense in a premise and in a different sense in the conclusion drawn from that premise
choices.rationale: This doesn't describe a flaw in this argument's reasoning. The meaning of “environment” doesn't change over the course of the argument. Both times the columnist uses “environment,” it refers to the natural world.

choices.text: treats an effect of energy-related damage to the environment as if it were instead a cause of such damage
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes a type of cause-and-effect flaw, and it's tempting to some test-takers because this argument describes a cause-and-effect relationship between producing energy and damaging the environment. The columnist claims that producing energy causes damage to the environment. This answer choice says the argument is flawed because that cause and effect could be reversed — implying that damaging the environment could produce energy. But that's not an issue here since producing energy (to make or recycle products) clearly precedes environmental damage. Moreover, this answer choice doesn't address the salient point in the columnist's argument — whether making products from recycled materials is as environmentally damaging as making products from nonrecycled materials. Therefore, this answer choice does not describe an error in the columnist's reasoning.

choices.text: fails to consider that the particular types of recycled products that it cites may not be representative of recycled products in general
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to consider” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the author's argument if true?” This answer choice wouldn't weaken the argument. The columnist's conclusion isn't about “recycled products in general.” It's only about “some types of products from recycled materials.” Even if almost all recycled products don't damage the environment as much as nonrecycled products, that wouldn't necessarily hurt the columnist's conclusion. To prove this conclusion, the columnist just needs to show that a couple of recycled products damage the environment as much as nonrecycled products.

choices.text: fails to consider that making products from recycled materials may have environmental benefits unrelated to energy consumption
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to consider” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the author's argument if true?” This would definitely weaken the columnist's conclusion. Suppose that making products from recycled materials can benefit the environment in ways that aren't related to energy consumption. In that case, making some products from recycled materials wouldn’t damage the environment as much as making those products from nonrecycled materials. If using recycled materials cuts down the amount of natural resources we use or the amount of waste we produce, then these recycled products might be significantly better for the environment than products from nonrecycled materials. So, this answer choice describes an error in the columnist's reasoning.

choices.text: presumes that simply because one phenomenon follows another phenomenon the earlier phenomenon must be a cause of the later one
choices.rationale: When we see “presumes, without providing justification” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, the columnist doesn't necessarily believe that one thing must cause another simply because the first came before the second. Although the columnist describes a cause-and-effect relationship between producing energy and damaging the environment, the columnist doesn't say that producing energy causes damage to the environment simply because producing energy comes first. In fact, the columnist never describes why they think that producing energy causes environmental damage. The columnist asserts that relationship as a premise, so we have to accept it when evaluating this argument's validity. Besides, this answer choice doesn't address the salient point in the columnist's argument — whether making products from recycled materials is as environmentally damaging as making products from nonrecycled materials. Therefore, this answer choice does not describe an error in the columnist's reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Making some types of products from recycled materials is probably as damaging to the environment as it would be to make those products from entirely nonrecycled materials. The recycling process for those products requires as much energy as producing them from raw materials, and almost all energy production damages the environment.

questions.stem: The statement that people who are constantly subjected to fire drills eventually come to ignore the fire alarm plays which one of the following roles in the physician's argument?

choices.text: It is presented as an example of the sort of warning referred to in the argument's overall conclusion.
choices.rationale: The last sentence isn't an example of the type of warning referenced in the argument's main conclusion. The argument's main conclusion addresses warnings about foods from definitive studies, not fire alarms.

choices.text: It is a statement that plays no logical role in the argument but that instead serves to impugn the motives of the medical establishment.
choices.rationale: The last sentence plays a role in the argument — it's an analogy that supports the argument's conclusion. Moreover, the physician never impugns (challenges) the medical establishment's motives. The physician describes what the medical establishment should do to prevent people from ignoring its warnings.

choices.text: It is an analogy offered in support of the argument's overall conclusion.
choices.rationale: This is correct! The last sentence is an analogy that supports the argument's main conclusion. After all, the last sentence shows why conclusions from initial studies are bad, supporting the last conclusion's claim that the medical establishment should only publish conclusions from definitive studies.

choices.text: It is an analogy that forms part of a specific objection to the argument's overall conclusion.
choices.rationale: It's true that the last sentence is an analogy, but it doesn't challenge or undermine the argument's overall conclusion. It supports the argument's conclusion. It shows why conclusions from initial studies are bad, supporting the last conclusion's claim that the medical establishment should only publish conclusions from definitive studies.

choices.text: It is an analogy offered to clarify the distinction the physician makes between an initial study and a definitive study.
choices.rationale: It's true that the last sentence is an analogy, but it doesn't challenge or undermine the argument's overall conclusion. It supports the argument's conclusion. It shows why conclusions from initial studies are bad, supporting the last conclusion's claim that the medical establishment should only publish conclusions from definitive studies.

questions.stimulus: Physician: We are constantly bombarded by warnings, based on initial studies' tentative conclusions, about this or that food having adverse health effects. If the medical establishment wants people to pay attention to health warnings, it should announce only conclusive results, the kind that can come only from definitive studies. After all, people who are constantly subjected to fire drills eventually come to ignore the fire alarm.

questions.stem: A questionable technique used in the club president's reasoning is

choices.text: drawing a conclusion on the basis of circular reasoning
choices.rationale: Circular reasoning is a flaw in which the conclusion merely restates a premise. They typically have this pattern on the LSAT: “X is true. We know this because, even when X doesn't appear to be true, X still must be true because X is always true.” This argument doesn't rely on circular reasoning. The club president's premise is a survey, and the conclusion rules out one explanation for the club's low attendance. The conclusion is not a mere restatement of the premise.

choices.text: making a generalization on the basis of a sample that is likely to be unrepresentative
choices.rationale: This describes the flaw perfectly! The author makes a generalization about the entire club's membership based on a sample of club members who attended a Tuesday meeting. This sample is likely to be unrepresentative because that sample doesn't include the members who can't attend Tuesday meetings. That's a particular issue in this argument, as the club president draws a conclusion about whether the club's low attendance at Tuesday meetings is due to scheduling issues. Note to the club president: you might want to ask the people who can't attend Tuesday meetings about that!

choices.text: treating a generalization that applies to most cases as if it applied without exception
choices.rationale: This is tempting because the club president definitely makes a generalization. The club president assumes that the club's members generally do not have scheduling conflicts with the club's Tuesday meetings. However, the club president does not say this generalization applies “without exception.” The club president's conclusion is just that the club's “attendance problem was not due primarily to schedule conflicts.” This conclusion doesn’t apply to all club members; it allows for some club members to have scheduling conflicts with the Tuesday meetings.

choices.text: drawing a conclusion on the basis of premises that contradict one another
choices.rationale: These premises do not contradict each other. The premises assert that the club normally meets on Tuesday, and the president's survey at a Tuesday meeting reveals that 95% of the members say meeting on Tuesday is fine. Both of these premises can be simultaneously true.

choices.text: inferring, solely from the claim that a change is not sufficient to solve a problem, that it is not necessary either
choices.rationale: The club president doesn't claim that any change is “not sufficient to solve the problem.” The club president doesn't say that changing the meeting to a different date won't cause meeting attendance to increase. The president never considers what would happen if they met on a different day. Because this answer choice misdescribes the argument, it does not describe an error in the club president's reasoning.

questions.stimulus: A club wanted to determine whether it could increase attendance by changing its weekly meetings from Tuesday to another day. At one Tuesday meeting, the club's president took a survey of all members present. Of those surveyed, 95 percent said that they had no difficulty attending on Tuesdays. On the basis of this survey result, the club's president concluded that the attendance problem was not due primarily to schedule conflicts.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following arguments?

choices.text: My pottery instructor says that making pottery will not cause repetitive-motion injuries if it is done properly. So I will probably not get such injuries, for whenever I do pottery I use the proper techniques that my instructor taught me.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” This conclusion makes a prediction. It doesn't assert that we should be suspicious of a claim. Moreover, there's no “person B” in this argument. We can eliminate (A) without even evaluating the premises. (If we did evaluate this answer choice's premises, we'd also note that nothing parallels the passage's claims about a “thorough review” or person A's lack of bias.)

choices.text: Gardner, a noted paleontologist who has no vested interest in the case, assures us that the alleged dinosaur bones are not old enough to be from dinosaurs. So we should be skeptical of Penwick's claim to have found dinosaur bones, for Gardner inspected the bones carefully.
choices.rationale: This one matches the generic version of our argument! We have a premise that parallels the claim that “Person A said X after a thorough review.” In this answer choice, that's the claim that “Gardner, a noted paleontologist ... assures us that the alleged dinosaur bones are not old enough to be from dinosaurs.” The argument also adds that “Gardner inspected the bones carefully” to parallel the “thorough review” part. We can also find a premise that parallels the claim that “person A has no bias in the matter” — the assertion that Gardner “has no vested interest in this case.” Finally, the conclusion parallels “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” This conclusion asserts that “we should be skeptical of Penwick's claim to have found dinosaur bones.” This directly contradicts Gardner's claim, so it parallels the idea that “X is not true.” Therefore, (B) is correct.

choices.text: The engineer hired by the company that maintains the bridge has examined the bridge and declared it safe. This engineer is the only one who has given the bridge a close examination recently. Thus, we should consider the bridge safe.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” This conclusion asserts that a bridge is definitely safe. That's akin to saying “X is true,” which is slightly stronger than “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” That's enough reason to eliminate (C). But if you weren't convinced, you could analyze the premises. The premises don't have anything similar to the claim that “person A has no bias in the matter.” In fact, if the engineer was hired by the company that maintains the bridge, the engineer might have a bias! Moreover, there's no “person B” in this argument.

choices.text: The reporter who recently interviewed the prime minister said the prime minister appeared to be in poor health. But despite the fact that the reporter works for a paper with opposition leanings, we should accept that the prime minister is in poor health. After all, reporters won't let their bias affect them when the truth of their claims will eventually be discovered.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” This conclusion asserts that the prime minister is in poor health. That's akin to saying “X is true,” which is slightly stronger than “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” That's enough reason to eliminate (D). But if you need more reason to cross off (D), you could examine the premises. The premises don't have anything similar to the claim that “person A has no bias in the matter.” In fact, it says that the newspaper reporter might be biased (since they work for a paper with “opposition leanings”) but that their bias won't affect their claim about the prime minister's health. Finally, there's no “person B” in this argument.

choices.text: The snowblower salesperson claims that there will be above-average snowfall this winter, but because the salesperson is biased, we can discount that claim.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” This conclusion asserts that we can “discount” the claim that there will be above-average snowfall this year. That's akin to saying “X is not true,” which is nearly the opposite of saying, “we should be suspicious of person B's claim that X is not true.” That's enough reason to eliminate (D). If we also evaluated the premises, we'd see that no premise matches the claim that “person A has no bias in the matter.” In fact, the argument asserts that the salesperson is biased. Also, there's no “person B” in this argument.

questions.stimulus: The railway authority inspector who recently thoroughly checked the tracks testified that they were in good condition. Thus, since the inspector has no bias in the matter, we should be suspicious of the newspaper reporter's claim that the tracks are in poor condition.

questions.stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.text: fails to consider the possibility that other types of pollution not involving ozone might rise, perhaps even producing an overall increase in health costs
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to consider” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the author's argument if true?” This answer choice wouldn't weaken the argument's conclusion. The argument's conclusion doesn't consider “other types of pollution not involving ozone.” Notice that the conclusion only applies to “ozone-related health costs.” So, it doesn't matter if other types of pollution increase health costs. That wouldn't change whether the air pollution measures reduce the “ozone-related health costs.”

choices.text: presumes, without providing evidence, that ozone-related health costs in the city vary roughly in proportion to ozone levels
choices.rationale: When we see “presumes, without providing justification” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, the author definitely believes that ozone-related health costs vary roughly in proportion to ozone levels. This is how the author gets from the premise that air pollution measures will reduce ozone levels by one-fifth to the conclusion that the measures will reduce the $5 billion worth of ozone-related costs by $1 billion. Moreover, this belief would strengthen the author's argument. If the costs vary in proportion to ozone levels, reducing the levels by one-fifth will also reduce the costs by one-fifth. So, this answer choice describes the author's potentially erroneous assumption, making this the correct answer.

choices.text: provides no explicit reason for believing that the proposed air pollution measures will in fact be adopted
choices.rationale: The author doesn't have to provide a reason to believe that the city will adop air pollution measure. They would have to provide such a reason if the author concluded that the city will definitely spend one billion dollars less on ozone-related health costs. But the author instead concludes that the city will spend one billion dollars less “should the proposed measures be adopted.” Since the conclusion is conditioned on this hypothetical, the author doesn't have to show that the hypothetical will definitely happen. In other words, if the conclusion is “If X, then Y,” the argument doesn't have to prove that X will happen.

choices.text: attempts to support its conclusion by making an appeal to emotions
choices.rationale: The author never makes an emotional appeal. Emotional appeals are very rare on the LSAT. When they do appear, the author will typically conclude that we should or should not do something by invoking our fear or pity to distract us from the facts. In this case, an emotional appeal might look something like, “Even though there's no proof that the proposed air pollution measures will reduce ozone levels, we should adopt the measures. The current ozone levels disproportionally affect the city's most vulnerable citizens, and any increase in the ozone levels may prove lethal to these individuals whom our government has let down.” The author doesn't do anything like that here. The author sticks to the facts about ozone levels but draws a dubious conclusion about ozone costs.

choices.text: discusses air pollution in order to draw attention away from more significant sources of health-related costs
choices.rationale: The author doesn't want to “draw attention away” from health-related costs. Their conclusion is about health-related costs! Besides, the two issues are related, as air pollution is responsible for the costs.

questions.stimulus: If the proposed air pollution measures were to be implemented, ozone levels in the city's air would be one fifth lower than current levels. Since the ozone in our air is currently responsible for over $5 billion in health costs, we would spend about a billion dollars less on these ozone-related health costs should the proposed measures be adopted.

questions.stem: The argument in the newspaper article requires the assumption that

choices.text: most of the recently discovered tablets that have not yet been translated contain literary writing
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. It isn't necessary for the argument, either. It doesn't strengthen the argument because it doesn't tell us when the Sumerians created literature. It just tells us that the Egyptians may have created a lot of literature. But if all this literature came after the Sumerian literature, we can't convincingly argue that the Egyptian tablets challenge historians' belief that the Sumerians were the first to create literature. This also isn't necessary to the argument because we only need one example of Egyptian literature to show that the Egyptians may have created literature before the Sumerians. We don't need a lot of examples, so this answer choice isn't needed to draw the newspaper's conclusion. Finally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “We found some Egyptian clay tablets from 3300-3200 B.C. Some clay tablets appear to have literary writing. But, it's not true that most of the recently discovered tablets that have not yet been translated contain literary writing. So, the Sumerians may have been the first to create literature.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. There's still a big gap between the premises — which are all about the Egyptian tablets — and the conclusion about Sumerians. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (A).

choices.text: every civilization that has kept tax records has also kept other written records
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. It isn't necessary for the argument, either. It doesn't strengthen the argument because it doesn't tell us when the Sumerians created literature. It doesn't even tell us that the Egyptians created literature. It just tells a civilization that keeps tax records keeps other kinds of written records, too. But “other kinds of written records” doesn't mean that the country makes literature. This also isn't necessary to the argument because the newspaper article only needs to establish that Egyptians and Sumerians created literature. We don't need to know about “every civilization that has kept tax records.” This provides information about far more civilizations than just the Egyptian and Sumerian civilization, so this answer choice isn't needed to draw the newspaper's conclusion. Finally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “We found some Egyptian clay tablets from 3300-3200 B.C. Some clay tablets appear to have literary writing. But, it's not true that every civilization that has kept tax records has also kept other written records. So, the Sumerians may have been the first to create literature.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. There's still a big gap between the premises — which about Egyptian tablets and civilizations that keep tax records — and the conclusion about Sumerian literature. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (B).

choices.text: historians generally believe that the Sumerians did not create literature earlier than 3300 B.C.
choices.rationale: This answer choice strengthens the argument by telling us that Sumerians didn't create literature older than these Egyptian tablets. These Egyptian tablets were created sometime between 3300 and 3200 B.C. So, this answer choice establishes that historians don't believe that Sumerian literature is older than the Egyptian tablets. This makes us more confident that the Sumerians may not have been the first to create literature. We also need to know this to draw the conclusion that the Sumerians may not have been the first to create literature. If the Sumerian literature was older than the Egyptian tablets, then we could not confidently claim that the Sumerians may not have been the first to create literature. We can also evaluate this answer choice using the backup plan. Here's the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the answer choice to make this easier to read): “We found some Egyptian clay tablets from 3300-3200 B.C. Some clay tablets appear to have literary writing. But, the Sumerians created literature before 3300 B.C. So, the Sumerians may have been the first to create literature.” This makes sense. Yes, we found old Egyptian clay tablets that may contain literature, but we know that Sumerians created literature older than these tablets. So, the Sumerians were probably the first to create literature, at least as far as we know. Therefore, no matter which approach we used, we can be confident that (C) is the correct answer.

choices.text: some historians are skeptical about the authenticity of the recently discovered tablets
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. It isn't necessary for the argument, either. It doesn't strengthen the argument because it doesn't tell us when the Sumerians created literature. In fact, it weakens the argument by calling its evidence into question. If we don't think these tablets are genuine, then we don't have good evidence to challenge the historians' belief that Sumerians were the first to create literature. Further, anything that weakens the argument won't be necessary to the argument, either. Additionally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “We found some Egyptian clay tablets from 3300-3200 B.C. Some clay tablets appear to have literary writing. But, it's not true that some historians are skeptical about the authenticity of the recently discovered tablets. So, the Sumerians may have been the first to create literature.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. There's still a big gap between the premises — which about Egyptian tablets — and the conclusion about Sumerian literature. Plus, what follows the “But” seems consistent with the premises that came before it, making the paragraph sound awkward. No matter which approach we used, we can confidently cross off (D).

choices.text: the Sumerian civilization arose sometime between 3300 and 3200 B.C.
choices.rationale: This answer choice strengthens the argument. If the Sumerian civilization rose between 3300 and 3200 B.C., then it almost certainly didn't create literature that's older than the supposed literary writing on the Egyptian tablets. For this reason, some test-takers believe (E) is the correct answer. However, this answer choice isn't needed to draw the newspaper's conclusion. Even if the Sumerian civilization arose before 3300 B.C., it still could have created literature after the Egyptians. Perhaps the Sumerian civilization arose before 3400 B.C. but created literature in 3100 B.C. In that case, we could still conclude that the Sumerians may not have been the first to create literature. Finally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan: “We found some Egyptian clay tablets from 3300-3200 B.C. Some clay tablets appear to have literary writing. But, it's not true that the Sumerian civilization arose sometime between 3300 and 3200 B.C. So, the Sumerians may have been the first to create literature.” This doesn't sound like a valid argument. There's still a gap between the last premise — which tells us when the Sumerian civilization was formed — and the conclusion — which tells us when the Sumerian civilization created literature. The Sumerian civilization could arose before 3300 B.C. and created literature older than the literary writing found on the Egyptian tablets. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (E).

questions.stimulus: Newspaper article: Recently discovered clay tablets from southern Egypt date to between 3300 and 3200 B.C. Though most of the tablets translated thus far are tax records, one of them appears to contain literary writing. Hence, these tablets challenge the widely held belief among historians that the Sumerian civilization in Mesopotamia was the first to create literature.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion drawn in the climatologist's argument?

choices.text: Some scientists have found evidence that the waters off the Pacific coast of North America have grown significantly warmer over the past 15 years.
choices.rationale: This omits the climatologist's belief that the scientists' conclusion near these warming waters is “far from justified.” While this answer choice is true, it doesn't capture the climatologist's main point.

choices.text: The warming of the waters off the Pacific coast of North America is not a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution.
choices.rationale: This is tempting, but it's stated with more bold language than the climatologist's conclusion. The climatologist concludes that the scientists' conclusion is “far from justified.” That means the climatologist thinks the scientists didn't provide enough evidence to prove that the 4-degree increase in water temp is a symptom of global warming. So, we can only conclude that the climatologist believes that the 4-degree increase might not be a symptom of global warming. We can't say that the climatologist believes that the 4-degree increase is definitely not a symptom of global warming. Arguing that a conclusion isn't justified isn't the same as arguing that a conclusion is false.

choices.text: The conclusion that the warming of the waters off the Pacific coast of North America is a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution is far from justified.
choices.rationale: It captures the climatologist's belief that the scientists' conclusion — that the 4-degree increase in Pacific water temp is a symptom of global warming — is “far from justified.” The climatologist supports this belief by referencing an alternative explanation — natural cycles that can change ocean temperatures. This answer choice captures the main idea the climatologist wants to convince us of, so we can select (C) and move on to the next question.

choices.text: The warming of the waters off the Pacific coast of North America may be the result of a natural cycle of ocean temperature changes.
choices.rationale: This is tempting, but it reflects a premise the climatologist relies on, not the climatologist's main conclusion. The climatologist concludes that the scientists' conclusion is “far from justified.” That means the climatologist thinks the scientists didn't provide enough evidence to prove that the 4-degree increase in water temp is a symptom of global warming. The climatologist supports this conclusion by referencing an alternative explanation — natural cycles that can change ocean temperatures. So, the climatologist uses the premise that the increased water temps may be caused by a natural cycle of ocean temperature changes to support the conclusion that the scientists' conclusion isn't justified.

choices.text: If the warming of the waters off the Pacific coast of North America is due to a natural cycle of ocean temperature changes, then it is not a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution.
choices.rationale: This does not express a claim the climatologist necessarily believes. This claim implies that the warmer Pacific temps cannot caused by natural cycles and global warming. The climatologist never says or implies that. The climatologist only says that the scientists' conclusion that the warmer temps are caused by global warming isn't justified. The climatologist supports this conclusion by referencing an alternative explanation — natural cycles that can change ocean temperatures. Even though the climatologist references an alternative explanation, that doesn't mean the climatologist thinks the two explanations are mutually exclusive. The climatologist could argue that, in some cases, a temperature increase could be caused by natural cycles but compounded by global warming.

questions.stimulus: Climatologist: The waters off the Pacific coast of North America have warmed about 4 degrees over the past 15 years. Some scientists claim that this trend is a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution. However, this conclusion is far from justified—it is known that there are many natural cycles of ocean temperature changes that last 60 years or more.

questions.stem: Their statements commit Robin and Kendall to disagreeing over whether

choices.text: the distinction that Robin makes between two kinds of cultures is illicit
choices.rationale: Robin would obviously disagree that the distinction made between nomadic and sedentary cultures is “illicit.” But we don't know whether Kendall would agree that it's erroneous to classify an ancient culture as “nomadic” or “sedentary.” Kendall may think these two classifications are completely acceptable. All we know is that Kendall doesn't think we can infer whether an ancient culture is nomadic or sedentary from the durability of its artifacts. Since we don't know Kendall's opinion on (A), we can eliminate it.

choices.text: it is reasonable to assume that a culture whose artifacts were not durable was nomadic
choices.rationale: This is close to our anticipation that the correct answer will discuss whether we can infer that an ancient culture was sedentary or nomadic from the durability of its artifacts. Therefore, we can be confident that this answer choice is correct. After all, Robin would agree with this claim. Robin says that we can determine whether ancient cultures were nomadic or sedentary from the durability of their artifacts. Robin says that if the artifacts are durable rather than temporary, then the culture was probably sedentary. Since Robin argues that we can determine whether ancient cultures were sedentary or nomadic, we can infer that Robin would agree that if the artifacts are temporary rather than durable, then the culture was probably nomadic. Kendall points out that the artifacts were largely influenced by which materials were available. So, Kendall doesn't think we can determine whether an ancient culture was nomadic or sedentary from their artifacts. A culture with short-lived artifacts may have just been surrounded by flimsy materials. Therefore, Kendall would disagree with this claim. Since Robin would agree with (B) and Kendall would disagree with it, we can select (B) and advance to the following question.

choices.text: any evidence other than the intended durability of a culture's artifacts can establish conclusively which of the two kinds of cultures a particular culture was
choices.rationale: Neither Robin nor Kendall addresses if we can determine whether a culture was nomadic or sedentary from “evidence other than the intended durability” of its artifacts. Both limit their arguments to the durability of the culture's artifacts. So, we don't know whether Robin or Kendall would agree with this claim. We can eliminate it.

choices.text: the distinction that Robin makes between the different kinds of cultures is as important as many archaeologists have thought
choices.rationale: Neither Robin nor Kendall addresses if the distinction between nomadic and sedentary cultures is “as important as many archaeologists thought.” Neither speaker addresses what other archaeologists think. Since we don't know whether Robin or Kendall would agree with this claim, we can cross (D) off.

choices.text: studying a culture's artifacts can reveal a great deal about the culture
choices.rationale: Robin might agree with this claim since Robin argues that we can determine whether ancient cultures were nomadic or sedentary from the durability of its artifacts. Still, we don't know whether Robin thinks this information tells us “a great deal” about that culture. We don't know whether Kendall would agree with this claim. Kendall doesn't think the durability of the artifacts tells us whether cultures were nomadic or sedentary. But perhaps Kendall believes we can learn other information about the culture from the artifacts. Because we can't infer Kendall's opinion on (E), we can eliminate it.

questions.stimulus:
Robin: Archaeologists can study the artifacts left by ancient cultures to determine whether they were nomadic or sedentary. If the artifacts were made to last rather than to be quickly discarded, the culture was likely sedentary.

Kendall: But what artifacts a people make is determined largely by the materials available to them.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the argument's overall conclusion?

choices.text: The volume of freight shipped by rail can be expected to increase.
choices.rationale: It captures the author's belief that “we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow.” The author supports this belief, showing that railroads have reduced their operating costs through automation while their main competitor has not. So, this answer choice captures the main idea the author wants to convince us of. We can select (A) and move on to the next question.

choices.text: Increasing reliance on automation means that fewer railroad workers are needed.
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes two of the author's premises. It's true that reliance on automation means that fewer railroad workers are needed. However, the author uses this fact to support their prediction that the amount of stuff shipped by rail will probably increase. The author claims that the need for fewer railroad workers will reduce railroad operating costs, which makes it more likely that more people will ship cargo by rail — especially because railroads' main competitor will probably not reduce its operating costs.

choices.text: No reduction in operating costs is predicted for the trucking industry.
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes one of the author's premises. It's true that the trucking industry will probably not reduce its operating costs. However, the author uses this fact to support their prediction that the amount of stuff shipped by rail will probably increase. The author says that railroad operating costs will go down. So, if railroads' main competitor will probably not reduce its operating costs, railroads will have a competitive advantage over the trucking industry. Railroads can offer cheaper shipping; presumably, more people will ship by rail.

choices.text: Operating costs for railroads have been reduced as a result of increased reliance on automation.
choices.rationale: This is tempting, since it describes one the author's conclusions. However, this describes a premise/conclusion, not the author's main conclusion. The claim that railroads' operating costs have been reduced is supported by the premise that railroads' use of automation means that fewer railroad workers are needed. However, this claim supports the author's main conclusion that we can expect that more stuff will be shipped by rail. If railroads' operating costs are reduced, more people will probably ship cargo by rail — especially if railroads' main competitor does not reduce its operating costs.

choices.text: The chief competitor of railway shipping is shipping by truck.
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes one of the author's premises. The trucking industry is indeed railway shipping's chief competitor. However, the author uses this fact to support their prediction that the amount of stuff shipped by rail will probably increase. The author says that railroad operating costs will go down. So, if railroads' main competitor will probably not reduce its operating costs, railroads will have an edge over the trucking industry. Railroads can offer cheaper shipping, so more people will probably ship by rail.

questions.stimulus: Railroads rely increasingly on automation. Since fewer railroad workers are needed, operating costs have been reduced. This means that we can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow. The chief competitor of railway shipping is shipping by truck, and no reduction in operating costs is predicted for the trucking industry.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.text: Boiled cow's milk makes less vitamin C available to infants than does the same amount of mother's milk.
choices.rationale: This inference must be true! Boiled cow's milk must contain less vitamin C (or, at least, provide less vitamin C to infants, as this answer choice states) than breast milk (AKA mother's milk). We know that the infants who got scurvy were fed boiled cow's milk. And we know that the scurvy was caused by vitamin C deficiency. If the kids who consumed breast milk didn't get scurvy, they were not vitamin C deficient. So, the breast milk must have provided more vitamin C to these tots. That would mean the kids who drank boiled cow's milk did not consume as much vitamin C. Because we can point to its support in the passage, we can justifiably select (A) and moooove on.

choices.text: Infants who consume cow's milk that has not been boiled frequently contract potentially fatal gastrointestinal infections.
choices.rationale: This inference is tempting because we know that doctors advised boiling because it would “prevent gastrointestinal infections potentially fatal to infants.” Many test-takers believe that it must be true that infants who consume unboiled cow's milk would frequently contract these gastrointestinal infections. However, this inference is not supported by the text. First, we don't know that the doctors were correct that boiling cow's milk reduces the risk of gastrointestinal infections. Perhaps if we knew that there was a dramatic decrease in gastrointestinal infections among infants once most people began boiling their cow's milk, we could infer that the doctors' recommendation was sound. But the passage doesn't provide that information. Moreover, even if people weren't boiling their cow's milk before the doctors made their recommendation, maybe they did something else that reduced the risk of gastrointestinal infection. Finally, even if infants who consumed unboiled cow's milk were at risk of gastrointestinal infection, we don't know that they “frequently” contracted these infections. Perhaps these infections were very rare.

choices.text: Mother's milk can cause gastrointestinal infections in infants.
choices.rationale: This inference is not supported. According to doctors, unboiled cow's milk can cause gastrointestinal infections in infants. But we weren't told whether breast milk (AKA mother's milk) poses the same risk. We also don't have any data on gastrointestinal infections among infants fed breast milk, so we can't infer that this claim is true.

choices.text: When doctors advised that cow's milk fed to infants should be boiled, they did not know that scurvy was caused by vitamin C deficiency.
choices.rationale: This inference is not supported. Presumably, if the doctors knew that boiling cow's milk reduces the vitamin C levels in cow's milk and that scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, they probably wouldn't have recommended boiling cow's milk. (Even then, they may have made the recommendation. They could have figured that the risk of gastrointestinal disease was more dangerous than scurvy. But let's ignore that possibility for now.) Since they made the recommendation, they either did not know that boiling cow's milk reduces its vitamin C levels or they did not know that scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency. So, it's entirely possible that the doctors knew that scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, but they didn't know that boiling cow's milk reduces its vitamin C levels.

choices.text: When doctors advised that cow's milk fed to infants should be boiled, most mothers did not breast-feed their infants.
choices.rationale: This inference isn't supported. We have no idea what proportion of mothers breast fed their infants. We could make this inference if we learned that “most infants” contracted scurvy, but breast-fed infants did not contract scurvy. However, the passage does not supply that information.

questions.stimulus: In the past, infants who were not breast-fed were fed cow's milk. Then doctors began advising that cow's milk fed to infants should be boiled, as the boiling would sterilize the milk and prevent gastrointestinal infections potentially fatal to infants. Once this advice was widely implemented, there was an alarming increase among infants in the incidence of scurvy, caused by vitamin C deficiency. Breast-fed infants, however, did not contract scurvy.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to resolve the apparent paradox described above?

choices.text: Fire departments tend to receive less funding during periods of severe drought than during periods of normal rainfall.
choices.rationale: This makes the paradox worse! If fire departments receive less funding during a drought, they're probably less equipped to contain the fires — especially if there are many more fires than usual. We'd expect these fires to spread and cause more financial damage, not less financial damage.

choices.text: Areas subject to grass and brush fires tend to be less densely populated than areas where there are few such fires.
choices.rationale: This fact doesn't resolve the paradox because it doesn't tell us about areas experiencing a severe and protracted drought. Remember, the drought conditions are at the heart of this paradox. If this answer choice told us that areas experiencing an extended drought are less densely populated than areas experiencing normal rainfall, it might resolve the paradox. Fewer people would probably mean less property, and less property would probably mean less financial damage. But because this answer choice doesn't tell us anything about places during a prolonged drought, it does not affect the paradox.

choices.text: Unusually large, hard-to-control grass and brush fires typically occur only when there is a large amount of vegetation for them to consume.
choices.rationale: As expected, this shows why extended periods of drought could produce more grass and brush fires but less financial damage. If grass and brush fires become uncontrollably large only when there's a lot of vegetation, we wouldn't expect grass and brush fires to cause a lot of damage during extended periods of drought. Common sense tells us there would not be much vegetation during an extended period of drought. So, during a prolonged drought, grass and brush fires wouldn't become uncontrollably large. Common sense also tells us that if these fires aren't uncontrollably large, they probably won't cause as much financial damage. (Yes, we're relying on common sense and outside knowledge, but that's OK on the LSAT — even if you may have heard otherwise. In fact, Paradox questions are basically impossible to answer if you dogmatically follow the bad advice to “not rely on outside information.”) So, (C) resolves the paradox at hand, making it the correct answer.

choices.text: Grass and brush fires that are not caused by human negligence or arson tend to be started by lightning.
choices.rationale: This doesn't affect the paradox. It doesn't matter what causes the grass or brush fires. We're just trying to figure out why the fires are more frequent but less damaging during periods of extended drought. Since this answer choice doesn't tell us why fires may be less damaging during these periods, it's incorrect.

choices.text: When vegetation is destroyed in a grass or brush fire, it tends to be replaced naturally by vegetation that is equally if not more flammable.
choices.rationale: This doesn't resolve the paradox. In fact, it might make the paradox worse. If there are more fires during periods of severe drought, the continuously destroyed vegetation would be replaced with progressively more flammable vegetation. With more flammable vegetation, we'd expect to see bigger, more damaging fires during periods of extended drought.

questions.stimulus: The only effective check on grass and brush fires is rain. If the level of rainfall is below normal for an extended period of time, then there are many more such fires. Yet grass and brush fires cause less financial damage overall during long periods of severe drought than during periods of relatively normal rainfall.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption that the medical researcher's argument requires?

choices.text: A surgical operation that is dangerous is ethically justified only for treating a medical condition that is more dangerous.
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. So, it isn't necessary for the argument, either. To get a better sense of why this answer choice doesn't strengthen the argument, let's take the flipside of it. We'll translate it to, “If a dangerous surgical operation does not treat a more dangerous medical condition, the operation is not medically justified.” This doesn't strengthen the argument because we don't know whether the procedure to remove a polyp is more dangerous than the malignant polyp itself. If a premise established that it was, this answer choice would strengthen this argument. But without this key piece of information, we can't say that this would strengthen the argument. And without knowing whether removing polyps poses a greater danger than a malignant polyp, this information isn't necessary, either. Finally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan (note that we used the “if-then” translation of the answer choice and negated that statement): “Doctors can now detect polyps before they know whether the polyps are malignant. Doctors tend to remove these polyps. Removing polyps is dangerous. Some removed polyps are not dangerous. But, even if a dangerous surgical operation does not treat a more dangerous medical condition, the operation can still be medically justified. So, these dangerous operations may be medically necessary.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. We don't have any premises about a “more dangerous medical condition” or a “more dangerous medical operation,” so it's unclear how the “But” statement undermines what comes before it. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (A).

choices.text: Surgical removal of nonmalignant polyps detected by the new screening test is not always medically necessary.
choices.rationale: This answer choice strengthens the argument by telling us removing nonmalignant polyps is not always medically necessary. So, this answer choice establishes that some doctors perform dangerous but medically unnecessary operations when they remove nonmalignant tumors. This strengthens the researcher's argument, making us more confident that this new screening test prompts dangerous but medically unnecessary operations. We also need this information to conclude that the new screening test prompts dangerous but medically unnecessary operations. If removing nonmalignant polyps was always medically necessary, we'd have no evidence that doctors perform dangerous but medically unnecessary operations. So, we need to know that some of these operations on nonmalignant polyps are not medically necessary. We can also evaluate this answer choice using the backup plan. Here's the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified and negated this answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “Doctors can now detect polyps before they know whether the polyps are malignant. Doctors tend to remove these polyps. Removing polyps is dangerous. Some removed polyps are not dangerous. But removing nonmalignant polyps is always medically necessary. So, these dangerous operations may be medically necessary.” This makes sense! Yes, we're removing nonmalignant polyps in a dangerous operation. But removing such polyps is medically necessary, so these dangerous operations might be medically necessary. That adds up and sounds like a cogent paragraph. Therefore, no matter which approach we used, we can be confident that (B) is the correct answer.

choices.text: If the new screening test encourages medically unnecessary operations, then probably it either should not be used or its use should be modified.
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. That means it isn't necessary for the argument, either. This doesn't strengthen the argument because the argument doesn't conclude that we should not use the new polyp screening test or that we should change the test. So, the “then” part of this answer choice is irrelevant to the conclusion. Plus, we don't know that these new screening tests encourage “medically unnecessary operations.” The researcher concludes that these operations are medically unnecessary. But this conclusion is flawed. The premises didn't tell us which kinds of operations are not medically necessary. Since we don't know whether these tests are medically unnecessary this answer choice might not even apply to the argument. Put another way, when an argument in a Strengthen or Weaken question concludes “X,” the correct answer won't begin with “If X.” The argument didn't prove that “X” is true, so the claim that begins “if X” is true won't add anything to the argument. Finally, this is the argument we'd make if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified and negated the answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “Doctors can now detect polyps before they know whether the polyps are malignant. Doctors tend to remove these polyps. Removing polyps is dangerous. Some removed polyps are not dangerous. But, even if a new screening test encourages medically unnecessary operations, we can still use the test and not modify it. So, these dangerous operations may be medically necessary.” This doesn't make a lot of sense. The part about modifying or not using the test doesn't relate to anything that came before it, so it's unclear how the “But” statement contradicts the previous premises. And the “But” statement discusses medically unnecessary operations, so it doesn't provide good support to a conclusion about medically necessary operations. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (C).

choices.text: A polyp detected by the new screening test should be surgically removed if it is malignant.
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. That means it isn't necessary for the argument, either. This doesn't strengthen the argument because the argument isn't about removing malignant tumors. The argument is only concerned with whether removing nonmalignant tutors is medically unnecessary. Whether doctors should remove malignant tumors doesn't help us establish that removing nonmalignant tumors is medically unnecessary. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, this is the argument we'd make (note that we simplified and negated the answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “Doctors can now detect polyps before they know whether the polyps are malignant. Doctors tend to remove these polyps. Removing polyps is dangerous. Some removed polyps are not dangerous. But, even if a malignant polyp is detected, it should not necessarily be surgically removed. So, these dangerous operations may be medically necessary.” This doesn't make any sense. The “But” statement is about malignant polyps, not nonmalignant polyps. Plus, if that statement suggests that we don't have to remove all malignant polyps, that might weaken the conclusion removing nonmalignant polyps may be medically necessary. This argument is a real stinker. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (D).

choices.text: The screening test is medically useful only when it detects a polyp that requires treatment.
choices.rationale: This doesn't strengthen the argument. That means it isn't necessary for the argument, either. To get a better sense of why this answer choice doesn't strengthen the argument, let's take the flipside of this statement. We'll translate it to, “If a screening test does not detect a polyp that requires treatment, then the screening test is not medically useful.” This doesn't strengthen the argument because the conclusion doesn't assert that the screening test is not medically useful. The conclusion asserts that the operation is not medically necessary. These are two different concepts. Even if the test isn't medically useful, the operation the test prompts might be medically necessary. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, this is the argument we could construct (note that we used the “if-then” translation of the answer choice and negated it to make the argument easier to read): “Doctors can now detect polyps before they know whether the polyps are malignant. Doctors tend to remove these polyps. Removing polyps is dangerous. Some removed polyps are not dangerous. But, even if a screening test does not detect a polyp that requires treatment, then the screening test can still be medically useful. So, these dangerous operations may be medically necessary.” This doesn't make any sense. The “But” statement suggests that the screening test for polyps may be medically useful. But that doesn't mean the dangerous operations are necessary. The screening tests could be useful for other reasons. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently cross off (E).

questions.stimulus: Medical researcher: A new screening test detects certain polyps at such an early stage that it is generally unclear whether the polyps are malignant. But the risk that a polyp might be malignant leads doctors, in most cases, to have such polyps surgically removed, which is a dangerous process. Yet some of those polyps turn out not to be malignant. Thus, the new screening test can prompt dangerous operations that actually are not medically necessary.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the psychologist's argument?

choices.text: Medications designed to lower blood pressure do not keep the people who take them from experiencing blood-pressure fluctuations when speaking.
choices.rationale: This doesn't address the conclusion's claim that the increase in blood pressure is caused by the stress of speaking and not by the physical exertion required to speak. It just shows that medications do not completely eliminate the increase in blood pressure. If the answer choice said that people who take medications that lower stress do not experience blood pressure increases while speaking, it would be an example of “no cause, no effect” and would strengthen the argument. But this answer choice does not say that, so we can confidently eliminate it.

choices.text: In general, the lower one's typical blood pressure, the more one's blood pressure will increase under stress.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is tempting to some because it affirms the relationship between stress and blood pressure increases. It suggests that stress increases blood pressure. However, that does not necessarily support the argument's conclusion that increased blood pressure while speaking results from the stress of speaking. Stress may increase one's blood pressure, but that doesn't mean people get stressed enough while speaking to have their blood pressure increase. This answer choice also doesn't strengthen the belief that increased blood pressure while speaking does not result from the physical exertion required to speak. Even if stress increases one's blood pressure, the physical act of speaking could increase one's blood pressure, too. So, this answer choice allows for the physical act of speaking to increase people's blood pressure. Finally, this answer choice states that there's a relationship between one's baseline blood pressure and the amount their blood pressure will increase. However, the argument doesn't compare people with low blood pressure to people with high blood pressure. It compares extroverts to introverts. So, the relationship this answer choice describes is not relevant to the researcher's argument.

choices.text: Introverted people who do not have chronically high blood pressure often sense the rises in blood pressure that occur when they speak in conversation.
choices.rationale: It's understandable that many test-takers are attracted to this answer choice since it affirms a relationship between introverts and increased blood pressure that the researcher's argument discusses. In a way, this answer choice resembles “same cause, same effect.” However, there are a few issues with this answer choice. First, even if introverts “often sense” that their blood pressure increases while speaking, it doesn't necessarily mean that their blood pressure is actually increasing. And even if their blood pressure is increasing, that doesn't mean their blood pressure is increasing because they're stressed. Their blood pressure might rise from the physical act of speaking or for some other reason. Additionally, this answer choice discusses introverts “who do not have chronically high blood pressure.” But the researcher's argument doesn't compare people with chronically high blood pressure to those with average or below-average blood pressure. It compares extroverts to introverts. So, it's unclear why information about introverts who don't have chronically high blood pressure is relevant to the researcher's argument.

choices.text: Deaf people experience increased blood pressure when they sign, but no change when they move their hands for other reasons.
choices.rationale: Many test-takers dismiss this answer choice out of hand, figuring that deaf people are irrelevant to the researcher's argument. But, before we do that, we should consider whether this argument presents one of the causal argument strengtheners we look for (elimination of an alternative cause; same cause, same effect; no cause, no effect). This tells us that deaf people experience increased blood pressure when they sign. Signing is how deaf people communicate, and we have no reason to believe that deaf people do not experience the same “psychological stress of communicating” that non-deaf people experience while speaking. So, if deaf people's blood pressure increases while experiencing the psychological stress of communicating, this answer choice presents an example of “same cause, same effect.” It affirms the relationship between the stress of communication and increased blood pressure. This answer choice also tells us that deaf people's blood pressure does not increase while moving their hands for other reasons. If a deaf person moves their hand for reasons other than signing, they're not experiencing the “psychological stress of communicating.” There's no stress and no corresponding increase in heart rate. Therefore, this answer choice also presents an example of “no cause, no effect.” If we take away the stress of communicating, we take away increased blood pressure. This last point is the most salient one. Remember, the researcher asserts that the physical exertion required to speak does not cause an increase in blood pressure. However, it would be difficult for the researcher to test that conclusion with people who communicate vocally. When these people speak, they will always feel the stress of communication and physically exert themselves. It would be hard for the researcher to isolate one of those variables with vocal communicators. But deaf people (or anyone else who communicates through non-vocal means) provide a way to isolate one of these variables. Deaf people do not experience the physical exertion required to speak. If their blood pressure still increases when they communicate, that suggests that the increase is due to the stress of communication and not the physical exertion required to speak. In a way, we can think of this answer choice as strengthening the researcher's anti-causal claim. In other words, the answer choice strengthens the argument by weakening the causal relationship between physical exertion and increased blood pressure. This answer choice provides an example of “effect without the cause” — deaf people do not experience the physical exertion required to speak while communicating, but their blood pressure increases all the same.

choices.text: Extroverted people are more likely to have chronically high blood pressure than are introverted people and are more likely to take medication to lower their blood pressure.
choices.rationale: This answer choice weakens the argument, as it provides an alternative reason why extroverts experience “milder surges” in their blood pressure while speaking. This answer choice suggests that these milder surges are not because extroverted people are less likely to feel stressed while communicating — it could be because extroverts are more likely to be on medication that suppresses their blood pressure.

questions.stimulus: Psychologist: Most people's blood pressure rises when they talk. But extroverted people experience milder surges when they speak than do introverted people, for whom speaking is more stressful. This suggests that the increases result from the psychological stress of communicating rather than from the physical exertion of speech production.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument is strongly supported if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.text: Most people who buy a frying pan with a manufacturer's warranty would seek reimbursement should the pan fail to work well or last long.
choices.rationale: This argument is flawed because it assumes that frying pan manufacturers would not offer a warranty on a bad frying pan. But there are some ways a manufacturer could offer a warranty on a bad frying pan. Perhaps the warranty is extremely limited (e.g., the warranty only lasts for two days), preventing most consumers from taking advantage of the warranty. Or, perhaps the manufacturer knows that most people are too lazy or busy or just don't care enough to take advantage of a frying pan warranty. In that case, the manufacturer wouldn't have to reimburse all the customers who aren't happy with their frying pan. This answer choice strengthens the argument by eliminating one way a manufacturer could offer a warranty on a bad frying pan. It shows that most people would actually take advantage of the warranty if they weren't happy with their frying pans. The frying pan manufacturer would actually have to reimburse all the unhappy customers who purchased a frying pan with a warranty. That supports the author's belief that a manufacturer would not offer a warranty on a bad frying pan. Offering a warranty on a bad frying pan would mean that the manufacturer would “need to reimburse many customers,” and we know manufacturers wouldn't offer a warranty if they had to do that. So, a frying pan warranty seems like evidence of the frying pan's quality. You could also select (A) using the backup plan. This is the argument we'd construct if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the premise, conclusion, and answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “If manufacturers thought a warranty would mean they'd have to reimburse many customers, they would not offer the warranty. Plus, most people who buy a frying pan with a warranty would seek reimbursement if they weren't happy with the frying pan. So, one should only buy frying pans with a warranty.” This makes some sense. The first sentence suggests that if manufacturers thought they'd have to reimburse many unhappy customers, they wouldn't offer a warranty. The second sentence adds that frying pan manufacturers would have to reimburse their customers if the customers weren't happy with their frying pan. The two sentences together suggest that frying pan manufacturers probably wouldn't offer a warranty on a frying pan that wouldn't satisfy their customers, which supports the last sentence's recommendation. No matter our approach, we can confidently select (A).

choices.text: All of the frying pans currently on the market that are covered by a manufacturer's warranty work at least as well at the time of purchase as any of the frying pans not covered by a warranty.
choices.rationale: This says that frying pans with warranties work as well or better than frying pans without warranties — at the time of the purchase. This makes it sound like we may as well buy frying pans with warranties, right? A lot of test-makers think so. Unfortunately, this line of reasoning is incorrect. This answer choice doesn't tell us that frying pans with warranties will continue to work as well or better than frying pans without warranties. If frying pans without warranties last longer or perform better long-term, maybe we should buy those instead. Plus — and this is the important takeaway point — this answer choice doesn't address the argument's reasoning. It doesn't show how a manufacturer's warranty provides evidence that the manufacturer is willing to put its money where its proverbial mouth is to stand behind the quality. Instead, the answer choice just introduces a new fact that seems to directly support the conclusion (but, for the reason mentioned above, doesn't actually support the conclusion). The correct answers to some relatively easy Strengthen questions will add a new fact that directly supports the conclusion. But the correct answers on harder Strengthen questions — the ones you might actually need our help on — will almost never do that. Instead, the correct answer on harder Strengthen questions will address the argument's reasoning by fixing a problem with that reasoning. You could also eliminate (B) with the backup plan.
