This is the argument we'd construct if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the premise, conclusion, and answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “If manufacturers thought a warranty would mean they'd have to reimburse many customers, they would not offer the warranty. Plus, frying pans with warranties work as well or better than frying pans without warranties at the time of purchase. So, one should only buy frying pans with a warranty.” This doesn't make a ton of sense. The claim that frying pans with warranties only work as well as warranty-less frying pans “at the time of purchase” does not provide strong evidence that warranties guarantee long-term quality. Plus, it doesn't relate to the first sentence's claim, which makes the argument sound disjointed and awkward. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently eliminate (B).

choices.text: The more a frying pan costs, the more likely it is to be covered by a manufacturer's warranty.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant to the argument. It doesn't show why a warranty would guarantee a quality frying pan. And we can't assume that a frying that costs more must be of higher quality. You could also eliminate (C) with the backup plan. This is the argument we'd construct if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the premise, conclusion, and answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “If manufacturers thought a warranty would mean they'd have to reimburse many customers, they would not offer the warranty. Plus, the more a frying pan costs, the more likely it'll be covered by a warranty. So, one should only buy frying pans with a warranty.” This doesn't sound like a cogent argument. The second sentence makes it sound like a warranty will make a frying pan more expensive, which sounds like a reason we shouldn't buy frying pans covered by warranties. Plus, the second sentence doesn't relate to the first sentence's claim, which makes the argument sound disjointed and awkward. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently eliminate (C).

choices.text: The most expensive frying pans are the ones most likely to work well for many years.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant to the argument. The argument didn't assert that we should buy the most expensive frying pans. It asserted that we should only buy frying pans with warranties. So, this answer choice doesn't show why a warranty would evidence a frying pan's quality. You could also eliminate (D) with the backup plan. This is the argument we'd construct if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the premise, conclusion, and answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “If manufacturers thought a warranty would mean they'd have to reimburse many customers, they would not offer the warranty. Plus, the most expensive frying pans will work the best for many years. So, one should only buy frying pans with a warranty.” This doesn't sound very good. The second sentence has nothing to do with the first or third sentences. It sounds like a complete nonsequitur, so this doesn't sound like a cogent paragraph that makes a convincing argument. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently eliminate (D).

choices.text: Most frying pan manufacturers' warranties provide for full customer satisfaction.
choices.rationale: This says that frying pans warranties provide for “full customer satisfaction.” Does this strengthen the author's belief that warranties are a mark of the frying pan's quality? No. Even if the warranties cover “full customer satisfaction” (whatever that means), that still doesn't address the argument's central flaw. The author thinks that a warranty will guarantee some level of frying pan quality since manufacturers wouldn't offer a warranty if they thought they'd have to reimburse a bunch of unhappy customers. But we don't know whether unhappy customers will actually take advantage of the warranty and seek reimbursement. If we knew that frying pan customers never took advantage of warranties, we could put a bad frying pan on the market and write whatever we wanted in the warranty. We could say, “If you are not 100% satisfied with your frying pan, we will not only give you a full refund, we will give you full ownership of this frying pan company in perpetuity.” Our warranty wouldn't show that we are 100% confident in our frying pan's quality. Our warranty would only show that we are 100% confident that our customers won't take advantage of the warranty. (E) doesn't strengthen the argument because it doesn't address that central issue in the author's reasoning. You could also eliminate (E) with the backup plan. This is the argument we'd construct if we used the backup plan (note that we simplified the premise, conclusion, and answer choice to make the argument easier to read): “If manufacturers thought a warranty would mean they'd have to reimburse many customers, they would not offer the warranty. Plus, most frying pan manufacturers' warranties provide for full customer satisfaction. So, one should only buy frying pans with a warranty.” This doesn't sound terrible, but it doesn't sound as cogent or persuasive as the argument we'd construct with (A). The claim that warranties provide for “full customer satisfaction” doesn't address the first sentence's claim about the manufacturers' reasoning in offering a warranty. This makes the argument sound a little awkward. No matter which approach we use, we can confidently eliminate (E).

questions.stimulus: One should only buy a frying pan that has a manufacturer's warranty, even if it requires paying more, and even if one would never bother seeking reimbursement should the pan not work well or last long. Manufacturers will not offer a warranty on a product if doing so means that they will need to reimburse many customers because the product did not work well or last long.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the journalist's argument?

choices.text: Court proceedings overseen by judges who are very strict in controlling lawyers' behavior are known to result sometimes in incorrect verdicts.
choices.rationale: This has no effect on the journalist's argument. The journalist's conclusion doesn't say or imply that the verdicts reached in cases where judges maintain close control over the courtroom are always reliable. The conclusion instead addresses verdicts in cases where lawyers use inflammatory language and badger witnesses, which sometimes occurs when judges don't control their courtrooms.

choices.text: Lawyers tend to be less concerned than are judges about whether the outcomes of jury trials are just or not.
choices.rationale: If lawyers are less concerned about the trustworthiness of verdits, they may be willing to engage in a level of obstructive behaviors that truly undermine the jury's effort to reach the correct verdict. Suppose lawyers are eager to use super inflammatory language and to really badger witnesses (instead of using these techniques sparingly to preserve the trustworthiness of the legal process). In that case, jurors will find it harder to reach valid conclusions. This gives us further reason to doubt jury verdicts when such techniques are used, slightly strengthening the journalists' argument.

choices.text: People who are influenced by inflammatory language are very unlikely to admit at some later time that they were influenced by such language.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the journalist's argument. It doesn't matter whether the jurors influenced by the inflammatory language will admit that they were influenced by it. They don't even have to be aware that they were influenced! To draw this conclusion, the journalist just has to establish that such language always influences jurors' decision-making enough to make their verdicts untrustworthy. (C) doesn't weaken the notion that inflammatory language always makes jurors' verdicts untrustworthy, so it is incorrect.

choices.text: Obstructive courtroom behavior by a lawyer is seldom effective in cases where jurors are also presented with legitimate evidence.
choices.rationale: This definitely weakens the journalist's argument. It presents a counterexample to the conclusion's bold, universal claim: it shows a situation in which lawyers use inflammatory language and badger witnesses but do not meaningfully influence a jury's verdict. If “[o]bstructive courtroom behavior” like inflammatory language and witness badgering isn't effective in cases with legitimate witnesses, it's not necessarily true that it's reasonable to doubt verdicts “whenever lawyers engage in such behavior.” Therefore, (D) makes the journalist's conclusion less convincing, making it the correct answer.

choices.text: The selection of jurors is based in part on an assessment of the likelihood that they are free of bias.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the journalist's argument. The journalist doesn't argue that we can doubt juries' verdicts because the jurors are biased. The journalist argues that we doubt the verdicts because the jurors are susceptible to lawyers' inflammatory language and witness badgering. An unbiased juror can still be influenced by the lawyers' obstructive behavior.

questions.stimulus: Journalist: When judges do not maintain strict control over their courtrooms, lawyers often try to influence jury verdicts by using inflammatory language and by badgering witnesses. These obstructive behaviors hinder the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict. Whenever lawyers engage in such behavior, therefore, it is reasonable to doubt whether the verdict is correct.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify Mateo's argument?

choices.text: Any industry has an obligation to pay for any damage that it should have known would result from its activities.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't quite resemble “if premises, then conclusion.” It's hard to say that the automobile industry “should have known” that automobiles would contribute to global warming, eventually causing permafrost to melt under several arctic villages. Mateo doesn't state that automobile manufacturers should have known they'd cause this damage, either. So, this principle doesn't bridge the gap between Mateo's premises and conclusion.

choices.text: Manufacturers should be required to produce goods in a way that minimizes harm to people and the environment.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't really resemble “if premises, then conclusion.” Mateo doesn't conclude that automobile manufacturers “should be required to produce” their cars in a way that “minimizes harm to people and the environment.” Mateo doesn't claim that the automobile industry should try to stop contributing to global warming in any way — Mateo just wants the automobile industry to pay for the arctic villagers' relocation. Therefore, this principle doesn't bridge the gap between Mateo's premises and conclusion.

choices.text: When the use of a product causes damage, governments should not be required to help pay for the damage unless those responsible for manufacturing the product are also required to help pay for them.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't resemble “if premises, then conclusion.” If we translate this, here's what it would look like: “if product causes damages and product manufacturers are not required to pay for damages, then government not required to pay for damages.” However, Mateo's argument doesn't touch on whether the government should be required to pay for the villagers' relocation. Mateo doesn't bring up the government at all! So, this principle doesn't bridge the gap between Mateo's premises and conclusion.

choices.text: Any industry manufacturing a product whose use contributes to costly damage for others should be liable for any damage generated by that product's use.
choices.rationale: This principle resembles “if premises, then conclusion.” Here's what it looks like: “if manufacturer creates a product that causes costly damage, then manufacturer should be liable for the damage.” This connects Mateo's premises and conclusion. Mateo's premises establish that automobile manufacturers created a product that contributed to global warming, thus causing costly damages to others when global warming forced arctic villagers to relocate. Mateo concludes that automobile manufacturers should be forced to pay for this relocation, which is synonymous with the manufacturers being “liable” for the damages created by the product. So, this principle establishes that if Mateo's premises are true, we have to accept Mateo's conclusion. So this answer choice is correct!

choices.text: An industry that contributes to global warming should be required to help pay for resulting damage to specific communities only if it has a general obligation to help pay for all damage produced by global warming.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't resemble “if premises, then conclusion.” If we translate this, here's what it would look like: “if industry contributes to global warming should pay for damage to communities, then industry has a general obligation to help pay for all global warming damage.” Experienced test-takers will immediately realize this answer choice is wrong because it places Mateo's conclusion on the “if” side of the “if-then” statement. Remember, we can only make conclusions about the “then” side. Moreover, Mateo's argument doesn't touch on whether the automobile industry has a “general obligation” to pay for global warming-related damages. Therefore, this principle doesn't bridge the gap between Mateo's premises and conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Mateo: Global warming has caused permafrost to melt under several arctic villages, forcing all their inhabitants to relocate at great expense. Since pollution from automobiles is a major contributor to global warming, the automotive industry should be required to help pay for the villagers' relocation.

questions.stem: The argument is flawed in that it

choices.text: relies on the opinions of certain unnamed people without establishing that those people were well informed on the matter
choices.rationale: Lindsey doesn't rely on the opinions of certain unnamed people when making this argument. If Lindsey relied on the opinions of “several people,” Lindsey would have used their opinions to justify the conclusion. But Lindsey doesn't agree with their opinions. Several people think the company acted unfairly, but Lindsey doesn't think the company acted unfairly at all! More generally, it's only a flaw to rely on people's opinions without establishing that they're “well informed on the matter” if you're using their opinions to prove a factual matter (e.g., “John believes Coke is the most popular soft drink, so Coke must sell more soda annually than any other soft drink”) or when they're clearly speaking outside their area of expertise (e.g., “John is a doctor, so we can trust his opinions on pop music”). This conclusion doesn't express a factual matter, and we don't have a strong reason to believe these people are uninformed about the company's policies. After all, Lindsey concedes that these people might recall one of the company's policies! Clearly, they are at least somewhat informed on the matter at hand.

choices.text: infers that an opinion is false merely because one potential reason for that opinion has been undermined
choices.rationale: This answer choice describes the error in Lindsey's reasoning. Lindsey infers that an opinion is false — several people's opinion that the company acted unfairly by refusing bonuses — merely because Lindsey undermines one potential reason for that opinion — the company's promise that it would give out bonuses if this year's profits were bigger than last year's. There could be other reasons the staff were entitled to bonuses! If the company denied bonuses despite those reasons, the company would have acted unfairly. Lindsey ignores any other reason the company's staff may have earned a bonus. Since (B) describes this flaw, we can select it confidently.

choices.text: dismisses a claim on the basis of certain irrelevant attributes of the people who made the claim
choices.rationale: Lindsey doesn't dismiss several people's opinions based on their “irrelevant attributes.” Lindsey doesn't bring up any attributes these people possess! Because this answer choice mischaracterizes Lindsey's reasoning, it cannot accurately describe a flaw in Lindsey's argument.

choices.text: confuses the size of a quantity with the amount by which that quantity has increased
choices.rationale: This is a confusing answer choice! Sometimes, it's best to provide an example of what this flaw might look like so we can compare the passage's argument to an argument that actually commits the flaw described by this answer choice. Suppose the argument said this: “Lindsey: Several people claim that our company was unfair when it failed to give bonuses to the staff. Perhaps they recalled that the company had promised that if it increased its profits over last year's, the staff would all get bonuses. However, the company's profit wasfairly small this year. Clearly, then, the company acted fairly.” In this version of the argument, Lindsey confuses the size of a quantity (the company's profits) with the amount the quantity has increased (whether this year's profits increased over last year's). The company promised to give out bonuses if the annual profit increased this year. Even if this year's profits were “fairly small,” they still could have increased over last year's profits, and the staff could still be entitled to a bonus. However, in the real argument from the passage, Lindsey doesn't confuse the size of the company's profits with the amount the profits increased. Lindsey doesn't say that the profits were “small” this year. Lindsey establishes that the profits did not increase this year (“the company's profit was much smaller this year than it was last year”). So, this answer choice does not accurately describe an error in Lindsey's reasoning.

choices.text: overlooks the possibility that a policy can be fair even when it is not generous
choices.rationale: When we see “overlooks the possibility” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the conclusion if true?” If a policy can be fair even if it's not generous, that would strengthen Lindsey's reasoning. Denying bonuses to your staff isn't very generous, but this answer choice would support Lindsey's conclusion that the company's decision was fair. It's not a flaw to overlook information that further supports your argument!

questions.stimulus: Lindsey: Several people claim that our company was unfair when it failed to give bonuses to the staff. Perhaps they recalled that the company had promised that if it increased its profits over last year's, the staff would all get bonuses. However, the company's profit was much smaller this year than it was last year. Clearly, then, the company acted fairly.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most help to justify the apparently paradoxical belief of the experienced climbers?

choices.text: It is difficult to recruit and train members for the rescue squads.
choices.rationale: This is irrelevant to the paradox. It doesn't matter if it's difficult to recruit or train members of these rescue squads. Apparently, we still manage to recruit and train members, and they do a pretty good job saving climbers' lives. This answer choice doesn't explain why experienced climbers think we need to get rid of these squads to reduce the number of deaths and injuries on mountains.

choices.text: The recording of deaths and injuries tends to be more accurate in mountain regions served by rescue squads.
choices.rationale: This doesn't resolve the paradox. It doesn't explain why experienced climbers think we need to get rid of these squads to reduce the number of deaths and injuries on mountains. It may suggest that the statistics on deaths and injuries in areas without rescue squads are less reliable. But that doesn't show why rescue squads may cause an increase in the number of climber deaths and injuries. Some test-takers are still tempted by this answer choice. It's possible to argue that this answer choice resolves the paradox, but that requires at least a few assumptions. Suppose the statistics on deaths and injuries in areas without rescue squads dramatically undercount the number of deaths and injuries. And suppose that experienced mountain climbers are using these statistics to argue that removing rescue squads is required to reduce climber deaths and injuries. If both of these suppositions are true, then the paradox is resolved. The experienced climbers look at the statistics and see far fewer injuries and deaths in the areas without rescue squads. The experienced climbers then argue that we'd see fewer injuries and deaths elsewhere if the rescue squads stopped servicing those areas. Still, neither the passage nor the answer choices support these assumptions. The statistics on deaths and injuries in areas without rescue squads could actually overestimate the number of deaths and injuries in these areas. Experienced climbers don't have to base their opinions on these statistics. And the experienced climbers may not be this susceptible to flawed logic. Because this answer choice requires unsupported assumptions to resolve the paradox, it does not truly resolve the paradox.

choices.text: People who commonly take risks with their lives and health do not expect other people to take those risks to rescue them.
choices.rationale: This might explain why the experienced climbers don't would be OK climbing without rescue squads. The experienced climbers know they're taking a risk, and they don't expect rescue squad members to take a risk rescuing them. But that's not the issue we're trying to explain. We're trying to explain why experienced climbers think removing the rescue squads is required to reduce the number of climber deaths and injuries. This answer choice doesn't give us any reason to believe that the number of climber deaths and injuries would go down without rescue squads, so it is incorrect.

choices.text: Most of the people injured or killed while mountain climbing were not adequately prepared for the dangers they would face.
choices.rationale: If most of the people who are killed or injured while mountain climbing weren't adequately prepared, it seems like they could use a rescue squad to help them out! This answer choice would resolve the paradox if it told us that climbers would prepare themselves more if they knew rescue squads wouldn't be there to support them. But, as written, this answer choice makes the paradox worse.

choices.text: The lower the risk of climbing a particular mountain is perceived to be, the greater the number of less competent climbers who attempt to climb it.
choices.rationale: Finally, this answer choice resolves the paradox. If climbers know that rescue squads can save them if they get into a difficult situation on a mountain, they'll perceive the risk of that mountain as lower. This answer choice tells us that when mountain climbers perceive the risk as lower, more incompetent climbers will attempt to climb a mountain. This explains why experienced climbers think that reducing climber deaths and injuries requires abolishing rescue squads. If there are no more rescue squads, climbers will think that climbing a mountain poses a higher risk. If climbers perceive the risk as high, fewer incompetent climbers will attempt to climb a mountain. And if there are fewer incompetent climbers, we can reasonably expect fewer injuries and deaths on the mountains. Therefore, this answer choice is correct.

questions.stimulus: It is widely known that the rescue squads serving high mountain areas with treacherous weather save the lives of many mountain climbers every year. However, many experienced climbers believe that the rising annual toll of deaths and injuries among climbers in these regions can be significantly reduced only by completely abolishing the rescue squads.

questions.stem: The dialogue provides the most evidence that Paula and Ashley disagree with each other about whether

choices.text: it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have developed radio communication
choices.rationale: It does relate to Paula and Ashley's disagreement over whether aliens would develop the same technology we did. And it uses the weak, easy-to-support language (“probable,” “there are”) we like a Connecting Facts question. Paula says that aliens develop the same technologies we did, and they both agree that we've developed radio communication. However, Ashley says that our technology is unique to ourselves and our environment, implying that aliens would not develop similar technology. She underlines this point by arguing that using radio communication to search for aliens is a waste of time and money, suggesting that aliens won't have radios to communicate with us. It is correct. Paula would agree with this, while Ashley would disagree with it.

choices.text: it is probable that there are intelligent alien beings who have the same legal or political systems that humans do
choices.rationale: We know Ashley would disagree with this claim. However, Paula never discusses whether aliens would share our legal or political systems. The way Ashley poses this idea as absurd suggests no one believes that aliens would share our legal or political systems. Even then, Paula and Ashley wouldn't disagree with each other.

choices.text: our technology is influenced by our cognitive makeup
choices.rationale: We know that Ashley agrees with this statement — she says technology is a “unique outgrowth” of our cognitive makeup. Paula never explicitly discusses our cognitive makeup. Paula suggests that technology comes from our understanding of mathematics and physics. Even if that counts as coming from our “cognitive makeup,” Paula and Ashley's opinions would be aligned on this issue.

choices.text: there is likely to be intelligent life on other planets
choices.rationale: Paula definitely agrees with this. But Ashley never indicates whether she believes intelligent life exists on other planets. She doesn't say she believes in aliens, but she doesn't rule it out, either. She doesn't think aliens, if they exist, would share much in common with us or be traceable by radio communication.

choices.text: scientists should spend more time and money on the search for intelligent extraterrestrial life
choices.rationale: Neither speaker has an opinion on this. Paula probably supports the amount of money we spend on radio telescopes. But she never says we should spend more money searching for aliens. And Ashley doesn't think radio telescopes are a good use of money, but she doesn't rule out spending more money to look for aliens some other way. Since neither speaker expresses or implies their opinion on this topic, we can eliminate (E).

questions.stimulus:
Paula: Earthlike planets seem to be the rule rather than the exception, so there probably are intelligent beings on other planets. Furthermore, we can expect our radio telescopes to detect signs of such beings. Alien scientists would have basically the same understanding of mathematics and physics that humans have. Thus they would inevitably discover gravity, electromagnetism, and other fundamental physical phenomena and then develop technologies such as radio communication.

Ashley: That is like saying they would inevitably have the same legal or political systems that humans do. Our science, mathematics, and technology are unique outgrowths of our physiology, cognitive makeup, and environment. Using radio telescopes to search for intelligent life is a waste of time and money.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, would most help to justify the developer's reasoning?

choices.text: If a construction project is necessary in order to strengthen a town's economy, then the residents of that town should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that construction project.
choices.rationale: This is very tempting! But it slightly misstates the premise. According to the developer, constructing the road isn't necessary to strengthen the town's economy. Constructing the road is necessary to build the apartment building. And the apartment building would strengthen the town's economy. But that doesn't mean we need to build the road to improve the economy. There could be many ways to improve the economy outside the road and apartment complex! (If you're following this “if-then” logic, we have “if Apartment Complex then Road” and “if Apartment Complex then Improved Economy.” We cannot validly conclude that “if Improved Economy then Road,” as this answer choice states.) Since this answer choice mischaracterizes the developer's premise, it cannot connect the developer's premise to their conclusion.

choices.text: The residents of a town should not vote in favor of a local tax to fund a construction project unless that construction project will produce results that benefit all of those residents.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't resemble “if Premises then Conclusion.” Here's what it does look like: “if Should vote to complete project then Project will benefit every resident.” Experienced test-takers will immediately recognize that this claim is backward (it goes “if Conclusion then Premise”). This won't help the developer prove that Sierra residents should vote to fund the road. (The flipside wouldn't help us either, as that is “if Project will not benefit every resident then Should not vote to complete project” — this would only help us conclude that Sierra residents should not vote to fund the road.)

choices.text: Whenever a town funds a construction project, it should do so by means of a tax rather than debt.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't resemble “if Premises then Conclusion.” It mischaracterizes the developer's premises and conclusion. Here's what it looks like: “if Fund a project, then Should use tax and not debt.” This principle could be used to make conclusions in situations where we know that a town will fund a project. In those cases, we could conclude that they should use a tax. But we don't know that Sierra will definitely fund a construction project. We need a principle that tells Sierra residents to vote to fund such a project! This principle doesn't compel Sierra residents to vote to fund a project, so it doesn't strengthen the developer's argument.

choices.text: Only those residents who will benefit from the results of a construction project should be required to pay a tax to fund that project.
choices.rationale: This principle doesn't resemble “if Premises then Conclusion.” Here's what it looks like: “if Resident required to vote to complete project, then Project benefits resident.” Experienced test-takers will immediately recognize that this claim is backward, more or less (it more closely resembles “if Conclusion then Premise” than “if Premises then Conclusion”). This won't help the developer prove that Sierra residents should vote to fund the road. This premise would only allow us to conclude that residents who were required to vote for the road will benefit from the road. But no premises establish that any of the Sierra residents are required to vote for the road. That's what the developer is trying to prove with the conclusion!

choices.text: Anyone who would benefit from the results of a construction project should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that project.
choices.rationale: Finally, a principle that gives us “if Premises then Conclusion.” If we translate this, here's what it would look like: “if Project benefits resident, then Resident should vote to fund the project.” This strengthens the developer's argument. The road can benefit every Sierra resident because the road is required to complete the apartment complex, eventually benefiting the residents. So, this principle gets the closest to compelling every Sierra resident to vote to fund the road, just as the developer concludes. Since this principle gets the closest to connecting the developer's premises with the developer's conclusion, (E) is the correct answer.

questions.stimulus: Developer: The builders of the Glen Veil apartment complex will not complete the complex unless a road connecting it to the town of Sierra is built. The completed apartment complex would strengthen Sierra's economy, and a stronger economy would benefit every Sierra resident. Therefore, the residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the historian's argument?

choices.text: Medieval epistemologists held some of the same epistemological beliefs as did ancient epistemologists.
choices.rationale: This doesn't affect the argument at all. Plus, it uses the weak, wishy-washy language (“some”) we don't like on Weaken questions. Statements expressed with this type of language usually do not meaningfully affect an argument, so answer choices expressed with such language are often wrong on Weaken (and Strengthen/Strengthen with a Sufficient Assumption!) questions. Further, it simply doesn't matter if medieval and ancient epistemologists shared some beliefs. This doesn't present a major downside to the historian's definition of “medieval epistemology.” This answer choice would mean that some beliefs held by ancient epistemologists would be included in “medieval epistemology.” But, the historian never says or implies that medieval epistemology cannot contain any beliefs held by ancient epistemologists. Finally, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Until recently, intellectual historians didn't have a definition of medieval epistemology. We can define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold. If we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes a belief, we'll ask whether any medieval epistemologists believe it. If they do, it's part of medieval epistemology. If any believe the opposite, the opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology. But, medieval and ancient epistemologists share some of the same epistemological beliefs. So, we maybe shouldn't define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold.” This argument doesn't sound very convincing. “Ancient epistemologists” pop up out of nowhere in the “But” statement, and it's unclear why they would present a reason why we “maybe shouldn't” use the historian's definition of medieval epistemology. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (A).

choices.text: The epistemological beliefs of medieval epistemologists depended upon their beliefs about nonepistemological matters.
choices.rationale: This answer choice doesn't affect the argument. It doesn't present a major downside to the historian's definition of “medieval epistemology.” It only suggests that medieval epistemologists' epistemological beliefs are influenced by non-epistemological matters. But, the historian never says or implies that non-epistemological beliefs cannot influence medieval epistemology. Moreover, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Until recently, intellectual historians didn't have a definition of medieval epistemology. We can define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold. If we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes a belief, we'll ask whether any medieval epistemologists believe it. If they do, it's part of medieval epistemology. If any believe the opposite, the opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology. But, medieval epistemologists' beliefs depended on their non-epistemological beliefs. So, we maybe shouldn't define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold.” This argument doesn't sound very persuasive. “Non-epistemological beliefs” show up without any rhyme or reason in the “But” statement. That statement doesn't seem to contradict or present a downside to anything that comes before it, so it's unclear why the “But” statement provides a reason why we “maybe shouldn't” use the historian's definition of medieval epistemology. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (B).

choices.text: The writings of most medieval epistemologists include passages that are clearly not about epistemology.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is irrelevant to the argument. It doesn't matter that most medieval epistemologists also wrote about non-epistemological matters. We wouldn't use those writings to define medieval epistemology. So, (C) doesn't present a major downside to the historian's definition of “medieval epistemology.” Moreover, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Until recently, intellectual historians didn't have a definition of medieval epistemology. We can define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold. If we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes a belief, we'll ask whether any medieval epistemologists believe it. If they do, it's part of medieval epistemology. If any believe the opposite, the opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology. But, most medieval epistemologists sometimes wrote about non-epistemological matters. So, we maybe shouldn't define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold.” This argument doesn't sound very persuasive. The “But” statement doesn't sound like it undermines or presents a downside of the premises that come before it. So, it doesn't provide a reason why we “maybe shouldn't” use the historian's definition of medieval epistemology. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (C).

choices.text: Some medieval epistemologists had epistemological beliefs that contradicted the epistemological beliefs of other medieval epistemologists.
choices.rationale: This answer choice is very tempting! If this answer choice were true, then medieval epistemology would contain some “contradictory” beliefs. If one medieval epistemologist thought we know things by experiencing them and another thought we don't know things by experiencing them, then medieval epistemology would hold that we simultaneously do and do not know things by experiencing them. That seems a little confusing! However, let's go back to fundamentals. This answer choice uses the weak, wishy-washy language (“some”) we don't like on Weaken questions. Statements expressed with this type of language usually do not meaningfully affect an argument, so answer choices expressed with such language are often wrong on Weaken (and Strengthen/Strengthen with a Sufficient Assumption!) questions. So, even if this answer choice seems to present a major downside to the historian's definition, its weak language suggests that the downside might not be so bad. If only “some” medieval epistemologists had views that contradicted other medieval epistemologists, medieval epistemology may not have that many contradictions. Maybe there's only like, one contradiction. That's not the end of the world. Especially because the historian concedes that medieval epistemology is a “complex” topic. And it's worth noting that the historian never said or implied that medieval epistemology couldn't contain contradictory views. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Until recently, intellectual historians didn't have a definition of medieval epistemology. We can define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold. If we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes a belief, we'll ask whether any medieval epistemologists believe it. “If they do, it's part of medieval epistemology. If any believe the opposite, the opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology. But, some medieval epistemologists had epistemological beliefs that contradicted those of other medieval epistemologists. So, we maybe shouldn't define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold.” This argument doesn't sound terrible! The “But” statement seemingly presents a downside of the previous claim. It shows that sometimes contradictory claims will become part of medieval epistemology. However, it's only a “some” statement. Saying that a definition “sometimes” produces confusing results is probably not the best reason to throw out the definition. This isn't the worst answer choice in the world, and it's OK if we keep it as a contender. But this isn't a slam dunk. It features the type of wishy-washy language we want to avoid. So, we definitely need to check the remaining answer choice before selecting (D).

choices.text: There is much debate as to which medieval thinkers, if any, were epistemologists.
choices.rationale: This definitely presents a downside to the historian's definition of medieval epistemology. The historian's definition hinges on finding medieval epistemologists and figuring out their epistemological beliefs. This answer choice presents a reason why that definition isn't workable — it's hard to tell who was a “medieval epistemologist.” It's possible, according to this answer choice, that no one was a medieval epistemologist! If either fact is true, the historian's definition is yet another definition of medieval epistemology that will not help us “determine what should and what should not be included in” medieval epistemology. Moreover, unlike other tempting answer choices like (D), this answer choice does not feature wishy-washy, weak language. That's another major asset for this answer choice; it should make us feel more comfortable eliminating (D) and selecting (E). Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Until recently, intellectual historians didn't have a definition of medieval epistemology. We can define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold. If we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes a belief, we'll ask whether any medieval epistemologists believe it. If they do, it's part of medieval epistemology. If any believe the opposite, the opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology. But, there's much debate as to which medieval thinks, if any, were epistemologists. So, we maybe shouldn't define medieval epistemology as the epistemological beliefs medieval epistemologists hold.” This argument sounds persuasive! The “But” statement presents a major downside of the previous claims. It shows that we may not be able to apply the historian's approach, as we won't be able to figure out “whether any medieval epistemologists” believe a claim. Whichever approach we use, we can confidently select (E).

questions.stimulus: Historian: Because medieval epistemology (theory of knowledge) is a complex subject, intellectual historians have, until recently, failed to produce a definition that would help to determine what should and what should not be included in it. Clearly, the solution is to define medieval epistemology simply as "the epistemological beliefs of the medieval epistemologists." That way, if we want to know whether medieval epistemology includes some epistemological claim, we just ask whether any medieval epistemologists believed it. If any did, it is part of medieval epistemology; if any medieval epistemologists believed the opposite, then that opposite claim is part of medieval epistemology.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the official's argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.text: takes a possible effect of a reduction to be a possible cause of that reduction
choices.rationale: This answer choice suggests that the official confuses an effect for a cause. Although the official commits a causation flaw, this answer choice does not describe the type of causation flaw the official commits. The official assumes that the increase in parking fines caused a reduction in parking violations. The increase in parking fines could not be an “effect” of this reduction, as (A) implies. After all, the increase came before the subsequent (“Since then”) reduction in violation.

choices.text: takes for granted that raising fines a second time will reduce parking violations at least as much as it did the first time
choices.rationale: When we see “takes for granted” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, the official doesn't necessarily believe that raising fines again will “reduce parking violations at least as much as it did the first time.” The official just says that raising fines again will result in “even fewer parking violations.” Because we don't have any reason to think that the official believes increasing fines will result in the same reduction, this answer choice is incorrect.

choices.text: fails to take into account the financial benefits the city is now deriving from fines for parking violations
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to take into account” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Would this weaken the author's argument if true?” The city deriving financial benefits from these fines would not weaken the official's argument. The official doesn't conclude that increasing parking fines will be a net benefit for the city. The official just concludes that it will reduce parking violations even more. This may cause the city to earn less revenue from parking violations (if the increased fines don't offset the reduced number of violations), but that doesn't affect whether there will be fewer violations.

choices.text: takes for granted that people who park their cars illegally would prefer to park legally
choices.rationale: When we see “takes for granted” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and would this strengthen the argument?” In this case, the official doesn't necessarily believe that people who park their cars illegally would prefer to park them legally. The official might assume the opposite — people would prefer to park their cars illegally, so we need to raise the fines as much as we can to deter them. Moreover, this answer choice would strengthen the argument if true. It may actually weaken the argument. If people who park their cars illegally would prefer to park legally, then fines may not deter them. If you would prefer to park legally but choose to park illegally anyway, there must be an issue with parking legally! Maybe there aren't enough legal spots! In that case, raising fines wouldn't persuade you to park legally — there'd still not be enough legal spots to park in!

choices.text: fails to establish that the initial decrease in parking violations was not due to the availability of additional parking spaces
choices.rationale: When we see “fails to establish” on an Errors in Reasoning answer choice, the question we should ask ourselves is, “Does the author believe this, and do we need to know this to draw the author's conclusion? The answer to both questions is “Yes,” making this the correct answer. The author assumes that parking violations decreased due to the decision to increase parking fines. So, the official believes that parking violations did not decrease for some other reason, like the availability of additional parking spaces from the new parking garage. Moreover, to draw the conclusion that raising fines again will result in even fewer parking violations, we need to know that the initial decrease in violations was not due to the availability of additional parking spaces. If the initial decrease was due to the availability of additional parking spaces, then we can't expect that raising the fines again will result in fewer parking violations. Raising the fines didn't reduce the violations the first time, and we're not adding more parking spaces, so we can't expect a subsequent reduction in violations.

questions.stimulus: Official: Six months ago, the fines for parking violations on the city's streets were raised to help pay for the parking garage that had just opened. Since then, parking violations on our streets have dropped by 50 percent. Hence, if we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken the consumer advocate's argument?

choices.text: As far as scientists know, none of the pharmaceuticals produced by genetically engineered crops would present any danger to public health if they were present in the general food supply.
choices.rationale: This doesn't affect the argument at all. The consumer advocate doesn't conclude that pharmaceutical drugs in the food supply will pose a public health risk. Their conclusion only states that pharmaceutical drugs might end up in the food supply. So, even if the scientists are correct and these drug-producing crops won't present any danger to public health, that wouldn't weaken the advocate's conclusion. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Scientists now genetically engineer some crops for pharmaceutical use. If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into another field, it can fertilize a food crop. The food crop would turn into a drug-producing crop. But, scientists don't think the drug-producing crops will endanger public health in the food supply. So, the drugs will not end up in the food supply.” This argument doesn't sound very convincing. The public health argument in the “But” statement has nothing to do with the conclusion's assertion the drugs won't end up in the food supply. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (A).

choices.text: If pollen from a genetically engineered crop is prevented from drifting into fields in which ordinary crops of the same species are being grown, then there is no risk of the pollen fertilizing the latter crops.
choices.rationale: This doesn't weaken the consumer advocate's argument. Sure, if pollen is prevented from drifting into other fields, then there isn't a risk of turning a food crop into a drug-producing crop. But what if we let our guard down? What if we can't prevent pollen from drifting into other fields? After all, the consumer advocate didn't say that pollen will definitely drift into other fields and fertilize food crops, converting them into drug-producing crops. The consumer advocate just said it “could happen.” Without knowing that we'll always be able to prevent pollen from genetically modified crops from drifting into other fields, we can't say that (B) would weaken the conclusion that there's a “possibility” that drugs end up in the food supply. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Scientists now genetically engineer some crops for pharmaceutical use. If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into another field, it can fertilize a food crop. The food crop would turn into a drug-producing crop. But, if we prevent pollen from drifting into other fields, then there's no risk of pollen fertilizing food crops. So, the drugs will not end up in the food supply.” This argument isn't awful. Still, the conclusion sounds a bit bolder than the “But” statement would allow. We only know that the drugs will not end up in the food supply if we continuously prevent pollen from drifting into other fields. Who knows if we can do that. This isn't the worst answer choice in the world, and it's OK if we keep it as a contender. But it's far from perfect, too. It doesn't seem like it prevents drugs from entering the food supply. So, we definitely need to check the remaining answer choices before selecting (B). (Upon checking the remaining choices, we’ll see there is a much better option.)

choices.text: The genetically engineered crops that produce pharmaceuticals are not among the crop species that comprise the largest portions of the general food supply.
choices.rationale: This doesn't affect the argument. The consumer advocate doesn't conclude that most people will consume the pharmaceutical drugs in the food supply. They only claim thats that pharmaceutical drugs might end up in the food supply. Even if the drug-producing crops are random foods very few people eat, they could still be “in” the food supply. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Scientists now genetically engineer some crops for pharmaceutical use. If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into another field, it can fertilize a food crop. The food crop would turn into a drug-producing crop. But, the drug-producing corps are not among the most commonly eaten foods. So, the drugs will not end up in the food supply.” This argument doesn't sound very persuasive. The “But” statement doesn't prove that the drugs will not end up in the food supply. It only suggests that few people will each them once they're in the food supply. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (C).

choices.text: In crops genetically engineered to produce pharmaceuticals, the drugs are not present in any part of the plant used for food in ordinary crops of the same species.
choices.rationale: This answer choice shows why the drugs won't end up in the food supply! This answer choice says we don't eat the part of the food crops where the drugs would be present. So, even if drug-producing crops fertilize food crops, converting them to drug-producing plants, the drugs still won't enter the food supply. So, if drug-producing carrots only store the drugs in the roots, the drugs won't end up in the food supply. Only carrot, which has no drugs, would enter the food supply. Therefore, this weakens the consumer advocate's conclusion that these drugs could end up in the food supply. Further, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Scientists now genetically engineer some crops for pharmaceutical use. If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into another field, it can fertilize a food crop. The food crop would turn into a drug-producing crop. But, the drugs in drug-producing crops are not in any part of the crop used for food. So, the drugs will not end up in the food supply.” This argument sounds pretty good! Yes, the drugs could end up in food crops, but not in the part of the food crop we use for food. So, it's fair to conclude that the drugs will not end up in the food supply. No matter the approach we used, we can confidently select (D).

choices.text: If pollen from a drug-producing crop turned an ordinary crop of the same species into a drug-producing crop, it would be possible for scientists to identify the latter crop.
choices.rationale: This doesn't quite weaken the consumer advocate's conclusion. Yes, scientists could identify the drug-producing crops, but could they do so before those crops entered the food supply? Could they always identify these crops and prevent them from entering the food supply. After all, the consumer advocate didn't say that drugs will definitely enter into the food supply. The consumer advocate just said it “could happen.” Without knowing that scientists will always be able to identify the drug-producing crops and prevent them from entering the food supply, we can't say that (E) would weaken the conclusion that there's a “possibility” that drugs end up in the food supply. Alternatively, if we used the backup plan, we could construct this argument (note that we simplified the premises and answer choice and are using the negated form of the conclusion): “Scientists now genetically engineer some crops for pharmaceutical use. If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into another field, it can fertilize a food crop. The food crop would turn into a drug-producing crop. But, if a food crop would turn into a drug-producing crop, then scientists could identify the drug-producing crop. So, the drugs will not end up in the food supply.” This argument doesn't seem very persuasive! Knowing that scientists can identify drug-producing crops provides no assurance that the crops won't end up in the food supply. Whichever approach we use, we can eliminate (E).

questions.stimulus: Consumer advocate: Some agricultural crops are now being genetically engineered to produce important pharmaceuticals. However, this development raises the possibility that the drugs will end up in the general food supply, since if pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into a nearby field in which an ordinary, non-drug-producing crop of the same species is being grown, the pollen could fertilize that crop and turn it into a drug-producing crop as well.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the argument follows logically if which one of the following completes the passage?

choices.text: most of the government employees who belong to Bargaining Unit Number 17 but are not computer programmers work in the Hanson Building
choices.rationale: This answer choice does not match our anticipation — that most or all of the Bargaining Unit Number 17 members work in the Hanson Building — so we can eliminate it. Besides, this answer choice wouldn't allow us to make this conclusion. If we symbolized this premise and added it to the argument's premise, here's what we'd get: if BUN17 (most), then Computer Programmers. if BUN17 and NOT Computer Programmers, then Hanson Building. We couldn't combine these to make a valid conclusion. When we have a “most” statement and an “if-then” statement, we can make a valid connection when both the “if” conditions are the same or when the “then” condition of the “most" is the same as the “if” condition of the “if-then.” Neither condition is met here, so we can't make any valid conclusions with this information, much less the conclusion asserted in this argument. So, we can eliminate (A).

choices.text: most members of the executive committee of Bargaining Unit Number 17 work in the Hanson Building
choices.rationale: This gets really close to our anticipation, but the “executive committee” specification means this answer choice does not match our anticipation — that most or all of the Bargaining Unit Number 17 members work in the Hanson Building. So, we can eliminate (B). Besides, this answer choice wouldn't allow us to make this conclusion. If we symbolized this premise and added it to the argument's premise, here's what we'd get: if BUN17 (most), then Computer Programmers. if BUN17 Executive Committee (most), then Hanson Building. We couldn't combine these to make a valid conclusion. When we have two “most” statements, we can only make a valid connection when the “if” conditions are the same. That's not the case here, so we can't make any valid conclusions with this information, much less the conclusion asserted in this argument. So, we can eliminate (B).

choices.text: most of the government employees who work in the Hanson Building are members of Bargaining Unit Number 17
choices.rationale: This gets our anticipation — that most or all of the Bargaining Unit Number 17 members work in the Hanson Building — backward. So, we can eliminate (C). Besides, this answer choice wouldn't allow us to make this conclusion. If we symbolized this premise and added it to the argument's premise, here's what we'd get: if BUN17 (most), then Computer Programmers. if Hanson Building (most), then BUN17. We couldn't combine these to make a valid conclusion, much less the conclusion asserted in this argument. So, we can eliminate (C).

choices.text: most of the members of Bargaining Unit Number 17 work in the Hanson Building
choices.rationale: Bingo. This matches our anticipation — that most or all of the Bargaining Unit Number 17 members work in the Hanson Building — backward. So, we can select (D) immediately. If we symbolized this premise and added it to the argument's premise, here's what we'd get: if BUN17 (most), then Computer Programmers. if BUN17 (most), then Hanson Building. We can combine these to make a valid conclusion. In this case, we have matching “if” statements. So, we can make a “some” conclusion with the “then” parts. That would allow us to draw the conclusion in the passage: Conclusion: Hanson Building –(some) – Computer Programmers. Therefore, this answer choice provides a premise that would allow the passage's conclusion to follow logically.

choices.text: most of the people who work in the Hanson building are government employees
choices.rationale: This doesn't match our anticipation — that most or all of the Bargaining Unit Number 17 members work in the Hanson Building — so we can eliminate (E). Besides, this answer choice wouldn't allow us to make this conclusion. If we added this premise to the argument's premise, here's what we'd get: if BUN17 (most), then Computer Programmers. if Hanson Building (most), then Government Employees. We couldn't combine these to make a valid conclusion, much less the conclusion asserted in this argument. So, we can eliminate (E).

questions.stimulus: Most of the members of Bargaining Unit Number 17 of the government employees' union are computer programmers. Thus it is certain that some of the government employees who work in the Hanson Building are computer programmers, since _______.

questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.text: All the students at Bryker School excel in their studies. However, students at Bryker School would not excel if they did not have good teachers. Thus, all schools should hire good teachers if they want their students to excel.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “C (and not A) must cause B.” This conclusion is causal — it implies that good teachers can cause students to excel. But it doesn't rule out another potential cause. So, we can eliminate (A).

choices.text: Whenever it snows there are relatively more car crashes on the highways. Yet in general, there would not be car crashes unless people were careless. So it is not icy roads, but carelessness, that causes car crashes when it snows.
choices.rationale: This one matches the abstract version of our argument! We have a premise that parallels the claim that “C (and not A) must cause B.” In this answer choice, that's the claim that “it is not icy roads, but carelessness, that causes car crashes when it snows.” So, we have “careless” as our “C,” “icy roads” as our “A,” and “car crashes” as our “B.” The first premise can be translated to “If it snows, then there are more car crashes.” The second premise can be translated to “If there are car crashes, then people are careless.” Although “snow” and “icy road” aren't identical, that's probably OK. After all, “Lab” and “breed” weren't identical in the passage. Given the resemblance between the structure of (B)'s bad reasoning and that in the passage, we can safely select (B) and wrap up this question.

choices.text: Every musician I know is a good dancer. Every mathematician I know is a bad dancer. Thus, it is a sense of rhythm, not the ability to count, that is most responsible for good dancing.
choices.rationale: This conclusion resembles the claim that “C (and not A) must cause B.” In this answer choice, that's the claim that “it is a sense of rhythm, not the ability to count, that is most responsible for good dancing.” So, we have “sense of rhythm” as our “C,” “ability to count” as our “A,” and “good dancing” as our “B.” The first premise can be translated to “If one is a musician, then they are a good dancer.” The second premise can be translated to “if one is a good dancer, then one is not a mathematician.” If “sense of rhythm” is implied by “musician,” then our C term comes first. And if “ability to count” is implied by “mathematician,” then our “A” term comes last. In other words, this answer choice mixes up the causes.

choices.text: All of the good cooks in my country use butter, not margarine, in their cooking. Thus, if you want to be a good cook, you must use butter, not margarine, in your cooking.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “C (and not A) must cause B.” This conclusion simply makes a recommendation — it says that you should use butter and not margarine when cooking. The conclusion does not express a cause-and-effect relationship. So, we can eliminate (D). If we did evaluate this answer choice's premises, we'd note that they don't resemble the premises in the passage either. choices.text: All of the students in my algebra class received an A, even though none of them can solve word problems. No student who is unable to solve word problems has an adequate understanding of algebra. It follows that the students in my class received A's not because they did any good work.
choices.rationale: This conclusion doesn't resemble the claim that “C (and not A) must cause B.” This conclusion only eliminates a potential cause (good work). It doesn't assert what caused the students to get As. So, we can eliminate (E). They establish an “if-then” chain, but there's an “and” condition in the “B” spot. This would be another reason to cross off (E).)
